You're an immortal warrior; every time you would die you instead come back to life. You were imprisoned for reasons that are not immediately clear to you as the player. Your only companion is the person who busts you out of your cell: a mysterious man in a pink rabbit mask. Your objective: get out of prison. Your adversaries are a series of powerful jailors, each residing on a "jail world" with their own theme in both aesthetics and combat. For instance, you may encounter a calm samurai on a beach whose entire fight is a difficult sword duel, or a high-flying winged combatant that does everything she can to evade melee and bombard you from afar.
The music and artstyle are the most striking aspects of the game. The OST is a collaborative album by hit synthwave artists such as Carpenter Brut, Scattle, the Toxic Avenger, and Waveshaper, while all the concept art of the game was made by Takashi Okazaki, the creator of Afro Samurai.
Mechanically, it's a challenging isometric bossrush game that plays like a combination between Hyper Light Drifter and a bullet hell (With notable influence from studios such as FROMSOFTWARE and Platinum Games). While you yourself have a limited - yet satisfying - move roster, each jailor you fight has an incredibly extensive array of attacks and patterns that grow increasingly complex, quick and damaging as you progress through their phases.
In every single encounter, you have three lives against a phased boss; the lowest amount of phases being 4, with the highest being a staggering 7. The enemy's phases are usually separated into two sub-phases: first ranged, then melee (though several bosses eschew one or the other during their bossfight). While the ranged phase permits you a full range of movement, upon depleting a boss's health bar you must close in to fight them in melee. Your movement speed is drastically reduced and your gun is replaced with the ability to charge up your next attack to do vastly increased damage (though this charge is lost upon taking damage). Similarly, the boss you fight loses almost all of the attacks they had in the ranged phase, instead getting a new moveset. This progresses until the final phase, which in most cases is a matter of surviving a veritable gauntlet of attacks in order to close in and get the finishing blow. Should you die during a bossfight, you lose a life and return to the start of the phase you were on. When you beat a phase, you return to full health and regain a life. If you lose all three, you must restart from the beginning of the fight.
The game is very solid; what it does it does incredibly well, and it provides a good challenge. However, it is not without its faults. The game's length entirely depends on how good you are at it, as there are a mere 9 mandatory bosses, with one optional. Its replayability comes from its speedrunning potential and the brutally difficult "FURIER" mode, which unlocks after the game's completion - if you aren't a fan of such things, you won't get much out of it beyond the first 3-8 hours. In addition, the downtime between bosses, though mandatory to keep the player from feeling fatigued due to constant action, is handled in a way that may bore; walking from point A to B with beautiful camerawork and ambient music (as well as exposition from your companion). Its animation work outside of combat and cutscene does not help the situation, as your character has a very stiff walkcycle. Dialogue in the game is very much hit or miss with inconsistent script quality and voiceacting delivery. Finally, its sound design (outside of music) is quite bizzare; what is there is quite good, but almost as often there is a dearth of sound accompanying actions that should have it - as though they ran out of money for a foley artist halfway through recording.
All in all, FURI is a solid 8/10-9/10 - spectacular, yet with clear flaws that, while annoying, do not ruin the game.
The jailor is the key. Kill him, and you will be free.

I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the genre, anyone who is looking for a relaxing gaming experience, and anyone who can appreciate a game for its art and music. Oh, and of course, likes cats...you get a cute kitten that helps you reach annoyingly out-of-reach objects.
The story promises a lot of mystery, magic and romance (although take heed gents - not much romance until the end scenes and a couple of love letters you find along the way). Initially what drew me to this game was the beautiful art-style, which did not disappoint. The voice acting was pretty lacklustre however, which was disappointing because it almost completely ruined the mysterious and intriguing atmosphere that the beautifully composed soundtrack combined with the art-style had created.
The story itself was interesting but cliche, making it somewhat predictable. Puzzles weren't too challenging, and I did get a bit tired of playing dominos to unlock necessary objects (dominos being the easier option than some other puzzle). "It's ok. I'm just in a hurry to save my sister. I've got time for more dominos." The final chapter had a LOT of puzzles, which I thought was a little over the top but was probably also serving to build suspense.
The link between some of the objects and objectives took a bit to figure out - who knew that you could use a diamond earring to cut an opening into a glass window? I didn't!  The amount of times I could have used my jewelry to break into my own house when I'd forgotten my keys will haunt me forever more...Thankfully the hint button refreshes quickly (on casual mode).
Artifex Mundi have created a beautiful-looking game, and it was the combination of the art, music, story and puzzles that was enough to keep me playing until the end of the dark abyss.

Circuits is basically Simon Says, with some fantastic presentation and some very puzzling design choices.
Being a game about music, it's right up my alley. I pay a lot of attention to how music is generally used in video-games, so I was somewhat eager to play the game.
Unfortunately, despite it being great in a lot of areas, it fails in the most important part: the game. The game and the part that music plays in it is incredibly disappointing, and, to me, it ruins the overall experience.
In this game, you are given a level, with some "holes" and pieces that you can use to fit those holes. Each piece plays a musical phrase, and your job is to reconstruct the song.
You can play the song at any time and go forward/backward to listen to a certain part exclusively.
... And that is the game. "Monkey see, monkey do". Or, well... "hear". There's nothing remotely interesting in how music is played. It's just a bunch of isolated tracks you have to place in the song.
This could be interesting. Music is a creative field, so, perhaps, we could have some similar tracks and try to make our own song... but no! The game often has very similar tracks, playing the same sets of notes, with a very very slight change, but you need to put everything in its "right" place. "Right" meaning simply the place intended by the designers.
If you misplace something, the game will tell you that "something is wrong" and you'll have to figure out what.
You have hints and you can isolate tracks (except in the last few levels, where the track isolation is taken out, for some reason... ""difficulty"" purposes, I assume), so you can get help if you make a mistake. But... then the game is telling you what to do.
Now, what's the biggest problem with the game?
Well, you don't construct the song from zero. You have several tracks already playing. This would be fine, as a baseline for the song, but here's the problem: the backing track is often much louder than the tracks you're trying to fit in the song.
Meaning that you often hear the backing track when you're trying to hear what's missing, and it gets frustrating. If you can barely hear what you need, what's the point?!
And this happens a lot!
Then, there's the second biggest problem. Some of the tracks that you have to choose from are incredibly similar! They play exactly the same notes, in exactly the same intonation, with very similar effects. But perhaps one more note (that fits!) is added, very lowly into the mix, and that track is "wrong". This is a very arbitrary wrong. The notes played are the same. The track fits the song just as well as the "correct" one. So where's the problem? Why can't I choose it?
It's a very artifical way of creating difficulty. And it completely defeats the point in have a game about music, to me.
In each level, you have X tracks, and you use them all. So, they're all notes that fit the song, there's no room for error, in that regard. It's literally just about listening (and trying very hard to discern the sound you're looking for amidst the other louder tracks) and putting the only piece in place that fits.
... It's really puzzling the me why this plays like it does. Maybe it's a very personal thing, but it seems to destroy what makes music amazing! There's no creativity. It's like a puzzle with every piece masked. The game hides information to increase difficulty, with no real reason.
I think I'm just hitting the same keys (heh) at this point. I really dislike the game itself, it seems to go against most of what I love about music.. so that's not good.
Now, how would it be better, using similar concepts?
Well, let the player build a song, from a set of rules. Perhaps the backing track already have its progression set, and the players have a larger pool of sounds and notes. Maybe the notes he has to place are already set, but the way they're played (instruments, sequences, effects, etc.) are to his liking. Maybe we could build an actual song that would be different from player to player, while obeying certain rules. Give the music space to breathe.
With some more thought, I believe this could work. As it is... maybe it does for most people, but certainly not for me. And that's fine!
Now, I've been negative enough.
The presentation and functionality of the game is actually really good!
The minimalist visual style works very well, it looks good and has a very novel, but solid way to presenting information in a pleasant way!
The songs themselves weren't much to my liking, but they sounded pretty good (sonically), for the most part! There were a couple of rougher edges in the track not connecting perfectly, but it was nicely done, for the most part!
It tries to change introduce a few mechanics, every once in a while, to keep things interesting.
The way you can listen to any point of the original song at any point is good, and you can fast forward your own song to listen to the exact part you want.
The interface is also fine, as I didn't have any problems with it at all.
I truly dislike the *game* and how music is used. And it's the most important part, to me, which is why I don't recommend this.
But the developers are clearly capable of a lot, as everything else is very well done!
So yeah, I'll be negative for now, but I'll be on the look out for their other games, the talent might be there!

A visual novel where the series of events are determined by the drinks you serve to your patrons. A good cast of people to listen as they talk about bits and pieces of their life. Some killer music to listen to.
Pros:
+ A variety of interesting and realistic characters (given the setting of the story)
+ Glitch City is an immersive setting I would never want to live in.
+ Killer music (You can even set up what you want to listen to while serving drinks)
+ A good game to play when you just want to chill.
+ Can serve a plum and perfume in a
fedora
Cons:
- Can't serve mead in VA-11 Hall-A
Other:
* No semblance of a central story. A bit different from most visual novels, but it doesn't take away much of the experience. The game is about being a bartender who listen to other people's stories after all.
Time to serve drinks and change lives.

This game has the most immersive and engaging storytelling I've ever seen in a video game. The world building is done in perfect pace - being slowly delivered using the dialogues, without overwhelming the player with too much information. You can literally dive into the atmosphere and life of Glitch City.
The graphics are amazing and fit the overall theme very well. Pixelated anime style is surprisingly good for the cyberpunk theme and it blends perfectly with the retro soundtrack. You can even turn scanlines on in the settings.
The characters are extremely believable, to the point where you can experience their feelings yourself (for example, by being sad when the main character is sad). The world of Glitch City, while being a cyberpunk dystopia, is very interesting and diverse.
The way you save game also greatly influences playability in a positive way - you can save the game during break from work or after you return home, which gives you opportunity to divide gameplay into shorter (but complete) sessions, without the urge to play even if you are too tired of reading. This counters one of the greatest problems of other visual novel games - the fact that reading may make you tired pretty fast. In VA-11 Hall-A, you can play as much as you want if you feel fresh - but if you are too tired, you have a well-placed milestones, where you can save without feeling too tempted to play over your limits. The result is that you never feel tired or bored by this game.
The bartending minigame, which is the main interactive aspect of the game (in a similar way to verifying papers in Papers, Please), helps to keep you active and focused on the story. It's also quite interesting to try doing every order properly. Oh, and by the way - it's a minor spoiler, but
, which makes things even more exciting.
So... overall, it's probably the best story/atmosphere-focused game I could ever recommend.

This game is a reminder to me that endings are real hard.
Everything about this game is so close to a thing I should love- it centers queer characters, mundanity in a fantastical world, emotional intimacy, bartending, the bleed through of the personal and the professional, all with an artistic style that is really vibrant.
Unfortunately, the writing trips it up, over and over, which is a problem in a visual novel. The actual ending is an atrocious cliched mess about, with the various 'endings' amounting to not even really epilogues but singular cards with a brief bit of dialogue, as though the writer didn't decide to include multiple endings until about the third pass at editing. There's a minor... twist? i guess? or introduction of a character who also includes an introduction of "meta" jokes and is largely just... so poorly handled and introduced that she feels like the act of an author who's afraid to leave their text alone and doesn't have an editor to help tell them something's a bad idea.
This is saying nothing of the way the lens that Va-11 Hall-A views both sex workers and women through feels... exploitative, a lot of the time. Between the moments of quiet intimacy and introspection, the game often feels... leering to me.
It's so frustrating, because the game is SO CLOSE to what I want, and has some genuinely lovely moment of quiet introspection and quiet intimacy. The boss coming over to drink is a nice moment and i love that scene so much. Some of the characters have some really lovely moments. but the writer desperately need another author, or at the very least someone to ask him "why is this this way" over and over to cut out the chaff which pollutes the back third of this game. You need to stick the landing with a narrative like this, and Va-11 Hall-A flubs it in just about every possible way in my opinion, and that bums me out.
If you need a number, it's a game I am mad that i want to give a 7/10 because that's far higher a score than it deserves.

First off I will say, this is definately a sequel to Far Cry 3. Most of FC4 is almost identical to FC3. For the most part, you get the same guns from its predesesor, but you do get some sweet new ones too. Suppressors sound and look better. Optics are more or less the same from FC3, just better looking. The main character is cool In my opinion. Also some new sweet signature weapons added as well. Suppressed Pump Shotgun anyone?? :) Story seems pretty decent, but Im sure its gets better since I am not very far in the game. Always random events going on. Saving your people from wild animal attacks, hostage situations, bomb disposal etc. New vehicles like hover craft, Buzzard mini helicopter and more. Breathtaking scenery as well.
Pros:
- Big map
- Lots of weapons to choose from
- More new signature weapons
- Always something going on in the world of FC4
- Different story paths, you choose
- Fun new vehicles
- Being able to shoot one handed weapons from any vehicle
Cons:
- Not optimized very well. FC3 was well optimized. It was easy to get 60fps with 1080p, even in high action missions. FC4 on the otherhand is not. I can get it to 60fps on 1080p, but it tends to drop while driving, running through dense wooded areas, fps drops in missions where there is alot of action, fire, smoke and explosions. Even with my settings on low and medium. But with FC3 I could crank up the graphics settings and it would be fine no matter what i was doing. So yeah I guess maybe if you have a super Intel machine you could get it to run better.
- The music you get to listen to in certain vehicles is kind of annoying. FC3 had way better music in my opinion.
- Certain weapons you could attach suppressors to in FC3, you cannot in FC4(unless you mod the game which I did, much much better that way. Check out Nexusmods for FC4 mods).
- Few bugs here and there, but not game breaking, unless you have Windows 10.
Other that that, FC4 is a good game. I recommend getting the game on sale. Also make sure to get the season pass to get all of the DLC missions and weapons, makes the game last longer plus Hurk missions are awesome. :)

Finally finished with the story and the dlc. Personally, I dont recommend this game, cause its boring. Almost everything is copied from FC3. If you're a solid fan of Far Cry series, get it. If not, dont bother. Get Far Cry Primal instead, or maybe Far Cry 5.
Graphic & optimization:
Graphic is certainly better than FC3, with slight stutter sometimes. I had 0 crash when playing in 1080p.
Gameplay:
If you have played FC3 before, then nothing is really new. The 2 new additions are karma system, the higher the level the higher discount you could get from the story, and the other one is elephant riding. Gameplay tips, get supressed sniper rifle as fast as possible, a bow, and grenade launcher, you're good to the end of the game.
Story:
Well, FC3 still topped FC4 in term of story, Pagan Min isnt as interesting as Vas, hell, they arent even in the same league in craziness part. Vas is iconic, but Pagan Min is just a generic dictator. But its interesting to know that you can beat the game under 20 minutes if you know what you are doing.
Conclusion: There is no problem with the game, its good, but its a copy of FC3 with new story, new characters, and new places. If you must get it, then get it on sale, definitely not worth full price

Firstly, I have experienced Deepworld for much much longer than it was on steam.
Admittedly, the Steam version is a bit shoddy. That's because the game was originally on Mac and iOS and is currently in the process of being ported to Windows. (I usually play on V2 Mac.) But if you check the updates, the V3 Steam version is slowly but constantly getting better, catching up to its v2 counterpart. Additionally, some of the microtransactions mentioned in negative reviews are on the way out. There's no more skill cap and now everyone gets unrestricted access to all biomes.
Anyway, I should tell a bit about what Deepworld is.
Deepworld is an online multiplayer sandbox game. A notable aspect is the fact that every single server/world is linked together via world teleporters. This makes it easy to travel between worlds, to go mining, exploring, questing, building, and so on. You can build something cool and show it to your friends or the public, or you can visit other people's creations. There's a place for everything.
The sandbox aspect means you can build whatever you can think of. Building materials are easy to aquire.
Remember: Deepworld is always in development. It will improve over time as more content is added to the game.

One could say Planetbase is a city builder that allows the player to build a base on a planet. Truth is, that’s exactly what it is. It’s also a ruthless test to your ability to manage resources while expanding your base and receiving visitors - good or bad.
Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Planetbase.
For those that aren’t familiarized with city builders, just imagine real life, but with no corruption, global warming, or religions/cultures. Sounds easy, doesn’t it? Fret not, as you still have to deal with hungry/dying/angry colonists.
The goal is pretty simple, to survive. And you do that by progressively expanding your base, while keeping an eye on your resources, as well as energy and water production. I’d dare say getting the energy system working properly, which includes having enough power stored for the night, is unquestionably the most important thing in the game. Without it, you won’t be able to produce oxygen, or food, or anything. Your colonists won’t even be able to enter/exit the base.
The base itself consists on singular pods, connected by bridges, with somewhat organic positioning. There’s a big variety of pods - from dorms, to med-bays, to bio-domes and even processing plants. All of which are important to keep the base up and running. There are also a few base components that aren’t pods, such as the solar panels, the water tanks, the mines, etc..
There are five types of colonists: workers, biologists, engineers, medics and guards. Each, as you can easily guess, has a specfic job, and some are more important than others, although that’s up to the player to decide how to run the base, and therefore choose the number of each type of colonist that the base should have.
As mentioned before, there are tourists, invaders and traders. They all come by ship, some bigger than others, depending on the landing zone. New colonists also come by ship, on a colonists ship, while tourists come on visitors ships, and traders on trading ships. Invaders, however, like to be special, meaning they’re sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that come on either the colonist or the visitor ship.
Once the basics are learned, and a good startup facility is built, the gameplay becomes entirely based on being able to sustain the prodcution cycle, while expanding the base and defeating invaders, serving tourists, helping crews in danger and trading some resources for new technology or even other resources.
After mastering resource collection and the architectural side of the game, there are a few other things to take into consideration, like oxygen production and the disasters. Oyxgen production is quite important, obviously, and it’s important to make sure there’s also enough oxygen for the current number of colonists and a few more, as the visitors also count.
Then, come the disasters. Disasters can be, literally, spotted from miles away, with the correct equipment. Although the word makes it sound bad, disasters can actually be a good thing, if the player wants it to be, as they can be a great source of energy, or even a great help when being attacked.
Oh, and there’s meteors! Did I forget to mention those?
Anyone that likes city builders can expect some good hours of fun with Planetbase. Even after learning the basics and being able to easily set up a base, the random events can easily disrupt the plan, adding to the challenge. There’s a total of three planets to colonize, all of which have their own specific characteristics.
It’s also important to mention that the Madruga Works team was, and still is, very active on the forums, taking notes of suggestions, even implementing some of them, as well as quickly correcting bugs reported by the community.
Despite its extremely addictive and enjoyable gameplay, Planetbase won’t be remembered for its cutting edge graphics, which are, as you’ve probably guessed by now, a mere drop in the vast ocean of good things it has to offer. Micromanagement is also somewhat/completely neglected, as it’s impossible to control one single character, or prioritise a single piece of equipment/production.
. From the get go I could feel Planetbase would be extremely enjoyable. I wasn’t wrong.
For those that want some sort of comparison, imagine Banished in space, with the addition of “disasters”, tourists and invaders. Let’s not forget robots, too.

Here is my first experience with this game, recorded on launch day here on Steam:
This game will fool you.  Once you play it, you'll swear this is no "indie" game but is instead a big AAA title!  The graphics, the UI, and the controls are amazing and very fluid.  The tutorial and the help menu's are very well done, very professional looking and not at all what you might expect of a typical budget indie title like this one.
There is a basic tutorial to show you the very basics of setting up the planet base you'll need to survive  on this game.  It is very easy to navigate, makes sense, and is well presented to prepare you for the oncoming challenges that this game will present you with, but it isn't too long and just shows you the basics you'll need.
Once you begin the game, you'll see an option of three kinds of planets, with the second and third options blacked out until you have achieved a certain level of success at the starting level and most basic planet which will be a desert planet with a decent wind pattern and o2 layer to help you succeed.
After selecting a location to start your base on this planet, you'll watch your little pod land on the planet with seven survivors and two robots.  Your humans consist initially of three workers, two biologists, an engineer, and a medic.  The robots consist of a carrier bot that will carry supplies around and a assembler that will do assembling of your base and interior components.  Each human has a basic needs status when clicked on that will show you his/her random name, profession, health, hunger, thirst, ovygen, energy, and morale levels all which will need to be kept up to prevent death or possible sickness.  The bots only have two bars to watch, one which is their overall functionality and the other their intregrity.
The cool this about this game is that you'll start off with a finite level of supplies you'll need to both survive and build your base.  These are steel, bio-plastic, basic food in the form of pasta, and medical supplies.  You can disassemble your landing pod and see the whole pile of resources in a big pile of blocks, each a different color, and each can be left clicked on to see exactly what it is.
The UI for this game is exactly what you'd expect with this kind of building game.  WASD or moving the cursor moves you around, the mouse wheel zooms in and out, holding the mouse wheel in or using the Q and E keys will allow you to rotate your camera and left clicking will select menu items or objects in the world.  It all works well and without any hassles and this is good.  The one knock or gripe I have is that I'd like to see all of your resources, food, metal, etc shown somewhere on the side or top of the screen but this is a minor complaint.  You can navigate through a simple menu at any time to see a list of all items you have in stock.
Production of your base will typically begin with an oxygen generator, a solar panel for power, a water  drilling machine, and a entrance hub so that your humans can get inside out of danger and get oxygen.  Once you build items, more items will become available to produce, for example the windmill will not be available to build until you have built a solar panel first.  Most space station rooms can also be built in three different sizes as well, the bigger the size costing more resoruces which is clearly shown before you accept it and also giving you more room inside for internal tools and objects to be assembled inside.
To give you examples of what you might build internally, a canteen is a basic cafeteria where your survivors can eat and a food making machine, tables and chairs, drinking fountains, and a tv screen can be placed in there.  However, a biodome is a room where food of different types can be grown as you'll need to be growing you own food very quickly to keep your survivors fed and living.
As long as you stay alive, soon your planet base will become a massive network spread out over the planet with chambers and rooms of all sorts to provide your base with everything from production rooms where goods can be made, rooms where bio-plastic and metal are manufactured from planetary elements like raw ore drawn from the planet through a mine.  You'll likey have a sick bay where your humans can go when their health isn't doing well for a number of reasons but you'll also need enough medics to attend to their needs in your base.
As you move on, outside uncontrollable elements can cause damage to your space station such as meteor strikes and your humans can be killed dozens of different ways.  Thanks fully, once you get you station in good status and livable, you can always bring in more people with a landing pad built and connected to your space base.
All in all, this game is a lot of fun, offers a deep level of building options, researchable options to expand your choices, and it really should never be the same game twice.  Because doing well can mean hours upon hours of gameplay for a single game, the game thankfully offers you the ability to save and load your game at any point.
So far, I am enjoying this game a lot and don't regret this purchase even a tiny bit.  I believe with just a small sample of playtime that this game offers you a big bang of value for your dollar and that almost any city building fan will enjoy this one!
Highly recommended!

There are no upgrades and no complicated combos, instead you get a handful of simple moves: a melee attack, a ranged attack, a dodge, and a parry. With this moveset you're expected to defeat 10 bosses that each play differently than the last. Every boss has multiple phases in which they get stronger and stronger, making every fight intense and grueling.  Winning in Furi is about staying determined and mastering the mechanics of each fight.
Adding to the tight gameplay are the stylish boss designs and music.
If you want a game that forces you to "git gud", this is it.

tl;dr The only difficulty in this game is timing button presses. This game is literally replaced by a factory job. That's it. The only thing that ever took lives off me is the arbitrary segments where they change the parry timings so you can't consistantly hit them without memorizing when the boss pauses slightly before their next attack. This whole review could be summarize as "Do you like memorizing when to hit B? Have I got the game for you!".
It's bad, don't even read this review because I summarized it for you.
Actual review:
This game is so close to being great it's actually even more frustrating than playing the damn thing.
Non-rebindable controller inputs are beyond stupid when you can rebind the mouse and keyboard just fine. Does your engine somehow break if you use anything but the 3 included configurations? Really arbitrary decision to allow M&K rebinds but not controller rebinds.
Parry mechanic is just, ugh. I've hit parries I know I shouldn't have and missed ones I know I hit perfectly. Because it feels like almost every attack, even those among the same bosses, have random timings associated with them. Some want you to parry almost immediately after the "shine" indicator, some want you to parry right before the attack actually connects. Some bosses will be SLIGHTLY too far away and hit you with the edge of their attack even if you parry correctly.
A lot of boss fights have really, really, really boring mechanics you have to sit through. Like, amazingly boring. One of the bosses literally makes you run in a circle during their fight. That's it. A child could pass this part easily, and even though it's short, there's a lot of mechanics that feel like time sinks rather than gameplay. Did I mention you have to walk to each boss?
Yeah this isn't even a nitpick, I was debating on calling it that but after doing this five times it justifies being a FLAW, not a nitpick. Walking is boring. Flat out. The dialogue isn't interesting or engaging enough (not to mention there's more dead space than talking anyway) to explain why you have to sit through walking sequences after each boss. I'm GUESSING the developer's intention was to give a pause to the action, or build anticipation to the next fight, all this did was make me walk into the other room or stare at my phone waiting for the auto-walk to complete.
So all in all if you're as easily put off by these things I'd pass. But seeing as the majority of people love this game I'm guessing I'm in the minority by borderline hating it. It's so much fun when it actually works, but it's SO BORING and finnicky the rest of the time I always leave frustrated. It's not even hard, maybe "Furi-er" difficulty is way more fun but it's taking forever to get there since I can only STAND playing one boss at a time. Maybe when I finally get around to beating this game it'll all "click" into place but man it's a slog getting there.
It's not fun. It's not fun enough to finish. I plow through the first 3-4 boring stages of the boss and then lose because they arbitrarily change the timing of the parries. The visual indicator is the exact same, but for some reason the attack is slightly delayed. That's called a QTE, and they're awful.
For two bosses in a row.
This isn't entertainment, this is just bad. The first phases aren't even enjoyable only to get to a terrible QTE. How do people love this game? It's a QTE in disguise rofl. I value my time more than memorizing when to press a button.

I generally expect good quality games from Artifex Mundi.  Even so, I was really pleasantly surprised at how GREAT this game was!  I would say this is one of the best, if not THE best, game of this genre that I've played (and I have played many, both on mobile and PC, over the years).

I don't normally bother reviewing every HOG I play, as they are pretty similar and existing reviews tend to hit the points people tend to want to know.
But I realized that I hadn't reviewed an Artifex Mundi title before, so now is as good a time as any to correct that.
Artifex Mundi is, at least on Steam, basically the state of the art of the HOG.
What's a HOG? Basically a "light" "point and click" adventure game characterized by hidden object scenes where you must find objects from a list.
Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride, the newest title of theirs I've played so far, represents striking production values.
Forsaken Bride hits upon all the key points that HOG players look for - pleasing art, a reasonably engaging story, astutely  placed items in hidden item scenes, a mix of not too difficult puzzles, ample handholding for those that need it - and takes it even further:
This title is highly animated compared to typical HOGs. Most scenes have moving/wiggling elements - people, vegetation, weather, etc. This makes the game feel much more "alive", rather than just a slideshow.
The numerous cutscenes are also quite well made.
In addition to using items from your inventory to solve puzzles and progress, sometimes you need assistance from... a kitten.
Yep, that's right. A kitten.
Really, it's quite a cheap trick to put a cute kitten into the game, but, of course, it works. Who can argue with a kitten?
Most of the time, the kitten sits quietly in the corner of your interface, but, sometimes, you can "use" the kitten like an inventory object to solve a particular situation. Sometimes the kitten starts meowing as a hint that he can be of assistance.
Every time this happens, you are treated to an animation of the kitten interacting with the scene.
This title has a feature I hadn't seen before. In addition to the more common trope of looking for a type of object (in this case, faeries) across all scenes (in this case, "regular", not HO scenes), you can also optionally find "elusive objects".
Elusive objects are basically objects that... do not quite belong. They also are not constantly present, instead appearing and disappearing at intervals.
This makes for a welcome change from the typical kind of object hunting. The visual challenge here is distinct - look for something that does not belong/was not there before.
This proves a quite difficult challenge, but the game helps you by indicating when a scene contains an elusive object.
These elusive objects, when found, fit into the illustrations of pages of an optional storybook. When you find all 3 objects on a page, you are treated with a small cutscene.
These pages also serve as another hint for what you are looking for - you can see the outline of the object in the illustration.
In an effort to be balanced, I'll mention a few things that were perhaps not as good as they could be:
* The character art is at times a bit awkward (but the voice acting is quite good). Faces especially sometimes come off as unintentionally "creepy".
* A few puzzles are unintuitive and not as well indicated as they could be (e.g. having to construct a water sprayer to put out a lantern), but this is not unusual for games of this type and is a very minor complaint.
Artifex Mundi develops and publishes high quality HOGs. I've yet to be disappointed by one of their titles, so this recommendation can basically be taken to extend to the rest of their titles - I won't bother writing a review for each one.
For achievement hunters, these titles tend to take about 10-15 hours to 100% without a walkthrough, usually(?) requiring two playthroughs.

Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride is a great Hidden Object adventure game. The game is a mystery plot where the story is driven forwards by object puzzles. Most of the objects are found on the various screens of the worlds, but for others you will need to solve a puzzle or find hidden objects.
The art is high quality and it is accompanied by a relaxing soundtrack. All dialogue is voice acted, and I have no complaints about any of the voice actors.
What makes Grim Legends stand out from other HO games are two things: first, the developer has made it so that every puzzle can be bypassed: either by using the hint/skip button, or by solving a domino slide puzzle instead of the object searching.
Secondly, during the main story you get a cat companion that helps you solve the puzzles. The cat is nearly always present on the toolbar and actually climbs out to enter the game world, which is a fun and pretty unique concept.
Highly recommended to all hidden object game fans.

Your sister is getting married today, and you're hurrying to get home in time for the ceremony.  Suddenly, a bear spooks your horse and almost sends your carriage over a cliff!  You must save the carriage, repair your wedding gift, rescue a cute helper, and get to the village before it's too late.  But this is just the start of your bad luck... it's not long before things take a turn for the worse, and thus begins your quest to rescue the victims, expose the villain, and learn more about your own history in the process.
Although I was a fan of point-and-click adventure games back in the day, I'd never played a Hidden Object game and wasn't sure if I'd enjoy one.  However, although there don't seem to be any demos on Steam, Artifex Mundi's own website allows you to try a demo of any of their games.  I spent a few hours on those, and now I'm hooked and want all of them!  :)  All their games of this style employ the same type of interface, which is very easy to use, so once you've tried one you'll be fine for just about any other title.
I found this game to have an engaging story and enjoyable gameplay.  The puzzles and hidden object scenes vary in difficulty and a few had me scratching my head for a while, but I only got frustrated once.  My husband helped me with that one by pointing out something I hadn't thought of, and saved me from having to consult a walkthrough!  Usually there will be some kind of hint in the dialogue or descriptions of a scene, and whenever I felt I couldn't progress it was generally because I'd missed something in a previous location.  There is a map available in this game which allows you to go directly to any previous scene if you wish, eliminating backtracking frustration, and sometimes going back to a recent location will present you with a new hidden object game to allow you to progress further.
In my opinion the graphics are well done, and although the character animations in the cutscenes can seem a little bit stiff (and the lip-synching is usually off) I didn't feel that this detracted from the overall enjoyment.  The hidden object scenes are highly detailed and beautifully drawn, and some objects in the scenes blend into the background so well that it takes quite a bit of hunting!  (Hint for newcomers to these games: if an item in the list is in a different text colour, you'll need to interact with something(s) in the scene to find or create what you're looking for.  Your cursor will provide clues!)
There is a hint option if you get stuck, and some (if not all) puzzles and hidden object scenes may be skipped if you wish.  Puzzles can also be replaced with a game of dominoes if you find one too challenging.  There are achievements related to completing puzzles and domino games, so if you like to collect them all you might wish to do one playthrough with puzzles and another with dominoes.
The music and sound effects fit the game well, with the music adding to the tension of the story at appropriate points.  I generally turn background music way down or completely off in games as I find it distracting, but at a slightly lower volume I found the music in this game added to my enjoyment of the whole experience.
There are many additional things to find while playing, such as woodland spirits and 'elusive objects'.  I missed one spirit somewhere, and only managed to spot three of the elusive objects.  These are items in scenes which change or are hard to spot, such as a face in the moon.  These objects work to translate text in a book in your Achievements screen, and once you find all the objects for a particular page there is an option to 'hear the story'.  As I haven't completed any pages yet I can't really comment on this, but it's something for me to work towards on my next playthrough!
This being the Collector's Edition there is an additional episode, taking place after the main story, which is unlocked once you complete the main game.  Although this is much shorter, it still added a couple more hours of fun!
In conclusion, I thoroughly enjoyed this game and will definitely replay it at some point to try for more achievements and elusive objects.  I would recommend it even at full price, and I look forward to playing many more Artifex Mundi games in the future!

I used to play the original Crashday back in ~2006-2007. I honestly don't remember alot about it, other than that I liked it at the time. As a remaster, I can't tell any difference from how I remember the original to be:
- The graphics are on par with a polished game from 2006, apparently they redid some aspects of the original but I can't see it
- The soundtrack is good if you enjoy rock and quirky electronic music
- The controls are surprisingly way more stiff than I remember, turning your car is kind of difficult. It's not that they feel weighty, it just feels like you aren't turning the wheel as far as you can
- I played the campaign for a solid 10 minutes and it says i'm 11% through it, so expect less than a 1 1/2 hour story mode
- The game modes are still fun, the minigames etc. are cool but aren't very substantial
- This game uses arrow keys for control by default but you CAN rebind them
The saving grace of this game is probably the online, which is the main reason I'd see anyone buying it. For $10, even with all of the faults I mentioned it's still a very solid choice for an online racer/vehicle combat game. If you've never played Crashday before, please recognize that the target demographic for this game is people who have nostalgia for the original and probably are viewing it from a much more rose-tinted perspective. If you have an extra $10 Rocket League is an infinitely better vehicle combat game with much tighter controls and a much larger userbase.
It's worth mentioning that this game also has a built in level editor and steam workshop support for those and mods; It's way too early to determine what the modding scene will be like for this game, but thats always something to take into consideration. I'd still say that if you have $10 and you want a fun racing game this is worth trying out, but don't expect amazing if you don't have any nostalgic feelings about it.
[Edit]
I just played the online, this game is balanced awfully. Since turning is so stiff you pretty much have to drift around every corner, but drifting is way too floaty and the maps are not big enough to accomodate for 3+ people drifting around a corner. For the capture the flag mode, the hitbox for taking the balloon is too big on the sides of the car so that you can grab it without even touching, but too small on the front and back so that you can hit the car but still not get it. Multiplayer seems to oddly favor the host of the match, as they always spawned closest to the balloon and seemed to move faster than the other players. Destroying peoples cars is way too underpowered with weapons and way too overpowered with ramming. The one match where I won, I made it through the final checkpoint and the game told me "Congratulations! You placed second" which is currently messing with me on a level beyond my conscious mind. So the main game is short, the multiplayer isn't balanced, and the controls are whack. I can't really recommend it.

TL;DR:
One of the better Far Cry's, a few characters worse than Far Cry 3 and one Coop and story better than it. Stealth is slightly better here than in the old one, enemies slightly smarter, and hostile areas slightly better designed from a gameplay perspective. Other than that - the same. It's a formula game, which, for me, is a flaw, but you decide for yourself. With coop, reduced price and an interesting story with a surprising amount of depth, I can give this game a cautios recommendation.
Been meaning to write this for a while. I completed the storyline for this game with my friend, which is what made it possible not to quit halfway through. The reason is the same as any formula game - it's very very similar to the previous ones built using this formula and everything has such a strong sense of deja vu, that if not for the "4" in the title, it just feels like an expansion to Far Cry [something that was made before].
All flaws still apply - annoying grindy progression, which is mostly aimed at increasing convenience rather than gameplay variety, locked down map, where you have to grind throught he same outposts to unlock fast travel points, rigid vehicles that feel like you are driving a piece of plastic without suspension on another piece of plastic (i.e. off-road/on-road, it all feels the same, this no Just Cause with it's fun arcady off-road vehciles and super-fast asphalt ones), and so on. You can read all about it on the previous games and all of it will still apply.
As for what's different - well, the storyline in Far Cry 4 is actually surprisingly clever. Despite the HUGE gameplay-narrative dissonance (small spoiler for explanation:
), it plays the context of your missions and the characters around you into the overarching plot very, very well. Much better than Far Cry 3, which had these well-acted psychopaths for villans, but honstly other than that the plot was very generic - kill all and get out or go rabid. Far Cry 4 actually has a lot more depth to both the player character, his history and the main villain, to the point when there's a hidden ending to the game 15 inutes in, that, only at the end of the game, if you complete optional objectives, do you actually realise might have been the best one. I really liked the storyline, even if it didn't have as many interesting characters as the third one.
Another thing is coop - it is (sort of) proper this time. You can invite your friend, they take the role of another character in the game's story, and you can do all activities together. Caveat? It is 2-player only, and the map progression is only saved for the host. But taking outposts in coop is a lot more fun than in SP, so I still recomend buying this game only if you have someone to play with, especially if you played any of the previous Far Cry games.
I could go on about gameplay, stealth being slightly better especially in coop, and so on, but honestly - it's all the same as other Far Cry games. That's the thing about formula games, and why I think they are never good value. Some parts may be better, but 90% of this 50€ title you have already played.

This game is amazing.  VA-11 Hall-A has some of the strongest character writing I have ever seen in a video game and I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it.
The game is placed in the dystopian future in mega-metropolis Glitch City.  You play as Jill, a bartender serving at the tihitualar VA-11 Hall-A bar.  Throughout the game you serve a number of clientele, each with their own backstory.  As the bartender you get to hear small slices of their lives and get to know them as individuals.  And the strength of VA-11 Hall-A is the portrayal of these characters.
Some will feel like people you know and you'll find yourself identifying with them.  Some you will come across as really sympathetic and make you want to give them a hug after all they've been through.  Some will make you want to punt them through a wall because they get on your nerves.  All of them have their hopes and hardships, and they all come to VA-11 Hall-A for reasons as varied as the characters themselves.
The protagonist herself is no exception to this.  Jill is far from a silent, faceless protagonist and has her own motivations, hopes, and fears that by far make her one of the most identifiable characters in the entire game.  She has her flaws but she deals with them in her own way and responds and changes to the events around her in the way an actual person would.
VA-11 Hall-A also makes full use of its genre to build a absolutely fascinating and complex world.  The world of VA-11 Hall-A is oozing with personality, with events that are currently ongoing clearly affecting both Jill and the characters she interacts with.  The world outside the doors of VA-11 Hall-A is clearly a living, breathing place and a great deal of thought on the developers part went into building the world.  Easter eggs are rife in this game and it's nearly impossible to count the number of subtle homages to science fiction both past and present are woven into this game.
Gameplay wise there is not much to the game beyond the mixing of drinks for clientele.  A customer asks for something, you look up the ingredients in your book on how to make, and then mix it.  Easy for the most part, no?  However, sometimes a customer doesn't know what they want, or they're being deliberately vague, or you know in your heart of hearts that one of your regulars always drinks sweet drinks so why they ordering a sour drink, ect.  Then it's up to your best judgement what's the proper drink to serve them.  Also, throughout the game there are a number of bills you have to pay that can lead to some bad things, so you have to strategize how to serve your drinks in a way that gets you the most money.
And oh my god is the music amazing in this game.  Much of the music you can play on the jukebox while you're working was clearly inspired by the 80s and adds an extra layer of that old school cyberpunk vibe to your gaming experience.
Ultimately though this is a visual novel with some gameplay elements to it.  If you couldn't care less about story or are more interested in dynamic gameplay over story writing, then VA-11 Hall-A probably won't do it for you.  However if you're a person who either loves 80s cyberpunk, enjoys strong character storylines, and interesting writing then I would absolutely recommend that you buy this game.

This game is stunningly good, by my opinion.
It is what it says on the tin, as silly as that may be. "Cyberpunk Bartender Action". It's an angle with a lot of potential, just  thinking about it. "People tell bartenders all kinds of stuff. This is a known cliche, so let's spice it up.", or something like that, and spice it up they did.
As the game sets up, life in dystopian Glitch City isn't great for a lot, even most people. It's a grim setting, and the game would be outright depressing at all times if it wasn't balanced by a silly, creative, and referential sense of humor. It explores some surprisingly dark topics. Topics that I consider very thought provoking. Such a bleak technological reality even possibly awaits us. That said, VA-11 Hall-A still manages to be a positive game, by my measure. It's a very careful balance. The game strikes somewhere on the slightly upper side of the 'depressing-to-not' scale, as it focuses more on the result of the premise, than the premise itself. Said premise being, that life is terrible in Glitch City and people come to VA-11 Hall-A to drink. Their escape is at the bottom of a glass. So the focus is more on the interactions between bartender/staff, patrons, and even patrons talking with each other sometimes, like with Betty and Deal.
All that said, the game definitely aims a chunk of itself squarely at a certain crowd. And while I'm sure it can be plenty enjoyable by many, a lot of the secondary humor aims itself at the weeaboo image board types, with stuff like the danger/u/ board that you can read ingame, and the fact that it literally markets itself as being a "booze em' up about waifus, technology, and post-dystopia life.". Not a lot of (good) steam games will use the "word" "waifu" in their pitch, but Sukeban has done it. Point being: It draws references to some pretty niche stuff, but I don't think that does it too much harm, and it certainly can be a huge bonus to people in those circles, or know well enough of them. I personally found it added to the game.
Anyway, VA-11 Hall-A is broken into mostly reading dialogue, and mixing drinks. The drink mixing part is largely the only real gameplay, unless you count reading as gameplay. Drink mixing is frankly quite easy and with a few exceptions, is never treated like a real puzzle, although it was clearly not designed to be a challenge in that 90% of cases. It's the way the game defines itself from other Visual Novels, as there are almost no situations where the game will squarely ask you to make a choice to branch the story, it's what drinks you give to who that defines the changes in what happens. It should be noted that the changes one can make to the dialogue/story by mixing drinks is relatively tame by VN standards. It's not a huge branching web, nor is there a huge amount of deviation to speak of in general, but its linearity didn't bother me much personally. Take this into account if you care about a lack of strong story branches.
As is the case with most Visual Novels, it lives and dies by its characters and writing. Although it's a very subjective topic, I'm confident in saying the characters/writing are quite fantastic, since the game has a staggering 98%(!!!) positive review rating out of 2,339 reviews as of writing this. I personally absolutely love the cast to death. The protagonist is actually one of my favorites. Since you don't make any choices for her, besides what drinks to mix, she tends to feel like she has a lot of agency, in my opinion. But the game wouldn't be weak without her, either. Although she is very solid, the cast of strange and interesting folks that come through the doors of VA-11 Hall-A are facinating, hilarious and can be surprisingly deep. It's also seriously one of the funniest games I've ever played, but I feel like its sense of humor fits me perfectly. However, humor is an extremely subjective topic, so I imagine it could be far less amusing to others. The only characters I didn't like were intentionally unlikable.
Also, the music is really excellent. The game works on a jukebox system. Besides certain events, the music that is playing is always off of a playlist that you set up for that half of the day, the work days being broken in half by a break in the middle, which allows you to change the jukebox playlist, as well as save/load. The interface for it could definitely be a bit better, but it's far from unusable. I probably took 45 minutes to set my jukebox playlists, total. The variety of different tunes is strong, with upbeat, fast tracks, as well as somber and slow ones, with some fitting a balanced middle ground.
Oh, I shouldn't ignore the topic of its art. VA-11 Hall-A has amazing art. It'd better, it's a Visual Novel, but they really nail the feel they were going for, on all fronts. Expressive, unique and colorfully realized characters. There are very few backgrounds, but that never bothered me.
I honestly have no real complaints about the game. Some elements could be more fleshed out, and the drink mixing is a little shallow as well, but it's a flavorful and quirky indie Visual Novel. I really just want more games from Sukeban, to be honest.
And that probably wraps up my review. I love this game. More than most probably will. I have an affinity for it. However, it oozes charm and heart, even ignoring my bias. Hell, if you're not much of a Visual Novel type, as many people are not, I still recommend this gem. I definitely wouldn't identify as a Visual Novel person myself, (until now, I guess) and this is the most time I've managed to put in one by far. It earns my recommendation.
NOTE: As of writing this, it's one of the games in the Humble Overwhelmingly Positive Bundle, over at Humble Bundle. With this and N++ at the $10 option, it's a steal. That's not even counting all the other stuff it comes with, as well! Like Shantae and the Pirate's Curse, or Deadbolt. I bought it for N++, but ended up completely falling in love with VA-11 Hall-A. It was a happy little surprise, so keep note of that bundle. It has 8 days left on it as of this review.

I spent a good amount of time playing through this game once and will probably only play it that one time. However, that's not to say I did not enjoy my time playing this game.
The game is a relaxing and chill experience with plenty of great characters, each with their own unique story and enough development to make you care for them. Without the choice of dialogue options it often feels like you're just watching Jill as she lives her life. The gameplay is mostly reading a how-to guide and following a book to the key.
The story of Jill and the bar is an enjoyable one, if not a fullfilling one. To me the game ended abruptly and without a full resolution of many of the stories that began within it. The arc of Jill and her ex had a weird and quick resolution that acts as if it was of utmost importance when I as the player felt no real reason to care.
In short, the ride is enjoyable but the destination is somewhat lackluster. I recommend if you care for fun characters and an interesting world but do not care for a solid ending. If you are like me and want a clear cut resolution to your game, then don't play it. Either way, it was worht my time and money, even if I felt a little peeved at the end.

WARNING: This game contains game breaking bugs. There are fixes available but they involve having to tweak the 'pcconfig' file for certain parts of the game only. This will be a minor inconvenience for casual players who just want to play through the game once, but will be a major annoyance for those looking for 100% completion. WB Games are aware of this, as they are ones who have informed other players of the fixes (easy to find in the discussions page), but they are unlikely to issue a fix given how old this game is. For many, this would be a reason to avoid purchasing the game.
Despite this however, this game still stands as one of the stronger LEGO games of the series before they brought in voice actors. One can only imagine how much better it could have been had they used the sound bites from the actual movies (see LOTR and Hobbit) but the humorous minifigure charades and expressions that made the original games unique and charming are still on top form here. The game stays true to both the novels and the films, making slight alterations here and there to suit the gameplay. You may actually find yourself wanting to revisit the books/films after playing, just to complete the experience.
Gameplay is mostly as can be expected from a LEGO game. You run through a series of episodes, completing the main story and then go back once you’ve unlocked special abilities to get all those extras. One of the interesting elements introduced is that the hub world of Hogwarts' castle actually contains a vast portion of the story itself, normally in the form of tutorials and minigames where you acquire the various spells (abilities). This actually helps the story flow a lot more smoothly and adds a lot more immersion into the game that often lacked in the earlier titles, where you were just going from one episode/level to the next.
The game does have some shortfalls however:
You can only change character in the hub world by drinking from a cauldron filled with polyjuice potions. While this is a nice idea as it keeps in spirit with the Harry Potter universe, it makes the quest for 100% completion a little more tedious as you often have to backtrack to find a cauldron in order to gain access to all the secrets in another area.
No maps or fast travel make Hogwarts a chore to explore. This is particularly annoying when trying to get 100% completion as you often have no idea (even with the relevant 'extras' enabled) whether you have collected all the items from a certain area.
Some of the puzzles/activities are very repetitive. This is actually something that plagues all LEGO games, but the variety here does seem rather thin at times.
Also, this is quite obviously an American game. All references to the first book are as “The Sorcerer’s Stone” and not “The Philosopher’s Stone”. Obviously American intellect is brought into question over whether they know what a philosopher actually is, hence the need for the publishers to change the book title overseas. This makes no difference to the actual game of course but, seeing as it is a British property, it would have been nice to have kept the original book title.
All in all it’s a great LEGO game. Exactly what you would expect, with a few twists here and there. Kids will love it. Adults refusing to grow up will love it. Just beware you will have to mess around with some of the game files in order to complete the game.

Let me start this off by saying that it has issues. A lot of issues. Seriously, what is it with LEGO Games and game breaking glitches? I was often blocked off from some parts of the levels because of glitches and had to restart the game. Also, the controls aren't optimized very well for the KB+M. There's no mouse support and they'll refer to your WASD keys as "Left Stick". That's how bad it is. Just use a controller.
However, all the unpatched glitches aside, it's not a bad game. It has the spirit of every other LEGO game, which is going around and building stuff. It's a game about creativity, and they couldn't have chosen a better setting than Hogwarts to let people explore in.
Keep in mind that this is heavily reflected in many of the "puzzles", too. The puzzles in this game aren't about testing your intuition. They're about innovation and creativity. Often when you are stuck on something that appears to be a puzzle, the answer is actually to BUILD something. It's not just about the LEGO aethetics, it's about the mindset. Looking at you, LEGO Marvel Super Heroes >.>
As far as the game's CONTENT goes, Hogwarts is actually a fun place to explore in the game, but it's very small and confusing to navigate, which necessitates Nearly Headless Nick holding your hand throughout the entire game.
I'd give the game a 7/10 because I enjoyed it and thought it was crafted together very well for what it was supposed to accomplish.

If you like Losing Is Fun games like Dwarf Fortress, Banished, Rimworld, Gnomoria etc then this is a fantastic game for you to pick up. If you're into more laid back city builders such as Cities Skylines then you may not enjoy the nature of this game. So what do you do? You are given a few colonists to... I'm sure you guessed it, colonise planets, the first planet being basically Mars. This isa  survival management game at it's finest, you are always in a precarious position and you never quite feel as though you can sit back and relax.
The easiest comparison to this game is Banished. yes, it's basically Banished in space but oh so much more. Like in Banished you need to strike a balance between all your different industries whilst maintaining an ever growing population of colonists. New colonists arrive in shuttles and the good thing is you can turn colony arrivals on and off to help control the population. There's technology upgrades to constantly give yourself a goal to work towards, ever making your colony bigger, better and more efficient.
The only negatives I've come across so far is that you cannoy rebind keys, which isn't a huge problem because there's not mnuch in the way of shortcuts but I do like to be able to pause the game with the space bar when a disaster hits. Also I've had the odd colonist trap himself behind things whilst building and the colonists sometimes prioritise certain tasks oddly such as going to work instad of getting a much needed drink.
Overall this just skims the surface of what this game has to offer, it's an excellet survival management game and very fairly priced. It's an instant buy if you like these kinds of games and if you're new to the genre I suggest watching some youtube videos to see if this is your thing.

tl;dr The only difficulty in this game is timing button presses. This game is literally replaced by a factory job. That's it. The only thing that ever took lives off me is the arbitrary segments where they change the parry timings so you can't consistantly hit them without memorizing when the boss pauses slightly before their next attack. This whole review could be summarize as "Do you like memorizing when to hit B? Have I got the game for you!".
It's bad, don't even read this review because I summarized it for you.
Actual review:
This game is so close to being great it's actually even more frustrating than playing the damn thing.
Non-rebindable controller inputs are beyond stupid when you can rebind the mouse and keyboard just fine. Does your engine somehow break if you use anything but the 3 included configurations? Really arbitrary decision to allow M&K rebinds but not controller rebinds.
Parry mechanic is just, ugh. I've hit parries I know I shouldn't have and missed ones I know I hit perfectly. Because it feels like almost every attack, even those among the same bosses, have random timings associated with them. Some want you to parry almost immediately after the "shine" indicator, some want you to parry right before the attack actually connects. Some bosses will be SLIGHTLY too far away and hit you with the edge of their attack even if you parry correctly.
A lot of boss fights have really, really, really boring mechanics you have to sit through. Like, amazingly boring. One of the bosses literally makes you run in a circle during their fight. That's it. A child could pass this part easily, and even though it's short, there's a lot of mechanics that feel like time sinks rather than gameplay. Did I mention you have to walk to each boss?
Yeah this isn't even a nitpick, I was debating on calling it that but after doing this five times it justifies being a FLAW, not a nitpick. Walking is boring. Flat out. The dialogue isn't interesting or engaging enough (not to mention there's more dead space than talking anyway) to explain why you have to sit through walking sequences after each boss. I'm GUESSING the developer's intention was to give a pause to the action, or build anticipation to the next fight, all this did was make me walk into the other room or stare at my phone waiting for the auto-walk to complete.
So all in all if you're as easily put off by these things I'd pass. But seeing as the majority of people love this game I'm guessing I'm in the minority by borderline hating it. It's so much fun when it actually works, but it's SO BORING and finnicky the rest of the time I always leave frustrated. It's not even hard, maybe "Furi-er" difficulty is way more fun but it's taking forever to get there since I can only STAND playing one boss at a time. Maybe when I finally get around to beating this game it'll all "click" into place but man it's a slog getting there.
It's not fun. It's not fun enough to finish. I plow through the first 3-4 boring stages of the boss and then lose because they arbitrarily change the timing of the parries. The visual indicator is the exact same, but for some reason the attack is slightly delayed. That's called a QTE, and they're awful.
For two bosses in a row.
This isn't entertainment, this is just bad. The first phases aren't even enjoyable only to get to a terrible QTE. How do people love this game? It's a QTE in disguise rofl. I value my time more than memorizing when to press a button.

Circuits is less of a puzzle game and more of an audio based game of memory. You must compare audio clips to a final version of a song, and sometimes the clips are a 8 seconds long, and the difference between clips doesn't make itself apparent until after halfway into the clip. It is less about challenge and more about patience and investment, and it feels far from rewarding.
It has a nice visual presentation, but it does little to change the slow, monotonous nature of the puzzles. It would be like having a visual puzzle piece fading in or drawing pixel by pixel then disappearing when you were no longer looking at it, requiring you to simply remember what it looked like. Perhaps there isn't a better way to do it with an audio based puzzle game, but hopefully that shares a bit of info for people looking for information on the game.

: If fast arena shooters a la Unreal Tournament are your thing, I heavily recommend checking this one out. The free version doesn’t give you access to all maps for example but TOXIKK is not a F2P game with ingame microtransactions – it’s a great way to test the game before buying it.
: After being in EA for some time, Toxikk now got fully released and offers an experience focussed on players who prefer the old-school way of competitive multiplayer games.
Of course the game has some kind of background story with you playing as a mercenary fighting for one of two giant corporations who’re battling each other over the newly discovered element Edenium but you can safely forget all this now: It’s an arena-shooter where you’re running and jumping around the level and killing opponents – there’s no big story stuff going on or even a real singleplayer campaign for you to experience.
On a couple of different maps, several being used for more than just one game mode (there are: Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag and Domination), you’re fighting with a variety of different guns: your standard Raven pistol, a shotgun and an assault rifle as well as more exotic weapons like the Stingray plasma gun or the Cerberes rocket launcher. All weapons have two fire modes, the assault rifle for example can also fire grenades and the Stingray either fires single plasma projectiles or a long-range plasma beam.
The maps vary greatly in design, from straightforward ones like the factory map Ehrgeiz over snowy environments (Twin Peaks) to far more complex ones like the city-map Foundation or the jungle and ruins mix Artifact. Most maps offer several paths as well as open zones and several height levels which means there’re a lot of ways to get to the objective but also a lot of positions to get shot from; some maps give you access to vehicles like a mech or an assault bomber. Mutators can be used to modify match-settings.
This old-schooly-ness (sorry for the creation) is summarised by the dev as “no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t”: there’re no loadouts, no health-regen, no cover and no classes. You have to collect health and armour on the map, weapons and ammo also have to be picked up but you can carry all the weapons in the game at the same time and then switch between them at any time you want.
The only type of progression system the game has are 16 levels of experience you slowly gain over time; this doesn’t have any effect on the game though and your skill is measured separately in 12 levels and then used for match making. This seems to work quite well, but as a beginner you will still need a thick skin and get used to getting destroyed horribly in several matches before celebrating your first successes – unless you’re a pro at this type of game to begin with ofc.
Game performance is, as expected and needed for this kind of game, very good with very moderate hardware requirements. It’s not a bad looking game under any circumstances but overall it’s nothing special art-wise; I much more enjoyed the colourful style of UT 2004 for example – TOXIKK looks a little bit…bland and generic sometimes.
Since this game screams old-school arena-shooter from every cell, I think I don’t need to say much about the controls: they’re spot-on and work perfectly.
For the exact differences between Free and Full version check the description page of the game; here’re just a few points: Free version means access to less maps, not the full contracts “campaign” and no customization options (which are purely cosmetically). In addition, you miss out on some nice features like the server browser or the vote-map system.
Personally I’m not a big fan of this genre, its’ too fast and too chaotic for me; I prefer games with a battlefield and frontlines and my performance in this game is accordingly bad.
Nevertheless, I can appreciate what Reakktor are doing here and for this low price of just about 15€ you’ll get a full package of action-loaded fun in a clean but cool environment. It’s nothing innovative or new but that also never was the dev’s intention. If you’re still not sure if this is your thing I recommend checking out the test-version and playing a few matches – you can even play against bots.
