I actually preordered this game from the dev's itch.io page in 2015 for $8 and it took me about 14 hours to get to one end.  I played entirely with just the mouse.
Glitch City in the 2070s is a pretty crappy place to live.  There are food and medicine shortages, on top of massive inflation and ever-rising crime.  But all of these serve as backdrop to the story.  You are a humble bartender in a hole-in-the-wall bar in Hall-A of the VA-11 building.  Instead of fighting a shadow government or an ancient conspiracy, this cyberpunk game sees you listening to your patrons' stories and troubles as you mix up a variety of drinks.
This game is a bit on the kinetic side of visual novels, at least at first glance.  There are zero dialogue choices, for one.  Clients can ask for drinks and it's your duty to serve them as asked...but you don't necessarily have to.  So the drinks are arguably your choices.  Will you serve as asked, will you serve at your whim, or will you try to get people drunk?  Would you rather get the flawless serving bonus, or just screw with orders to see how people react?
Gameplay is easy, but that's how visual novels are.  Read a bunch of dialog, and when prompted for a drink, find the drink in the catalog (by name, by flavors, by type), and it'll tell you how many of each of the five ingredients it needs, if it needs ice and/or aging, and if the concoction is mixed or blended.  Some might call for optional Karmotrine, which controls how alcoholic a drink is, or someone might have a vague order.  If Jill isn't distracted, she might have a comment to help you in the mixing screen.  It helps to pay attention and you might be rewarded if you remember what your clients like.  You are paid by commission and by performance, too.  There's a lot of dragging-and-dropping involved and clicking to advance the text otherwise.
The game is spread across a couple of weeks near the end of December, each day starting in Jill's apartment and then working in the bar proper.  You are given notice about incoming bills and also items that have caught Jill's eye, which you are encouraged to buy to keep her focused at work.  You can read the news, and later read up on a forum and a character's blog before you start the day.  This naturally means that the scenery doesn't change very much, but I didn't see it as a problem.  This is more a game for the text and the story as opposed to fancy CGs and all.  Art is retro-inspired but vibrant and the characters are fairly detailed, several with a number of expressions.  There was a minigame you could buy but I was dutiful and kept my spending to aa minimum...and still got the "bad" ending.  Whoops.  You have 24 save slots with opportunities to save in Jill's apartment and on her mid-day break, so there's opportunity to see alternate dialogs if you're willing.
Music is really catchy and there's a lot of ambient music.  The start of each shift and return from break sees you interact with the jukebox and pick 12 songs to randomly play during that part of the game.  There are quite a few songs to start with, but some have to be unlocked during the story or buy buying them between shifts at work.  There is no voicework, but tones play when characters speak.  There are a couple of other sounds effects too.
Overall, the experience was great.  I loved the dialog and the varied cast of characters, like the shameless robot ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or the camgirl or the idol singer...or the pompous oaf with the cryptic drink orders or the dog with the Hawaiian shirt and sunglasses.  This is on the funnier side, but there are still some sad and serious moments.  There were quite a few "did they really just say that??" moments with the dialog too.  Like the story camgirl had about her former manager (papercuts, ow).  Nothing naughty is actually shown but the text makes up for it, all right.
The only thing I didn't like was at the very beginning, a crucial thing about the shaker that you're not told about and this tripped up a lot of people going by the discussion forum.  I thought that you just let the shaker stop on its own (and it never will), thus getting stuck on the very first drink you're told to make.  Mixed drinks are in the shaker for under five seconds, blended drinks are in there for longer than five (the shaker speeds up).  After that, the rest of the game is smooth, and I didn't really have a problem with anything else.
Edit:  It turns out that if you actually make a Sugar Rush as Gil originally tells you at the very start, he'll explain about mixing and blending, as well as how to age/add ice.  So making the Piano Man is basically the "I already know this tutorial" option, so watch for that!  So really, that problem was my fault in the end.
If you're someone more into gameplay than story, you might not like this one since it's very heavy on the story side.  But, you know, visual novel.  The dialog can be off-putting to some, and there can be issue raised with a few characters, but I just attribute it to the kind of place Glitch City is.  And it's your bar that attracts the interesting ones...

This was definitely a good purchase. The story has wonderful atmosphere, interesting characters, and a simple, but ultimately important mechanic of making drinks for the patrons. Guys, the older reviews for this game honestly DO NOT APPLY (anymore)! Seems like because of how long it has been in EA it has gotten a pretty crappy rep.. and it's not fair.
This is everything SOCOM 1/2 was and much more at this point. Some of the maps are done so well by the community it's like I am re-living my childhood again.. which is a wonderful, heart-warming experience. Honestly, it brought a tear to my eye replaying some the of the greatest experiences I have ever had while gaming.  Who would have guessed, that after all these years, there was actually something much deeper to the Socom 1/2 style formula that honestly had not until this game released been fully utilized.
The Amazing:
Maps (Community made)- I have never seen a more dedicated community than the Socom fanbase. The vast majority of the best maps are present, or have been present and need updating. Some exclusions that are needing to be updated to the current UE 4 before the map would be active are (Crossroads, Fish Hook, Frost, Blizzard) however we still have (Off Shore, Desert Glory, and some other favorites)
Gameplay- Damn near perfect if I do say so myself. It has all the features of a tactical shooter and some sweet additions that honestly feel like the quality of the old Zipper Interactive ® (RIP) at times.
Community- Almost every person I talked to in-game was super helpful, and I have yet to meet one toxic person.. which is always cool haha. It's defiantly small, but that will change over time once the PS4 release sees the light of day in its current state.
Devs- They seem to really care at this point. I wish the two original Zipper employees had not left the project... but I can easily understand why.. they should have raised much more money.. It simply was not enough to have the project fully staffed and retain what is now senior (A+++) developers. That's heartbreaking honestly.
The Good:
Engine- It's a custom Unreal Engine.. which is a double-edged sword. On one hand, if you are comfortable developing within that engine it's wonderful... However, I can't help feeling like something is lacking. (Discussed down below)
Graphics Fidelity- In all honesty, I think they are near perfect and I am perfectly content with what is currently being rendered.. however, some people are spoiled.. so to be fair it's not next level holy crap, then again I am pretty sure it's not intended to be. Think Socom 2.5 HD.. you will not be disappointed.
Gun Mechanics- Pretty good, there is defiantly some room for some net-code optimization and hit detection. However, it's perfectly acceptable. Just could be improved.
The WTF!?!?:
Grenades- They are so horrible.. and I honestly can not stand how scrubby it feels. I would host my own dedicated server (Setup a limit), however, that's not really an option considering it's unable to be ranked at this point. I want to be able to host a dedicated ranked servers on my 1Gbit connection.. not use some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ data center gimped environment. I think I can host it better than you.. so how about you let me?
Map creator/mission editor- I was super excited to create my own maps, and bring back what was missing.. however, the learning curve is ridiculous and I have never had a worse feeling of pure hell trying to get something off the ground. I am not honestly even sure they let you use the assets they created to create your own maps.. Spend some time on actually documenting the editor instead of just saying it's an unreal engine "thing". It's unacceptable, and I think you guys should really reevaluate the effort that needs to be put forward in creating a good foundation for a newer user to UE 4 map creating. The documentation right now is pathetic, and honestly is my biggest disappointment in the game.
Sound- it's crap, you know it's crap. I hope you guys fix it.
Much Love and respect for what you guys/girls created. Thank you for the passion you have put into the project, and I look forward to the future of the game.

I'm a few hours in and I can see there are some problems with the colonist behavior, there's also some information about the game mechanics you wont get without experimentation or by reading the help documents in the game.
Some of the wierd things I saw for colonist behavior:
* Say a solor flare is coming. You set the base to Yellow Alert to make everyone stay inside. They appear to check for alerts only after completing their current task. So the guy who's just left the airlock to go drop off materials for your new complex... he'll keep carying his box all the way out there then come in. Even if he's only 3 steps out the door.
* Robots will also sit in line to get inside on Yellow and Red alert when priority obviously should go to humans getting to safety.
* Trade ships will leave before getting trades done when large numbers of resources are being exchanged.
* You have a bunch of sick people so you set a priority on the Lab that makes your medical supplies. As you're currently out of medical supplies an bio plastics (one of their 2 ingredients) your medics are off getting coffee or something. A worker finishes making the needed bio plastic... and caries it to a building site rather than to your Medic's workstation.
A lot of the above sounds bad. It's not nearly as big of a deal as it sounds like and a lot can be fixed by the devs allowing you to directly tell a colonist what to do or where to go, or just putting in a check for "Wait this priority thing like an alarm should change what I'm doing" to the colonist state engine. While I'd personaly be the nutso who wants to make the shift schedules for all my colonists I also understand the choice to not have players exhibiting that level of micro-management. This isn't Prison Architect on Mars.
All of that said... I'm still hooked on this game. Sitting at work and watching video of other players and getting ideas on how to change my planning and playstyle is not something I do for most games but I'm doing it here. Despite the flawed colonist AI the basic game of balancing colony growth is still delightfully well done and I still reocmmend this game to several of my friends, though I do tell them to swing by and try it at my place a bit first before they buy.

Video Review:
TLDR: This is an example of a game that needs a maybe button. I enjoyed my time with it, Overall a solid management game and it looks great. It does have a number of issues in the form of poor AI and camera controls. However, the biggest issue the game has is a lack of content past a certain point. After about 8 hours of play I lost all motivation to progress and had unlocked all of the buildings. If it was cheaper or had a few more months in the oven I would be able to recommend it. As it stands I can't. For more please watch the video.

The game is fun but the AI is extremely simplistic. The main goal other than expansion is to always balance the various demands of the population. The minute one key criteria becomes scarce things can go wrong quickly. I state the AI is simplistic because you are unable to micro manage situations, for example the chain of events to restore stability may start with one item needing to be produced to complete the construction of a structure. Whilst you have the ingredients and machine to do this your people may not focus there. Instead they will often undertake daft trivial things like carry boxes to storage as that's on the queue already. You end up feeling a strong sense of frustration as you watch "general duties" being undertaken instead of the one thing which will lead to a chain of production to resolve an issue. Even the Sims have that level of control and its lacking in this game.
Aside from that I would have preferred to see some R&D rather than trading for capability. Also perhaps exploration/discovery where you send an explorer off and perhaps they uncover a crashed ship with alien tech to advance things. Or mining zones of varying quality to give a reason where you place a mine. Harry Potter in LEGO, what could you possible not like about this combination? In this game, you'll play through years 1 to 4 at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry during the time of the rise of Lord Voldemort. This was a huge undertaking by the development team given the excitement and anticipation for the game, and unfortunately I don't have many good things to say about the first installment.
You'll find yourself battling from Dudley's house, through the secret canals and dungeons of Hogwarts and all the way into the forbidden forrest. And for what you might ask? Simply to graduate from school, but it wasn't that hard when I went!
I genuinely feel that this game would be better suited to hardcore fans of the franchise, and I also genuinely feel that the development team didn't take this game seriously enough. The games mechanics are much like all the other LEGO games, and it is a successful business model so there's no arguments there. It does however lack unique mechanics, engrossment and immersion. Overall it does feel too much like too much of a kids game for kids.
With all of this said, I would still recomend it. It's charming, mindless, nothing unique and short-lived. If you're a huge fan of the franchise it's definitely worth the time. I wouldn't recommend it so much for those who aren't huge Harry Potter fans. So given you understand all of this, you're able to make your own judgements.

From what I managed to play, I love this game; it's fluid, fast-paced and fantastic. The parry system is rewarding as the timing window is tighter than [censored]. The first boss serves as a rather challenging but helpful tutorial to get you into the game, and the narrative and atmosphere is simply epic (for lack of a better word).
However, due to my current hardware, for the game to run smoothly with no input delay, I have to play it on the lowest settings. As such, all the graphics are blurred at best; the fast-pace of the battles means that what would be clear signals of an incoming enemy attack are more akin to pixel-hunts that require a lightning reaction time to spot. I compared my experience to watching some gameplay on Youtube and the visual difference is clear as day, so to speak.
For me, Furi was manageable up until the 4th boss, who constantly blurs your screen with his attacks; I quite literally could not see the dark-green boss against the dark-green water, made only worse by the incessant water effects. Of course, the dark-green boss is adorned with light-green lights, but those are the exact same colors of his attacks; under these conditions, it was nigh impossible to tell what was the boss and what his attack was, and the constantly moving camera did nothing to help with this. To put it in perspective, try playing your favorite fighting game but wearing beer goggles. The graphics are already blurry as-is, and a boss incessantly inducing a blur effect on your entire field of vision in tandem with the fast camera movements makes the game quite literally unplayable on the lowest settings.
In conclusion, I can only recommend this game to people with proper gaming PCs. If you have a low-end machine, avoid this game.

For us Planeswalkers, there’s a desire to cast Memory Lapse on our minds and view the game again as beginners. We long for those trampling monsters, the overpriced yet devastating spells, and the bliss that comes from winning a game by bashing your opponents face with a 9/9 dragon. Unfortunately once the maturing mage explores more refined planes—constructed, limited, EDH—he leaves behind the naive yet slightly more satisfying battles of his youth. He trades primordial wreckage for strategy and precision. “Expensive” is now defined in RL currency, rather than mana. The ingenious creations of an adventurous mind are replaced by the fine-tuning of imitation. Suddenly the love of the game is “promoted” to the love of the metagame. And we feel with this evolution that something was lost.
Magic 2014 lets us revisit those simpler times. Picking your flavor of magic, whether it’s the rampage of green’s creatures or the scalding of red’s spells, every player can pilot decks attuned to their style and fight the personalities of the Dominarian multiverse. The games are straightforward yet rarely frustrating, and the addition of new cards for every win makes progress enjoyable. The diversity of decks keeps things fresh, and the power of later challengers or revenge campaigns puts your deck to the test. I say deck, because it is your ability to structure your deck that makes the most difference. Games are often too simple to reward strong plays, and unlocks are the only meaningful way to improve your chances of success.
For veterans, this makes the game a joke if you know what to look for. For new players, or experienced ones with discipline, this makes exploring the game a joy. Challenges, achievements, personas, and titles all round out the package to burn time and steep yourself in flavor. Probably the best part of the game is multiplayer, where playing a few constructed or sealed games with your mates makes you feel like the (albeit pleasant) grind was worth it. Mercifully, Wizards of the Coast lets you buy decks for a dollar, so those with cash to burn can skip the monotony.
Duels of the Planeswalkers, as a series of games, is inferior to both MTGO and the real thing. But for a journey to a more innocent past, where the game is what mattered, not your meta-strategy or budget, these are refreshing and enjoyable. For those who can’t help but unlock the best decks and smash the computer’s face in, this probably isn’t the game for you. If you owned the previous titles, you likely already own this one, but if you’re on the edge I would say it’s my favorite one yet, but not a big enough improvement to justify the buy. But if you do grab it, I also recommend the expansion, which simply adds more magic love.
Any platform, short of finding 13 year olds just entering the fray, where I get to swing with giant dragons and drop game-breaking spells for twelve mana, is worth the price tag. It’s Magic at it’s core, unfettered by efficiency and pretension. But it’s certainly not Magic at its best.

I saw this game several times passing by, and told myself that I had to try it... some day. I knew this game was made by Mr. Blow, the creator of Braid. And I have to admit that I was not a big fan of Braid. But I finally bought it and started the game. Just... wow
There is no menu at first start, no help, no explanation. You just arrive in a place you don't know. Quickly, you'll find a simple puzzle, and then another one a bit harder, and so on, to finally arrive in a magnificent place. As you can see in the screenshots the graphics touch is a bit "uniform" (I mean no very detailed textures), but this makes the place wonderful. Very quickly you go out of the place and discover other puzzles, other elements. The goal is always the same. Go from start to end, with respect to the puzzle elements. But you never get bored !
As I said before, no help. But only with careful observation and experimentation, you can understand how the elements work, and how the puzzles need to be solved. This is great ! So great design that you can understand and play the game without a freaking line of text. Also, this helps to the immersion in the game (since you are alone here).
And so on, element by element, puzzle by puzzle, you gonna discover this very environmental-varied island, advance, and perhaps... understand what you're doing here.
This is the first game in history where I shout "THEY DARED!" each time I solve a new puzzle type. They are very well thinked, and the elements are pushed to their maximum. Each time you think that this puzzle was the trickiest, you'll find a trickier one. This is pure genius.
Finally : A-MUST-HAVE. The best puzzle game, and one of the best game I never played in my whole life. Even at it's initial price, it's totally worht it.

An intimate story of a little bar in the not too distant future.
I think it’s fair to say that VA-11 Hall-A has a very narrow focus. Most of the game, save for a few cutscenes, takes place in either the titular bar or at the main character’s apartment. You see most of the game through the eyes of Jill, a bartender who sees to the requests – which are sometimes unspoken – of the clients that come by. The world does feel very anime-esque, with catgirls, talking dogs and power armour. A lot of thought seems to have been given to the interplay between characters and the world they inhabit and you can discover details about people if you treat them properly and remember what they like.
The story is, well, muddled. There’s a lot of threads that seem to be left hanging by the end of the game. I wonder a little if the writers let the characters lead the story instead of having a plan of where they wanted things to end up. While there are bookends to certain character stories, it ends fairly abruptly, not letting you know the fate of the people you’ve met over the course of the game. I managed to get most of the “good endings” and they felt terribly disjointed. The characters all have a certain type of personality and charm (or lack of), but that wasn’t enough to carry the story for me.
Playing the game honestly felt like a little bit of a chore. Mixing drinks is simple, easy and low stress with the focus being on character interaction, but it’d be nice to have something more to do. Yes, there are little interludes, like being able to choose what Jill’s apartment looks like in a limited way, playing a retro bullet hell shooter or a brief truth or dare game. Unfortunately, you’ll be spending most of the game mixing drinks off a menu with minimal chance of actually screwing up unless that’s your intention. I suspect it’s the equivalent of dialogue choices in a visual novel, but you’re really only given yes-no options here. With the occasional maybe.

I've been a longtime fan of the game since its original launch in 2006. When I heard that Crashday was getting a re-launch with improvements, enhancements, and Steam Workshop support, I knew I had to get this game.
Crashday: Redline Edition provides EVERYTHING that fans of the original have come to expect. There have been no un-necessary changes, meaning that longtime fans will be able to pick this up and start playing online or in the game's single player right away. The improved gamepad support is greatly appreciated, and whilst it does take a bit of time to memorize the buttons, a bit of playing will definitely help this out.
The gameplay is addicting and rewarding. Being able to demolish your opponents or friends online and at times even escape with the victory is always a great feeling. Thanks to the addition of powerups, it can keep matches going for longer and adding more depth to the matches. The car handling is exactly as it was 11 years ago, so its easy for me to get back into the hang of things, but newcomers might need to take a bit of time to master it down. Once you've got it down however, its solid and responsive.
The graphics are largely the same from the original release, however there are some enhancements made to keep the game from looking as if its aged poorly. For a small game like this, it still looks rather good considering its original time of release.
The online at the time of this review isn't exactly the smoothest. Sometimes races may fail to start, but when they do it seems to be pretty consistent. Lag is dependant on the person's connection, but if you are racing with others who have good connection, you shouldn't have many issues.
The music is the same as original. Which is nice.
Thanks to Steam Workshop support and the built-in track editor, this game provides plenty in terms of replay value, allowing you to mod and create to your heart's desire. Kudos points to Moonbyte for providing a Mod Manager at startup, so you can set it to your liking. Reminds me of the old fan-made mod managers from Need for Speed: High Stakes. OH, and you can use mods online! Take-Two should take some lessons there..
If you've never had the chance to play this game before, DEFINITELY consider getting this Steam release. Its 100% faithful to the original and has several bug fixes, optimizations, enhancements, and many more to make this the definitive release of the game. For longtime fans like myself, I am going to enjoy the many hours I spend in this game.
I highly recommend this game.

My uncle got me this game called Crashday when I first started PC gaming back in 2013. I tried it out, and I hated it. For me, still being a console peasant, it was hard for me to pick up with the issues it had with controls, menu navigation, difficulty curve, etc. It sat on the self for years, until I found out the game I hated was being remastered. It got me thinking, so I bought the Redline Edition. Lets just say that have a 'different look' on the game now.
Crashday: Redline Edition improves on the negative aspects of the original, while still keeping the same feel that set Crashday apart from the other generic car combat games.
This game does run over 60FPS. I want to point out that even the original game had amazing settings. I was surprised that I could set the game to my 1080p 16:9 resolution at 144hz for a 11 year old game! The Redline Edition improves on every aspect. Not only that, it can run on a lot of computers, making it a great game for low end, mid range, and high end computers. However, the game still has noticable pop-in, and dated graphics, but this is made for PC. No ports here!
"Download and play mods, cars, tracks and more from the newly integrated Steam Workshop, or create your own using the Crashday SDK. New: modded gameplay is now fully online-play compatible!"
It speaks for itself. However, the mod loading system doesn't work well, and you have to restart the game in order to enable mods.
They improved the HUD & UI so much. Not only did they fix the controller issues, it is much cleaner now. It also is now red, which makes sense compared to the baby blue of the original game, which really didn't set the mood well. Simple, clean, and clear cut HUD and UI.
(I only used a controller) The controls feel different than the original, but in a bad way. They don't feel as responsive, or as fluid. They are hard, but they aren't anything like the original, which is something to get used to.
The camera in the game is good, but lacks in a full 360 view. It only has a front, and back view which limits your field of view, especially from the side.
The AI is a mix of smart and dumb. A lot of times, the AI can be very hard to beat, but other times they screw up bigly, and give you the advantage. The racing AI is clueless, while the destruction AI is top notch. It is a mix bag of results which gives it a mixed bag rating.
This game has a very difficult learning curve. It is easy to pick up the controls, but the AI is very aggressive, and doing stunt combos are so difficult, unless they are done just perfectly. The new pick-ups in the games, like the ammo, and repair vehicle help to lower the difficulty. The difficulty for this game makes sense, however, it is something you really need to get used to before you jump right into career mode, and online.
The game features 6 gamemodes: Wrecking Match, Stunt Show, Hold The Flag, Race, Pass The Bomb, and Bomb Run. There is a Test Drive mode where you can drive around a map, but it has no real goal. Each mode has setting to adjust the gamemode to your liking. These modes are really fun, although they can get repetive over time. Their techinque of combining car combat, and stunting really pushed the game into a whole different style of car combat games than any other similar car combat games I played.
Career mode is very difficult, but in a frustrating way. I wanted to pull my hair out trying to complete career mode due to the relentless, instanity of the AI. You really need to practice, and practice in Single Events before you jump right in. Also, career has a plot, which really doesn't fit the game. They made this wacky game into a story that tries to make it intriguing, but really it isn't. Of course, you need to complete career mode to unlock vehicles, and upgrades, but with a frustratingly hard career mode, it just isn't fun at times.
The game features 6 minigames: Long Jump, Long Jump II, Vehicle Blast, Vehicle Blast II, Checkpoint Chase, and Checkpoint Chase II. These are fun minigames, but I would have liked more included than just the original ones. There are so many cool minigames made by the public for the original game, that hopefully can be put into the workshop, but the minigames supplied in the main game are fun, but more would be appreciated.
I think they improved it, but I can't even tell, no one is playing online!

There are 12 vehicles, all from the original game. Each one is very unique, with so many different cars combined into one. I wish there were more, as they could have easily included more vehicles in the Redline Edition.
I find the car customization a bit weak. Many cars only have a few parts to choose from in each category. Some cars don't even have parts for certain categories! Also, not many performance upgrades are available to choose from. I am glad customization is there, but it needs to be developed on.
The vehicle weapons consist of single, and double missles, and a machine gun. There is not much to say other than the weapons have a lot of punch to them, and you just need to angle them perfectly to hit the target.
The vehicle damage is very dated. It was good back in 2006, but now it looks more like a spikey car.
The physics feel really good. Cars crash quite nicely, and doing barrels roles, and flips can be easly done. Nothing feels very unnatural.
The track designs are really nice. Each map is very special, with the stunt maps being the real highligh of the tracks. This style of tracks is kinda weird, but fits perfectly with the tone of Crashday.
The track editor takes a while to master, but once you do, the track editor is a amazing tool. Even for more inexperienced player, you can easily make maps to share with everyone. Although it is not perfect, it is still an amazing tool that will help to extend the life of the game.
One of things I hated about Crashday was the soundtrack. They decided to bring back the original soundtrack, which makes a lot of sense, to keep the original game intact. I feel that the music still doesn't fit the atomsphere of the game well. The songs just don't get me in a "let blow up♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; mood, which sours the gameplay. However, what I learned from my other indepth review is that I am going to have people yelling at me for giving the soundtrack a low score, especially people who grew up with this game, so I better not rate this category...
Compared to the original release of Crashday, Redline Edition should be the one you pick up. Some issues still remain from the original Crashday v1.2, but all in all, the Redline Edition is a great upgrade from the original, which shows the company still cares about this game, something that companies just don't do anymore.
A classic PC game, now has new life. Moonbyte decision to take a classic PC game, and rework it means old, and new players will have a lot more Crashdays to enjoy.

The TL;DR version:
Ultimately, when it comes to base-building strategy games, there are only 2 types of them - the ones that are done right, and the ones that are not. There is no middle of the road option. Thus, I am very happy to say that Planetbase actually succeeds in being a good open-end base-building strategy with survival mechanics, very much like Banished, for example.
The longer version:
I really like this game, I will make that clear right off the bat. I am a huge sucker for survival colony-building or base-building sims like Banished and Startopia where your role is to set tasks and watch your little minions carry them out. The concept of Planetbase (build, survive, expand) really reeled me in and I asked the devs for a beta testing key, and they actually came through for me - much to my surprise, as I am not a popular youtuber and I upload unmonetized youtube vids just for fun. This is also the only game I ever asked a beta test key for - and I did it because I saw some of Negark's and Blitzkriegsler's youtube vids and loved the concept. I tested the game throroughly, gave lots of feedback and loved every minute of it. So in true fashion in all my reviews, let's take a look at the good and the bad.
The Good:
1. Great graphics - I was pleasantly surprised, because many 20€ games on steam boast way poorer graphics. I have an ROG 751 laptop and the game played flawlessly on max settings, without a single hiccup or drop in the frame rate even in a 300+ pop base.
2. Great music - although some people might expect more tracks, I really like the relaxing music that the devs selected for this game.
3. Good challenge - the game provides a big challenge at start, and once you get everything set up and running, it still keeps you on your toes. It is surprisingly easy to destroy a whole colony of 200 citizens, as I so painfuly learned. Solar flares, meteors, attackers and other detrimentals will constantly keep you on your toes.
4. Good pacing - you don't need to grind or mine materials for hours and hours on end before you get to the endgame (meaning 200+ population). And 'bout that...
5. A planet takes 10+ hours to complete once you've learned the ropes, which is good value for the money.
6. Great replayability - every planet has a full 180 degree lattitude and longtitude representation, in essence making for a ton of possible starting locations - and yes, if you find yourself a good location, you can write it down, share and challenge your friends, as it will always stay the same.
7. Great help menu - I love games with decent help menues, like Cilivization, for example. Planetbase is one of them, having everything in a very in-depth help menu that will explain everything perfectly. No need to spend hours and hours looking for wiki pages or faqs to help you cause the devsgot lazy.
8. Great tools to keep track of your base - the game has a great base overview system that can even track every single base resource and give you a very precise information how it changed over time.
9. Approach the game as you want - you can just dive in, or spend a good amount of time looking at the map and planning how you want to build your base. I personally love looking at the map and making a mental image of the base and then just going for it. And as a consequence...
10. The game promotes creativity - while you can still build haphazardly and win, making a beautiful base with a well planned layout that runs smoothly and efficiently is extremely satisfying.
11. Good tutorial - the game does a great job giving you the basics of base-building, and letting you go on from there.
12. Fun to look at - it's a lot of fun to look at your little colonists, analyze their paths, schedules, duty or leisure time, etc.
And now let's take a look at the Bad.
1. Very punishing at start - until you learn the ropes of the game, you will decimate a good number of colonies. You really need to play for 2-3 hours in order to get better acquanted with the specifics of the game and that could be a turn off for some gamers. But then again, that's the case of most simulators, really...
2. Once you have a good system running, it's all expand, trade and survive - pretty much like Banished. That could be another turn off for some gamers.
3. The camera is a bit static - while you can zoom in and out freely, I expected more in terms of minimum and maximum zoom distance.
4. The settings menu could have been better - while to me it has never been that big of a gripe, and let's face it - this is a simulation game - some gamers want better graphics/audio/gameplay menues, and not an all-in-one menu.
5. The pathing is wonky sometimes, but a good base layout will remedy that.
The conclusion:
I thoroughly recommend Planetbase to anyone who enjoys base-building, sci-fi, and/or survival games. At the current price tag of 17€ (15% reduction at launch) it is a great value for the money, and you can expect to dump at least twice as many hours in it. If you liked games like Banished or Startopia, you will absolutely enjoy this one. It is a great open-end experience with lots of unlockables, achievements, and ultimately relaxing gameplay once you have every all nice set up. I, personally, never felt bored - I always felt like having something to fix, improve, and adapt for the mid or late game.
I would love to see the devs build up on this concept. I would love to see things like first person camera mode, more buildings, more colonist classes, more things to trade, more structures and more unlockables. Will the devs do it? I guess we will have to wait and see.

Really enjoy playing this game it is fun to play and relaxing. Rather than trying to be overly complicated game the game is simply yet fun.It is about making a self sufficient colony. The 1st planet acts as a sort of large scale beginners planet with the others becoming more difficult due to harsher conditions.
Basic resource needs in the game are metal,water,power,air,food.From that needs branch out and mechanics get more specific to what your colonists need. Water,power,metal,food are infinite so this will make the game easier to master for those who take advantage of this. However the main draw to game is in building  your colony to a self sufficient level and grow it out as much as you want.
There are a variety of mechanics in the game that can throw wrenches in your works.Environmental conditions,intruders,pro-longed injury,starvation, etc.Learning how to overcome these is part of the fun and challenge. The game works beautifully as far as I can tell, runs absolutely fine. However it's incredibly shallow and consists of nothing more than a very repetetive balancing act, battling with the map you've been given to place increasingly large numbers of structures whilst hoping things pan out with your factories and such.
It's far too shallow and requires an inhuman amount of patience to deal with production misery for me to recommend this, but if you really want a game about colonising a planet, then this might do it for you.
Someone called me out on my profile for only having played just over an hour, so I'll explain why I didn't need any more time - Once you've completed the absolute bare essentials of a base which takes around 20 minutes of getting the balance right and building things in a pretty set order, the game becomes a repetetive slog of repeating the process of adding things to your base as you need them (which is sometimes difficult because the connections system is often interfered with by the terrain with no real way to understand why), there is almost no complexity to the game, I'd compare it to Banished with far less content.
In addition, simply checking your resources requires several clicks through menus, a lack of resource display on the main UI and decent hotkeys makes the game a pretty miserable experience unless you're really committed to it.
I guess I need to add another edit explaining why my low game time isn't a good enough reason to ignore this review. The game showed no form of complexity or advancement in the first 2 hours, if a game is incapable of getting you on the hook then that's entirely the game's fault. You can unlock the majority of the buildings you'll be using all the time within 15 minutes of starting the game, and you'll be using them so often that I got bored incredibly fast. The game doesn't go anywhere and the only thing you've got to worry about is randomly having your life made even harder by one of the "disasters" which amount of having to spend more time alt tabbed out waiting for things to be repaired.
The game is as shallow as a puddle, there's simply no reason to play this over one of the many other far more interesting citybuilding games which have far more freedom and a lot more content. Quite why people are attacking me and coming to this game's defense so quickly - smells very fishy to me.

- BETA REVIEW -
SPOILER ALERT!
I must start by saying, that developers of this game have been very active in forums. I havent seen topic out there without some kind of dev (martino) reply. I was part of beta, and this review is based only on beta state:
When you start game, you can pick planet and starting location. You can unlock other harder planets later by playing first one and achieving milestones. Game starts by group of colonists/bots landing on planet and then everything is up to you to keep them alive. You have to build different kind of buildings like bio-domes for food production, oxygen generators, solar panels etc. which all are needed for basic survival. Then you can place landing bay, where tradeships (and potential intruders) can visit your base. Survival itself can be hard sometimes, as it's very easy to expand too quickly which leads to several problems. Colonist AI tends to build new buildings first and when everything are build, they focus on production inside base (which leads to situation where you lose all your energyproduction when buildings break down  if you arent careful).
AI can be nasty sometimes, but there was very nice update just before release which fixed lots of problems. There's still some problems left with AI/pathfinding, mostly with priorities on what colonists are doing and will they finish their job before going to eat/sleep etc. But then, point of this game isn't to micromanage everything. You do plan building layouts, activate alarms and such, but rest if up to colonists who are living in base. And I'm sure that small problems what are left, will be quite easy to fix as they already did big deal in last update. (Problem WAS Biologists who are supposed to keep people fed, stopped working when little a bit hungry... leading to snowball effect having whole base waiting in canteen for food, but no-one working for it).
Graphics are nice. There's day/night cycle in game with some events like solar flares and sandstorms which are looking great for basebuilding game. Sounds are quite basic, but ok for theme.
I have been playing this game quite a lot already in beta. For me, it has replayability as I love to build different kind of bases and try to minmax my production and survival. But in "end-game" this game mostly has content like avoiding solar flares, sandstorms, signalling ships, helping out people who visit your base and most importantly, dealing with intruders who try to invade your base and kill your colonists. I hear from forums, that some people have found way to max 200 buildings limit which means HUGE base. This means you at current state of beta, there's limit in how big base you can build. But I never were even close that big.
I recommend this game to anyone who likes games like Banished or other survival/management/building games. It's already very good and I never had problem with bugs/lagging/crashes or such. It just runs flawlessly. Only thing I wish from future is some extra content here and there to keep people challenged and small changes in AI behaviour.

I'm 2 hours in on the default difficulty and currently facing the third boss. These two hours have been filled with happiness, joy, anguish and despair, usually all simultaneously. The tagline of the game "The jailer is the key, kill him and you'll be free", is almost poetic in how it lures you into a false sense of security. The beauty of this game however, is that it totally does not matter whether you fail miserably or by a miracle succeed, I always found myself wanting to try again, until I had conquered that (&*()&^#!@ jailer. The combat system feels impactful and requires some effort until you master them in conjunction with the various bullet hells you will get thrown into. This paired with multi-phased bosses with differentiating attack patterns, make it an absolute joy to play. In addition, the rough yet polished look in combination with the amazing soundtrack will give you one hell of a ride.
A minor point of annoyance for me personally were the transitioning points between each boss. the controls (mouse and keyboard) felt a bit clunky. Next to that, I feel like they simply ate up too much time. The narration about the bosses was interesting, but could have been implemented in various other ways (the transition visuals were great though, depending on which boss you were facing).
All in all, I would defintely recommend the game. Especially with the current sales, I would see this as a little hidden gem.

There is a part of me that loves many elements of Furi.
And there's a part of me that absolutely hates many elements of Furi.
It's got style, gameplay, challenge, and a great soundtrack.
It's got control issues, camera problems, and it's unforgivingly frustrating.
There's a story which doesn't completely unfold until the very end, and it's ok if not a bit obvious.  It does it's job moving you forward.  The ending was rewarding and done well.
There are 12 boss encounters in this game and that's all there is.  But each boss has 4-6 phases and if you fail on any of them you must restart that boss completely.  You can't just go in and wail on the boss (in normal mode) because they will kill you fast.  You must dodge and parry constantly, rapidly, over and over until there is a weakness you can use to hit the boss.  You do this for every boss, for every phase.  Sometimes it's a bullet hell and you have to clear a path and move carefully until you get a chance to hit the boss.
I have played every Dark Souls game to completion (multiple times NG+, etc.) and the thing is, Dark Souls is a balanced and polished game.  To compare Dark Souls to Furi would be like comparing a Porche to a Pinto.  The only thing they have in common is that they are challenging.
Furi gets a lot of things right.  And a lot of things wrong.  I can't recommend it unless you just really want to play an extremely hard game that is both brilliant, and yet deeply flawed.  If there was a neutral option I'd pick it.  For a rating I'd give it a 6/10.
I believe it was Shigeru Miyamoto who said It's simple to make an easy game.  It's simple to make a hard game.  It's nearly impossible to make a balanced game.

If you enjoyed Far Cry 3, then you'll enjoy Far Cry 4, as it offers more of the same open-world adventure as previously experienced. A bit dissapointed that it did not vary to much from it's predecessor, however it was enjoyable nonetheless.

If you liked Far Cry 3, you will like this.  It's a very similar open world game with lots to explore, do and find.  The  overall plot is OK, but no particularly clever bits nor anything particularly original.  The voice acting is excellent.

I did have a few quibbles with the game though.

There is no reason for 90% of the weapons.  I got access to the"Shredder" early in the game and there was nothing else that could compete with it in terms of effectiveness for must situations until very late game when I got the "Bushman", and even that is debatable.  You have space of 3 other weapons as the game progresses, so one will be some sort of sniper weapon, another will be a single-handed weapon that you can use from vehicles leaving space of one heavy weapon.  For the last, I almost always carried a flame-thrower to get at the high propiganda posters that you have to destroy.  The only reason to even try some of the other weapons is to get ranking in the "arena", but even then, that's more of a grinding/time filler thing than any real  game reason to use the others.

Along the way in the game you gain experience and "karma". Both of those will hit the cap quite early if you are completing most of the extra quests and missions.  Money is  also very easy to  come by, so that hits the limit of what you can carry (which can be expanded over the course of the game) fairly often.  This also relates to the weapons you can buy.  Over  time, most are given to you for free, but since money isn't really a limit, you will likely have bought them well before that time comes.

There are lots  of places to explore, but usually not much comes of finding them (no extra missions, although  often a bit  of cash, which, as I mentioned above, you don't really need). Still, the game is pretty much wide-open right from the start, so there is a lot to explore and do.

The game is gorgeous for the most part, but I did definitely notice the "pop-in" of objects in the far distance, especially when flying.

Colorful images and haunting sounds are the key points of attraction in Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride, a hidden-object adventure game from Artifex Mundi.
A good fantasy story ties together the simple gameplay: use logic to piece together items you find in the environment so you can solve puzzles and proceed with the story. Some of the solutions don't make a lot of sense (nor do some of the hidden objects you have to find), but if you ever get stuck, you can fall back on the hint system to make regular progress.
While it can be absorbing to seek solutions hidden within the beautiful images, it bothers me that there is only one solution to every puzzle. Sometimes the “correct” solution makes less sense than something I came up with on my own. Also bothersome is the protagonist's tendency to leave behind useful items like a knife or a rope, only to search for new ones in the next puzzle. I'd like Artifex Mundi games more if they had flexibile puzzle solutions (like the Deus Ex games), encouraging creativity and improving replay value.
As long as Artifex Mundi sticks to their formula, they are unlikely to make a game better than Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride. I can't complain too much, though; simple, bite-sized games like this can be very satisfying to play once in a while, especially in an environment populated by so many long games.

Ok, I have to admit....out of all the Artifex Mundi games on Steam, this is one of the few that feels most like an adventure game, even though it is a casual game.  It feels more like an adventure than any of their others, with a bit more varied array of puzzles and locales, along with the beautifully rendered scenery and objects typical for them.  Scripting still feels like a middle-school play, and CG isn't top-end, but hey, it's a casual game from a non-AAA publisher.  Playtime's around 4-5 hours including the extra adventure unlocked after the main game is completed.

This is easily the best hidden object adventure I've ever played in terms of production quality. The quality of the visuals, music and voice acting are both superb for the genre (I was especially amazed by the smooth, but still painted-looking animations.) The game brings all the features of modern HO games, map, hints, selectable difficulty level, easy puzzles, lots of achievements and collectables and an alternative for HO scenes (in this game it's domino).
The plot is good too for the genre, not too blatantly obvious, though not that surprising either. I liked how it's not about a guy saving a love interest, but a woman trying to save her sister. And I loved the ending a lot! The focus was different than most HO games I've played.
In the first half of the game instead of word-list HO scenes, the player has to combine items based on images. I haven't met with this type of HO scene before, it was refreshing after the endless word-lists of other games.
The only thing I kinda missed is the feature they had in 'SEASON OF MYSTERY: The Cherry Blossom Murders' where if you click on an object in a HO scene, it shows the item's silhouette.
There were some genre-typical ridiculous elements, like having to light up a torch with a ray of focused light in a multi-step puzzle, next to a field of dozens of candles. Also having to be basically a cleptomaniac and steal quite a few things from your innocent neighbours. (I had to steal a candle, a crochet needle, a fan and a teacup from the same windowsill throughout the game + even had to cut off a piece of their curtain ^^;; )
PS: That kitten helper is the cutest thing ever :D

Circuits is one of those increasingly-popular, sleek, simplistic puzzle games, with very simple (yet complex) concepts that grow as you play. Similar to LYNE, Splice, SpaceChem, KAMI, or Perfection., Circuits is polished to perfection, very easy on the eyes, and EXTREMELY easy on the ears. Circuits has one of the best soundtracks of any puzzle game ever, and for good reason: the gameplay revolves around the music. The object of the game is to construct certain songs piece by piece, by listening to the full thing in sequence, and then doing your best to remember what it sounded like. It gets more and more complex as you go, as it has very nice progression. It stays entertaining as it introduces new methods of completing increasingly difficult and complex songs, such as looping certain clips. My only complaint is the difficulty and length: it starts way too easy for the first 10 levels, and then hops up the difficulty quite a bit. But after that it has beautiful progression. It also only took me 85 minutes to complete, but since it's so enjoyable to listen to the music and such a pristine and refreshing experience, the shortness doesn't matter that much; I played through it one and a half more times before I got bored. Also since it only costs $4.99, it's a great deal even for an hour-and-a-half-long game! (especially if you get it on sale) Circuits is a little gem that went unnoticed by most. If you like sleekly designed and simplistic puzzle games and love good, crisp music, then don't hesitate any longer: get Circuits!

I saw this game several times passing by, and told myself that I had to try it... some day. I knew this game was made by Mr. Blow, the creator of Braid. And I have to admit that I was not a big fan of Braid. But I finally bought it and started the game. Just... wow
There is no menu at first start, no help, no explanation. You just arrive in a place you don't know. Quickly, you'll find a simple puzzle, and then another one a bit harder, and so on, to finally arrive in a magnificent place. As you can see in the screenshots the graphics touch is a bit "uniform" (I mean no very detailed textures), but this makes the place wonderful. Very quickly you go out of the place and discover other puzzles, other elements. The goal is always the same. Go from start to end, with respect to the puzzle elements. But you never get bored !
As I said before, no help. But only with careful observation and experimentation, you can understand how the elements work, and how the puzzles need to be solved. This is great ! So great design that you can understand and play the game without a freaking line of text. Also, this helps to the immersion in the game (since you are alone here).
And so on, element by element, puzzle by puzzle, you gonna discover this very environmental-varied island, advance, and perhaps... understand what you're doing here.
This is the first game in history where I shout "THEY DARED!" each time I solve a new puzzle type. They are very well thinked, and the elements are pushed to their maximum. Each time you think that this puzzle was the trickiest, you'll find a trickier one. This is pure genius.
Finally : A-MUST-HAVE. The best puzzle game, and one of the best game I never played in my whole life. Even at it's initial price, it's totally worht it.

First impressions; Steampunk Terraria clone. Sounds lame, but I love steampunk, and terraria was fun. Anyways, It's KINDA like terraria, sort of how an ice-cream sandwich is kind of like a Klondike bar. Its fun, it seems to have a fairly steep learning curve, has there isn't much of a wiki or guide yet (disappointing really, considering the game has been on IOS since 2012, it really should have a better guide) A lot of the ingame stuff is there but not polished (example, Metal pipe description is: Not a lot is known about this item. and that's pretty much what it says for every item in the game.) It IS free to play, and a lot of the stuff you have to pay for can be obtained free ingame through much grinding / farming / hopelessly searching for the one onyx that happened to spawn.
Cons: Although there are LOTS of free worlds to explore and enjoy, They are all explored / looted for the most part. I have not noticed any sort of loot respawning, or item respawning, but then again I havn't been playing that long so perhaps it's there. I payed for a "private world" to explore and build on, and that's probably the easiest cheapest way to get a good feel to the game. Another gripe I have though, is your private world is only one biome. So if you want to get diamonds for example, you need to go to an arctic world, (which is probably depleted of all natural resources) Which leaves you to either trade for it (again, most free worlds are depleted, besides the chests hidden around some of the developed worlds that give every player loot the first time they open it) or to pay for an arctic world (250 crowns is the cheapest, which works out to about 2/3 bucks)
They are working on their business model, trying to move more and more stuff outside the "paywall" which is really pretty non existent as it is, How they have stuff set up at the moment is more suited to a tablet or Ipad then a PC, Hopefully they start trying to bring in some "mixed biome" worlds. Kind of like terraria, but then again, I'm content to play the game as it is. Crafting in the game is fairly well done, besides the aforementioned lack of tool tips on the items, I'd say the crafting is more diverse than terraria, but not as diverse as Minecraft.
Pros: You could easily get 30-40 hours of enjoyment without having to pay a dime. “It’s time to mix drinks and change lives” – Jill.
Edit: I would highly implore you to buy this game on Humble Bundle alongside many other games while it's still available till next week or so. The summary of my thoughts can be seen at the bottom of my "review"
Plot:
Without any spoilers Va-11 hall-a is a “game” that puts you into the perspective of a female protagonist simply named Jill. You’re a bartender in a bar named Va-11 Hall-a in a cyberpunk dystopian world.  Va-11 hall-a is much less of a game as it is an experience and it is primarily a Visual Novel over anything else.
Va-11 Hall-a’s plot takes a much more realistic approach considering their situation. The game’s plot is where the game shines and the more you’re into it, the better. Va-11 Hall-a’s plot is primarily about dealing with life. Not the life of a super hero, a life of a super villain. This is you experiencing an average life considering the world the characters are living in. Which is what I love about this game.
Va-11 Hall-a’s story is one where you meet a variety of different characters who each have their own problems, usually talking them out with you while also having your own set of problems that need to be dealt with, like paying rent or some more serious personal problems.
I think one of Va-11 Hall-a’s greatest strengths is that you can’t twist the grand scheme of things, you can’t stop a bank robbery from happening or a huge turf war from not causing collateral damage. You can’t, you can however, help change the lives of close people that were seriously affected by the events themselves. This game shows you how people from different walks of life deal with grief, stress, pressure and many other things and how although you can’t ultimately make things work how they did before and reverse major events, you can try to help make things work as they are now.
Characters:
All the characters were really interesting and none of them really stood out way more than the others. Sure there are characters that have much less development and much less screen time than the others but the main side characters do shine equally and it was and still really is difficult in finding a true favourite. An extra positive in the game would also be how Jill, our main character isn’t some boring, bland main character that we usually get. She herself has great character development and is relatable enough being the most “normal” out of them although she is a bisexual
The characters also feel real, none of them have any ham fisted plot forced into them, instead, they all feel like characters that are relatable to some extent and varying to person to person and even things like their sexual preferences are given out in a so to speak normal condition.
Now that is to say that the plot of the game isn’t flawless. There are some side mysteries that ultimately never get concluded but they aren’t too huge. They feel like stuff that you want to know but don’t exactly need to know. Hopefully means that the company does want to make a second game for this series.

The game also really only makes you have choices by the drinks you make, you can’t exactly ask them this specific question or that one, your only real choices are what and what not to serve a customer.

Gameplay:
Huge warning to anyone that is expecting any real gameplay that’s truly engaging, fun and interesting you are not going to like this game one bit. This is primarily a visual novel and the less you are interested in story-centric games the faster you will drop this game.
The gameplay is fairly basic but the gameplay also heavily relies on your interest in the story and your memory for some specific occasions. Meaning, the less you are interested in the story, the less likely you will care about this game’s just enough gameplay.
Now in the gameplay department this game obviously lacks, there really isn’t much for you to do asides from clicking left mouse button over and over until the person you’re talking to asks you for a drink.  You can also buy stuff for your apartment which is also a plus. I guess.
Even so, the gameplay, again, heavily relies on your interest in the story. The less and less you’re interested in the story, the faster you will realise the gameplay does get repetitive. Which is really the game’s only flaw, it can feel repetitive as you get further into the game but since I personally was engaged and intrigued by the story I managed to one sit the entire game in one day and never really felt like “omg stop I just need a break”. So if you’re not a person that’s a fan of things like Visual Novels do not, by any means buy this game.
The way I see it, when and if you end up getting interested into the story you don’t just make a drink, you’re making a drink for a friend that you care about which kinda helped me continue on and disregard the game’s repetitiveness.
The game’s world is also built through looking at Jill’s tablet/phone(?) at her apartment, you won’t exactly find out how this or that works or how this entire organisation’s infrastructure works but you get a small gist of everything here and there.
Music:
The music is fairly interesting which features a more techno type soundtrack which ranges from emotional type of music to energetic up beat ones. I however, could not get myself to fall in love with the music at all. I tried to listen to the game’s OST in multiple occasions, sitting down and relaxing, working and heck, I even tried to listen to some of it while typing this review out. I just couldn’t really say I loved it, there are some nice songs but none of them truly felt iconic or really stood out. I feel like this is due to how when you’re playing the game you can select your music so when you’re listening to this girl talking about how she’s completely stressed out about her family you might possibly end up listening to the same song when another girl is fan girling about a singer. Which means that there was no iconic music.
When you’ve played Undertale and you listen to a piece of music from that game after a month or so you will remember where that piece of music is taken from and who you fought. In Va-11 hall-a… I just couldn’t really get myself to fall in love with the music, most of the down beat music has the same vibe and feel to them. No, I’m not saying this song is just an alternate version of that one, I just felt like they were too “samey” in terms of feel.

Now I guess a good comparison would be Doom 2016’s OST. Pretty much the music that plays through the game is just pure rock and heavy metal but each piece truly feels unique from one another. I can’t really say the same about Va-11 Hall-a’s OST.
Summary:
This game is aimed towards more people that just want to chill and read/watch a visual novel more than play a game. You will be severely disappointed if you’re expecting an actual game with fun filled content and not want a story.
If you’re a fan of VNs or just want a different story based game experience than I would highly recommend this game if it goes on sale and as of time of typing this review Va-11 Hall-a is packaged with Humble Bundle right now for 10$ alongside many other great games and I implore you to get the 10$ bundle just for this game. In fact, I bought the bundle primarily just to give the key to one of my friends.
I would highly recommend this game IF you know what type of game you’re getting into and if a VN about being a bartender in a cyberpunk dystopian world interests you. You should get it.

Back in 2014, Sukeban Games managed to pull the wool over my eyes with two words "waifu bartending". At the time, VA-11 Hall-A was a submission to a game jam and was little more than a neat little prototype of what could be. I kept my eye on it because, hey, I like anime girls (shut up) and the bartending mechanic was something different. I didn't figure it would be too deep with a tagline of "waifu bartending".
Fast forward to X-mas 2016, and I finally get around to playing this and discover that this is not the onslaught of fan-service and moe tropes that I figured the original descriptor would dictate. Instead, VA-11 Hall-A present a well fleshed out, engaging story in a compelling and contemporary cyberpunk setting. But the setting is not what is terribly important; rather, it is the characters that inhabit this world that will draw you into Glitch City and the Neon District. The gameplay mechanic of mixing drinks, as well as managing the main character's personal finances, allows for different branches in the story. Putting together a cocktail for your customers is never a chore, and every character has their own backstory and charm.
Visually, the game has a retro, PC-98 look to it. Everything is consistent, though, and it all looks authentic to its inspiration. The soundtrack is ambient, and is worth a listen to on its own. About the only gripe I have with this game is related to an easter-egg that is found (and has an associated achievement) where you play a game-within-a-game.
Anyway, this is highly recommend to visual novel fans looking for something new to sink their teeth into.

Grim Legends: The Forsaken Bride is a hidden object adventure game by Artifex Mundi. Most of the Artifex Mundi games on Steam are hidden object games, and all of the ones I've played have been of very high quality. But when I started playing The Forsaken Bride, I knew it was something special.
First, lets talk about the gameplay. The hidden object scenes and puzzles are basically the same as any other Artifex Mundi game. Items are collected or created through hidden object scenes, and are also collected through exploration of the world. You explore and interact with the world using items you collect, and some of these items are used in various puzzle games. Many puzzle games are similar to those found in other Artifex Mundi games, but I found the ones in The Forsaken Bride to be more refined, varied and challenging.
I've always found the atmosphere and music to be phenomenal when it comes to Artifex Mundi games, and The Forsaken Bride is no exception. In addition, I found the artwork to be hauntingly beautiful.
What stood out to me most was the story. The execution was nearly flawless, and there was a depth and subtle intricacy that I had not found in previous Artifex Mundi games. That's not to say that the stories in other Artifex Mundi games are bad (they're actually quite good), but the story in The Forsaken Bride is truly a step above the rest.
The Forsaken Bride is the best hidden object game I've yet played, and may very well be the best Artifex Mundi game to date.

The free version is pretty seriously trimmed down, and it's disingenuous to try to sell it as something more than a demo -- especially saying "it's the same core multiplayer experience!". You can only use 'quick match' matchmaking, which seems to prefer to throw you into basically-empty servers, and playing games with friends is out of the question, unless you happen to accidentally be thrown into the same quickmatch server. You seem to be restricted to two maps, neither of which have vehicles, although there's some interaction with vehicles in the singleplayer boot camp missions. The game is still fun, but it's definitely not a replacement for the real retail version, as they might lead you to believe.
It's unfortunate that TOXIKK has adopted a full-retail no-microtransaction model... I'd rather play a free arena FPS and pay the occasional $5 for a custom hud/weapon skin/player model, versus dumping $20 into a game I can't even play with friends that run the free edition.
That being said, the game is BEAUTIFUL, and is playable maxed-out on even modest systems (I'm on a xeon w3520, 8gb of ddr3 1066, and a gtx 570). There's a lot of advanced movement mechanics similar to warsow -- lots of wall jumping and sprinting up slopes, air strafing, etc. It seems like it'd be a lot of fun to play at a high level.

I think this is the third review I have ever written, so it must be something big!!! And friends, let me tell you, it sure is.
The Witness is a much needed game. Not only for the intention of making people think again, but also for the way it does so. Many, in fact almost all, new games cater to the young and those with extremely limited attention spans. These games are supposed to be fast-paced and easy to learn and etc.
The Witness, on the other hand, will challenge you. Challenge you completely, and there will not be any sugarcoating. There is no extensive tutorial that will show you how to solve the puzzles. You will have to use sight and sound and brains to figure that out by yourself. It will challenge your preconceived notions of how things work and teach you the concept of "confirmation bias" - which basically is a way of saying that people more often selectively believe in things that fit their pre-existing beliefs, and that people tend to seek out similar information in the future.
If you want to play this game just prepare to get annoyed at your own lack of neuroplasticity. Expect that you will have to rewire your brain to allow it to stop believing that the knowledge you already possess is the one truth and the only truth.
This game can teach you how you should view life in general. It is about perspective. It is about to be able to accept certain truths that at a first glance will seem false, or incorrect.
This game is philosophy!

"Overwhelmingly Positive" for many reasons.
Honestly one of the best games I've ever played. The amount of immersion and learning about the world and the people within it that the game takes you through is truely stunning. I felt like an actual member of the city; a real, living, breathing city. It felt like a real world that I got completely lost in.
How the characters react to you and how you react to them feel like legitimate social interactions. You get opportunities to give people drinks based on what you've learned about them so far, such as what their favorite drink might be or what kind of flavors they prefer. Serving drinks based on how deeply invested you are with a certain character changes the path the game takes, and makes it feel as if you've formed a real bond with that person with how you've gotten to intricately know them.
However, if you're hoping for amazing, involved gameplay, this isn't so much that. You serve drinks to people throughout your shifts and that is what determines certain outcomes, but the time it takes to serve drinks isn't timed and there is no real challenging factor (unless you count memorization of someone's particular drink preferences). This is a visual novel and you should expect to go into it as one. Still, it feels as if the tasks you do perform within the game have real meaning to them. It doesn't feel like you're constantly doing a "minigame" where you serve people whatever they ask for, but rather that you are changing people's lives by what you serve them. Many orders are open-ended and up to you to determine what drink they would like or what would be the best for their current situation. Many orders even let you decide how much alcohol to put in their drink, which can affect some things.
After doing the first main route (which took me about 10 hours), I can honestly say that I was at a complete loss of what to do with my life at that moment.
Highly recommended, if it wasn't obvious enough. I managed to purchase VA-11 Hall-A for $10 from a Humble Bundle. However, I would have gladly paid $30, if not more. You won't regret playing this.

This is a very fun and easy to play game, but is very difficult to win. Previous reviews have explained what this game is about, so I will try to share some things I have found out the hard way. Please note that all my suggestions are for Normal Level.
New Game:
After creating a new game check Army Chief and Police Chief Ambition. If it is too high better start another game and don’t waste your time. Is already hard enough as it is to avoid a revolution from the various parties, the Guerillas or the Prisoners. The most common way to get overthrown and lost this game is if your Police or Army Chief betray you and try to seize the power.
After playing several games I noticed that with an ambition rate below 6 is very rare for a Chief to try to overthrow you.
In the other hand try to have a Police Chief with high Ability. Without his monthly reports you will be blind!
Also an Army Chief with low ability is very difficult to win a war or inflict high damage to the Guerillas.
And here the difficult thing and the hard decision. Is very rare to find a Chief with high Ability and low Ambition.
First Action:
Attack the Guerillas! To keep them week is of paramount importance. Is not only the danger to start a revolution but they can also make other actions like steal banks or burn plantations or industries if they are strong enough.
Taxes:
I like to keep taxes as high as possible just below the point that a party will grow unhappy enough to start a revolution or try an assassination attempt. This gives you more money of course but has a risk. If something goes wrong and any party starts the revolution all unhappy parties will join in. So be really careful there.
Every month:
Spend the 5.000.000$ for the personal campaign. In general you trade some of the 2nd most important resource of the game to lower the opposition against you and buy you some of the 1st most important resource, Time!
Must to do action:
There are too many actions (around 25) to explain here in detail (like the personal campaign above) but the game gives you a detailed report of the effect it will have on the society for each one so are self explainable.
I just want to point out that one of them, to give a general amnesty and release all the prisoners at the beginning of the game is a must. It really lowers the opposition and at the same time cuts a lot the state expenses. After that you must always attack the Guerillas though as most of the released prisoners joins them. The only thing that is better than doing this action is if the people make a request about it and you approve. But you might need to wait many months for this.
The Americans:
I have never seen an Assassination attempt from the Americans to fail in this game, so try not to♥♥♥♥♥♥them off. Maybe you can say no to 1 or 2 of their demands but at the end you must play ball to remain in power.
There is a Kiss Americans’♥♥♥♥♥action. Use it if necessary.
What to do when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan:
1. Increase your personal army (will give you some basic protection against assassinations and will help in a civil war if you select to stay and fight after a revolution starts.
2. Buy an escape helicopter. I tried to escape on foot several times and I ended up dead all of them!
3. Arrest your enemies and even execute them in the prison.
4. Tax the parties that will for sure take part in a revolution against you to decrease their power. Also make any of the actions in the action page that further cut their power. Notice thought that parties that are too weak will try an assassination attempt and not a revolution.
5. Only if you select to flee the country, collect all the money you can. Sell an island, ask Americans for aid etc. Then transfer all money to your Swiss bank account.
Of course I haven’t covered all aspects of the game but I hope I have helped. I will continue to add to this guide as I find new things.
