That was a worthy challenge, for certain. Economic simulations are a nice little niche, a self-sustaining genre if you will, that I really enjoy playing from time to time. Didn’t expect Computer Tycoon to go so further into details, yet it was a pleasant surprise nonetheless. As the Steam debut of a single talented individual called Andris, Computer Tycoon aimed high and didn’t miss its target. Progorion, is the game’s publisher and they already had a presence on the platform, with a casual game/translator between English and Spanish. So educational value seems to be a defining factor for the dev team.
In Computer Tycoon’s current Early Access stage, the Historical Mode is not implemented. Players shall instead learn the ropes through the Random Mode and I mean it, since even the tutorial hasn’t been fleshed out yet. Andris explains that since it’s an ongoing process still requiring constant improvements, a crash course into the game’s mechanics shall suffice for now. You’re encouraged to explore the options for yourself, learn as you play and from those potential failures, you will gain experience and eventually regard obstacles as merely an incentive to better yourself and the fictional IT&C company that you’re leading. As the newly appointed chief executive officer of a company whose name, brand (no logos yet, just colors) and business practices rely entirely on the player’s choice, there’s not much I can write about in terms of a standardized storyline.
Most economic sims follow the open-ended method in conveying their story, no matter how flimsy it may be. Currently, Computer Tycoon is all about that random or sandbox mode in which you are not restrained by anything but your own creativity and business acumen. Savy or ruthless? It’s up to you to keep the company afloat, making a decent profit and changing the world of electronics while you’re at it. That isn’t even an exaggeration since the ultimate invention that you may research and develop in-game is one of my favorite topics: technological singularity. Human consciousness melding with Artificial Intelligence and thus creating a new chapter in world history.  Rather than seeing it in the simplistic perspective of machines surpassing their creators, humans will embrace the change eventually. Rejecting it is not an option.
Transhumanism, the boundries between robotic labour and slavery, the self-aware AI taking over or not, Moore’s Law going sideways. These are either dreams or nightmares about humanity’s future. It just depends on who you ask. Many tech geniuses are present in Computer Tycoon, at least in the form of easily recognizable avatars for your competitors. Household names such as Elon Musk, Steve Jobs, John McAfee, Paul Allen or Steve Wozniak. Only good ol’ Bill Gates is missing from the picture and you’d have a full dream team of industry giants which shaped technology into what it is today. It was only natural for a game focusing just on the computational segment of electronics, to honor the pioneers, the few determined nerds which took seemingly ludicrous ideas and turned them into both financial successes and ubiquitous objects, crucial for humanity’s never-ending progress.
I had my “suspicions” about Computer Tycoon’s graphics engine and I was right. It is indeed a Unity project and Modb confirms it along with the settings menu and the flawless performance on all tested resolutions. Didn’t encounter a frame rate drop or glitch. This isn’t a simulation that’s leaning heavy on the looks department, yet you’ll never see me complaining about staring at pie charts and  especially at maps. Cartography is fun, trust me. You will be given the chance to develop even the HQ and the nearby industrial park linked to it. More like a logical chain, actually. We’re talking of factories, marketing, R&D and last but not least, the leisure buildings ensuring well rested and motivated employees. So there is some 3D acceleration with appropriate assets, not just 2D maps and lots of fictional reports. But you don’t play economic sims for “shiny graphics” and you know it. Gameplay complexity is everything to a genre which takes role playing to a new meaning.
Only a mildly annoying soundtrack is available so far in Computer Tycoon. No voice acting or any sound effects. Yes, it’s an early stage and it can still include more sound assets by the time it shall reach its full release. I don’t think there will be any work for the voice actors though, since the player can’t interact a lot with his AI-operated competition. More on that in the gameplay, just keep in mind that you’re fully excused for muting the sounds and blasting your favorite tunes. That’s what I did. Better than listening to a couple of elevator songs being played on a continuous loop.
What’s an economic simulation without tough competitors to remind you that you’re never good enough for the game? Well it would probably be like capitalism if it relied on the barter system. As basic as it useless. “Survival of the fittest” translates perfectly in the world of business. It may be the brain and not the brawn that wins the fight, but neglecting the body and overworking yourself, is nothing but a quick route to an early grave. That’s what happened to a certain Steve. You know who I’m talking about. The man that changed the way we interact with personal computers, smartphones and a few other devices which had saved his company from bankruptcy more than once. Steve was a smart man when it came to always being a step ahead of his competitors but in the end, he was dumb enough to reject conventional treatment in favor of “alternative medicine”. You can’t beat cancer with a vitamin smoothie. My point is, Computer Tycoon has an entire segment of its gameplay dedicated to the well-being of the company’s CEO, both physically and mentally. “A healthy mind inside a healthy body” as as anonymous phrase would have it.
Stress can kill even the best of us. This is just a facet of financial success. Or failure, since nothing in this title can guarantee that you won’t fail the first few times you start a new game. As long as you learn from those mistakes and never repeat them, Computer Tycoon shall award thinking outside the box. Speaking of boxes, it’s not coincidence that the Historical Mode shall have its start date set to 1974. The golden age of the home computers was on the horizon and crude prototypes were starting to appear, first in boardrooms and then on store shelves, once streamlined enough for the consumer market. That’s were you, the CEO, comes in. Steering where the company’s heading to, is just one step. You will have full control over the technologies being tested, the machines, their components being assembled and the marketing campaigns surrounding those end products. I could go on about it for a few more pages, but I’m certain that you can discover all features once you play the game for yourselves.
Suffice to say, I am impressed by this simulation and I see a lot of potential for it once it leaves Early Access. I do expect some fierce “fighting” with the competitors and an interface overhaul along with comprehensive tutorials that might introduce the genre even to players that still refuse to play it, out of fear for its steep learning curve. All in due time, I’m certain. Congratulations, Andris!

The games intentions are very genuine and respectable, it is the way they are executed and paired which makes the game extremely hard to have fun playing.
The biggest intricacy and downside to the game is that the protagonist uses a wheelchair, and the wheelchair physics are decently real. The tank controls are awkward but more significantly moving around is slow and tedious. Because, the protagonist is in a wheelchair. It cannot be understated how much the lack of mobility hinders the gameplay when it revolves so much around the player moving around. Players must move out of the way from enemies, weave through doorways, go to specific corners of the rooms to pick up items; all while struggling around to turn and move their character. This is the first big mechanical pairing that is unfun, the game involves a lot of moving yet the way players move is hindered.
The other huge problem is the general structure of what the player is supposed to do. Players, while in a wheelchair, must explore a semi-labyrinthine map with randomly generated item and objective placements. To complete the floor players must; find the initial objective trigger somewhere in the map, complete the objective after they are given it which often involves tracking one or more things down elsewhere in the map, returning to the objective trigger, then returning to the elevator. So basically, the entire game is a fetch quest. Which would be fine if moving the protagonist around wasn't so frustrating and slow, or if the lighting was better, or if the objectives weren't often hidden away in little corners where you can miss them, or if there was something more eventful to do with enemies then either instant kill them or flee.
The main enemies in the game damage the player by blowing themselves up. At first it is intimidating, but when players realize they can easily trigger the enemy then wheel away to avoid the explosion then it's completely lost the threat factor. It mostly comes down to getting hit by the explosion if you mess up the awkward controls, if you get caught in a bad spot, highly subjective things. Players can shoot enemies to kill them instantly, but there is an extremely limited supply of ammunition so it is not meant to be a proactive feature. There is also a glitch that can cause enemies to lose the ability to explode so they just stand still and become a permanent damage field in the map, since they don't blow up but the damage hitbox is still there forever.
The existence of a highly mobile floating ball texture which zooms through the map and damages players when they get too close, even though the ball is too fast to dodge half the time, is not only unfair but also a stupid and uncreative hazard.
The game never tells players that most inventory items must be interacted with via double clicking on them. This includes taking items from found containers or using items from the players inventory. You have to figure that out by yourself. Players barely use the cursor in general, so you either have to just have your hand idle on it for up to a minute at the time just so you can double click on found items; or take your hand off it and have to grab it each time you do actually need to click. Players also aren't told anything descriptive about what their objectives even are, the objective is very generalized and thus it is up to players to identify what the objective is actually pertaining to all on their own. Find the sacrifice, well what's the sacrifice; the system brain will guide you to the transmission nodes, what are the transmission nodes and how is the system brain guiding me to them.
The art and the animation of the game however are just fine, the music and story being extremely thematic despite the unusual translation-esque dialogue. Although the arbitrary objectives players must complete to advance make no sense.
There is zero horror however. The game takes place in a slightly macabre setting and has ominous surreal music in the menu and dialogue scenes, but there's nothing scary about any of it.
It's also possible for the protagonist to get literally stuck on objects and surfaces and become immobile or require effort to get them out of it. It's also possible for objectives to be locked behind doors players literally can't open unless you shoot them, which costs ammunition, ram into them, which costs health, or make an enemy blow up adjacent to it; which costs lots of time.
Honestly it's a good try, but the developer just ended up making the wrong decisions about what the gameplay was to be about. The gameplay mechanics do not pair well with eachother at all and it makes the game very abrasive to play.

I'm not amazing at writing reviews, but, this is my favorite visual novel.
I enjoy story-based games, especially ones with other charming features. For VA-11 Hall-A, the magic comes not just in it's story writing, but the effort put into the other aspects of making this VN into a real game.
It's not an easy task, I'm sure - VNs are typically lacking in legitimate gameplay. VA-11 Hall-A's primary game is mixing drinks while talking to your customers. Instead of being tedious filler that derives from the story, it adds to the connection you make with the characters.
You start memorizing what drinks they enjoy, overloading your little drink shaker with Kamotrine (alcohol) and experiencing the stories every unique character presents you with.
Aside from the captivating world the story takes place in, Glitch City, the magnificent soundtrack, art style, and secret gems hidden in this game are enough for me to fully recommend this game to just about anyone.
Thanks for creating this, Sukeban Games. It's been a wild ride, and I can't wait for the next installment, hopefully coming soon. ~Rydia.

Weeeeeeeell.. I haven't finished it yet, and there is no neutral recommendation, so I'll give it a thumbs up for now. Since I feel so on the fence about it, I hope my review will be objective.
Without spoiling any of the story, you're a bartender in a dystopian future society. You serve drinks and listen to people's stories. You can't change the storyline very much, but that's not a problem because the story is ok.
Pros:
-The 8-16bit style art is good for the genre
-The story is well fleshed out with several avenues of exploring it
-The characters are diverse and sufficiently consistently different
-The story is pretty imaginative and interesting
-The gameplay is simple for a graphic novel
Cons:
-The drink making gets old and eventually seems to be a distraction more than something fun to do
-The process of dragging each drink REALLY slows down the story (tip for this below)
-The ticking of each letter of the dialog onto the screen is too loud and too slow. Clicking to skip it will inadvertantly and unavoidably cause you to miss a little dialog here and there
-There is no way to go back to previous dialog in the event that you accidentally miss something
-The story can be a little slow at times
Tips that don't spoil gameplay:
-Find that sweet spot where you can position the mouse on the corner or edge of a drink ingredient and get it to automatically drag itself on the the shaker when you click. It will take a little practice, but it will speed up the drink making by a whole lot. Making drinks becomes less of a hassel.
-Click once to skip the text ticking, but if you click once, read, then double click, you won't have to bother with any of that text ticking at all. If you're not a robot, you will probably screw up a little and miss a line of dialog here and there. Still, this is prefereable to making the game take hours longer to complete for no reason.
Overall:
I like the graphic novel nature of the game, but it isn't really utilized well. There aren't enough settings depicted in the game (as in locations), and the gameplay gets boring after a little while. The story is good enough to keep you coming back, but at the end of the day, I'd prefer an ebook.
Buy it if you're really into this sort of thing, but know that it isn't going to be the best thing ever.

Story: 10/10
Music: 9/10
Art: 7.5/10
Interface: 10/10
Longevity: 7/10
Writing consistently good and plausible dialogue is hard, but Sukeban Games nailed it. This game has some of the most compelling and believable characters in a visual novel in a long time; it's almost guaranteed you'll find someone to root for along the way, and there's plenty of incidental worldbuilding and lore to lose yourself in. It's a cute and often silly game, but it doesn't shy away from serious life issues like loss and not knowing what to do with your life; the protagonist, Jill, is particularly relatable in her mood swings and efforts to simply make it by and figure out what she wants and can reasonably expect from the world around her. She would not be out of place in the 2010s. Above all it's thought-provoking and sweet (without being saccharine or over-the-top), and often very witty.
It's always refreshing to find a good cyberpunk setting where the heroes are not larger-than-life mythical figures setting themselves against dystopian corporate antagonists, but instead relatable individuals dealing with day-to-day problems. If you've ever wondered 'what is it like for ordinary people in a dystopia?', you should play this game. There's also some really good sci-fi in here in here. Topics like AI mortality, tech ethics, and solipsism are dealt with naturally, as everyday concerns.
It's ultimately a pure visual novel, and things like the bartending mechanic are just substitutes for dialogue choices, but it works surprisingly well, particularly with the amount of endings and content unlockable in the game. A lot of it has to be worked quite hard for too, so attentive and caring readers will be rewarded, as in any good VN. Investment in nearly all the characters pays off. And there are quite a few characters, with a lot of variety and all of who have something interesting going on, so you'll never be bored. All characters were designed with thought and care.
In terms of what you'll get for your money, the story can be finished in 5-10 hours, although you might want to go back for endings and side content (it does have a NG+ mode). There's quite a lot of situational and unlockable dialogue; what this game is really remarkable for is how much high-quality content it squeezes in, and I've played it several times because it'd be a shame to miss any. Never does the game feel like it ignored your choices. You'll be sad to see this end, but the game gives you great closure on most character arcs.
The art style is exactly what you see in the promo images. It's charming, but if you're not into pixel art you won't find this game very pretty. I am, personally. I think it suits the game well and the characters easily transcend their two dimensions. I think that they're low-end isn't a bad thing; the game will run on anything, and there's quite a lot expressed through the pixels, which always look nice. A good and consistent art direction can make up for a lot.
The interface is easy to use, never clunky, and features a log of text (really important for a VN). Shout out to all the save slots as well. I encountered no annoying glitches. Most things are self-explanatory, and if not, you're told pretty quickly how to do it.
The soundtrack is incredible, with lots of songs that you can unlock, and a playlist function for your daily work; it's a cyberpunk-themed chiptune glory with lots of love poured into it and songs for every mood. I always felt engrossed by the music.
A really special game that touched me deeply. I'll remember this one always.
Would recommend to pretty much anyone who likes narrative games, cyberpunk/futuristic settings, AI, alcohol, dystopias and post-scarcity worlds, emotional games, and especially to anyone who played Read Only Memories.
It's very relaxing and the characters are compelling. The writing isn't perfect but it is still a very good game.

Furi is an incredibly fun boss rush game, but it's not for everyone. Furi's design heavily revolves around the intensive use of colors, neon lights and overall this kind of 80's retro neon / TRON looks, supported by absolutely fantastic soundtrack matching in theme - gameplay has nothing to do with the music, but the developers create some background system that matches the music's tempo and specific parts to your actions so it's full of those great moments when "our swords clashed and the music exploded, man best feeling ever!"
The gameplay is combining a rather simple combat system - you can shoot, charge up a shot, melee hit, dash, and that's it. However the colors are also used to show you when you are getting healed, when you are charged up to deal 5x more damage with your sword, when the enemy is invulnerable, and so on.
Every bossfight is a puzzle on it's own, much like Dark Souls you have to learn through experience and failure, but here each boss have an average of ~5 different phases with drasticly different tactics required - sometimes speed and precision, sometimes timing and patience is required, but more often a good mix of them all. Each phase you defeat gets your health back up, so we can almost say the bossfights are turn based - you lose, you lose 1 "heart", you win, you get back 1 "heart" and the boss loses 1 "heart" and moves to the next phase with all new moves and tactics.
Furi also has a rather hectic story - it's really a sad story if you piece it together, but it's also presented as a puzzle for you  to learn about the world around you and each boss, who they are or they were, and most importantly - who YOU are. If you are into criptic storytelling and fantastic boss battles, and also happen to like synthwave and the oldschool arcadeish feeling injected into a modern game with highly stylized looks and artistic direction (man those walking parts between bosses are fantastic!), Furi is an absolute must for you to have and an ageless classic to return back to if you are that type of Devil May Cry / MGR: Revengeace / Dark Souls player who wants to go through and through the content again to learn more, perfect your performance more, be better and just enjoy the stunning style of the game - which is again, not for all, but those who sympathize with it, you won't find any better than this. Despite that, I must say 25 euro is a rather expensive price for the game, but anything around 15-18 unquestionably a must have.

LEGO Harry Potter: Years 1 - 4
What can I say about this game that hasn't already been said? It's got that same LEGO charm and goofiness that we've all come to know and love since 2005's LEGO Star Wars: The Video Game. Parodying the first four Harry Potter movies (The Philosopher's Stone, The Chamber of Secrets, The Prisoner of Azkaban, and The Goblet of Fire), this game has the potential to bring new people into the Harry Potter fandom. It inspired me to watch the eight movies, and I must say that they're all wonderful. The puzzles in this game are clever, the satirical humor is an amazing thing to have considering how dark the movies get, and the idea of having the 'Dexter's Diner' and level select rooms as the Diagon Alley and Hogwarts Castle (respectively) overworlds are truly fantastic.
But, I'm afraid I can't give this game a perfect score like I would for other titles in the series. LEGO Harry Potter: Years 1 - 4 falls just short due to one fatal flaw in the game: Game breaking glitches.
In Year 3 Act 6, right near the beginning of the level, there are two switches that you need to hit to melt ice off a door to continue on. Hitting either of these crashes the game. But there is a workaround to it, thankfully. Just go into 2 player mode, place player 1 in a corner far away from a door, have player two hit the right switch, and have them drop out back to player 1. After waiting for a few minutes, do this again, but this time have player 2 take blind shots at the left switch, and then wait after you hit it. I know, it's convoluted and crazy, but it works. In the same level, there's a glass window that you need to break. The first time I tried to break it, the sound played but the entity in the map remained. This is fixed by a simple re-entering of the level, or restarting the game if you want to be sure. Just remember the glitch before that window.
But in Year 4 Act 2....there's a huge problem. The third dragon you take care of, a blue one, is supposed to be raised up on a platform whenever you walk onto a certain spot on the walkway on his cage. Instead of working like he should, he instead falls right through the platform. As this is a glitch in the physics engine for the game, I kept trying again but had the same result. But one time the dragon went through the ceiling of his cage. And another time, he worked. BUT, the fireball that he shoots teleported as soon as it left his mouth, and hit the back left corner of the platform. I had heard that you, again, needed to go into two player mode to get this to work. The first time it almost did, but then he went through the ceiling again. Which is, admittedly, kinda funny. But the other two tries just had the same result as the first time I encountered this glitch. As of yet, I have not found a workaround or fix in the files to remedy this problem.
Overall, I give this game an 8/10, and highly recommend it to any fan of Harry Potter, or the LEGO games in general. But, for the time being, I would also recommend that you get it in physical form just in case the above glitches are Steam exclusive. I will edit my score later on should there ever be a patch released for this game that fixes the above glitches.

They release a new one of these every year and continue buying them, despite the numerous restrictions that come with this game.  Why?  Because for a sub-casual Magic player like me, it's good enough, and $10 is peanuts compared to the cost of playing Magic in a live setting.  I'll get at minimum 10 hours out of this, and probably more due to multiplayer with friends.  If you're new to Magic, this is a nice learning tool, and the limitations inherent in DotP are actually a good thing for a novice player with no deckbuilding experience.  And really, those people are the target audience for this product; If you're a seasoned Magic veteran, you know there are alternatives that give you greater freedom with deckbuilding.
So, with that out of the way, different things about DotP 2014 (as compared to previous DotP titles): there's more lore-related stuff throughout the campaign, though the story may as well be non-existent, which I consider neither a virtue nor a flaw for a title like this.  (You don't play Magic for the story.)  The client seems more stable and less sucky than the one for DotP 2013.  There's no way to skip encounters during the campaign, which is a bit annoying for someone who isn't really interested in "puzzle" games and just wants some vanilla Magic against an AI opponent.
The alternate game mode in DotP (replacing Planechase in DotP 2013 and Archenemy in DotP 2012) is sealed play, where you get access to two random card pools out of the gate--if you want to have additional sealed pools after that, you'll need to buy them for $2 apiece.  Some people loathe this, but as someone who has spent $25 a pop for sealed play in a live setting, I personally don't mind too much, and as extras go, I find it sealed play to be more substantive and enjoyable than Planechase in DotP 2013.  I've paid more than that for new deck DLC in previous versions of DotP which have offered substantially less replayability and enjoyment.
Magic is a good game, and one that you'll probably enjoy if you like turn-based tactics games.  DotP is just one way to experience Magic, and if you've never played Magic, it's probably the best way.

The visual experience of Far Cry 4 was one of splendour, the fictional country of Kyrat being a war torn adaptation of Nepal. There are so many visually superb sections to this game. The stone Buddha in the ice cave on one of the arms dealer missions was amazing to see. The forests and rivers look lush with the graphics settings on Very High with a decent card (e.g. GTX 780+).
The gameplay was a great blend of sneaking, storming, and exploring. Capturing the various fortresses with no alarms and no detection becomes a nerve-wracking puzzle that you can keep replaying. Riding elephants is kinda fun although the novelty wears off quick. The skill tree has some perks that make the game easier to enjoy. There's weapons galore, with more to unlock through special missions and levelling. Eventually you unlock the Driller machine gun and at that point most enemies become easy.
The main story (and some of the DLC) has some colourful characters and cutscenes that add occasional enjoyable breaks to the shooter format. The game also asks you to make some tough choices during the plot where there are no nice options and you have to shaft somebody, which isn't nice but then this is art after all, so it should make you feel something.
If you want DLC, the ones I recommend are "Escape from Durgesh Prison", the extra Hurk missions, and "The Valley of The Yetis".
Multiplayer was also fun, very challenging for the soldier side against the magical Rakjasa, but of course may not have many players online by the time you read this. If you like the FPS genre you'll still be pleased with this game without ever playing the multiplayer, as it is foremostly a single player title.
Above all else I have to recommend this game simply for the Shang-ri La missions, which are essentially a game-within-a-game. This part has the most imaginative gameplay mechanic that I've ever seen in a first person shooter. You basically get your own pet tiger that you can command to attack your enemies for you. I thought I was the dumbest person in the world when I finally solved the puzzle - the solution was so simple, all along! Then, later on, there was another puzzle, the rules of which were different. I solved it immediately and felt like a genius. Combining the rules of those puzzles I constructed a solution to a third puzzle. My doing so opened a locked door. The door led me to an underground cavern lit by torches and full of mysteries waiting to be examined.
It's beautiful. It's complicated. It's difficult, but sometimes - inexplicably - not.
It's The Witness.
Perfect.

You definitely need to approach this game with an open mind. It's essentially puzzles for the sake of puzzles. A bare-bones plot, minimalist art style, and a nearly absent soundtrack make for an unusual video game experience.
It might not sound like it, but I had an amazing time playing The Witness. I had only the most basic idea of what I was buying (I watched someone play through the 'tutorial') and I loved every minute of it. Exploring an (almost) completely open world filled with puzzles that had little direction to them other than what could be inferred was refreshing.
The puzzles themselves are rarely
*. It's more about understanding the theme of each area and how it applies. The reward for completing a puzzle isn't some cosmetic item or plot device, it's more puzzles. To that end, the real pleasure of the game comes from making the aformentioned connections, the "Ah-ha!" moments.
However, it is very likely that this game will test your patience. There is no hint system. If you don't get something, too bad. Mull it over, sketch out a diagram, try a different puzzle, sleep on it, come back to it later - whatever works for you. When it says it respects you as an intelligent player in the description, it's a pledge of faith in your ability. Every unspoken rule is simple, and the clues are there, but it really is up to you to discover it.

Ok, so I've had a bit more time with The Witness now and it is a genuinely enjoyable game with great puzzles, many of which require an extra level of lateral thinking to solve. Original Review:
I have only just started playing The Witness and I'm pretty shocked there are no options to rebind keys. There aren't many buttons required for the game anyway, but the walk speed is PAINFULLY slow and you have to hold down the shift key to run (which takes a moment to get up to speed as well). There is no autorun toggle either.
This game has been out for a while now and there are plenty of discussion threads online requesting this feature but I doubt it will ever be implemented.
I will continue to play and probably enjoy the game for what it is, but it is unacceptable to not include basic control options. Also pretty overpriced for an indie puzzle game.

It is easy to dismiss the game as simply a puzzle game with pretty scentery to move around in, but do not take it so lightly. The use of the enviroment to hide both puzzles and solutions is incredible, and occasionally pretty mind-bending. However, this also hurts the game. The puzzles can become not simply obtuse, but deliberatly frustrating - nausiating color-cycling and obscure audio cues being two particularly troublesome mechanics required.
What makes the game truly remarkable however is the vast amount of material that the game does not require you to find or solve. The 'rewards' are minor: Brief quotations of a dubiously profound nature, and snippets of video of a similar nature. None of this ticks any boxes or unlocks any achievements. It is simply... there. It's a fascinating art project, if nothing else.
And finally, and in all seriousness: Screw 'The Challenge'.
The Witness is a masterpiece. No game has ever lodged itself in the back of my brain as well as The Witness. "The Challenge" was really hard, and really awesome. Buy The Witness.

This game, in my opinion, needs a lot of work to make it interesting, to begin with, and afterwards, to be playable.
The concept of world domination in the business space has been done better already.  This game isn't, at the moment, adding anything to the genre.
Buy access to a country to sell, build a facility and design a product.  Sell your product, make money, buy access to another country.  Dominate.  I tend to like these sort of games, but not this one. Many of these tycoon games have a charm or a sense of humour, or both.  This game is lacking in those regards.
The UI is not well done, at all.  For a game that is essentially static 2D views of data (numbers mostly) the layout and colour schemes are not "pleasing" to me.  I know pleasing is hard to define, but I would like better.  The data itself is both confusing and confused - I cannot "double check" numbers, which always seems like a good thing to be able to do in a management/tycoon game.  There is not enough consitentency between screens when looking for data.  There is no ordering of the data.  Please add order by as a clickable element to the columns of data - order by date, order by price, order by units sold, order by name.  Please no lurid green colour for the annual balance on the light cyan background - it is not easy for the eye - well, not my eye anyway.
Feedback - well, there isn't much of that.  Why did my company dominate?  What are/were the opposition selling?  What does their research consist of?  What are their products composed of?  Why are they selling more than me in a particualr sector?  Well, sure I can see that the country values Ease Of Use over other aspects of the product, but I have no way to know HOW MUCH Ease Of Use a competitors product has and why it is outselling me.  There is not enough feedback about  the impact of your decisions in building a product and the outcome when it meets battle with your competitor's products.
This game, at the moment - and I love Early Access games in principle and sometimes in particular - is not one that I am ever likely to play again sadly.  It needs a re-think in it's presentation, direction and playability.  It is competing in a market of better quality games, in terms of ideas and execution, in this genre and needs to up it's own game considerably or it will become Archived, but unlike the in-game products not 5 years, just 5 hours.
[EDIT - after 0.9.1.28 release]
The developer has made some additions to the game.  Namely a "Crash Course" instead of a tutorial.  A crash course is supposed to be to give enough detail to survive the oncoming crash.  This developer likes words, as can be seen from his lenghty responses to negative reviews and the "Crash Course" - oh and tooltips too, but the dev knows this already.
The facts remains that this is game is not very enjoyable to play.  The challange, for me at least, is trying to peer under the hood to see and understand what is going on inside.  The dev response is "NEVER" will he add competitor information.  I conclude that there is no competitor information to hide or present.
A competitor consists of a coloured part of the map and a slice of a not very useful pie-chart or two.  You "feel" a competitor how exactly?  Nah, I've decided that they don't exist.
This game, by the developers own admission, is easy when you know how.  I agree.  It is easy and without challange.
The developer did me the courtesy of responding at length to my review - something I think is personally valid but professionally counter-productive - you cannot win an argument with a customer as he is ALWAYS right.  The least I could do, as a paying customer, was to see if I could get some value of money in "enjoyment" out of my £10.  I couldn't.
But 4 hours for £10.  That's ok.  It's still cheaper than going to the cinema.  I wish the project well, but I won't be part of it.

Ok, I really like this game. Its really rather addictive. However, there are some things that deffinately need to be improved upon.
So obviously at the moment it is a early access game, need for improvement is to be expected. But I certainly think the developers need to explain some things better.
For instance there is not much information as to what each building on a particular site actually does. Like thje office building. Supposedly it has the effect of making upkeep costs less expensive. I done really see any improvements.
Marketing is confusing and somwhate complicated to do. And it does not seem to work in your favour if you do try and dabble in marketing. Perhaps I just dont know how to effectively use it. So please developers if there is any use for marketing as of now please be more clear as to what marketing does and how best to use it because for me it just seems to cost a lot and I don't see any improvements.
One thing that really bugged me is not being able to meet market demands for a computer in the late game. As far as I know you can only have 7 sites. The only problem is that for each additional site you aquire the next site is much more expensive. Making it almost impossible to get the last sites durin a campaign.
Even if I did manage to get all sites the production points I would be able to get would not be suficient enough for me to be able to supply the demand. This I think needs looking into by the devs.
Finally the npc's seem a little imbalanced. As in they are crazy good at pretty much loking you out of the share markets so you have to ressolve yourself to a little slice of the market and try and just win the game through research.
The fact that you cant see any information on your competitors other than what countries they are currently in and what share they have in the markets you really dont know what your rivals are doing. As in what computers they currently have on the market. What level of tech they are currently at and other such things that would be most useful to know.
Now maybe Im just bad at the game, but given that this game is so very new and is so very good I wont hold anything aganist the devs.
They are charging a most reasonable price for their game and they do seem to be somewhat active in updating the game and in all honesty I think that this game will be one of my favourites as I do love tycoon games like this.
Im sure that in time the game will become better as the developers patch and update the games. In one of my newer worlds for instance the NPC's do infact seem more balanced than they where before. Not just loding into the world and 5 minutes later all the NPC's just snap up every region of the map.
I hope this game turns out as great as I expect it too. I also hope the devs allow mods from the comunity. As green heart studios did with their Game Dev Tycoon.

Finally there is a game which anyone who loves Cricket can play and enjoy which actually represents the game. Brian Lara used to be the benchmark but this redefines it. With codemaster and EA no longer developing Cricket games it's great that Big Ant developed this.
Initially I was suspicious of having to play with a controller, all other cricket games were quite happy to be played with a keyboard. However once I tried it with a controller I could definitely see why it requires one.
With one stick being used for foot placement and the other stick for direction, combining these two inputs with the modifiers (power,defensive,fancy) and the need for having proper timing means the array of shots becomes diverse and unpredictable. Also unlike other cricket versions this does not just descend into a boring slog match with every shot going for a 4 or a six.
I have been able to use this to explain the game of cricket better to my children which means they enjoy cricket even more now and just for that alone I would recommend this to everyone who loves cricket.

- Community generated content
- A great physics engine
Cons

- Superhuman fielders
- The cricket grounds are not particulary diverse

A great game for nostalgia and worth getting if you enjoyed the old dungeon adventure experience.
Castle Torgeath harkens back to the olden days of dungeon rpgs such as Shadow Tower with the attempt to recreate that experience for more recent times, something the game does very well for people who remember or liked those kinds of games. Combat is somewhat slow at first and takes a bit getting used to but then becomes modestly enjoyable for at least a short while after. The story that I uncovered so far was fairly interesting although I wish more than just the npc dialogue was voice-acted, however it doesn’t really affect your ability to get into the game so long as you don’t mind pausing and reading for a bit here and there. The little I’ve seen of the rpg system is somewhat basic and bare-bones but it seems to get the job done if you really stack your points into one particular stat or another.  The game does a good job of keeping you in suspense and forcing you to consider whether it’s wise to engage a group of enemies for xp or not. I had my reservations for the strange monster types that seemed to randomly spawn after killing enemies sometimes, but the system ended up feeling exciting and interesting rather than frustrating so long as you kept your wits about you and roamed carefully most of the time. As it stands the game is fairly decent for what it is and is more than likely to satisfy that dungeon crawler itch if you’re the kind of guy who is into dungeon-themed games. More than anything else it was the low price point of the game that made me feel like it was very good for what it was. So with all that said I can resoundingly say the game definitely gets a positive recommendation from me.
tl;dr: Game is pretty decent for the price especially if you're really into dungeon games.

Furi is an incredibly fun boss rush game, but it's not for everyone. Furi's design heavily revolves around the intensive use of colors, neon lights and overall this kind of 80's retro neon / TRON looks, supported by absolutely fantastic soundtrack matching in theme - gameplay has nothing to do with the music, but the developers create some background system that matches the music's tempo and specific parts to your actions so it's full of those great moments when "our swords clashed and the music exploded, man best feeling ever!"
The gameplay is combining a rather simple combat system - you can shoot, charge up a shot, melee hit, dash, and that's it. However the colors are also used to show you when you are getting healed, when you are charged up to deal 5x more damage with your sword, when the enemy is invulnerable, and so on.
Every bossfight is a puzzle on it's own, much like Dark Souls you have to learn through experience and failure, but here each boss have an average of ~5 different phases with drasticly different tactics required - sometimes speed and precision, sometimes timing and patience is required, but more often a good mix of them all. Each phase you defeat gets your health back up, so we can almost say the bossfights are turn based - you lose, you lose 1 "heart", you win, you get back 1 "heart" and the boss loses 1 "heart" and moves to the next phase with all new moves and tactics.
Furi also has a rather hectic story - it's really a sad story if you piece it together, but it's also presented as a puzzle for you  to learn about the world around you and each boss, who they are or they were, and most importantly - who YOU are. If you are into criptic storytelling and fantastic boss battles, and also happen to like synthwave and the oldschool arcadeish feeling injected into a modern game with highly stylized looks and artistic direction (man those walking parts between bosses are fantastic!), Furi is an absolute must for you to have and an ageless classic to return back to if you are that type of Devil May Cry / MGR: Revengeace / Dark Souls player who wants to go through and through the content again to learn more, perfect your performance more, be better and just enjoy the stunning style of the game - which is again, not for all, but those who sympathize with it, you won't find any better than this. Despite that, I must say 25 euro is a rather expensive price for the game, but anything around 15-18 unquestionably a must have.

The Witness is a beutiful looking game with a unique mechanic that teaches you as you go along, but without using words at all.  It's like a cross between Harpo Marx and a cryptic crossword, but with shapes and colours instead of letters!
It seems, initially, like a small island, but there are many, many more layers than are first apparent.  It's a pretty big game and will take dozens of hours (at least) to get the full experience.
The puzzels have been very cleavery designed and (eventually) seem to keep you right at the limit of your intellect.  Depending on how your brain is wired, you might sail through some things than others find difficult and get stuck for a while on things that other people find easy.  Chances are though that you will, usually, find the last few puzzles of each section a head-scratcher, at least for a while.
Personally, I find the spatial (pattern, colour, position) challenges easy, but the logical (chess-type) ones more difficult.  The unlocks in the Ewok-style section were a particular nightmare for me and I confess I cheated a couple of times by looking up solutions on-line when it all became too much.  For some of the others, I persevered but only got the solution by sheer fluke!  That may sound as though it's a frustrating and unrewarding game, but that's not so.  Sometimes those "WTF, how did that work" solutins are a major revelation and you suddenly see how to move on to a new large section of the game.  When those great "Ah-ha!" moments come though, it's really satisfying and you feel wonderful.
Overall, a firm recommendation from me.  Stick with it, even through the tough times, or just wander away to another part of the island and try something different and new: or you may find that what you just learned will help you unlock another puzzle that seemed impossibe before.
8/10 for me.  Would have been highter, but the game sometimes made me feel so cross and stupid that I switched the PC off!  Get it though, especially if on sale.

Tedious and without reward, The Witness tries desperately to capture the spirit of something much grander than the sum of its parts can deliver, but fails at virtually every conceivable turn. Offering only occasionally interesting puzzle mechanics that long overstay their welcome, pseudo pensive and ultimately pointless commentary in the form of purposefully abstract quotes delivered as if read the night before by failed art students, and agonizingly slow video clips picked straight from the brain of a teenage philosopher, all to pad the corpse of a treatise written by someone that values the appearance of thought more than the content of thought, and culminating in the weakest non-ending ever laid to disc.
If you've ever had anyone attempt to convince you that their well trodden ideas are deceptively deep, you've experienced the bulk of The Witness and the rest isn't worth anyone's time. Armchair philosophy in pixel form.
The visuals are occasionally pretty.

The game is ok. There are some serious balancing issues I feel, but its a good start to the game.
Lets start out by my experience thus far. I won my first game in 3 hours, not making it past 1985 before the competition all went bankrupt and the game "ended" I say ended because it pauses after the message about you having good products and there are no competitors left. You can't do anything... no exit button.. nothing. Just sits there, so that was somewhat unsatisfying. I was also researching techs that probably shouldn't have come out in 1985.. like Blue Ray drives... micro SDs.. SSD drives,  things like that. [Update: There is now an implemented ending screen and a limit on when tech can be researched to 7 years before official release]
The menu system is a little tedius to get some things done. First, buying each country is obnoxious, not the mechanic of buying access into a country but the fact that you have to click on every single one of them on the map, and some of those suckers are really small. It would be nice to get a list view which an option to buy each one... and maybe a few numbers of what that population wants. A data list beats clicking on some random island off the coast of australia.
Another section that gets tedius is updating your headquarters. You quickly outgrow them and I found myself buying up 3 new HQs, then proceeding to upgrading the 5 or 6 tiers one by one (You have to click on each section, hit upgrade, click on next section, hit upgrade). Would be nice to get a "upgrade all" or again another list view that I can just click down a line. Also changing HQs while waiting for past upgrades to happen requires again, 2 clicks into a menu at the bottom of the screen and then click through each category one by one and hitting upgrade. I know this may be picky, but I spent a good 30 minutes of my gameplay just clicking on menu items to upgrade... when good UI could eliminate this for me and get me to planning and playing instead of repetative click tasks.
Upgrading your computer parts is fun, and the game descibes your choices as important and that to make a good product you need to hit a niche and focus on that. I took a look at the global population and it seemed a majority of countries just wanted ease of use. So, I researched those techs... while every other competitor had superior processing, displays, essentially creating hardware that beat mine by 80% I still out sold them pretty much everywhere, taking up 60% market share in the first year. After that I didn't even bother to research anything particular, just added everything to the list. It appeared later on when I made a concious decision to make a cheap computer that was very easy to use... it actually didn't sell... so I made one with everything maxed, a PC that cost about 9k to buy.. and it sold like the dikens... even though 9/10 countries I sold too were poor... that didn't make sense to me at all. So at this point I didn't even make new computers because after a couple years I was at 80% market share.. had almost all the countries purchased and my HQs almost maxed so no one could keep up with my research. There was no strategy to winning.. it was just inevitable.
Manufacturing is maxed at a 5 tier, and even with 8 HQs maxed I could never keep up with demand. This didn't make much sense to me.. I felt like I should be able to create manufacturing centers outside of my HQ to keep up with demand... hey maybe sell leftover production to other companies if I had too much? But.. at 15 trillion per new HQ it ended up being more of a pain to match production.. and I just upped the cost until demand met what I could produce. It would be nice to be able to create production areas outside of the HQ to meet demand if needed. A real company would just hire more manufacturers if the demand was there.
Some other nice features are missing... like, seeing what products your competitors have released and sold to compare to your own... or seeing how much market share they all have (I can see mine, but can't see theirs).. or seeing how much cash they all had on hand (Since we can pretend were are publicly traded and see that type of stuff). At the moment I didn't not see any way to look into anything the competitors were doing other than their market share in a specific country that I clicked on.
All in all, while the game had a lot of things to do and has a lot of potential, it really didn't feel like it had any real depth. I am going to try again on the hardest difficulty to see if strategy comes more into play... but in the end it just felt like very limited strategy was needed to win and it was pretty boring after the second hour of destroying everyone.

I was encouraged by a friend who did not have the game to not purchase the game. His reasonaing was that the game is still in development and an early release and to stay away because most devs do not finish the games. I've had really good luck if you would with early release games. I actually prefer that the developer tell me that it is unfinished and that they are still working on it as opposed to tossing out some garbage and calling it finished. I knew the developer, solo dev mind you, was active based off of others reviews. You are always welcoem to check the update history as well.
As to the game, my opinions were mixed going into it. I read reviews about tons of bugs, so I was immediately on the look out for some. I found none in the 12hrs of play time preceeding this review. I point this out because often times we believe anything might be a bug when we really do not have an understanding of how the game works yet. A few times early on I thought I had, and I was wrong.
My reactions over the 12 hrs went from excitement to confusion, to one of bewilderment. All the while I was having fun.
Now this all means nothing unless you know why I say this.
The game states I need 3GB of available harddrive space. When I started the download steam told me the download was 2.6GB. I thought since when does a Mogul or Tycoon game take 2.6GB. Turns out the download ended up being 380 or so MB. I don't know if this was zipped or what the deal was.
The startup screen has an option to make countries, populations, and economies random, so that everytime you play it is a unique experience. The option as of right now is permanently checked. So when you play this game, the population of New Zealand might be 400 million and Rich, while the US might be 50 million and enpoverished.
Another small quirk of mine is that when you start/restart the game, your name is always cleared. It might be cool if it saved your name or company name from the previous game. Small quirk but doesnt hinder gameplay.
Once the game starts up, in many tycoon games, you have a base factory, in this one you have nothing. You start with 7,500,000 of some mystery currency (another quirk, you cant switch in the options to your desired currency.) You choose a country to Sell in. Once you have chose it, You click on the same nation and pay additionally for a factory or HQ if you will. Upgrade some buildings. This can be really confusing starting out especially if you have the game frozen, because the buildings wont be contructed immediately, but over a period of time.
If you select research you will find the options to be a bit odd, you start with some items already researched. But because of the UI you likely won't realize this. Each item you have available also does not tell you what options you have to research beyond this either. IE the research tree isn't really a tree, but a list. A cool thing though is there are so many things to research even some of the most experience computer guys won't know all the techs you can research unless you are maybe an electrical engineer working in the semi conductor business.
Next step is to build some hardware components and then stash then develope a computer. Another somewhat annoying option is there is no way to remove an option feature that was input into a computer design, only replace it with another one. With the hardware creation process, it is confusing, you can add multiple features, you arent just choosing one or another. Once you figure out how the hardware creation works, it is no longer a problem just confusing at first. Not overly intuitive.
The concept of the game works somewhat like this, open sales region, build factory, build hardware, build computer, research, use a poor concept of marketing, and then open up more sales regions. When demand gets high open another HQ and factories or upgrade teh existing ones. Keep researching and then release another computer as tech increases.
A really good feature of the game is that having a quality product isn't enough to win market share, some people will make decisions based off of price, features, permance, and so forth.
Bottom line the game is good and there are several UI features that suck (like the moving around the 3D screen as you toggle between upgrading certain buildings, and the lack of tooltips) but the game is playable in its current state. I would recommend this game. Hopefully the dev takes some consideration of "Requirements Analysis" a bit more as the game developes, his interface isn't designed for the typical user. Have some patience and you will have some fun.

Really nice software, easy on the computer, no crashes at all so far (and I use it in a VM, which is probably not the best environment).
Now let's be clear, this is NOT a DAW, it's complementary to a DAW.
It's here to help you quickly draft a chord line, a melody, a bass line and some drums, then you export all this to a proper DAW and polish everything.
I strongly disagree with the reviewer who said it doesn't bring anything that a DAW can't do, it's a ridiculous assertion. No DAW, as far as I know, provides you with so many building blocks for creating a quick tune. That's not the role of DAW anyway.
What Odesi gives you really is this, hundreds (thousands?) of MIDI patterns that you can mix, match and edit, while making sure evrything stays coherent and in-scale.
Nos I understand "purists" might dismiss this as "cheating", but this also is kind of ridiculous. What you learn in music school is exactly this: learning lots of scales, patterns, how to make then fit together and sound good. And, yes, also how to break the rules when you have mastered them well enough.
Odesi helps you skip the tedious learning by putting all this at your fingertips. And, yes, it does let you take things in your hands and modify notes yourself to break the rules and add your personality.
Last but not least, the tutorial videos are great, simple, and useful, they make you want to jump in the software and start playing.

OK, I just used this tool successfully, although not in the way one might expect. First off, I find it unpolished UX-wise. It looks nice enough, but the very, very first thing I did when I started a new project was to type a title with a capital R. It doesn't let you type a capital R. It lets you type other capital letters. But not R. The way it turns alt-tabs into "start/stop playback", its inability to fit my laptop screen correctly, the way it makes my trackpad freeze up occasionally(this is a thing I've seen Unity games do too, I have no idea what the common cause is) - all very irritating stuff.
Regardless, after a few minutes of negativity, I did have a chord progression and bassline going, roughly as fast as the claims said. This is where I stopped following standard procedure and moved over to OpenMPT to track in the chords in by hand, and threw a melody on top of them. The melody was great but did not fit the progression I had, so I threw away the chords and plugged in some of my own. My workflow tends to lead with motif and melody and has chords follow, which presents a sort of philosophical problem for tools like these: Did it actually help to employ all this technology? I mean, I did write something that I wouldn't have written otherwise. But I did it in a strange "sidechannel" way where I did not simply sketch the thing in Odesi and then build on that: I more-or-less assumed that I was going to go roll the dice again as soon as I made the jump from MIDI to tracker sequence, and make destructive changes in the process of arriving at a more final arrangement.
This isn't the only tool of this type that I have. I also have Sundog Scale Studio, B-Step, and Rapidcomposer. I like any tool that tries to make building and editing a sequence a more fluid process. But I find that I only take them out rarely, none of them are a silver bullet, and they each do things quite differently despite sharing some concepts. This one is less polished-feeling than Sundog and B-Step, but more so than Rapidcomposer(or least, more than the last time I checked in on that program).

I'm hardpressed to call this an actual game, but alas it's a fantastic experience if you enjoy a more comical spin on cyberpunk. It's more in line with a visual novel with a dialogue system, however the actual dialogue system itself is replaced with the ability to mix drinks. You're given five ingrediants and two modifiers to craft one out of a multitude of drinks, each one unique. Certain characters will like certain drinks for a certain reason, and you're tasked with figuring out which drink each character will like and remembering drinks that are special to them. Simple, but very effective and very innovative when stood next to games in it's genre as it really sells the premise that you're playing a bartender.
It's a system that forms the branching dialogue you expect to see in RPGs, which is great because the writing is fantastic. Characters vary strongly, feel unique and are instantly likeable. The Sukeban's efforts in characterising their cast paid off. You'll have no problem laughing with the character's joy, sympathising with their frustrations and feeling down when they're feeling low. The plot itself doesn't drip with the philisophical substance or conspiracy thrills you expect to find in typical cyberpunk fiction, however the plot gets away with it as a) it was intended to be simplistic and b) nails the dystopian feeling, for the most part. The plot is really just an excuse for solid character interaction, which it does well. Intercharacter chemistry is strong with this game. One small downside of this game could be it's heavy use of internet references. Now, this isn't all bad. They're never really on the nose so even if it goes over your head, you're not left scratching your head thinking "what the ♥♥♥♥ was that". On top of that, they're not quite overused, placed in sparcely enough to never have a negative impact on the story. They feel like occasional nods for the player to think "aah, I get it!" whenever they're in on the reference.
All of this is packaged in fantastic art and presentation. If you're not a fan of sprite art or the art styles popular in many Japanese cartoons/video games, then you're gonna be hardpressed to feel the same as me, but the art in this game is gorgeous. The art does a lot to sell the cyberpunk setting of this game, as it uses a lot of dark and moody colours that convey the dystopian vibe. The sprite art also invokes a retro feeling that puts the game closer to the more 80s flavour of cyberpunk like Bladerunner and less like the more modern era like Deus Ex: Human Revolution. I also the think the anime inspired aesthetic also invoke's Japans take on the genre, such as Ghost in the Shell or Akira, so the setting has this lightweight feeling of a combination of Bladerunner and GitS.
Overall, I think VA-11 Hall-A has beautiful art, great writing, strong bartending gameplay and top waifus, so I highly reccomend the game to anyone who's a fan of visual novel style games and the cyberpunk genre.
Very original experience, great soundtrack, I had a blast. I highly recommend this game.

Let's put this straight. I'm a sucker for cyberpunk stuff. The neon colors, the general aesthetic of a futuristic city is literal scenery porn at its finest.
VA-11 Hall-A is a visual novel that mixes that psychedelic dream world with everyone's favourite waifu trends, mixing drinks, kickass music and what ends up being a much deeper story than what it looks like on the tin. A story about life, taking opportunities at the right time, and everlasting friendships.
The cast is made out at first glance to just be 'waifu filler', but they all manage to stand out and be special characters. The main protagonist, Jill, is a 'snarky ♥♥♥♥♥' type but with a very warm and also lighthearted side, even being as immature sometimes as to always laugh at the name of the drink 'Bad Touch'. The bar also begins with two other workers. Gillian is a fellow bartender with a mysterious past and a very 'loner' aura, but still comes off as a real chill dude. The other is Dana, the boss of the establishment and one of Jill's best friends, if not her absolute best.
Common visitors to the bar are not limited to but include Stella and Sei, a very close and sister-like pair of 'White Knights', authorities that instill order around Glitch City, the game's setting; Dorothy Haze, a 'Lilim' (robotic) sex worker and fetish actress; Virgilio, a pompous buffoon who is constantly cryptic and unclear with his orders, making them into riddles for Jill to work out; Alma, a professional hacker and very close friend of Jill; and Betty and Deal, two best friends who are hardly ever seen apart, with the latter fearing for how the former would cope if he were to leave her to her own devices.
Being a visual novel, VA-11 Hall-A's gameplay is very streamlined and admittedly repetitive most of the time: talk and mix drinks. There are 28 drinks available to make (24 in the recipe book, 3 bottled, and 1 hidden via the first 5 integers in the Fibonacci sequence) and how you respond to your clients' orders affects the paths you take throughout the game, not unlike dialogue options in other visual novels, which VA-11 Hall-A lacks in favour of its bartending mechanic.
Other gameplay shake-ups also include one-on-one conversations with clients, Dana or Gil, often during breaks; a Truth or Dare game that is played on MEGAChristmas Day, the game's interpretation of Christmas Day; and a Model Warrior Julliane bullet hell game that can be played once Jill buys a video game console and cartridges for her apartment.
Similiar to some games, "Papers, Please" first coming to my mind, VA-11 Hall-A also features Jill being paid for her work and having to issue out money to either make purchases to prevent herself from being distracted, or pay bills, online subscriptions and rent. Subscriptions and bills cause distractions if not paid, with rent being the top priority; if Jill fails to pay her rent on December 30, she will be evicted, resulting in the bad ending.
Last but most certainly not least, VA-11 Hall-A has a soundtrack that mixes together funky drum beats, eerie atmospheric synth pads and electronic chiptune to create a great range of music that puts the cherry on the top of this 'kick back, grab some soda and crisps and get ready to mix drinks and change lives' attitude the game proposes.
The game's main portion; serving drinks in the bar; has a jukebox of songs that can be changed at the start of a day and after Jill's mid-shift break. There is many songs to choose from to begin with, with even more being available to unlock, some being received through secret dialogues and many other being purchasable from a shop in New Game Plus for a total of forty-four tracks. The soundtrack is composed by Garoad and can be purchased on Bandcamp for a minimum of $7.
All in all, I definitely recommend VA-11 Hall-A. It's a great visual novel with a story that pulls you in and ends up being way more than you'd expect, alongside music, visuals and overall tone perfectly mixed together to create a relaxing and comfortable attitude.

Extremely fun, charming, and at times very compelling visual novel... but it's probably not for everyone. I'll touch on that a bit later.
First I should probably address the elephant in the room: is this game "worth it for $15 dollars?" In my opinion, after 15 hours of play, between a few lengthy play sessions because I honestly didn't want to stop, absolutely. Given that the entire game portrays a job with a large social element, you may or may not like the people you're dealing with. At first, some clients may come off as abrasive or one-dimensional, but as you talk to these clients, you'll find your reasons to tolerate, like, or straight-up love them as characters. While they're not Vonnegut-tier levels of writing quality, they have enough depth and good quips that I grew to really enjoy all of the cast.
While the core of the game is a visual novel, there is of course the element of mixing drinks and tending to your clients. Most of your time will be spent conversing with the myriad of characters and making drinks for them. The drink making is relatively simple and comes down to simple memorization and consulting your bartending UI, which contains a handful of mixed drinks that clients have preferences for. At critical points in the story, there are some other activities that present themselves, and there is a 'fail state' per se, depending on how good you are at tending to your clients and managing your money. At the end of the day, it's a virtual novel with a very unique way of presenting plot forks/dialogue choices, and one that is extremely charming, at least to me.
VA-11 Hall-A describes itself as a 'comfy' game, one that's best enjoyed in a comfy chair in front of your PC with a drink of your own in hand. The distinctive classic PC game style is one that I'm an absolute sucker for, but some could probably find a bit kitschy or lame. Some of the UI and interstitial between-scenes action is greatly reminiscent of Snatcher and Metal Gear Solid codec scenes, as well, if it does anything for you. (Because it certainly does for me.)
I mentioned in the opening line of this review that VA-11 Hall-A may not be for everyone, and I'd like to touch on that.
VA-11 Hall-A was described as a "Waifu Bartending Simulator," and that wrapper might scare some people off. The writing has plenty of pokes and prods that all not-so-subtly say "hey, you;ve probably been around on the block when it comes to the internet." At the same time, it contains a lot of nods to various anime/manga, western pop culture, and even professional wrestling, (one of which is probably my favorite exchanges in the game,) and I can see it being grating to some.
As always, make your own decisions when purchasing games; go out and find some gameplay, use your better judgment and always make that decision yourself. But if you're looking for a recommendation, here you are: In the end, VA-11 Hall-A is probably one of the many satisfying experiences I had with video games in 2016, (and the first few days of 2017,) solely because I was able to just sit in my room with my space heater at my feet and enjoy a story I just didn't want to stray away from for a few hours.

I remember seeing the E3 trailer, with the gameplay of the Burst, and I thought it looked kinda cool. The music was what caught me off guard. So I did some pre-launch research and found the trailer music (and the music for that boss) was done by Carpenter Brut.
So I got hyped.
My hype paid off though. My initial interest was the music, and I expected an alright game, but I got a very fun and exciting action game to go along with it. The game is minimalistic to the right degree, as you only have 5 real abilities: Shoot, slash, charge, dodge, parry. No intricate combos, no juggling, and no damage sponge bosses. The pacing on every stage of a boss feels just right. In addition, to quote a favorite long time reviewer of mine Acornflims, "a testament to a good game is that it makes you get better." And Furi does exactly that. It teaches you the basic controls, keeps them basic, then expects you to learn how to utilize them. But it's also very fair in its difficulty. There is only one boss who can one-shot you, and the move is very well telegraphed and delayed. Also, bosses never chainstun, so one mistake will very rarely ever cascade into your defeat. You can always recover.
All in all, Furi turned out to be my GOTY 2016, pretty easily. I highly recommend it, as it lived up to my hype. Even despite the claims that it's short (which it is, to be perfectly fair), it keeps you coming back. Try your best to go in blind, as difficult as that may be so long after launch.

Pros:
- Awesome graphic
- Flashy battles
- High skill cap
- Intense Action
- Interesting mechanics
Cons:
- Weak tutorial
- No storyline
- Confusing interface
- Medium learning curve
This game is amazing shoot-em-up game. The control is complex yet intuitive once you can remember all the functionality. I definitely love the concept of having the ability to pilot spaceship that can switch into mobile assault units. This game is really fun and the controls reminds me of Freelancer (Another great space action game).  The detailed environment and flashy weapon animation is really great.  They are so good that I am willing to overlook the fact that there is no storyline. The graphic itself really let you experience what you would expect piloting a cool hybrid spaceship feels like. I highly recommend this game if you are looking for a fast-pace shooting game that have a high learning curve.  The better you are at making complex manuever of your ship, the more enjoyable this game will be.
Unfortunately, the tutorial fell short. For those that are new to flying action games, you will be left with a lot of things to figure out. On top of the fact that you will spend a large amount of time to learn basic flying mechanic, you will have to deal with very fast pace action and lots of small details on the battlefield like: incoming missles, incoming mines, shield level, lock-on timer, EMP timer, dodging, aiming with different guns that have different fire-rate, etc. All the details can be overwhelming for those new to the genre.
The interface tries to be straight forward so you can enter the action quickly. But. This means that you can easily be confused of what the interface try to convey. They gave a list of ships you will encounter each level. Okay? Can I get the stats of each ship to plan out what I want to do? They gave you ship upgrade screen. Yet they did not mention that you don't interact with the upgrades on the screen, the only time you get upgrades is when you kill certain optional ships in the actual level.  The screen is there to review the upgrades you own.  They gave you a fleet information screen so you can get allies and upgrade your fleet. Yet they do not give enough information for the upgrades and ships so you can make good decision. I still don't know the damage, durability, and abilities the different ships have. and I definitely do not know the detail of what upgrading ship crew will do to my fleet.
I suggest this game to those who are used to the genre or those who are willing to explore the game until they master the basics. The game really get interesting once you get the details out of the way.

The witness is a open world game set in an absolutely gorgeous world with striking colours and beautiful environments. It is quite ironic that the actual game element is solving mazes within the environment which are very few and the majority of times you will be solving 2d mazes based on various rules. there are about 10 or so different rules used and you learn the mechanics of each rule in different places which encourages exploration as you will find puzzles which combine rules which you have not yet seen. The exploration is absolutely thrilling to do as the environments are gorgeous and breathtaking. there is no story I could gather in my incomplete playthrough though you see some audio files which ramble about philosophy or something which I completely ignored
Now coming to the gameplay you will be solving 2d mazes based on the environment or based on rules you learned before incorporating various symbols,colours and shapes. the mazes may sometimes be in the environment which is optional to solve. On solving the mazes various doors open and various mechanisms work through. There are a set of lasers in the 15 or so areas which when completed will open the last area I figured that out seeing a vieo walkthrough. I will come to that in a bit as to why i did not complete the game. You are given tutorial puzzles to solve so that you can understand the mechanic and solve a set of increasingly complex puzzles which might require you to combine 3-4 rules.
Now coming to my biggest gripe as to why I played 24 or so hours and left the game incomplete. It depended on this 2 basic questions for me
Am I enjoying the game?
Could I bear solving any more mazes?
Is the game fun at all?
the answers to all three were no. the game IMHO just did not give me that AHA moment on solving the puzzle. When I got to figure out a rule solving 50 or so puzzles adhering to the same rule just seemed a chore and the puzzles just seemed like math homework where the rules constantly change and you are given a set of problems to try and figure what the solutions are and match up the solutions so you reach something consistent. The rules are incredibly conssten but using the rules in increasingly complex puzzles was not fun for me at all. At the 200th puzzle I simply was not enjoying the game. The mazes themselves disgusted me and I had no inclination to solve them.
I would recommend this game only to people who like figuring things out based on no prior inputs. There is absolutely no hand holding here and no text to guide you. The rule you figured out might not even be the correct one. So it requires patience to find out what exactly is the fail case for the tutorial puzzles which is not as easy as it seems.
This game feels like Sudoku where the rules keep changing and you have to figure them out and then get hammered with tons of puzzles on that rule and the rule again changes. Rinse and repeat and in between they will combne 2 rules. If you like this type of gameplay then this a perfect game for you. It just not fo me.This game would be really appreciated by a very selected audience and I get that. It just not is not a game for everybody and it might take you sometime to actually figure that out. I figured that out once I was constantly irritated and frustrated seeing the puzzles and was more inclined to see a walkthrough and get things done. Thats the time I questioned why am I even continuing playing this in that way when I am no longer enjoying it.
The reviews and video walkthroughs do not give you a feel of the game, I recommend to atleast try out this game. If it is your cup of tea you will adore and admire the game. If not you will help Jonathan Blow with his maybe future projects which might be to your liking. I absolutely loved Braid and would love to see what he brings in after this game. This is an absolute masterpiece of a game only with the big caveat being whether you will like it or not. I will say take the plunge and go ahead, Buy the game experience it at least once. If you do not like it thats fine accept that it is not your type of game but you would really contribute to this masterful game designer. I have absolutely no doubt that Jonathan Blow is a masterful game designer and like Braid was mainstream this game has its niche audience. I hope the next game is more mainstream with the unique game design of the previous game.
