It's a decent enough game. I have 2.4 hours in-game currently and basically use it as a time waster when I don't have anything else to do. I appreciate the amount of levels in the game, but judging by some videos I've seen of the final levels, I realize that I will never be that good at the game. At some points Dungeon Escape tends to be rage-inducing because of tight jumps and trap spikes. I also have spent a decent amount of time attempting to beat levels while friends were at my house. Overall, it's a decent game, but at some points I feel that it's copying Super Meat Boy.
(P.S.: I got the game for 50 cents and probably wouldn't reccomend at a price higher than 1-2 dollars)

- Controls are too stiff - There is no option to fine tune your jump, you always jump the same height; predefined movement range when you touch the keys, makes finetunning your position impossible
- Jump is registered after movement, so if you want to move->jump (close to the edge or spikes) you have to jump first and then move while in the air; apparently its registered after everything else in the game, play level 49 to see for yourself
- Terrible hitboxes - spikes and saws kill you before you touch them because they can predict the future and know that you are gonna land on them; monsters kill you if u hit them on the edge; cannot double jump when standing on the edge of a block
- Too much focus on timed jumps - for a game with such simple jump mechanic, it focuses WAAAY too much on timed jumps, which together with bad hitboxes, makes for lot of frustration
- Achievements are stupid - you basically get achievement every stage + when you get score >5000
- Coins are useless - just a distraction, you gonna die a lot until you figure out they have no purpose but give you mere 10 points (you can get easy 5k just by killing mobs and completing levels)
- Music - interesting and diverse at first, but gets annoying as time goes by; obnoxious after a few hours
- Graphics - very simplistic, maybe too simplistic
- Tries be like Super Meat Boy as seen in some of the levels, but what worked in SMB doesn't work here - lack of certain mechanics present in SMB (run, wall jump and slide, controlled jump height) makes it so that levels don't work as developer intended to, they are just outright frustrating
+ 50 levels, each progressively harder along with achievements for hunters
+ Enough challenge for masochists that want to finish the game
+ Simple to learn - hard to master
+ Runs well on most of the systems (I didn't know what else to put...)

no ads no nothing, just updates ALL your drivers without any fuzz.

Game Mechanics are good, fun stealth elements, far too much chaos going on in the world around you.  The animals are hyper aggressive and more dangerous than the vast majority of the human enemies. Pagan Min is by far my favorite villian for sometime (think Handsome Jack meets Saddam Hussein) rooting for him all the way, I hope he wins :D
BIggest Drawback-
Story sucks a big one so far.  Allow me to explain
The only way the story even works is if you are willing to believe that a soft skinned spineless kid from America is the ONLY hope the downtrodden people of Kyrat have for being free.
Ajay, Stand up for yourself in the face of undue criticism from the so called leaders of the Golden Path? NO THANKS!  Ajay, do all the work and liberate Kyrat without any one of the incompetent Golden Path lifting a finger to help?  YES PLEASE!
Everything one would expect from a modern day hero-
natural born weapons expert, marksman and stealth prodigy with zero training? CHECK
Utterly incapable of forming a cogent sentence or using his brain? DOUBLE CHECK
Pagan Min is the only character worth paying attention to in this whole game so far.  We'll see what the rest of the game has in store but I get the feeling it's going to be cringe worth character "development" and a lot of flimsy pretexts for story advancement. Thank God the main character is a maleable lump of goo....

Now that I've played it enough, I feel I can give a decent review comparing to Far Cry 3 (since so many seem to hate this one over 3 and wouldn't suggest buying this one). I'll edit if the ending is absolutely terrible but for now I can't see that happening...
Overal gameplay is much better, the first-person effects for all that added realism and immersion really makes playing it fun and engaging, while all the added weapons and a few new vehicles and a lot of new types of missions all make it all the better. Most of the side missions don't feel like too much of a chore, and some of the main missions require you to make (usually) difficult decisions while choosing sides. I'm 23 hours in and I still am probably barely half-way through with the story...Far Cry 3 took me 36 hours to beat without doing nearly everything. Overall seems about the same if not better, all except possibly the story which I can't say for certain now...although I felt like your overall goal in 3 is much more reasonable and larger than the reason you end up where you are in 4.
Probably my biggest thing against it is the lack of skill trees and how quickly it seems you can unlock most of the useful skills, like all the takedowns. You still have most of the skills you would from far cry 3, some being combined a bit I believe and new ones being added, but it seems like less overall. In fact, a lot of them in the survival/defense side seem to be mostly unlocking syringes I never use and health stuff. But it's alright for the most part.
I've been having a little more fun on 4 than 3, even though I liked the jungle a bit more and the lore of the WWII Japanese on the islands. But 4's gameplay is really good and I've NEVER had issues with uplay ever or with it crashing with my 2 GTX860m's on SLI. I don't know why everyone seems to have problems on uplay but there's even an option to play singleplayer online without needing a stable connection, so I imagine it wouldn't matter as far as possible 'bad servers' and stuff goes.

So, I bought this game expecting it to be kindof underwhelming, even as someone who likes management games. Unfortunately, it didn't even match my lowered expectations.
Initially, I thought I could have input into the skyscraper's design; fiddle with floorplans and construction methods and so forth. What I got was 3 arbitrary choices for sky scraper design and 4 slider bars to tweak quality/quantity/type of rooms in the building, and the number of floors. That's it.
At this point I thought 'oh well, maybe they make up for this with complex and engaging mechanics in management of the actual construction. I could dig that.' What I expected now was a game with plenty of 'make sure this resource is managed well' and 'hire/fire staff as needed', but also a game with slightly complex decisions like choosing companies to contract with, or buying resource sources. Also random events, and a solid progression as described of 'start with multistory houses, and work up to mega skyscrapers'. What I got was a game of 'hire/fire people as needed. that's it.'
By the time I finished the tutorial/learning process (completed one skyscraper), I decided I'd build another. I maxed the speed the whole time, and found myself entirely and utterly bored. This isn't really a game so much as an add-on for some other, non-existant game with the other 90% of the process. I am generally not critical of games, but this game is only worth a dollar or two as it stands. These simulator games seem to be turning out to be a money grab, rather than a genuine simulator. Much less a fun game.

It's pretty. It's like Myst. If you liked Myst, you will probably like this. Some of the puzzles are fun, but what were the devs thinking, making you go back and re-solve puzzles you've already solved? I cannot fathom what was going through their heads.
So, for example you have to solve a maze, draw a path through this grid so it covers all of these dots and none of those dots. Okay, good, you do that, find the solution, and then you move on to the next one, which is the same idea but harder this time. The problem is, if you fail the hard one, you then have to GO BACK to the one you just solved, erase your solution, and enter the exact same solution again. Every time. Every single time you need to retry the hard puzzle, you have to go back and erase and re-solve the one you already finished.
What in the world could have possessed them to put such a tedious and boring mechanic in a puzzle game? It's like being forced to erase all your answers from a crossword puzzle and then write them in again, exactly the same. Over and over. Who would want to do that!?
Meh. The puzzles are fine, although some of them seem to be a bit less "solve this logic problem" and more "guess what I'm thinking of", since I'm faily sure I found working solutions to a few puzzles only to have the game reject them because a different solution was expected. So then you get to go back and try to find another solution, even though you already found a perfectly good one. Maybe there was some reason why the solution that eventually worked was better than the one I initially came up with, but if so I can't work it out.
Anyway. The world looks good. It would be great if it supported VR--which it doesn't. Having to go back and fill out puzzles you've already completed is a boring waste of time. If that sounds like something you're okay with, play it. But wait for it to go on sale.
I don't regret buying it. But I don't recommend it.

The Witness is a difficult game to review.
This game seems to generate some very polarizing opinions and a common theme I see from people who dislike the game is that it seems they didn't really know what they were getting into.  Some expected a more narrative experience.  Some expected a more explicit instructions.  Some expected a more directed experience.  These are all fair points, but I think it's exceptionally important to define what kind of game The Witness is:
The Witness is a Puzzle Game.  You solve puzzles.  If solving puzzles is not your jam, or if you need a overarching narrative to keep you interested, then this is not your the game for you.  If the idea of solving clever and complicated puzzles that tend to ask a lot out of the player makes you excited, then this is a game you will probably enjoy!
I enjoyed The Witness immensely, but I knew what I was getting into:  A game about solving puzzles.

I had seen this game recommended to me by way of various Youtube videos, and upon just looking at the game, I immediately purchased it and started playing.
This game is legendary. The gameplay involves only boss battles (and the various build-up walking sections) and thus is very centered on the gameplay element. Your character has moves such as dashing and parrying, hacking and slashing, shooting and strafing, and an extra surprise should the player find the secret at the very end. These gameplay mechanics make the bosses fast, intense, and suspenseful; I can guarantee that one will end up holding their breath throughout most of the boss fights (especially mid-late ones). Each boss fight is memorable, presenting unique fighting styles that force the player to adapt to more techniques than simply hacking away with their katana-esque weapon.
The art style is gorgous; designed by the artist behind Afro Samurai, the character art doesn't dissapoint, each one having an individual look, paralleling their fighting style. The environmental art is astounding as well, with its vivid colors and cool imagery. Added on top of all this, the music, composed by a small group of famous musicians, perfectly blends with the game's visual flair and charisma, and makes the fighting feel almost nostalgic, in a way, as if one was playing an old arcade game.
While the storytelling is subtle and meticulously told, it indeed holds a candle to the other aspects of the game, providing each character with a background that not only connects them to one another, but also to the player character himself. The story becomes especially climactic in the ending of the game (which I will not spoil, as it is quite the ending).
The only problems that I had with the game were some input lag (which is always a thing in games anyways), and a few moments where I found the game mechanics to be working against me, but not in a way that made the game unbeatable.
Long and short of it is this; if you are prone to rage quitting or getting mad at games, this is not the game for you (although there are difficulty modes, if that suits your fancy). Otherwise, if you are the kind of person that loves a challenge, than this game is the one.

I bought this game because it was extremely cheap. I still regret it.
Pros:
- The price
- Controls aren't awful
"Meh"s:
- The graphics
- The music is okay at first, but gets a bit headache inducing and repetitive after a while
- The difficulty is fine, though it does feel cheap at times
Cons:
- Bad hitboxes (not being able to double jump off of a corner of a block, not killing enemies if stomped at the edge, randomly being able to stand on the side of a wall)
- No tutorial whatsoever, and while the controls and the concept of keys and doors are rather intuitive, it took me a long while to understand that you can stomp on enemies to kill them (in a lot of similar games, like Super Meat Boy, hitting any part of the enemies' hitboxes instantly kills you)
- No story to speak of
- No cutscenes
- Can't navigate the main menu with the keyboard, despite the whole game being keyboard-only otherwise
- Score doesn't appear to do anything, which makes collecting coins pointless
- There don't appear to be any secrets or easter eggs
- No unlockable abilities or characters (or at least not ones that I've been able to get to before quitting the game in frustration [not due to difficulty, which is fine, but due to the sheer amount of problems this game has])
- No bosses or bonus stages (again, that I've been able to get to)
- Bland enemies (the 2 I've seen so far, one blue and one red, are both effectively just moving square hitboxes with no abilities)
- Bad level design (saws and enemies that can't possibly hit you, odd platform placement, coins that require no extra skill but extra time wasted)
- Your character's falling speed is absolutely ridiculous, giving you no time to react whatsoever if the fall is just a few blocks down
- Very basic move set (no running, no wall jumps, no dashing, etc.)
- Awful achievements (Complete level 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7... are all separate achievements, and it doesn't feel rewarding, it just feels like the devs are trying to bribe you with free achievements)
Overall, I don't think this game is worth your time even if it's free.

Plain in simple in it's delivery, but engaging while playing. T.E.C is a 3D linear running game.
This game feels like it was greatly paid attention to, from the gameplay to the visual details and music. There are three basic modes to T.E.C. The first requires you to run in a straight line and commit to certain dodge techniques. The second sort of works like a grid system, where acceleration and top speed rise sharply and quick manouevers are needed. The third mode consists of free running, where the player is in full control of every tilt their player makes. This last game mode is what makes this game unique. There are levels where I've felt I've barely made the turn but still managed to make it to the end. The free running is extremely fun as you'll quickly be jumping platform to platform (which go in all directions).
One thing I've noticed in free running is some courses require the player to make 360 degree turns running up a platform. As the joystick is held in one direction, the player finally starts leaning inwards making a sharper turn, while the camera begins to rotate over the shoulder. This is a cool concept, and makes for a great visual, but can make it hard to control the runner accurately. I also have no idea how to reset the camera back to normal when that happens. On top of creative level design and good control schemes, the game offers local co-op on top of multiplayer. Third and first person views are also a feature in the game.
The visuals are appealing, and game (and menu) colors change with each color-icon you hit. Graphics are sharp but there seems to be more room for improvement here. The backgrounds are quite plain. Level designs are immaculate as there is no one way to go about your business, which makes it welcoming to local co-op. Sounds are few but on point. I like when the runner jumps from a height and that smashing metal sound plays. Music seems to be original and some tracks are quite catchy.
For future T.E.C games, perhaps make a "fight" mode for local co-op where players can run into one another, or perhaps strike each other as a distraction. Also, maybe having an options to designate sensitivity of the joystick would be appreciated, unless the dev's wanted this certain feel.

This game is incredibly fun and addictive if you like the sense of speed. Be warned though, it's not a relaxing casual game. Most levels are very hard and require you to learn to manoeuvre your robot very precisely. And even then, a lot will often depend on sheer luck, and you will die dozens of times before you succeed.
There is a large variety of stages, from high speed ones, to the more aerial ones where you perform numerous jumps between platforms, and so on. Some take a form of drag race, where you must time your boosts accurately, others are more open and have multitudes of paths to take through a level.
The main 'campaign' has 41 levels. There are a lot of tough, frustrating moments, but strangely enough you will keep coming back to the game repeatedly to try and beat the level you're stuck on. Once you complete the campaign, you unlock several bonus levels, which, from what I played so far, seem even harder than the original campaign ones. You also have an endless run level, where you keep running and dodging obstacles for as long as you can.
The game has a very nice visual style and cool electronic music. All this helps to enhance the virtual reality atmosphere the game is going for. If high speed challenging games are your thing, then give this game a try.

It's pretty. It's like Myst. If you liked Myst, you will probably like this. Some of the puzzles are fun, but what were the devs thinking, making you go back and re-solve puzzles you've already solved? I cannot fathom what was going through their heads.
So, for example you have to solve a maze, draw a path through this grid so it covers all of these dots and none of those dots. Okay, good, you do that, find the solution, and then you move on to the next one, which is the same idea but harder this time. The problem is, if you fail the hard one, you then have to GO BACK to the one you just solved, erase your solution, and enter the exact same solution again. Every time. Every single time you need to retry the hard puzzle, you have to go back and erase and re-solve the one you already finished.
What in the world could have possessed them to put such a tedious and boring mechanic in a puzzle game? It's like being forced to erase all your answers from a crossword puzzle and then write them in again, exactly the same. Over and over. Who would want to do that!?
Meh. The puzzles are fine, although some of them seem to be a bit less "solve this logic problem" and more "guess what I'm thinking of", since I'm faily sure I found working solutions to a few puzzles only to have the game reject them because a different solution was expected. So then you get to go back and try to find another solution, even though you already found a perfectly good one. Maybe there was some reason why the solution that eventually worked was better than the one I initially came up with, but if so I can't work it out.
Anyway. The world looks good. It would be great if it supported VR--which it doesn't. Having to go back and fill out puzzles you've already completed is a boring waste of time. If that sounds like something you're okay with, play it. But wait for it to go on sale.

The Witness is a difficult game to review.
This game seems to generate some very polarizing opinions and a common theme I see from people who dislike the game is that it seems they didn't really know what they were getting into.  Some expected a more narrative experience.  Some expected a more explicit instructions.  Some expected a more directed experience.  These are all fair points, but I think it's exceptionally important to define what kind of game The Witness is:
The Witness is a Puzzle Game.  You solve puzzles.  If solving puzzles is not your jam, or if you need a overarching narrative to keep you interested, then this is not your the game for you.  If the idea of solving clever and complicated puzzles that tend to ask a lot out of the player makes you excited, then this is a game you will probably enjoy!
I enjoyed The Witness immensely, but I knew what I was getting into:  A game about solving puzzles.

Spoilers: I have 100% completed this game.  Then I went to bed.  When I woke up I found myself asking a few questions about it.
First, did I enjoy the experience while playing it?  Yes.  I enjoy a good puzzle and this game offered plenty of them.  They varied in difficulty and strategy and combined in interesting and creative ways.  I relished the "Ah-Ha" moments of finally solving a puzzle that had been stumping you for 10 minutes.  It was a well realized and truly enjoyable experience.
Second, would I play this game again?  No.  The primary issue of this game is that once it is learned then no challenge remains.  This is hardly a unique criticism of a puzzle game as the same can be said of Myst and it is still held up as a classic, but it does degrade the overall joy the game can bring me.  I have found that the best games are ones that can be played over and over for years bringing something new each time.  Unfortunately this game can not offer that.
Third, what did it all mean?  On this I am unsure.  If we are to take it at face value as a puzzle game then it holds up well for the reasons given above.  This does however raise an issue.  If the game is really about just solving puzzles then the only plot and story we are given is philosophical readings then why bother to include it those readings at all?  The Witness quickly teaches you that nothing is arbitrary.  If something is shaped in a strange or odd way, then it is a puzzle.  The game, from the onset, demonstrates that it is not haphazardly constructed and that all of the minute things that are included are deeply necessary for some reason that may not yet be clear.  It shows you that if you just dig deeper you can find the answer; you can solve the puzzle.  From this core concept of the game we must conclude that the philosophical readings have a function, a purpose, in the larger game.  Unfortunately, that is the flaw in this experience.  No plot resolution is given.  (Yes even with both endings.)  Saying "It was all a dream, or a simulation" doesn't inform the philosophy discussed.  It doesn't illuminate the goals or purpose of the people whose voices we have heard.  Who are they?  What are they doing?  Why should we care?  The game spends its entire span showing you that answers will come to those persistent and clever enough to find them.  Then it changes the rules with 10 seconds left on the clock and unfortunately declares: None of that Matters.  It wasn't real.  This is a critical mishandling of an otherwise perfect setup.  I can and have thought of literally 10 better endings since I started writing this.  Sadly this game falls woefully short in that respect.
With that said, perhaps overly harshly, I still did truly enjoy the game as I played it and I will recommend it to friends.  Unfortunately, I will be recommending it as a puzzle solving game.  Just a puzzle solving game.  This had the potential to be so much more.  There is perhaps nothing so tragic as a wasted opportunity.

Suguri is a very challenging bullet hell style shooter with a few major differences to the normal style.
If you don't like games where you have to try levels over and over again to get through you will NOT like Suguri. If you do, then read on.
Suguri's plotline follows a girl named Suguri who has been given powers by her father after she encounters hostile enemies in the sky. She meets several members of a race of humanoids along this journey who wish to inhabit her planet... forcefully, by killing everyone else.
You go through 7 levels usually with the stage-miniboss-stage-boss layout however some stages divert from this norm.
The main thing that sets Suguri apart is the 'dash' feature. This makes it so she can just pass through most energy based attacks whilst taking no damage. However this raises her heat gauge, and the higher her heat gauge is, the more damage she takes. Another thing is her 'hyper'. This varies based on which weapon she has equipped but will unleash a large attack whilst protecting you from damage for a few seconds.
A thing I find in a lot of bullet helly games is that they just feel cheap. You could be going through after making a lot of progress then something OHKOs you or there is an attack that you can't dodge. I never felt this in Suguri. This is because they have warning text when something big is going to happen so you can prepare and if you're cornered, you can just dash or hyper your way out.
A main part of this game are the bosses. I never actually disliked any of them character wise EXCEPT one, but that's kinda spoilery so i'll move on. Each boss felt like they were like you, and I always felt slight remorse after killing them, after the RUSH OF EXCITEMENT. This game makes boss kills feel REALLY REWARDING.
Onto the graphics, they're definitely dated, but I still like how the game itself looks, especially the characters. The game really suits it's graphics style and the fact that the graphics were bad by today's standards never got in the way of gameplay.
The music though, is very good. It never failed to make me pumped up for the level ahead and to me it never felt repetitive although I had played through the levels countless times.
In conclusion, Suguri is a very difficult game with a lot of features that make it feel like it's your fault when you die, not the game's. The game never fails to make me want to try new things and carry on until I finally beat that boss. The only thing that I felt could be improved, was the segments where you were 'indoors' as the bullets kinda glitch when hugging the wall, but thats 2 of 14 segments, so it's really not that big a deal. I'd reccomend it to anyone seeking a challenge and a decent story (towards the end).

An interesting spin on bullet hell games that allow some shots to be passed through with dash and some that you can't. Most of the ones that you can't dash through are the ones you can destroy by shooting at. While there's not much story the character design's pretty nice even though I still think Iru's a guy. Gameplay is very fun and features an Arcade mode but if you can't get through all the missions without dying you can tackle them one at a time.

Before you buy this game, keep aware that the game is insanely hard (even on easymode) on players who are new to bullet hells. (I learned this the hard way). Suguri is a fast paced action shooter, kept my heart beating a lot faster than your average horror game.
Pros
-I found this unique, there were an arsenal of many weapons with different kinds of tactics to put into use.
-The dash ability was a very crucial yet fun way to progress through the game.
-Game is very fast paced, there won't be a time when your body is relaxed (except when you're talking the bosses). It really keeps the excitement in the game
-1st stage soundtrack was the best c:
Cons
-There wasn't any tutorial, nor any guide to tell you that dashing can dodge beam attacks unscathed. You would have to also check the keyboard controls to realize its function before starting the game.
In conclusion, this game is one of the best bullet hells I have ever played.  9.5/10
P.S I prefer keeping the game under a window mode.

Suguri By Orange Juice. Its an Addictive Fustration making game that has something very special about it.
The first thing you will want to know considering it tags itself as Bullet hell is, "Does it feel cheap when you lose?"
Absolutely not, and its one of the main reasons why I love this game. Theres never been a point where I have dies and felt that it was impossible. Losing in this game is down straight and true to Player error. Theres always away to beat the level and its that wanting to come back and finally beat that level that makes me want to play more. The game is very fustrating yet at the same time extremely fun to play at the same time.
Another Big highlight I want to point out is the Soundtrack. I don't know what it is With Orange juice but all the games they have developed have a great soundtrack. QP Shooting Dangerous had it. 100% Orange had it and if anything Suguri has it even better. It's a key point that people overlook in these kind of games. The right music adds so much more to your experience and Suguri has the perfect soundtrack to make you want to play it.
Performance wise. It plays at a solid 60fps smooth and silky. I haven't experienced any slowdown when things have got rather manic on the screen and it helps to the overall experience.
The Game also accomadates a good number of different guns and weapons, Allowing for a more personal experience. However, You may find that what works on one level may not work on another. Its like the game actively encourages you to either master your primary weapons or change your loadout to suit the kind of level and projectiles that you will face.
Finally I will say the visauls of the game may look dated, but they are certainly acceptable. A game of this age is never gonna look the greatest but the quality is there in the right places when it is needed.
Overall while its still early in 2015 and this being a rather oldish game, I certainly put it up there with my favourites of the year so far. It sits there in your library, taunting you to give it another go. To beat that next level and when you do, The rush of excitement and joy are on another level. Check out the tracklist if you can as well, it will not dissapoint you.

First off, this feels really good as a shooter. Just you, your weapon and your skill. The mechanics are very 90's shooter. You know...Unreal Tournament, Quake...That sort of thing. No sprint, no health regeneration, armor pickups, no reloads... And it's a good thing. With no powerups, the only thing keeping you on the winning side is how you play. How did I find it, though? I like it. The dodge mechanics and a camo ability (albeit for a few seconds only) help you get out of a sticky situation, and I find myself getting the heck out of there pretty handy. It's very ability based though, so no matter how well you dodge you still have to learn how to shoot straight and overcome your enemy through wit and ability.
Weapons? There's a few. You have your classic slew of automatic rifles, shotguns and rocket launchers. Nothing too unique other than a mega weapon that has the ability to wipe out an entire team although I haven't seen it in a public match yet. The weapons have no reload though so your entire inventory is loaded already and the only way you can top up your supply is through pickups either from specific points on the map or from dead enemies. Health and armor are scattered throughout the map. These come in pretty small amounts save for the larger yet rarer mega versions. You can also customize your player's appearance as well. These are unlocked by progressing through the ranks. You've got a helmet, body, primary and secondary colour, camouflage pattern and the glow of the lights on your body. You can add initials on your body and that's about it. Nothing too fancy or deep, but then again with the very fast paced action this game boasts I'm guessing you catch only a glimpse of your assailant before either he or you bites the dust.
One thing of note to me and which I like a lot is the options and settings. You can customize a lot of the settings HUD-wise, including crosshairs (which you can set up individually for each weapon) as well as a weapon selection display where you can change colour of each weapon so you know what weapons you have from a glance.
Overall, if you really like old shooters or just barebones, skill-based FPS then maybe this is for you. There's a free version out here that omits a server browser, game host option and character customization. Just to get a taste of what to expect and if you like it enough, you can get the full thing. They're not forcing anybody, so that's a plus.

The game starts out well...collect items on the way to the finish line while trying to get the best time possible.  The first problem becomes evident fairly early on:  the controls stink.  The second problem revealed after several levels in, is that the path you are to take near-impossible to tell.
I reached level 26 before I finally threw in the towel.  I then did the "Endless Run" mode a couple times just to round out my experience with the game.
They have checkpoints, but on the difficult levels they are too far apart.
Which game are they making?  Seems like the devs couldn't decide between a (all-too-common) 3-path run/jump/slide game as on mobile devices, and a first-person runner.  These completely distinct play styles are used on different levels.  They should have picked ONE and made THAT game.
No additional 'bonus' as far as I could readily tell for collecting additional batteries along the level or finishing much quicker.  I suppose the 1, 2 or 3 lightning bolts for your 'grade', but when there's upwards of 20 to 40 items on the level does an extra few matter?  Or an extra few seconds?  To me, I just got the minimums and moved on and still had many 3-lightning bolt rankings for the levels, so why bother?
I have no idea how you score points toward the leaderboard.  I reached level 26 and ran over 2000 "units" in endless mode, yet still have a score of "0".
Too many times where perfect timing is required.
It's not so much a game of skill or reflexes if they put things just out of sight that will kill you (a turn or a hole) unless you prepare on the previous obstacle "just so".  Impossible NOT to die the first time, leaving you having to memorize the course.
Jumping from one "I-Beam" (your path) to another "I-Beam" next to you is incredibly difficult given 1) how far apart they make the beams, 2) how slowly you turn, and 3) how narrow the beams are.  This becomes an increasingly common event.
You can reach a checkpoint at too slow a speed to complete what is just after that checkpoint.  Thus when you die (as you will), you start at the checkpoint again
to complete the next obstacle.  Leaving you no choice but to quit and restart the level from the beginning.
It's a good infinite runner.

This game is so good I couldn't keep myself away from it for too long!
The atmosphere is amazing. I love the colour palettes the developers chose, and the way there is so much happening on this fairly small island. They packed so much stuff in there! It looks so meticulously designed!
The puzzles are quite well thought out. It takes this kind of path tracing puzzle concept and runs with it; it goes through many different rule sets all based on this one type of puzzle. The way in which it is done is awe-inspiring. I found myself excited whenever I figured out what one of those variations was.
The game definitely lived up to the promise of a challenge - nothing was given for free (or at least, not much). However, as a puzzle game fan (and adventure game fan) myself, I found that to be quite entertaining. I was often faced with a puzzle that I at first thought was impossible. However, in every case, I would come around to the answer. It was really cool how they managed to get the puzzle's rule set accross without actually saying anything. I love games that give me these mental exercises without holding my hand, but still make it just enough of a challenge to be solvable without breaking your brain.
The only drawback with the game (and it isn't a big one at all), is that some of the clips you find on the island are a little long. They vary from 10 minutes to more than an hour. Thankfully, though, there aren't that many to find. If you play this game, you'll know why I know about the lengths... ;) The videos overall (mixed with the audio clips strewn about the landscape) give you an interesting mix of perspectives on the human condition. However, I do feel that while they don't exactly fit within the context of this game, they do provide food for thought.
In short, I would recommend this game to any puzzle or adventure game fan out there. As some have mentioned, there isn't much of a story, but I really don't care. It gives just enough to be mysterious, and that's enough for me.
With the ammount of content in the game and the level of quality, it's well worth the $40.

The software does mostly what it says it's supposed to, but I wouldn't recommend it at this stage of development.
1. Program crashes a lot, especially when performing an operation for the first time, such as entering the serial code or downloading a new driver.
2. Despite being managed through Steam, this software requires you to sign up an account with them. Kind of a hastle considering it's managing drivers on your local machine. This isn't exactly an MMO. If I can get my Skyrim save-games through the Steam cloud, anything you're storing could probably go there too.
3. Auto-login option doesn't always work.
4. Downloading is still a very convoluted process:
- When you're downloading something, the rest of the program is inaccessible.
- You can't pause a download.
- You can't queue multiple downloads.
- When viewing potential download candidates you can't view the current drivers info and compare them. You have to memorise one and then compare to the other.
- Downloads aren't filtered by whether they are signed. If you're freaked out by Windows warnings, be brave!
- The program will offer the current driver as a download, even if it is currently installed. Unless you've check that it's not the same one, you might perform a redundant download.
5. There are a few little finishing touches that are lacking. For example, when looking at an installed driver's release date, the format is (m)m/dd/yyyy. When looking at prospective new drivers, their release dates are dd/mm/yyyy (my preferred). Its just the little things.
Probably not worth the full price, depending on your rig and your resourcefulness, so try getting it on sale.

95 hours later, I remembered I do not have a review for this.
Unlike most shoot em ups, SUGURI is surprisingly easy to get into. Even for the people that do not typically enjoy shoot em ups for more than 2 hours such as myself. So unless you really hate the shmup genre, I believe you should buy it.
SUGURI is a type of game that theoretically should have no replayability, there's no randomisation in game outside of boss moves. All enemies come in the same order every time. And is the type of a game I normally abandon without ever finishing. However, the music and the game mechanics make it stand out rather well from traditional shmups and keep it enjoyable to play even after you've completed the game.
At the core, it does not differ much at all from a traditional shmup : Start a stage, enemies come from the right, you use a weapon to blow them up, then comes the midboss and finally the stage boss. Defeat that and continue doing this until the end of the game with minor variations to that formula. Except you have health instead of lives.
The difference comes from the fact that the game includes two types of projectiles, I am not sure how they're actually called but I just call them solid and non-solid for ease of understanding.
The way it goes is that Suguri, the same-named protagonist of the game has the ability to dash, which allows her to completely avoid non-solid projectiles and charge her Hyper attack meter. Dashing also increases her heat which on a direct percentage amount increases the damage she receive (eg 5% heat you will receive 5% more damage). This and the solid projectiles prevent you from using dash all the time to be completely invincible.
Suguri herself carries two weapons (out of total 16) of your choice into battle, and when her hyper attack meter has built up, can use it to deliver a powerful attack with either of the two weapons. Hyper attacks replace bombing that you normally have in a shmup. Although, while it gives you short temporary invulnerability, it does not clear projectiles.
What makes this game so special for me is the complete freedom you have where the larger enemy fights don't have a real timer set over how long you're going to be fighting them for. You think you can kill something in 5 seconds? Go ahead and try, if you do not die in the process you might just pull it off. Alongside the ability to experiment with different ideas of what might or might not work with the weapons you chose.
And then there's the music, I can't find words for how much I like the music. While obviously not the type of music for everyone, it is really enjoyable.
As fun as this game is, there are some flaws, three of these being steam release exclusive and one is a general flaw with the game :
Although, despite not really a flaw. One minor oddity is that for some reason, the Story mode and the first option of the game (Complete a stage, unlock the next one to play at your will) was renamed to Stage Select upon localisation. While Arcade (Play all stages consecutively in one go) was moved to be the first option of the game.

So far, I've been plaing with the free version of the game, so some elements of the game aren't up for review. But that does bring up one huge aspect of this game. It's PC release.
There is a lot that game companies could learn from the title when it comes to PC releases. Firstly, the free version. This isn't some EA Access, play one hour and tough luck affair, it provides the core and impotant parts of the game for you to play and try, for free...forever. Yes a lot of the functionality isn't there, but it's for you to try the game out and it's a method of marketing I wish I saw more of. When first seeing TOXIKK, my first thought was, "Oh, here we go again! Another Quake clone trying to 'bring me back to the '90s'. We need these like we need more zombie games." Honestly, if it wasn't for the free version, I would never have played TOXIKK. Now I'm buying it. The devs are attracting more customers, I feel more confident in my purchace, and I have confidence in the devs. A truley excellent trial like this, is worth 1,000 pre-rendered trailers.
Though of course, the game. Does it play well? Is it fun? Are we back in 1999? Well, yes and no. Though first, is it a good PC game? We PC gamers are only seeing more and more dodgy releases each year. Just yesterday, I re-installed The Division to check out PTS, and still, there is a bug where running Rainmeter caused the game to lock up when  the mouse was moved. Halo 5 Forge, released by Microsoft for God's sake has a locked 60FPS and locked 55FOV, making my sick when playing. So I'm glad to report that TOXIKK is a shining pillar of star-light in the ocean of♥♥♥♥♥♥ports. Framerate going all the way up to 242FPS, a plethera of in game options, an FOV slider with a huge range, and nigh-on mouse lag-less Vsync, and 100% lag-less when off. It even feels snappier than CS:GO. Which really is saying something here. Though of course, performance. Does it run well? Yes. My God yes. The game looks great, not amazing, certainly not ground-breaking, but runs like a dream. No stuttering, hitching, spikes of any kind, pop-in, and only one-or-two blurry textures. When stood still. Staring at something. Which will last 1/2 of a second before you're shot in the head. Using a GTX 1080 @ 4K w/ maxed settings, I see a range of 105-133FPS. Very, very impressive. And excelent news for high-refresh rate users.
Though the game. Is it 1999. No. More early 2000s. And that's what stopeed this game being another Quake clone, and made it a killer game. The weapons, their designs and charecter movement, are all 1999 to the bone. But the enviroment and charecter design is very 2001. Big burrly blokes in metal clad armour with seeimingly pointless blinky lights, that you'd assume would make you more obvious to other players. Ancient ruins of an unspecified people covered in highly detailed lights from torches, in-explicitly lit during the day. Huge furistic bases made wholey from whit metal and sharp angles with tubes of...stuff in them. All because of one reason. It looks cool.
So really, all-in-all, we're not fragging like it's 1999 here in TOXIKK. But that's it's best quality. It's light Quake if it was to have had it's debut in 2001. A beautifully old school shooter with all the pro-PC user features you could ask for, at two price points that instantly make my little niggles with the irrelevent. Or at least that would be true until I tried "Quick Play". One major niggle is the servers ping times in quick play, which brought a last minute rejig of the score.
8.9/10
Keep fragging Reakktor Studios. Wait. Reakktor. Oh, that's the reason for the double 'K'. Thought it was  them emulating the '90s edge.

PROS: Beautiful graphics, solid physics, awesome sound, clans.
CONS: Game economy, server quality, development team communication, lack of respect for playerbase.
Sadly, I can no longer recommend this game in good conscience. Since update 1.2.3, so much has changed the game is hardly recognizable. The game still looks and feels great, but progression is a nightmare; even for paying players!
Update 1.2.3 removed the tier system and reduced equipment requirements to ranks. So now modules can span multiple ships, even if there is a better module available. This can be nice for new players, as it helps reduce the power gap when levelling. However, if you were a vet like me, you lost hours of your progress, as tons of ships gained access to new parts that required more grinding to max out.
And that is ultimately why I am finally laying this game down to die, despite my 500+ hours of gametime (I was playing before it was added to Steam), the money I have spent, and the unique ships I have in my hangar.
This latest update undid hours of progression, and would have required hours more of my time to get my favorite ships back to their maximum potential. I have spent $80+ on this game, and all of it was a waste. Because ultimately, despite this game being based on a pay-not-to-grind model, the amount of grind you get to skip for your money is crap.
You can not get a decent experience for the price of a new triple-A title. This game's economy is ultra greedy and targets the 'whale' demographic who have too much money to spend. And the developers know it.
The amount of information withheld from the playerbase is astounding. They removed the in-game player count to hide the dwindling numbers (I estimate we are currently at 5K players MAX, with only 1.5K of those players from the non-Russian demographic), they refuse to discuss the game's economy and the decisions made regarding the ever-increasing level of grind, they have repeatedly patched the game in ways that have destroyed player progression, and continue to show blatant favoritism toward the Russian community with only minimal resources being directed at their English forum (mainly for the purpose of damage-control).
Well, they got my $80 and 500+ hours of my life. They're not getting any more. Goodbye Star Conflict, and good riddance!

The Witness is a beguiling game of deceptive simplicity. You'll see a lot of criticism aimed at it from people who have only scratched the surface of the game distiling the game down to "just tracing line puzzles". While it is true a large selection of the game are maze-like puzzles where you attempt to trace one unbroken line to the end without overlapping itself, the variations on this are vast and fascinating. Whie traversing this beautifully constructed digital island you unravel the various ruleset of these puzzles with non-verbal communication. This game has a lot more in common with the Cyan Worlds games (Myst, Riven, etc.) but instead of pushing an archaic, aging button to activate a portion of a puzzle like in Myst, The Witness unifies all contraptions into a unified puzzle language which serves to thematically tie all puzzles together.
But the true beauty is in the story and narrative provided. You have to work hard in order to piece together the "story" of this place you find yourself in, but its a grand combination of philosophies from a myriad of schools of thought presented in a way that only video/computer games can provide. The story being told in The Witness isn't one of sci-fi mysticism, but instead the story presented wants you to meet it more than halfway. It wants to hear your own ideas and preceptions as much as it wants to present its own.
This is also a hard game to talk about without giving away a lot of what makes it so special, and that discovery is a large part of its genius. So $39.99 is really a cheap ticket of entry for an experience that is priceless, but I also realize that the experience isn't for everyone but it was definitely an experience I enjoyed thoroughly.

Circuits is essentially a music puzzle game, where you get to reconstruct melodies by putting little sound hubs in their right positions to build a track. The game mechanic is based on you listening to certain melodies and then identiying the proper sounds and putting them in the right order. Note that you will probably have to listen to some parts repeatedly to get them right, since it is something not everyone has the patience for.
The difficulty is generally not high, except towards the end (levels 24-25). You can, however, choose to *not* break up the music into layers in the previous levels, so it will be harder for you to distinguish the different sounds playing at the same time. The game is a tad short, I finished it in roughly 4 hours, but that can vary depending on the person. However, the developers have promised more levels in the near future, so this might change.
Overall, I would say that circuits is worth your time.  It is simple, yet elegant and relaxing if you are generally musically inclined. It is hard to comment beyond personal preferences for this type of game, since I feel it is mostly a matter of taste, so if you think what I have mentioned so far is something you will like, you will probably enjoy this game as I have.

The last two puzzles were the most interesting, since the game forces you to figure things out by listening to all of the song layers at once. What a ride Furi was.
It’s not necessarily a long game, unless you keep dying over and over and over and over and over and … you get the idea.
However it’s still worth it every single penny.
The gameplay and the whole experience was just amazing.
Excellent question! Next! … What? I do have a idea what the game is about! It’s about … oh look a
Did you see it?
…
Let’s get on with the review.
Look. If you’ve got high blood pressure or anything like it: think twice about diving into Furi.
Also if you can’t handle getting your♥♥♥♥♥whooped big time: think twice about diving into Furi.
However … if you’re one of those crazy people out there who, not only like, but love a challenge and fast paced gameplay: Buy it. Play it. Love it. Now.
Look. Here’s the thing. I can’t get into what the game’s all about because that’s exactly what you’re trying to discover by playing it.
What I can say is this. You’re trapped. Tortured. You have no idea why.
By fighting against the Guardians of the game you’ll learn more about yourself and what’s going on. It’s all pretty cryptic but you get an idea the further you make it.
The character design gave me a pretty big
vibe so I checked it out whether I had the right idea and yup I was right.
The talent behind the incredibly good and fitting character design is none other than Takashi Okazaki - Afro Samurai creator.
Let me tell you one thing. The design is just so good. I’ve seldom seen a game where the whole design and by that I mean the world, the characters, just everything fits.
Thanks to that the whole game has a certain flow to it. Big reason besides the design is of course the combat but more on that later.
There’s nothing, absolutely nothing, that I could point out and go: That looks♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ That doesn’t fit. Dafuq were they thinking?
Everything. Fits. You wanna know why?
The music. Oh my god. I swear to god I had multiple eargasms while playing.
In fact I’m listening to the
right now.
Folks like Carpenter Brut, Danger or Kn1ght make their appearance and blast your headphones right of your head with their intense and explosive tracks. If you think the boss fights are intense by watching some videos or looking at some screenshots:
All kidding aside you really have no idea how intense the game gets once you’ve played and listened to the track. The soundtrack gets your heart pumping and the combination of the fast paced combat against bosses with the soundtrack: adrenaline rush.
Every fight in the game. Every single one will test you. You’re up against several Guardians. Those are the Bosses you have to kill to be free.
The bosses, and you, have tanks beneath their health bars. Those indicate how many phases you have to survive. Or how often you can get bodied.
A sword. A gun. That’s all you have and need.
Furi isn’t about leveling up. About finding the right gear to make your way through the game.
There’s no divine intervention, magic, or NPCs helping you. What determines the outcome of every fight is one thing and one thing only: your skill.
Getting better at something, be it in a game, sports, you name it, and feeling your skills improve, is what we all strive for and what we all think feels best.
You’ll die. You’ll get bodied. You’ll be mad but once you finally beat your enemy it’s celebration time.
In order to beat the game you have to know what you can and can’t do. What you can’t do is one shot anyone.
What you can do is dodge at an incredibly fast speed, parry attacks (that way you can also replenish a bit of health) and counter them (strive for a perfect parry every time), use your gun to damage your opponent while you’re trying to dodge several bullets and shockwaves and more.
Personally I think that the less you know about the meat of the game, the actual combat, the better. Find out for yourself what you’re capable of. Level up not ingame but as a player.
The experience you gain by playing Furi and by dying over and over and over again will not only aid you in this game but in all others.
It’s a game about testing your limits. About making split second decisions which can determine your fate.
Will you manage to fight your way through and to free yourself? Are you going to keep trying after you’ve been bodied?
Or are you going to give up and let yourself be captured again?

Higurashi When They Cry is a sound novel. The music, backgrounds and characters work together to create a world that is the stage of a novel for the user to read. They laugh and cry and get angry. The user takes the point of view of the protagonist to experience the story.
The 58th year of Shouwa, early summer.
It’s June, and the summer heat has arrived earlier than it does most years.
By day there are crickets, and by night there are cicadas.
We’re in Hinamizawa, a small village in the countryside.
There are fewer than two thousand people here. But every year, there is an event.
This event is a mysterious death.
On a certain day in June, someone dies, and someone else goes missing.
The series of deaths is connected to the upheaval surrounding the dam construction project.
A murder case that was covered up is being reenacted.
Is it a conspiracy? A coincidence? Or perhaps a curse?
Someone who was supposed to be there isn’t.
Someone who wasn’t supposed to be there is.
Someone who was alive last night is dead now.
And someone who is here right now isn’t alive.
So, there is no way to avert tragedy. There is no choice but to give up.
But don’t give up.
Only you can stand up to this.

Suguri is, as you probably have gathered by now, part of the Bullet Hell subset of Shoot 'em Up's, but a very unique take on it.
You're given a lot of freedom in movement, thanks especially to the dash mechanic, which has the added bonus of allowing you to dodge certain bullets. None of the stages dragged on too long, and they actually seem to get shorter with each passing stage. You have a large range of weapons to choose from, but you only start out with three of them; the more you try the stages, however, you unlock more weapons.
The story is simple, but it's actually pretty good; the characters all seem unique, thanks in part to their fights, but you don't see too much of their personalities until the sequel, Acceleration of Suguri. The art is also a bit simple, but it did grow on me; the sprites on the other hand look amazing, with the enemies sharing a distinctly different style compared to the chibi-esque style of you and the bosses.
The music, on the other hand, is overall a bit above average; while there were certainly standouts, namely the final boss and the entirety of Stage 4, the rest is pretty good at best.
Oh yeah, and this game is insanely hard. On my first playthrough, I could only manage Easy Mode, and even then it took me quite a few hours just to beat it. After getting more accustomed to how the game worked, though, I did finally manage to beat Normal Mode; it did take me a bit longer than it should have, however, thanks to my save data getting corrupted (I still don't know how, either).
Overall, if you're looking for a difficult game that takes a while to get used to, but is a blast once you do, I would easily recommend it; it's easily become one of my favorite Shoot 'em Up games I've played, though I do still prefer its sequel.

It would be a real shame if fans of the shooter genre passed this one over as being too generic, or too similar to Touhou/Cotton/CAVE/etc games, because it has its own flavor that's really unique. Rather than simply firing in a straight line, or at fixed angles, in SUGURI, your character -- the eponymous Suguri -- actually aims at targets directly, with a simple lock-on system, and depending on the weapon, she has to pause briefly to fire.
This completely changes the dynamics of the game, with enemies doing the same, as well as firing rapid-fire homing attacks! I'd be lying if I said SUGURI is a difficult game, because it's much more than that -- as a danmaku veteran I was getting destroyed on Normal! Excellent timing, clever use of the grazing dash, and mastery of both of your equippable weapons are all required to win in SUGURI.
At the time of this review you can pick up SUGURI and the fighting-game sister title Acceleration of SUGURI for just five dollars together, which is an absolute steal for two inventive and fun games that will run on any computer, anywhere. I highly recommend both titles.

There are a couple of challenges games like this face, one being actual gameplay, does it actually have any or is this basically a visual novel? Vallhalla has plenty of gameplay, presented at first as a kind of bar-tending minigame (granted with no real ingredients so maybe not actually drink making) that's as liesurely as can be, no time-limits, no game-overs, and the recipe book never more than a mouse-click away. At first this seems like there's not actually any impact, and you've fallen for an excellent visual novel (and it IS excellent) with a minigame tacked on, but you couldn't be more wrong. Very subtly at first, but then more and more present the true gameplay emerges, where the story and characters becomes important, where what seemed like a "follow the instructions and click next" has suddenly become a "how best do you cheer up your friend?" and I think that was truly magnificintly done, something I haven't seen employed as successfully in any other game.
The second issue this style of game faces is the world, if it's not engrossing why would the player bother sitting through the many, many dialogue boxes? And it is, almost from the title screen I found myself pulled into this cyberpunk quasi-dystopian world filled with likable and interesting characters (even the ones I wanted to hate) with the feeling of a much larger story playing out in the background, but also one that somehow feels less important than the vignettes playing out inside your tiny bar.
Oh and the soundtrack is absolutely wonderful.
I remember when reading reviews (even though I'd essentialy already decided to buy the game at "Cyberpunk Bartender") that someone had said this was "The antithesis of Dark Souls" or something along those lines, meaning that whereas Dark Souls is stressful and demanding you can (and I highly recommend that you do) play this while kicking back with a couple of beers and very casually working your way though this game. And while that may be a very apt description but it misses so much.

It's no actual bartending simulator (as you can screw up as many times you want), but the story-telling, humourous dialogues, memorable characters, and soundtrack is enough to win your heart over.
And yes, I'm writing a review for this game because of the Steam Awards 2017. It fits the "The world is grim enough lets just all get along" award because it IS set in a dystopic cyberpunk future, yet the comedic tone and the characters lighten up the mood of this game. After all, the objective of the game is to serve patrons with drinks and even listen to their stories, even befriending some of them. There are no "big bad evil guys" to fight. Just a cute bartender trying to pay off her end of month rent.

The Witness is a beguiling game of deceptive simplicity. You'll see a lot of criticism aimed at it from people who have only scratched the surface of the game distiling the game down to "just tracing line puzzles". While it is true a large selection of the game are maze-like puzzles where you attempt to trace one unbroken line to the end without overlapping itself, the variations on this are vast and fascinating. Whie traversing this beautifully constructed digital island you unravel the various ruleset of these puzzles with non-verbal communication. This game has a lot more in common with the Cyan Worlds games (Myst, Riven, etc.) but instead of pushing an archaic, aging button to activate a portion of a puzzle like in Myst, The Witness unifies all contraptions into a unified puzzle language which serves to thematically tie all puzzles together.
But the true beauty is in the story and narrative provided. You have to work hard in order to piece together the "story" of this place you find yourself in, but its a grand combination of philosophies from a myriad of schools of thought presented in a way that only video/computer games can provide. The story being told in The Witness isn't one of sci-fi mysticism, but instead the story presented wants you to meet it more than halfway. It wants to hear your own ideas and preceptions as much as it wants to present its own.
This is also a hard game to talk about without giving away a lot of what makes it so special, and that discovery is a large part of its genius. So $39.99 is really a cheap ticket of entry for an experience that is priceless, but I also realize that the experience isn't for everyone but it was definitely an experience I enjoyed thoroughly.

The Witness starts off great. It has beautiful visuals and just leaves you to its devices, which teach you how to play the game without just flat out telling you, making you feel very rewarded when you learn a new mechanic. However, The Witness starts dragging its feet after the first few hours. Everything The Witness has to offer is centered around solving geometric puzzles on panels, very few of which are easy, and there's roughly about 50,000,000,000 of them. Maybe the designers didn't want the player lacking for content, or maybe they didn't want to you finish the game so quickly and just take in the world, but they went to the other extreme. There's just too much of it. You'll start to get bored, and progress will be too slow coming in the game. Opening a can of soup in the world of The Witness is a 20 puzzle affair and 3 hour ordeal. As this drags on, the beatiful visuals and atmosphere will start to become meaningless, and The Witness will feel like a very large Sudoku book. Fun to play in very short bursts when you're bored, but you don't go through the whole book in few sittings like you do a game. If you play this game, I'd have a walkthrough near by, take 30 seconds to solve a puzzle on your own, and if you can get it, look at that walkthrough and move on to the next one. Don't worry about feeling cheated, there's plenty of opportunity to solve puzzles on your own. But there lies the problem with this game. It doesn't respect the law of diminishing returns. All there is to The Witness is these mountain of puzzles, and by the end of the game, you'll be sick of them and sick of The Witness.

This game requires you to listen to some soundtracks and reconstruct them from individual parts. You can separate the soundtrack into individual layers, which makes it easy to listen and compare the music pieces and find the right place for each one... but that's not even a challenge, and I think there is no point in playing the game like this.
But if you have a good musical ear (and headphones), you can choose not to use layers (there is an achievement for that), so you can only listen to the complete unmodified track, with up to 3 "instruments" playing at the same time. And that makes things interesting, in some cases nearly impossible. But that's when hints come into play! You just need to get things mostly right and then you may use hints to logically deduce the rest, which is also quite fun.
Oh, and if you want more, then you can play with layers but without hints (which is another achievement), so there's some replayability.
In conclusion, Circuits is an interesting game, but I wouldn't recommend it to most people.

TL;DR - Furi is a good game that I recommend. I do have a few issues with the game. But overall it was a solid pick up.
Furi is a really solid game that I would recommend for many of the reasons that others here do. The game has amazing character design (same artist as Afro Samurai and the comparisons are easily seen), the art direction is great with the game, the soundtrack is amazing, and the gameplay itself is nice and tight. For more in depth on the positives check out almost any other positive review. My review is mostly to point out some of the negatives, that don't keep me from recommending the game, but a buyer might want to be aware of.
Firstly, while the game's artwork and character design are amazing, sometimes the visuals themselves look silly. Mostly the main character's hair and his cape. The hair often behaves erratically and both the hair and the cape often clip through the outfit. The sword's sheath cares little for the cape and often sticks right through it. It's a small complaint but the clipping makes the cutscenes where you're the stoic and silent protagonist look silly as things just don't behave correctly.
Secondly, while I don't mind the sections of forced walking between boss fights, they seem incredibly unnecessary. The point of the walking sections is to show off the new area you're entering and give exposition. These sections are where a majority of the story is revealed, but in the end the story is still incredibly cryptic and sparse. While I didn't really care about the crypticness and lack of story (as a Dark Souls fan I'm used to it) the ending brings it to light. The end of the game presents you with a choice. Choice A or Choice B. Knowing little to nothing about what's actually happening in the story the choice feels really arbitrary. Like the main character would know what the outcome of each choice would be, but as the player I had literally no clue. And apparently one choice let's you do an additional boss fight while the other does not. Once again, a small gripe but it made the ending feel less than stellar.
Lastly, a complaint I wouldn't usually make. As someone who has beaten Dark Souls 1, 2, and 3 plus Bloodborne and more games of that nature, I like games that present a challenge. But personally I think Furi's difficulty is incredibly unbalanced. Furi mode (normal mode) usually gives the boss about 4-6 life bars and gives you about 3. This already puts you at a disadvantage but the ability to gain life bars back kind of balances the game out. However, the game is still difficult. On the other hand, Promenade (easy mode) is disgustingly easy. It's utterly ridiculous. Promenade gives you about 5 life bars, bosses about 2 and you each do about 3x damage to one another. Furi Mode makes boss fights take multiple tries until you learn the patterns and Promenade makes boss fights take about 5 minutes max. The disparity between the two difficulties is insane. Furi mode would leave me frustrated on certain bosses (especially during the bullet hell segments that I felt were a bit much) and towards the end I started just getting annoyed by bosses rather than enjoying the game. Losing on the bosses final bullet hell phase and restarting the fight from scratch multiple times made the game feel cheap instead of fun and challenging. But Promenade makes the game easy to the extent where I felt like $25 is wasted for this difficulty. I honestly think the game could use an extra difficulty between Promenade and Furi. A difficulty where you and the boss are way more evenly matched than it being unbalanced one way or another. Also, the ability to not switch the difficulty back means that if one boss if giving you trouble, have fun playing the rest of the game in 20 minutes because Promenade makes it a joke. It's weird to not have an option to switch back in order to experience the other bosses as intended after lowering the difficulty for a particularly hard boss.
Anyway, the game is good. Those three complaints don't make the game not worth buying. But they may be something to consider before dropping $25 on the game. If you don't think you can't beat the game on Furi mode don't bother purchasing, because your only other option is a cakewalk. Unless you really just want to experience the character design and artwork (because you're definitely not picking up the game for the story).

For ages 6 and below. Not challenging. One of the only simulator games where anyone that can read will probably get everything right since the first attempt. If you sell your buildings, you'll get rich. If you rent them out, you'll get rich. You can just set the price to maximum and ensure maximum profits. Nothing to calculate, no need for operations research. Any building will sell for maximum price within one year. And you can't build a new one faster than that anyway... no need to hurry then. If you set the rent out price to the maximum, you'll get the maximum sale value every 4 years. You'll start slower, but will build up steady income faster (exponential income growth). You can use your steady income to ensure you won't run out of money when investing more than you have.
As a matter of fact, your only job is to allocate workforce and machinery. Too bad that's about half a thousandth of the skyscraper building costs. In other words, you can fail pathetically and will still look successful.
For some reason, you can rent out your skyscraper as soon as it's about 20% done constructing (60% total building time). That means you only need money enough for 60% of the building process. From that point on, the rent will give you more than you can possibly spend on its construction.
No maps or modding. No scripting to fix their bugs. Simulators really need modding capabilities. Especially if the developers decide not to finish the game before (or after) selling.

Dungeon Escape is a sadistically-difficult 2D-platformer that is surprisingly fun even if it is a stripped-down clone of Super Meat Boy.
The game features 49 increasingly hair-pulling levels for you to die repeatedly in. While incredibly infuriating at times, it feels very satisying to beat levels after you've tried and failed an innumerous amount of times.
One thing to note: The hitboxes feel a bit funky at first, but after enough play-time you learn their boundaries.
PROS:
-Solid and responsive controls.
-Game mechanics are simple and easy to learn.
-Pleasing visuals.
-A fairly good soundtrack with some catchy tunes.
MIDDLE-GROUND:
-It's frustrating as hell (but that's to be expected).
CONS:
-Hit-boxes can be weird.
-Some jumps and maneuvers are nearly pixel-perfect.
-I don't think 5 dollars is a fair price for a game of this simplicity and scope.
SCORE: 6/10

Got that picture in your head? Nice.
NOW THROW IT OUT THE WINDOW, BECAUSE THIS GAME IS JUST COMPLETE MADNESS.
So, true, you start in a pretty standard vehicle and try to find your way to said country.
But, oh boy, the ride couldnt be any wilder, even if it's name was Gene.
Much like a chocolate factory, this game is filled to the brim with joy, humor and sweet remarks about the pop culture we're living in.
You can encounter an exploding Anime Girl, Gordon Freeman, Jason, Garfield, Men in Black, Santa Claus, Knights, Cavemen, Skeleton Queens, Rick Grimes, Link and like a hundred more of special characters.
All of them are playable.
All of them have different abilities.
All of them can be a big pain in the bum or your last hope of making it to the paradise of maple syrup.
If you think you're a creative fella, well then make your own survivor with his or her own special abilities! (But some of them are only useable after you unlock them with zombo points, which you gain during the game, so.... this game even has an upgrade-system - pretty swell, right?)
And much like the original adaptation of "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory", this game is also filled with brutality and death.
The difficulty level varies with the gamemode you're playing and did I say "Gamemode"? Indeed, I did!
Wether you like the normal experience, only like to encounter your own made characters or only rare, special ones; if you like to have a short ride or a long one or just want to torture yourself, this game can deliver.
So it goes from somewhat challenging to "Sweet embrace of death, please end this eternal suffering".
"But what after I made it to Canada? WHAT THEN, BAMJAM?", I hear you all asking.
First of all, good luck getting all the achievements, meeting all the special characters and beating all the gamemodes.
After you did all of that... Well, what do I know. I'm not at that point yet.
You're probably gonna fall in an abyss of pure depression, because this game is just that outstanding.
Did I mention that this game has no loading times, doesnt need internet and can run on a toaster?
Now I did.

Gameplaywise it's like a mix of top-down hack-and-slay scavenging missions, micromanagement - much like "Oregon Trail" and a textbound CYOA.
Really, there's something for everyone.
I'd say that it's worth the full price.
What are you waiting for?
Get your sweet cheeks to Canada.

A good visual novel game. That genre of course means that the main attraction is gonna be the story, dialog, atmosphere and the characters, and this game does pretty well in that regard.
You are a bartender in a future cyberpunk city. So that will mean serving drinks and listening to the stories that characters tell each other. The people you meet include cyborgs, robot girls, a talking dog.. and many even weirder things than that.
While it has a pretty cute art style, don't let that fool you, this is very much an adult game. The themes, discussions and the language...
+ Very nice art style and pixel art
+ Fun cast of characters
+ Generally has a cool atmosphere

- The drink mixing "minigame" is not very interesting and after a while it may just feel pointless. Sure, there are moments where you can choose to make different drinks to change how the situation will develop, but the actual drink mixing is always just looking at the manual and then doing the drink as it says, there is no actual thought involved.

What can I say. From playing far cry 3, completing it and absolutely loving it from front to back I basically had no choice but buying the fourth game in the series expecting nothing less than a smaller masterpiece like the third one. I must admit that the first 5 hours of this game did not impress me that much. The story did not engage me much at all and I felt that the world seemed very cramped combined with way too much going on around me (wildlife, people in need and everything in between thrown in my face). I decided to push on and I'm glad that I did. All of a sudden it all makes sense and the world opens up and everything that I thought I'd be annoyed by got more and more intruiging and fun to deal with.
The game is still an absolute stunner in many ways if you crank up the detail levels. The game physics are great most of the time and Ubisoft has done a truly great job in emulating a world that is savaged by a civil war with constant clashes with rebels fighting I guess government troops. There are ton of things to do and the world is pretty god damned big. If you've played the third game you know what to expect, radio towers to sabotage, outposts that need to be taken over and loads of loot to grab. I sometimes miss that feeling that fc3 gave me, that feeling of relaxation everynow and then where I could truly enjoy the scenery, like I almost was on vacation, less of that in fc4 since it's always somehting going on, hostages that needs rescue, a cargo truck that needs to be blown up or simply fierce wildlife that terrorizes the locals. All of this gives you precious "karma points" which opens up possibilities to call in reinforcements for you when you're for example trying to take over an enemy outposts.
It does get a bit repetetive in the end with the identical side quests that comes with conquering an outpost and so forth but I think all in all it is a great game and a worthy sequel to fc3 and I had loads of fun with it. Time for Primal!

The Witness is now officially my favorite game of all time. It takes a bit of getting used to, but the beautiful world, coupled with brilliant puzzles, and a mysterious world with few answers creates a game I have spent hours in and many more to come. Negative reviews of The Witness may state the game has no sense of progression, but I believe that the progression people seek is constant reward, with the game saying GOOD JOB or whatever. This game isn't like that, but what it is is a study on your own mind: a test to see if you are determined, logical, and observant enough to solve what Jonathan Blow and his development team has come up with. Since this game was announced, I had been eagerly waiting its arrival, and I am very pleased to say the seven years of waiting did not disappoint. Play The Witness, forget the price (if you can buy it on sale, even better), and envelop yourself in that world for at least a few hours. The Witness has hit just the right notes and I will always remember the time I spent in it. Yet again, I now deem The Witness my most favorite game of all time.
