Furi is a great boss rush challenge game.
The game starts with a first boss fight where you are taught the basic game mechanics. It's very simple, you have a melee attack, a range attack, a dash and a block move.
In addition, the game has a defined set of rules (melee attack will make a distinct sound helping you to time the block, projectiles come in certain flavors like purple ones will always follow you, etc). The game is consistently sticking to these rules, which makes it very fair, as opposed to games like Titan Souls.
The fights are fast-paced, but the clear set of rules makes the screen completely readable. Perfectly timed blocks will give you an advantage, which is very cool.
Boss fights all follow the same pattern: bosses have a set number of phases. Once you empty the boss' HP bar, you enter a close-ranged short fight, where you have to clear the HP bar once again to progress to the next phase.
Boss phases are like rounds: you have three lives, and if you run out of HP, you lose a life and the round restarts: you and the boss are back to full HP. Progressing to the next phase also refills your HP and one of your lives.
Of course, patterns also change at each phase, with the last phase usually being more survival based.
There are initially two difficulties, which correspond to Easy and Normal. I didn't try Easy mode yet, but Normal mode is a light challenge: it's not too easy, but I wouldn't say it's hard either. I read several reviews saying it was frustratingly hard, but now that I've completed it, I don't even get why you would say that. Even when you get killed, it's not frustrating at all.
A third difficulty is unlocked once you clear the game. That one is really challenging and completely changes the boss' attack patterns.
The story is a bit ambiguous and not very good at all, and walking between bosses while you learn about the story and characters background is a bit tiresome. That said, the character design is pretty cool.
The most annoying thing is when some bosses get you stuck in short QTE scenes, where you have to wiggle your gamepad sticks around. This is stupid, but it doesn't matter too much.
Otherwise, boss design is consistently good (3rd boss is a blast) and the attack patterns can look super pretty.
If you want a few hours of good, fast-paced action, this is the game you're looking for.

An incredible, but short game. Fantastic soundtrack, great gameplay, unique art style. One of my all time favourite games.
This is a boss rush style game. There's no fighting hordes of enemies, leveling up, looting, or exploring. (If you DO want that, but with the same core gameplay as Furi, try Hyper Light Drifter.) Every boss you face is drastically different than the rest. No two bosses are alike and each one has it's own strengths and weaknesses.
Your character has the ability to teleport short distances, a "blink" if you will. This can be used infinitely, charged up for longer teleports, and has no cooldown. You also have the ability to parry most attacks. Successful parries heal you. You're equipped with a fully automatic pistol and a sword. The gun has infinite ammo, the sword never breaks, and you can charge both up for more powerful attacks.
The gameplay isn't deep or complex. It's very simple once you get used to it. Attack the enemy, dodge attacks. The hard part is not dying. The story isn't extremely deep or convoluted either, but it's interesting enough that even when I felt I couldn't complete a level, I pushed forward to hear what happens next.

Never heard of this one til it popped up on steam, but might be the best surprise of the year.
The game consists entirely of top-down boss battles. The bosses alternate between shot patterns and melee strikes, and are made up of multiple phases. All but one I've encountered are 6 phases each. Each phase, usually, consists of a large arena section, where they let off bullet patterns and the occasional melee strike, and close quarters sections, where you dodge and parry certain strikes while constrained to a small radius around the boss, and you can't shoot.
Never been one for bullet hells, but this one managed to put it in a language I can understand, swords and twin stick shooting. Controls are elegance. Move, Slash, charged slash, rapid shooting, charged shot, dash, charged dash, parry, and the elusive perfect parry. They have interesting interactions and situations. Charged shot is an instant knockdown, giving you a breather, charging slashes slows you down but doesn't prevent you from dashing, leading to satisfying bit where you dodge through a massive volley then unleash a mighty strike them when they're vulnerable. Fully charging a slash or perfect parrying stuns the enemy, allowing a followup combo. Certain bullets can be shot and neutralised, and most can be parried back.
As with any game with simple, elegant controls, Doom, Super Meat Boy, Hotline Miami, the level design makes everything. And boy are those bosses designed. Each works by the same rules, but twists them in different ways. The first boss tests you at a little bit of everything, though after the second phase, he goes all 'Tutorial's over, ♥♥♥♥♥'. The second has you focus dodging powerful beams and waves, the third primarily spams bullets at you, tests your shooting skills, and has you deal with deceptively delayed delayed parries, and the fourth has you dealing with a small amount of durable and tricky shots, and fast and frenetic melee attacks.
The game is difficult. Death is a reverse of the Dark Souls/Hotline Miami/Super Meat Boy situation. In those games, you die, but the distance between progression is quick. In Furi, boss fights are a 15+ minute slog, but your character is durable, you have plenty of opportunities to heal, and there's a life system. Parrying strikes or shooting green bullets gives you healing opportunities. Beating a phase restores your health to full and gives you one life, however, losing a life means you start the phase again, you and the boss go back to full health and have to go through whatever setpieces there were at the start of the phase. This only really becomes obnoxious on the third boss, who has a rather lengthy set of stuff you have to dodge before you can actually start hurting him. Losing all your lives, however, puts you back at the start of the current boss fight.
Artistically, the game's got a synth soaked, neon colored totally radical 80's anime style. Heck, the character design was done by the guy responsible for Afro Samurai. The music's synthwave, what seems to be the music du jour of the post Hotline Miami indie scene, but it's used to great effect. It's even got Carpenter Brut, responsible for some of the best music from Hotline Miami 2.
I wish I could comment on the story, but for what I've played it's particularly cryptic. In between each boss you have a bit of downtime walking from one boss to the other while a vaguely sinister guy wearing a giant pink rabbit head rattles of exposition on each boss and offers you encouragement to help both of you escape the bizzare plane you're in. I'm told it's a Platinum kind of short game, where the game's short but tough but you try to chase those S ranks in addition to a brutal bonus difficutly.
My criticism's are minor. The third boss is really the only weakness largely because it's quite annoying. Not particularly harder than the others, fun in places, but you spend about 2-3 minutes in each phase just trying to get the the point where you can fight him directly. The walking between bosses sections have fixed camera angles, which are beauiful, but this is paired with an absolute control scheme, meaning you probably get a bit disoriented when the camera shifts. The walk to the 4th boss is also particularly frustrating, lighting preventing you from clearly seeing what part isn't blocking you off, and at one point sent me the wrong way.
Still, a beautiful, well made game.

This game is beyond phenomenal.  It oozes style in every way, from the beautiful and varied visuals, to the mysterious unwinding story (admittedly light but holds you and keeps you guessing) to the unbelievably amazing soundtrack worthy of note on its own.  The gameplay style is an odd yet perfect blend of a twin stick shooter, action game (DMC), and bullet-hell sh'mup.  The feel and difficulty are the epitome of "hard, but fair": nothing but boss battles that keep ramping the challenge up 10 more notches at each step, with controls and abilities that feel great and precise but require near-perfect use in order to stand a chance.  It is the kind of game that frustrates you when you fail, wondering if that last-phase is even possible, but keeps you coming back for more a few seconds later.
The really nice thing is that it blends old-school arcade hard with reasonable more modern checkpoints:  You have 3 "lives" in which to beat a boss, and if you lose all 3, you have to start the boss over again.  Once you beat a boss however, you can always continue from the start of the next boss fight, or go back and revisit them in "practice" mode.  The bosses themselves are long, having multiple stages (seeming to average 6 stages), with the overall fight taking around the 10 minute mark the first time you beat it.  Whenever you beat a phase though, you not only refill your healthbar for the next phase, but also regain one lost life (up to the 3 you start with), giving more leniency.  Overall it seems very well balanced to kick your butt while allowing you a fair chance to keep trying without feeling too punishing for failure.
I've only played for a few days and already this may be one of my favorite games of all time.  It's great for quick sessions with practice mode, and has continued replay value with the somehow even harder Furier mode, ranks with art unlocks for the individual battles (watch as your "solid win" still is only D rank and wonder what it takes to get S rank), and a boss-rush style speedrun mode (Furier/speedrun mode require you to beat the standard difficulty).  The artstyle and music are just a joy to watch/listen to, which you can tell if they're for you based on the trailers (basically more of that, with some nicer more tranquil notes as well).  And playing it just feels so satisfying, from when you're struggling with the initial challenge to feeling like the amazing badass main character as you perfect runs.  While after I beat it all the way through I might not keep playing it every day for the rest of all time, it's definitely the type of game I can see myself revisiting regularly for years to come, and more than worth the price already.

Highly recommend this game if you're into space flight sims and like me are waiting for Star Citizen. This is ok as it's better than waiting longer than that for real players when potentially there's just none on in my time zone (GMT+8). I found i was connected to South Asia i think and i didn't notice any lag. The players i did play against were good and although it looked like they may have had better ships/items, i still killed them as many times as they killed me, often finishing top of the leaderboard for that game.
The repetitiveness of the pvp matches is balanced with pve missions that gain experience with your chosen faction - i went with the Empire. Am looking forward to doing more contracts for them and gaining reputation for good rewards/upgrades. I haven't dabled too much into the workshop/crafting but i can see some potential there after looting a few crafting components and having the ability to craft items. Am saving them for now though as the upgrades are easy to obtain so far.
Am looking forward to putting some more hours into the game this week, especially with some friends picking up the game too. Highly recommend for fans of space flight sims.

For me The Witness is by far, the most provoking game in an intelectual scope that I have ever played. Not just by the puzzles, but by the subtle touch of Phylosophy and Scientific thinking. The game does not hold your hand and make things easy... Just like a scientist, you have to begin from scratch, find correlation between symbols and patters, test your hypothesis on what they mean, and keep making progress. Sometimes, you need to understand that you lack the specific knowledge to solve a puzzle. You need pursue that knowledge before trying, or you will be simply wasting your time.
The Witness is not just about solving puzzles. It's about YOU. And when I say 'you', I don't mean you as the character of the game, but you as a person.
I've never thought I would see things as profound as "The Demon Haunted World" on a game... This is the most important book of my life.
Fragments of B. F. Skinner are also thought provoking and very well placed in the game. I'm not going to say more to not give any spoilers on this review, but that moment made me realize how brilliantly Jonathan Blow breaks the fourth wall in a way that is very rare and unique.
I highly recommend The Witness.

This game is brilliant.  If you like games like Myst (puzzle solving games in a 3D environment on a lonely island) you want this game.  You have to like solving maze-like puzzles, because there are a lot of them.  But with that caution in mind, this not just a "puzzle game."  This game has provides a number of "A-HA!" epiphany moments, as you unwrap layers, and realise there is more going on than you originally thought.
The game is constantly teaching you.  Be observant, and trust that almost everything you see in the world was placed there specifically for a reason.
My one bit of advice is, don't get frustrated if a puzzle doesn't make sense, and don't reach for the spoilers just to get through it.  Go elsewhere in the world and work on other puzzles.  Frequently the game will teach you what you need to know and you can come back to the puzzle currently stumping you.  The game is quiet non-linear and very playable "out of order," so enjoy your own personal path through the world.
Finally, one warning.  Don't buy the game if you want a straight forward narrative story.  You won't get one.  You will tease out a story from observation, but the game invites interpretation and introspection.
Buy it, seriously.

Spore was the first ever PC game I got; hell, it was the game that convinced me to get a PC in the first place.  I remember booting it up back in grade school and just... *POOF* Mind blown.  I know that many people consider it an underwhelming experience in contrast to what it promised, and now that I'm an older and wiser boi, I can see their argument, but to my young mind, it was the most amazing experience to create a creature and actively see it move through the world, help it further its species.  I've recently picked up Stellaris, and while that is no by means an uninteresting game, I find it lacks a certain heart, a whimsy and deep personal connection that I personally associate with the wonder of discovering new worlds and civilizations, that we have all seen and felt in such franchises as Star Wars, Star Trek, and many other novels, games, and movies.  This game took that ethereal strangeness that space embodies in our collective psyche and it made it personal, close.  You felt the weirdness of the world around you, and there was some seriousness to the situation, of course, but there was always that underlying sense of wonder to it, to seeing other people's creations and ultimately driving them to extinction, buying them out of whole solar systems, or just plain ignoring them.  Well, that, and the technology that went into the consistently fluid animation that was employed in the creatures you built still impresses me.
This expansion has taken all these things I loved about the original and multiplied them extravagantly.  To me, GA holds about as much nostalgia as the original, and for good reason.  It took the experience that extra mile by letting you explore other planets, go on adventures of battle and friendship and mystery and horror, and create your own!  While it has its limits, the Adventure Creator is fairly versatile, and I appreciate the moderate fluidity and easy interface that Maxis worked into it.  Making adventures is as fun as playing them for me, and the new weapons, upgrades, and other parts that  were added to this expansion are really neat, although I do wish there was a bit more variety to them.
Such a shame that Maxis had to be dissolved.  I had a preexisting account before getting the Steam version, so I can access the online community just fine, but for others who are first-timers with this version, I have heard that they cannot play online, which is a damn shame in and of itself.  This game is at its best when you are witnessing, interacting with, commenting on, and sharing content with others; it really creates the sense of an ever-expanding universe, and I appreciate that there are still people posting content on this game even after all these years.
This game may not be the most limitless universe sandbox you'll find (Lord knows that I've mulled over the potential of this franchise plenty, potential that will now sadly never be reached), but you'll still find a lot to enjoy.  Galactic Adventures is merely an expansion, but it multiplies the experience quite a bit and brings the game that much closer (but not quite close enough) to reaching its true potential.  I've heard Creepy and Cute is good as well, but I have yet to buy it.  Do yourself a favor and at least try out Spore, or Spore: Galactic Adventures if you've already got the main game.  Together, they still constitute one of my favorite gaming experiences, and that's not the nostalgia talking.
I highly recommend this game.  I've made so many memories playing this, and I hope other people get the chance to make some of their own.

If you like endless runners, T.E.C. 3001 is perfect for you. It's not really endless, but the gameplay is similar--run around at ridiculous speeds collecting stuff and avoiding obstacles. It's a simple concept done well. The controls are extremely responsive, and it's not all just the same thing. There are 3 level types. One where you have full control of T.E.C.'s movement, one where he's on 3 tracks, audiosurf style, and one where you have to just go straight and boost when needed. This manages to keep it fresh enough to stop you from getting bored. There's a ton of levels and it can get pretty challenging. For the price, there's no reason that you shouldn't buy this game.

After playing a bit of this game now I feel I can write an honest review on it, so here goes.
T.E.C 3001 is a runner, where you control a robot through various courses in different game modes. The campaign consists of 3 game modes, a freerun mode, a speed run mode and a drag race mode. On top of these campaign gamemodes there is a seperate mode to play which is the unlimited runner mode.
In freerun mode, you get full control of your character to jump between the various levels and layers of the pre-generated worlds. You can use all the controlls, boost, slide, jump and double jump to traverse the areas, being faced with obstacles like barriers and walls you can slide under, and speed boost power ups. Freerun requires you to take full advantage of these abilites, by facing you with walls that require precision timing for you to dodge past. This is where the game really shines, as you are not on set tracks and are free to jump away from the path entirely, only to come back in having looped around a tough obstacle. Throughout these stages there are checkpoints, so if you muck up right near the finish line you won't have to start from the very beginning which is a very forgiving bonus. These levels don't require you to take a set path, you can alternate between the many layers of the track at will which gives every replay a unique feeling and keeps the track fresh, for a time anyway.
Speed Run mode is a more traditional runner mode, reminiscent of games like Temple Run. You are stuck to one course where you must simply dodge the obstacles that are presented. You use the arrow keys to switch between the three lanes, having no option to jump out of the track like you can in Freerun. The tracks are usually straight forward and require you to pick up the collectables to finish.
Drag Race mode requires you to time your boosts, bound to the up arrow, to speed up and finish the course before the time is up. The obstacles in this mode are straight forward, and unlike the other two modes there is no way to switch between lanes. You are bound to the middle lane and must time your boosts with the icons on the track to get enough speed in time.
Unlimited Runner is more of a side mode, you won't be spending as much time on it as the campaign unless you like the feel of an endless track runner. It is a randomly generated track, built on the Speed Run mechanics, so there's not much to say about it.
Now these are my opinions on the gamemodes. Freerun, as I already stated, is certainly the strong point of the game. It is interesting and tries its best to stay that way, and will be the mode you look forward to while playing the campaign. Speed Run is fun, but gets old quickly. It is more enjoyable to play in the form of Unlimited Runner in my opinion because this really extends the longevity of it and allows for high score beating and the like. Drag Race feels like it was thrown in as a filler, because I honestly don't have much fun with it at all. It's repetive, and feels like a grind to complete, and not a unique experience. It gets boring quick and you probably won't look forward to playing it, or not as much as other modes.
For the price, T.E.C 3001 is an amazing game. It offers quite a bit of gameplay while staying fresh and interesting besides a few letdowns. It has simplistic yet beautiful visuals and a nice soundtrack, and is a great experience. If I were to change anything about it, it would be to remove the Drag Race game mode and try to add even more variety to Freerun (Tracks that curve upwards, requiring you to run on the roof?) and possibly some more variety to Speed Run to make it feel less repetitive. Other than these slight hinderances, it's almost a garaunteed buy for me and a rating of 8/10.

This is no rhythm game, this is a musical game. Solving a puzzle means composing a musical piece from short snippets, layered on several tracks (you get extra symbols for bass, drums, solo etc.). After all, if it still sounds great, can you really say you were wrong?
If you have an ear for music, listen to the trailer, and if you enjoy that synthetic sound, go for the game.
If you don't have an ear for music, stay away from this game: you'll be solving it by trial and error, if at all, and that's no fun.

This review might contain spoilers, be awared. Keep in mind that this is solely based on my opinion.
Furi can been seen as the game 'Hyper Light Drifter' in 3D arcade. The game has an nice unique style. However, it is not really worth the price you are paying. The reason why this game is so pricy is because of the soundtrack, which cost roughly 15 euro. When buying the game, you basically pay 10 euro for the game and 15 euro extra for the soundtrack which you don't even own. You can buy and own the soundtrack together with the game for 10 more extra euro (35 euro!?)... sorry but I see this as a rip-off. Nevertheless, I am not saying that this is a bad game. Furi is for those who love arcadish games with a high challenge curve and also potentially for people who likes to speedrun. Only for them, there is a replayability (which is my main concern).
You only fight bosses in this game. For some, it will take couple of hours against each boss and for others it might take less than 3 hours to beat. From there, hard mode will be unlocked. For me, it was already the finish line. I did not try hard mode and I did not feel like I wanted to replay the bosses again. Two reasons why: walking sequences are too much of a hassle (explained in the next paragraph) and this isn't a game you play for just 5 minutes. The bosses can eat a lot of your time because of the many phases you have to beat from a single boss and you cannot save mid-way (as expected from arcadish games).
What I also don't like about the game is the long walking pace between the bosses, which I think is the most useless part. There is like less than 30 min of walking throughout the whole game and you cannot skip it. The camera angle in these sequences really messes up your control. It forced me to use the auto walk function. During these sequences, you will get to hear bits and pieces from the guy who freed you. There are so many better ways to tell the story. I can imagine they wanted to have an unique approach to the story telling or give more of a cinematic feel to it. For me, it horribly failed.
Lastly, most music from the original soundtrack is not my favorite either (I only like the music in the trailer). Compared to Hyper Light Drifter, this music does not feel immersive.
As a verdict: The gameplay during bossfight is immense fun, but that's about it. I would recommend waiting for a sale on this game before buying. The price is too much.

Do you like bullet hell and the mechanics of Metal Gear Rising Revengence?
Well boy do I have a treat for you.
For those who are looking for more info, the game is simply bosses only with a total of
bosses. The rest is  just a "playable" cutscene I say playable, because you are simply walking towards the next boss while some random guy start saying♥♥♥♥♥♥ and even then, just press A(xbox controller) to auto walk so you can take a♥♥♥♥♥♥and get a drink if you don't care about the story, or have a wireless headset.
The bossfights themselves are split into multiple phases, you yourself have 3 life's, if you complete a phase you get a life back. And of course every phase will be harder than the last.
The gameplay itself is pretty well done, 9/10 bosses are fun to play and have some cool weird designs. The 10th is just an overglorified bullet hell.
The basics of combat is parry, dodge and shoot. Depending on the situation, all the patterns in the game are very well taught to you, and rarely should you feel you have no idea what is going on.
All the controls (with controller) feel great making for some really fun bossfights.
Personally I like the design, it looks cool, and the music complements it well. The story... I really tried to care, but honestly, couldn't at the end. Don't buy this game for the story.
In complete honesty though, is it worth €25? No, there is not much content in this game, and to prolong game time it asks you to play the game again, but harder, or go for speedrun mode. Currently not in the mood for trying that, maybe I will in the future. But those mode's don't make up for the price compared to the content. I completed the main game on normal difficulty in 5.4 hours. And to be fair, that is a bit short.
Although overpriced, I do recommend this game because it is a lot of fun. And if it is ever on sale for 40% or higher, it is definitely worth it.

Well.  I don't tend to write reviews, so take this one with full meaning in that I took the time to write this:
I knew nothing of Furi until it popped up in my Steam queue and I watched the 2 videos. (Cinematic & Gameplay)  The videos had me intruiged and wow was I right to pick this up.  This game hit me hard and fast from the beginning and kept pounding on me with the "get good or go home" mentality and it is addictive.  I haven't felt the fulfillment of completetion I was getting from Furi since my 1st playthrough of the original Dark Souls, and I'll tell you what, this may be a slightly different kind of hard, but this is harder.  If you're looking for a challenge this provides.
Visually the game is stunning, I love its art style, and the choreography was incredible, from the most wimpy of slashes, to the most brilliant of executes, you will be wowed over and over again.  Audibly, the sound effects are spot on and the soundtrack is incredible.  The song that plays for boss 3 & boss 8 are some of my favoite electronic songs ever now.
Bosses are challenging, varied in style, and will force you to improve at each turn.  The boss design rivals the best in the video game industy in my opinion, and that includes the "death mechanic" simple, but effective, and while not forgiving, it gives you a chance.
And crazy enough if all that doesnt convince you, the story is also pretty good, alot better than you may expect from a game like this.
--------------------------
TLDR:
Art & choreography: 9/10
Sound & music        : 8/10
Combat                    : 9/10
Boss design             : 10/10
Story                        : 8/10
All in all.  If you like a challenge, and are willing to put some effort into it, GET THIS.  You'll love it.

TL:DR - Fun with brilliant reply value thanks to randomly generated scenario's/characters.
I had the perfect party:  Danial, my randomly generated starter with tons of ammo, a lassie with a sphere to keep zombies at bay, an other guy who recently joined that I also gave guns/ammo to, and Alvis. A martial artist who sings after he attacks and he wore a wolf mask.
The final siege started and I was ready to rock. I played through DRTC multiple times and I never got this far and I knew my party was more than capable. I entered a building and found 2 grenades. I picked them up and either I pressed the wrong button or someone in my party used it. To my horror, a grenade was thrown in our faces and it all happened in a flash. Danial was blown out the building and he had that skull mark above him while 2 of my other members died inside. My heart sank.
Alvis, had low HP from the blast and survived but at this point I didn't care because there was no way I would survive the last siege with one guy at low HP and no guns.
Miraculously, I managed to weave between zombies using martial arts on any lone ones in the way. I swear if Alvis had stood for a second longer near the Zombies at the border he would have died but alas, he didn't. I made it to Canada!
The fall and rise of emotions that whole scene gave me was a blast.
PROS:
.No game plays out the same, so many different things can happen with the RNG
.Funny and light-hearted, not an edgy Zombie game does not take itself seriously.
.The music is good and wacky, it fits the tone of the game surprisingly well
.Just when you think you saw all the game has to offer, you have not.
.That feeling when you get good rng: AKA, finding a room with loads of food/ammo
.Every door you have not yet opened is marked with a small flash - Very Helpful!
.Risk for Reward gameplay - its getting dark, the music has turned ominous, the zombies are now faster. Do I enter this last building for more supplies or run back to the car?
.I have never felt too O.P. A lot of Zombie games make you a one man army near the end, but
DRTC can turn the tables on your supplies with random events
CONS:
.Gets addictive, losing in the game can be frustrating and makes you go"Just one more time"
.When the game gives you bad rng. (Group members arguing over a fart, etc) Be warned, this
game is a Troll but its the rng that makes it so interesting.
.Its hard to make out your characters in hordes of zombies.
.Sometimes you will be doomed by the hordes and you just have to accept it.
Overall, I totally recommend DRTC. It surprised me by how good it was because I normally don't like Zombie games yet this is the best zombie game I have ever played.
(Resident Evil 4 does not count, they are not Zombies)

as of 30th September 2017 they still have no dedicated servers for the game available so you can't host your own server without playing it at the same time.
Two years later the game now contains 4 maps rather than 2 maps (double the content!) unless you count the community created maps the devs just bundled with the game. From the store page right now:
The singleplayer/coop campaign is not existant yet to my knowledge.
I pre-ordered during Kickstarter and I can't say I regret it because the money went towards development. The game is not worth buying in it's current state though regardless how much I originally backed it for, it's not presently worth $25. It should be $5, MAYBE $10 at this stage due to the truly incomplete status of the game. It contains 2 maps, 1 weapon and a handful of incomplete animations. Seeing the state the game has been put into Steam at I would not buy this product, check back in a year or two if the game has not been cancelled due to lack of funds.

This game gets a big thumbs up from me. I love the tactical team-based gameplay which the developer has managed to bring back from the early Socom days on the PS2. These types of games have been far and few between for far too long, and I miss how the Socom series brought people together as a community. Most of the gaming friends that I have today, are from way back while I was playing Socom 2, 3 and Combined Assault on the PS2, and I feel that this game is already developing that same type of close-knit community.
H-Hour is certainly a breath of fresh air from the over-saturated first person shooter market. If you were a fan of such games as Socom 1, 2, 3, & Combined Assault(PS2), Socom: Confrontation(PS3), Ghost Recon Advanced Warfighter(Xbox 360 Version), Ghost Recon Advanced Warfighter 2(PS3/Xbox 360 Versions) and Metal Gear Online(PS3), then you will most likely enjoy the heck out of this game. If you've never payed a Socom game before, or any of the other games that I've just listed, then you're in for a pleasant surprise. The gameplay offered in H-Hour is extremely addictive, and just completely different from your typical run of the mill shooter on the market today.

In its current Early Access state the game is simply a shell of a full game.  It gives the players an idea of what the graphics will roughly look like in the final product and allows you to shoot some people along the way.
From what I understand, they had this game nearly completed with many more features and animations to the point of being a fairly finished game, but it was using the Unreal 3 Engine.  Now they are in the process of taking what they had on the Unreal 3 Engine and converting it to the Unreal 4 Engine, which isn't as simple as copy pasting.  So this is the current state of the game we are able to play, the beginning of this conversion.  So there are currently a lot of features not yet in the game that were in the Unreal 3 Engine version of the game, they took a slight step back to take a bigger step forward.  But it will take more time, clearly.
The game may not currently be worth the money for the gameplay in the current state, but I would argue that if you are a socom fan, it's worth the money for the support and funding so they can get the job done, because you can easily see and feel that even in this shell of a game, socom is in there, it has huge potential if it reaches its final state.

Land Plots (Since they're purely decorative as they are now):
- Farming capabilities
- Be able to set up automated shops (Sell items/buy from other people's shops.)
- Machines that do different things
Inventory/Loot system:
- Item drops with randomized stats and rarities
- Armor slots
- Crafting (Not too complicated, but just enough)

- Option to quickly trade items with other players
Combat/Exploration:
- Improve hit detection
- Ability points/tree and a clear leveling system
- More incentive to explore (Maybe be able to find rare strongholds with good/unique loot)
- Increase movement speed or make it possible to improve through items/ability tree
Social
- Make an ingame friendslist that's easier and quick to use
That's all I can currently think of. Summed up, I think the biggest improvements would be a loot system and improved inventory, ability tree/clear leveling system, and make land plots more interactive.

While similar to Race the Sun, I had much more fun with T.E.C. 3001!  A great run/dodge game to test one's hand-eye coordination, I whole-heartily recommend T.E.C. 3001 - especially if you like racing games!
Since I am an old fart, I appreciated the levels that locked you to your lane; this actually made it like a different game, as the "regular" levels have momentum to think about... can't just twitch through it!  Excellent variety!
The graphics are clean and crisp, nothing jaw-dropping, but this game should not be played for graphics alone (should any game?); the soundtrack is well-fitting, techno-based that completes a solid package of a game.  For the price, just buy it.
I use Linux (Mint 16 x64 Xfce) and the game runs very smooth (nVidia driver).  It is a great casual game that one can play for 30 seconds or 30 minutes.

T.E.C. 3001 is a nice little runner-platformer (of the 3D variety). Things get difficult quick, there will be lots of deaths, and the game is all about quick reflexes and precision in timing jumps and moving your character.
I like these types of games that are suited to a shorter playing session. Yes, it is on iTunes for iPhone/iPad (launched 2013), but worth noting it was on XBLIG even further back in 2011. So to disregard this as a cheap mobile game is folly.
Graphics and soundtrack in the game are fine. Nothing spectacular, but not bad either. Worth noting you can choose your color/theme, and also which soundtrack to play. Content is aplenty, and certainly worth $4. Game starts off slow, but within 10 levels you'll start feeling the challenge. For completionists, the 41 levels should keep you occupied and challenged for a bit.
All in all, if you're a fan of precision platformers, then this would suit you. Or if you just want a challenging game to take your mind off the "AAA" game you're been playing. But if you dislike games of this nature (everyone has their own tastes, right?), then maybe you should stay away.
UPDATE: Really loving the game the more I play it. The achievements are well-done and make you go back and play certain levels either faster, or to get all collectibles. Only complaint now is that...the level-specific achievements are too sparse!

This review contains no spoilers.
Warning: I would be very cautious about reading other reviews and being robbed of some of the best experiences the game has to offer.
The Witness is hands down the best puzzle game I have ever played.
The bite-sized puzzles never feel too imposing - you just about never look at a puzzle and think "I don't think I'm up for that. I think I'll come back to it tomorrow.".
The essence of the gameplay is the combination of those basic logic puzzles (the fundamental concepts of the puzzle boards) and a huge variety of environmental complications like colored panes of glass and tree limbs and erased lines and more. No other game mixes environmental puzzles and symbolic logic puzzles together so masterfully.
Another consequence of this unifying concept of the puzzle board is that you always know when you're looking at one. The game almost entirely lacks that Myst situation where you're wandering around unsure of where the next puzzle is. It also lacks the Myst problem of puzzles that are available, but impossible to solve until some other puzzle is solved first.
The method of teaching the "rules" of the symbols on the puzzle boards through carefully designed challenges without ever using any explicit explanation is downright brilliant. They're carefully designed to make you think you understand a rule, to give you a series of puzzles where the rule you've come up with will work, but then to suddenly confront you with a puzzle where you have to rethink. You'll frequently discover that you convinced yourself something was impossible without ever seeing evidence of that.
And none of the puzzles ever require guess-and-check.
If you're guessing and checking, you're making a mistake. You can play Sudoku by guessing numbers and seeing how far they get you - you'll eventually solve any Sudoku puzzle that way - but you're not really playing Sudoku if you do that. So it is with The Witness.
Once you understand all the pieces of the puzzle, it is always possible to solve it completely deductively. Learning the different ways to do this is a huge part of the game. Many complaints about the game center around the idea that the reviewer "learned all the rules" and then just spent hours and hours boringly brute-forcing puzzles. Learning the "rules" is just the start. The bulk of the game is not spent learning the rules, but learning the logical consequences of the rules that allow you to deductively solve puzzles. It isn't just about learning the rules of the dots, it's about learning that the rules of the dots imply that certain configurations are impossible. After you learn the rules, the subsequent boards will be about teaching you these implications.
The audio logs and videos can feel a bit preachy at times, but having listened to all of them now, I understand a lot beter what purpose they served. They can initially come across as a pretentious affectation, like some college student going around spouting random philosophy quotes to seem "deep", but in time I think the game does actually reveal a fairly legitimate depth to what it's trying to express.
And the final challenge, past the "end" of the game, is downright beautiful. While opinions may differ, I also found the reward for completing it to be far more worthwhile than the final rewards in most other games.
Fundamentally though, The Witness is a game about changes in perception. It's a game about looking at something again and again and then suddenly and very viscerally seeing it in a totally different light. Sometimes that's puzzles - sometimes it's re-examining how you think a symbol works or how you reason about a certain kind of puzzle. Other times the shift in perspective is more profound.
Penultimate warning: You will almost certainly want some paper and a pen. Maybe even some scissors.
Final warning: If you use a guide to get through much of the game, there is a very real possibility, thanks to a brilliant pieces of design near the end, that you will find yourself unable to complete it.

For the price of upto $3, I think the game is overall worth it. It's a nice experience, although short and not too challenging gameplay wise, it's a relaxed casual music game with great music that's enjoyable to listen to.
Sadly, it gets boring to listen to the same song over and over while trying to find out what node you were wrong with, and when you finally get it right, you'll just skip the song because you've heard it so many time until that moment of actual victory.
I think it would've been better if the song were to remain 'bland' (only the nodes you put in, no extra music), and when you actually try to play it (to check if you were correct) it adds all the other layers, to feel some measure of success and progression.
Apart from that, having actual parts of music development that don't occur from the nodes you've placed is rather confusing at points and there should at least be a way to disable that while testing out your song (apart from switching between layers).
At times it was hard to figure out which node was playing what type of music, and some nodes were mostly too quiet to hear and comprehend which required me to guess and check with the hint tool if I was correct or not.
The game doesn't really have any replayability, because once you've finished all 25 levels (I think I finished them in about an hour or two), you've heard all the songs and you wouldn't really go back to play those songs again.
There should be some sort of difficulty level per song (maybe something like 'easy' 'medium' 'hard') which include more/less nodes according to the difficulty, and more song complexity accordingly. Some sort of rating (according to time or some other measurement of performance) may improve replayability.
Lastly, a 'free-creation' mode would've been great, using all the nodes in the game to create your own levels or songs to share, or just to enjoy on your own. That would've changed the game immensly, making it a whole new experience.
Overall, it's a pretty nice game, lacks in a lot of respects, but for $3 it's pretty worth it just to give it a try, and hope the developers will make a 2nd version with some gameplay improvements :P

This is a love-it-or-hate-it thing.
Yes, the whole game is maze puzzles. Yes, there's barely any explicit narrative -- and the little bit that *is* there is buried very, very deep. I went 50 hours in The Witness before I felt I understood what the island was, or why I was there. And there's still some doubt there, frankly.
And... none of that bothers me. I found the puzzles tremendously engaging. I felt like a genius when I solved them, and discovering the endless, clever twists on the mechanics was a constant delight. I was happy when my puzzle-solving prowess was, inevitably, rewarded with more puzzles to solve. That's what I wanted to do: it's just like an FPS game rewarding you with a bigger gun, and more things to shoot with it.
So this all hinges on whether or not you personally enjoy the puzzle mechanics of The Witness. If you do, the game will absolutely fascinate you; if you don't, it'll seem an interminable slog. I don't think there's much middle ground there, and there's just no way to know until you try it.
If $40 seems like too big a risk, there's no shame in waiting for a sale. For me, though, the game was worth every penny, and then some.

This game is a masterpiece.  It takes the best elements of the puzzle/exploration genre (i.e. Myst, etc.) and completely eliminates the more frustrating elements of that genre.  For example, in Myst you could be stuck forever because you didn't realize some teeny-tiny pixel was a button that you needed to push.  The developers probably didn't even intend for that to be a hard puzzle, but you just didn't see it.  Well in The Witness every single puzzle is plainly displayed and very obvious.  Furthermore, the sequence of puzzles is obvious and the game does an incredible job of very fairly teaching you each rule you need to learn to solve each puzzle before later testing you on that knowledge.  This teaching was one of the more impressive elements of the game.  The end result is a type of puzzle where you could easily imagine the majority of them being in a straight puzzle game (no adventure or exploration, etc.) but that would be somewhat boring and The Witness has an excellent atmosphere of intrigue that makes you want to find out what is beyond the next gate.  The downside of this puzzle approach is that The Witness does not have the same immersive feeling as a game like Myst which had puzzles seamlessly integrated into the environment itself.  However, if that kind of immersive puzzle is something you love then The Witness actually has you covered there too!  I won't say anything that spoils the fun, but there is a whole set of puzzles that are not required to finish the game that do not show up on clearly marked panels...
My recommendation to anyone who plays this game: DO NOT look up walkthroughs!  Seriously, you can figure it out.  If you're stuck on a puzzle just walk away and come back another day.  I can't count the number of times I was so close to giving up and looking up a walkthrough and when I came back the next day I was able to figure it out.  I'll admit I did use one hint and that was for one of the bird call puzzles.  But most of the fun of this game is in the moments of finally figuring out a hard puzzle by yourself.

I would describe the game as a fast paced boss fighting arena paired with a bullet hell. You move freely around the arena while having a top-down perspective. The camera zooms out as you move farther away from your oponent, and zooms in as you close the distance. I will make an own section about the combat-system.
You are fighting an enemy one vs one (later in the game a boss spawns in weak minions), which are progessivly getting stronger and more difficult to fight. The enemies are more like an old school boss fight with multiple stages and health bars. They change the way they fight with each new stage, and each stage has mostly two phases. Some opponents have only one phase in their earlier stages.
You are in a top-down perspective fighting the enemy. Dodging projectiles and melee attacks, while trying to hit the enemy.
You zoom in having more of a side perspective and the focus changes to sword play.
After each stage, your HP is maxed.
At the last stage, the enemy stays at one position and is invulnerable. This is when the pure bullet hell starts. I hope you played some because they can be quite difficult. After you dodged enough projectiles, lasers and waveshocks, they are a one hit kill.
The opponents have around 6 stages, while you have 3 lifes, with which you can try the same stage again, but at full HP. If you run out of lifes, you have to fight the boss from the beginning again.
Before and after each fight, you have to walk (slowly) to the next area. Luckily you can auto-walk by using the Dash button. In this phase the story will be advanced. If you are not interessted in the story though, and just want to fight, you will be held back since this progress cannot (to my knowledge) be skipped.
You are a prisoner locked up on floating islands above earth. For what reason is not known (to you as the player), but will be told by progressing through the game by a side character talking to you. The side character, a mysterious and weird looking man with a rabit mask, freed you from your confiment, and wants you to escape with him, since he wants to get out of this prison as well, and needs your help to do so.
The combat is held simple and in my opinion responsive enough.
You have one button for your melee attacks with which you can perform a 4 hit combo with a slower knock down attack at the end. You can hold the attack button to charge it up to dash forwards, deal more damage, and stagger the enemy. This also destroys normal projectiles, and some give you a health drop. At maxed charge you can stun your enemy.
Luckily you are equiped with a pistol with which you can shoot your opponents form a distance. The projectiles have relative slow speed, but you can also charge your weapon up which deals more damage, while also having fast speed, and knocks down the enemy. In phase two this is replaced for charging up, which gives you a damage boost on the next attack.
Upon a succesful block you regain 1 segment of your HP back, and if timed right you will parry your opponent which will additionally stun them. Blocking a projectile will shoot it back on your enemy at a very fast speed. Some will spawn a health drop, which gives you 1 segment of HP back. The enemy is also able to parry you, and then tries to attack you. This attack (or attacks) can only be blocked, but you don't regain health from that.
You can punish an enemy while they are stunned. It deals decent damage and shows you a short cut-scene. Punishing an opponent removes all projectiles from the arena.
With this you can dash around and dodge the enemy's attack. This can be charged as well, which then lets you cover more distance. Bear in mind that, if the arena has an edge, you can fall down and take damage (1 segment of your HP). You can charge your melee attack and dash at the same time. The enemy can also evade you. Keep that in mind!
You are running quite fast, but if you are shooting or charging your weapon, you will be walking really slowly.
Both you and the enemy can be knocked down. While on the ground, there can't be any damage dealt. You stand up when you want to move or after some time automatically.
Enemies can't fall off the edge and if they evade your charged melee attack there, you'll fall.
If you wanna play the game for fun and for the story, go ahead! It's a good game and fun to play!
For my personal taste, it has too many little, annoying things, that drive me mad, so if the things I listed could potentially drive you mad as well, you should maybe wait for a discount.

My opinion of this game has bounced back and forth a number of times - my hopes were high, and comparing it to full price game like Revengeance would not be fair. As the gameplay went on, however, the novelty begins to fade, and it wasn't until I unlocked Furier (the hardest difficulty) and began aiming for speedruns and S Ranks that the game really started to shine. If you don't see yourself playing this game more than once, IT IS HARD TO RECOMMEND if it isn't on sale, but if you get hooked, it will provide many more hours than the three it took for my initial playthrough.
Pro: This game is purely about fighting bosses, and you can see the love poured into some of these fights, where some bosses have purely unique ideas like briefly turning into a 2d fighting game perspective with a view similar to oldschool Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, et al. Bosses also differ wildly in design, making you wonder what will show up next. Designs including futuristic glowing warriors, dual-crossbow-wielding angels, samurai, and fishy mutants.
Con: At the same time, however, the protagonist has a relatively threadbare move set, and there's only so many ways you can re-use mechanics, like ground-circles reminiscent of WoW or FFXIV (aka "move out of the fire") and keep them interesting, especially when most boss fights take place in circular arenas, perhaps with a hole in the center or without a railing on the side. In this regard, once you've played the game for an hour, you've seen most of what it has to offer, except for boss-specific mechanics like "oh, they have a sniper rifle and can one shot me."
While the arenas themselves are pretty much circular, their designs do change quite a bit, from rain-soaked stone during a thunderstorm, a swampy sewer, an unfortunately unused astral arena you only walk through, and windy / snowy floating platforms. The different environments paint a pretty full spectrum.
The game is short. Without trying to spoil, expect slightly less than a dozen bosses, and expect only a couple hours of gameplay. I was walled by 2 bosses briefly, the 3rd and the 8th (who wields a weapon similar to the player's - you'll know him when you see him), but nothing that kept me stuck for long. In this regard, it seems like the difficulty has been overhyped, as I was hearing comparisons to Dark Souls but I managed to pump this whole game out in one sitting without much frustration.
Pro: The player has infinite ammo, but the game finds neat ways to mitigate your gun's effectiveness, ranging from a warrior with a shield that reflects your bullets in more dangerous ways (such as homing shots, ways, or giant clusters). Other ways include a boss who stops time, so all bullets, both yours and theirs, just hang in the air, turning what was originally a pretty ranged boss into a melee fight. Ideas like this are where the game grabs your attention and doesn't let go.
Pro: Many boss fights try to end dramatically with an intimidating last phase, many briefly turning into a bullet-hell style affair (although obviously not on par with a real bullet-hell).
Con: Going back to "there's only so many ways to use this mechanic and feel fresh," the bullet-hells begin to feel pretty samey after the first couple times. Shoot enemy bullets to make room, and dodge out of bad waves / pulses. Got it.
Pro: All parry-able attacks are indicated by a flash, so you're never left wondering "could I have parried that? Did I screw up?"
Pro: After beating the game, there are numerous unlocks, including a practice mode to fight any boss at the difficulty of your choice, a speed run mode, and a new difficulty. This new difficulty is not just a scaling up of boss damage and hp - it adds new effects to existing mechanics, which is a massive plus in my book. Furier (the hardest difficulty) is what feels like the real game, where you don't have time to react and there's much less healing available, forcing you to master reacting to bosses, learn how to parry their combos, and learn when you can boost to do more damage.
Let's talk about healing - you can parry boss moves to heal yourself. You can interrupt some boss' attacks to bait them into doing a parryable combo, effectively feeding yourself more hp, assuming you can always parry. Missing one parry and getting hit will mitigate multiple successful parries - you take much more damage from 1 attack than you can recover parrying the same hit. There are also green bullets fired by bosses, that you can break for healing. This provides an overabundance of healing in several of the boss fights on normal difficulty, but the green bullets, to the best of my knowledge (I'm only halfway through Furier atm, I'll update if I learn otherwise) are non-existent in Furier, the hardest difficulty, providing more of a challenge.
Pro: While music taste is subjective, the music does change according to boss phases, getting more and less intense. I love it when games do that.
Pro: Lastly, let's talk about boss phases. Bosses have many phases, broken up into subphases. A subphase may consist of the boss running around and being a relatively ranged fight, then the next subphase is a close encounter melee fight that you can NOT run away from. In this example phase, once those 2 subphases are done, you move on to the next boss phase, typically with the boss gaining a new weapon or a new moveset, for example, pulling a scythe *almost literally* out of their ***. You can see the number of phases the boss has in the top right, and similarly, you also have "phases" of your own, except in your case, it is your lives. In this way, the player and the boss seem almost like equal players in the game, sharing the same "lives" / "phases" mechanic. Why does the distinction beween these phases and subphases matter? When you lose a life, you go to the beginning of the boss phase you're currently on, so any progress on subphases is lost - you must beat all relevant subphases in one go to make it to the next phase. Lose all of your lives, and its back to the beginning of the entire boss fight.
Story: simply put, do NOT play this game expecting a great or coherent story. The game largely revolves around its bosses and not much else.
If you're in it for the long run, playing the harder difficulty, trying to S rank bosses, or want something to speed run, then give the game a shot. If you think you'll only play it once, however, you're better off passing or waiting for a sale due to its very short length, as well as the fact some bosses and mechanics feels pretty similar as the novelty of the game and your few mechanics begins to wear.

All in all I absolutely love this game, and cannot wait to see what The Game Bakers have in store next.

The Ball is neither good or bad, and feels crude and mostly empty. Areas are consistently walled-in with invisible walls that bring back memories of late 90's shooters, and full of giant arena-like spaces that feel a lot like Serious Sam but filled with only four enemy types that are so sparse that it just makes one wonder why such expansive maps were necessary, while you are bunny-hopping for 5-10 minutes straight to get to the other side. The story would be good, if a giant ball and hammer could pass off for advanced alien technology that could subjugate a people. Instead, I just kept wondering how that giant boulder I was lugging around could make or break a civilization, or how anyone could have the patience to traverse those puzzle-ridden rooms every time they needed to get to the neighboring town.
Survival levels do not really add anything to the game either, and boil down to standing in a corner, methodically rolling down wave after wave of the same enemies. Adding bosses, or larger enemies that require traps to kill, would have made survival mode a lot more fun. The Portal map is probably the standout of the game, with the additional mini-campaign being quite the opposite as it is way too long and does not allow saving mid-level.
All-in-all, The Ball is worth playing, especially if you mock with the configuration file and make it run in modern resolutions, but you would not miss anything if you skip it and play something better instead.

A solid game.
Definitely feels like an A grade game rather than AAA grade. with minor bugs and a lack of polish. It feels like a game that stayed within its modest budget and scope. Despite all this, the puzzle and environment is kept very solid and considering the small, unheard of dev team, that's quite an acomplishment.
The game feels fresh throughout with new locations and puzzle elements constantly thrown at you.
Story is surprisingly uniqe and interesting, trickle-fed through text found in secrets.
A few minor complaints would be average sound design, getting stuck on terrain multiple times and having to restart the whole level, or the max resolution being 1080p (though this being a Unreal game, perhaps it can be fixed with .ini tweaks). There was nothing game breaking like crashes or corruption.
I feel like this game takes an old school approach to puzzles, more of a trial and error style with little information given to you as you enter a room. You have to walk and analyse your surroundings before you can even start puzzling. At first this was a bit jarring to gameplay, but once I got into the swing of things I really enjoyed it - a breath of fresh air.

WARNING LONG REVIEW...
It's P2A = Pay-to-Advance with a small splash of P2W (Pay-to-Win).  It's not necessarily pay-to-win because there are comparable free ships, if you don't mind being slightly: slower, less damage, less hull...and other minor differences in most cases, but regardless it will take you forever to get to rank 15 without premium.  (((WARNING SHIP PACKS RANK YOU INSTANTLY TO THE RANK OF PURCHASED SHIP PACK....ugh = Pay-to-Advance failure.  I personally got top rankings in PvP, played PvE and was always top scorer among friends and especially solo-queues (a bit too easy) and it still would take forever to rank up.  So buy premium?  This is what they want more than anything and their thoughts are obviously wanting people to buy at least the 30-day premium per month ($10.50 USD).  At least it's not standard $15/month.  This game has more of an app game franchise feel, but more on the negative end example = beautiful, fun, can be exciting and eventful, but centered around spending money and of course it should be in free-to-play, but last year to last 6 months especially got worse.  Game keeps getting better, community has its ups and downs, but not really getting all that big and it never will; due to people realizing just this.  I have personally got around 50-60 people to play this (friends & viewers) and only 2 play anymore and I asked around and the responses were all the same or close to similar. #1 reason = Pack Prices
The best F2P games are the ones that have more aesthetic in purchasing options than the racing past your friends and/or one of the best ships for money to instantly rank up (This makes people feel left out if they can't afford the fast advance).  My argument is even in top ranked matches the Tiger can still rule over the Lions, so player skill still plays a major role and guess what?......If you are the type to take the very slow road to top pilot ranking = you will own those (majority) that raced ahead due to having 10 times the amount of matches to achieve your experience.  Plus you will have the most rewarding road as far as modules, credits, more daily login rewards, weapons, etc, etc....
CONS__________________
1. Anywhere you see a reward of some kind you will always see what you could've had if and only if you had premium = "VERY ANNOYING" to most!
2. Buying Ship Packs (needs a Markdown) advances players instantly to the highest ranking ship in that pack. (UNSKILLED COMMUNITY at higher to max pilot ranks)  This cheapens the very quality of the player community.
3. One of the slowest advancing games I have ever played in over 22 years of gaming experience......sigh
4. Premium missiles ...ugh
5. Additional Devices = one is Galactic Standards only (Real Money in-game Currency)
6. Missions that are twice your rank are available in one or more of your allowed quests quite frequently.  Say you are new and rank 2....well a suggested for rank 10 can show up...odd right? Maybe just another one of their snares set to Pay-to-Advance method.
7. Admin immaturity.  Don't get me wrong there are some good/bad in all games, but the majority seems to be very young and/or very inexperienced, they will show favoritism openly, not very supportive or helpful compared to most game communities.
8. Cost of things.....not really talking about the real money currency, but the modules, weapons and anything that can be equipped to your ship.  Especially the costs to level up these parts...crazy expensive!  Well unless of course you have premium.  So BUY IT NOW! .....or some galactic standards.  Even the faction based costs are crazy in cost starting at blue to purples.
___SPECIAL NOTE: For fastest ranking up possible for free just save your money until you are higher ranks, this way you will have tons of money once you hit higher ranks, but in turn you may rank up slower due to using less than mediocre gear most of the time, but you might have some luck at looting who knows.
9. No group?  Not going to be as much fun until you do.  Feeding off of PUGS, which mostly care less about win/lose is not the best way to start.
10. Community is not growing the way it easily could.
11. Many changes over time to the point new players are confused very easily.  Example = my viewers, subscribers and followers responses
PROS__________________
1. Beautiful Game!  I mean the ships are all amazing looking and the hangar over time got great in its own right.
2. Best control out of all (realistic) space flight simulators I have ever played. I love Space Engineers, = worst for example.
3. When in Team the game is crazy fun. (Join a corporation)
SPECIAL NOTE: The best corporations are the ones that do not recruit less than rank 10 or some other similar requirement (Shows that you will stay around)[At least none I know of].  So your best bet is to join and grow with a newer corporation then later on moving onto a better setup corporation, if you’re not lucky enough to find a rebuilding corporation to take advantage of.  To explain a bit further you want a events, weekly runs, and many other opportunities a structured corporation can offer (really can change your gaming experience), but like everything else you have some that are too demanding so move on.
4. Constant Evolution & Growth.  What I mean here about growth is not the community size, because that is not changing much at all, but in game mechanics, visuals, available ships and updates.
5. Ship Customization.
6. Maps & Game Modes.
All in all not a bad game, I have more reasons to hate this game than I do to like it, but the true fact of the matter is that in moderation I enjoy playing at times.
Final Rating = 5.75 = 0.75 over not recommending
5.75/10
**Note my original rating over a year ago was around 7.5**
Conclusion:
Although a very fun game to play.... Admins are the worst, Prices are crazy (Packs, GC, Credits and Premium) and will decide this games fate = already has with the lack of growth. In my circles 90% played and will not return.  Hope not all circles have this same experience and they wise up and price things better for a F2P game.  Maybe one day they will figure out that even at 1/3 the costs to the consumer with 5 times the sales they would have a greater chance to get closer to a mainstream game and have greater success all around.  When people talk about space games this game is not on the lists...I truly hope things turn around one day :)

As a fan of puzzle games, I find it hard to recommend The Witness.
The price point is very steep, the storyline is very barebones and pretentious, the (normal) ending is a royal kick in the balls, and the rules to new puzzles are often poorly represented. There are even some solutions that require you to take screenshots and solve them outside of the game. I'm not sure about everyone, but I prefer to have all the tools to solve a game within the game itself. I'm not a fan of solutions that break immersion.
It's a shame because I would consider myself a fan of Jonathan Blow. Even with the game's faults, the environment is gorgeous with thought provoking set peices. Despite everything feeling 'dead' and 'sterile', there is a persistent sense of mystery that makes you want to explore all that the world has to offer. Every zone has a theme, every theme has a new rule, and every new rule causes you to think differently.
On paper, this sounds like a lot of fun, and I would be lying if I said I
have fun, but in practice this game is designed to be solved very slowly with every zone containing several mental road blocks. While I'm all for challenge in video games, it should not come at the cost of proper pacing. There are quite a few puzzles to solve and though some are genuinely clever, most involve contorting the camera to the 'exact' angle required to complete a path, look at the environment a certain way, see through a specific window, look at just the right reflection, and so on. It gets to be more awkward than enjoyable.
If you're a fan of puzzle/artsy games, I would pick this up for a 1/4 of its current price. Everyone else: Avoid.

Review:
The beginning of a game has too many repetitive puzzles. I was forcing myself through the beginning and the middle of it. Sometimes I felt frustration because of seldom rewards from puzzles. Too many of easy puzzles there and that felt like a drudge-work. Where is all the fun? The worst experience was when I solved couple of puzzles and nothing just happened. What was the point?
The end-game puzzles were really good and they gave me a feeling of hand crafted experience. But I am sure that not many of you will get to the end-game to enjoy it. End-game puzzles cannot compensate for the overall boring process of the game.
The game has ended too-indie-like (read it as no real ending at all). This game lacks the story, in fact it lacks almost everything except nice views here and there and puzzles. Sad face.
The whole island feels like a crazy big tutorial with too stretched learning experience of too many puzzles. The end-game felt like the game finally has started, but it was not long enough to compensate for boring exploration experience of the island.
But again. No mystery gets uncovered in the game. There is no plot, no story, no nothing to think about afterwards. Random philospohy felt like a sand into my eye. Too cheap, sorry.
Compared to Braid it is:
a) a step back as a game
b) a step forward in nerdiness of puzzles.

This might be the most polarizing game experience of my life...
On one hand, The Witness is both beautiful and brilliant from an artistic and design sense. The lighting, materials and rendering are pure eye candy. The entire island integrates perfectly to form a continuous chain of incredibly intelligent puzzles.
On the other hand, The Witness is also one of the most boring, poorly paced and non sensical games I have ever played. The story is told through audio logs which have no consitant theme and are mostly told out of context. While the rendering is great, the envirronment itself is bland comprised mostly of generic trees, rocks, cave walls, brick walls, wood planks, etc. Almost nothing has character in this world. The vast majority of the puzzles consist of standing in front of a grid and drawing lines to separate different icons. This gets very old and repetitive.
Regardless of the low entertainment value, I have to reccomend this game beacuse it is just too inteligently designed to pass up. There are a lot of great ideas here.  Everyone should witness at least the first few hours of brilliance before the repetitive bordem sets in.

A very good game, though not without it's share of issues. The core gameplay is where it shines, boss fights are satisfying and engaging, though some are rather lackluster at time.
The game's difficulty at Furi mode is...decent. I felt that it was a little too easy and I hope that Furier will provide a little more of a challenge.
Story wise there's not much to go on, and that's either great or annoying depending on the person playing. The game continues not telling you much anything until the very end. Questions are answered pretty conclusively at the end as well. But I enjoyed what there was; and I definitely think the game wouldn't be as strong without it.
The walking sequences give you the chance to look at the really beautiful scenery; but if you aren't invested in the little bits of flavor dialogue they can be lengthy, ardous breaks from the action. The camera going every which way without the controls switching up made it feel confusing and harder than it should have been. There were points that I honestly felt it should have just auto-walked me through, then at least I could enjoy the scenery without fighting the controls.
Price tag feels just a tad bit too high for my liking. If you're a speedrunner/challenge gamer you'll definitely get your money's worth out of replaying it, but for normies like myself the experience felt just too plain short for the $25. Especially if you're like me and found the normal mode rather easy (I died a total of once against
and 3 chances for a phase seems crazy to me. Though there were incredibly tense moments were it all came down to that last health pip, only to pull back.
Boss design is nice, very No More Heroes inspired from the looks of it. They all have these kind of wierd quirky bits to them that make them unique. Some will challenge you more than others, there's some that'll annoy you more than others, but they all feel *good*. The post fight cutscenes also feel a bit lackluster sometimes; the ones I think are the most important seem to have little to no dialogue. Then again, story may not be all that important to a challenge gamer, and it keeps up the pacing.The ordering of them could have been revised I think, but they'll all challenge you in one way or another.
Looking at the above, you may wonder why I'm rating this up. Remember the "core gameplay" I mentioned? I'll elaborate on it a little. First of all, IT'S ♥♥♥♥ING GREAT. It feels fluid, fast, skillful, and fair. There's no handholding, there's no improvement trees, there's no absurd unlockables. It gives you the controls, and that's what you get. All the improvements happen when you learn to time your parries, when you learn how to perfectly dodge that one annoying attack, when you develop strategies to help play better and faster (For example, purposely normal parry all of a combo string for the health, and learn how to super-parry the final blow to mooch health from each string and get the counter hit.). It switches between bullet hell and close range action frequently enough to feel balanced. I can't stress this enough, the gameplay is what you're here for. The story is ok, the music is good, the fighting is great.
Overall, it could be improved, and I sure hope it does if it ever gets a sequel. But it's worth the time if you're willing to pay the toll. Just be ready for it to be a bit high for the content.

What can I say about this game?
Well, when I found this game I was just lazily scrolling through games on steam. When I saw it in my suggestions, I didn't think much. The description had me confused and I just didn't really see it as something I would play just based off of that. Then, I watched the video and I found myself unable to stop thinking about the game. A day later, I found it on my wish list. The day after that, I found it in my library and I was starting it up. I was scared I'd regret it considering I never buy games that fast. But all of the reviews I'd read were positive. I only saw 28 negative so I didn't think it'd be that bad. So then I began to play.
When I started, I didn't understand some of it. I felt like it wasn't my type of game before I even had my first customer. Then as I began to talk to the customers, I'd laugh and cry and find myself absorbed in the conversations. Without saying any spoilers, I found myself in love with all of them. Stella and Dana ended up being my "favorite" characters but honestly? All of them are fantastic. Alma felt like the best friend I could just b.s. with about nothing. Dorothy became my comfort when things seemed bad. Joh-I mean...Gil, was that guy I could just tease because it was fun. Dana is the best boss. 'Nough said. Stella is so full of love. Plus, those "ears" <3 I love her. Sei...I found myself genuinely worrying for Sei and honestly adore her. Virgilio was a bit annoying but in the end, I found myself enjoying his visits as well. Kira*Miki was such a sweet girl. Kim inspired me. Streaming-chan....Annoyed me but she was still a cool character. Jill...What can I say about Jill? I relate...So hard to this woman. As a main character she's exactly what I want. I love her so much and I don't think I can even say why without spoiling things.
Look, if I really try to talk about this game, we'll be here all day. What all of the above boils down to, is that this is a fantastic game. If you're unsure about buying it, just buy it.
This game gets a 10/10 from me.

They may not be able to get toiler paper, but they can make a good game. VA-11 HALL-A is what you get when 2 venezuelan weebs get together and put their love of cyberpunk, anime, and cute girls into one package and sell it for 14.99. Valhalla is a good game. Or is it? Can it really be considered a game? Are VNs games? All valid questions, questions that don't have a single answer:
Valhalla does have a lot of reading, and there's no voice acting, so reading is the only way to play the game, but it's not like a traditional VN where you read a bunch of stuff, make some choices, choose a girl you want to ♥♥♥♥ and go into her route, Valhalla is a cyberpunk bartending simulator, and most of your interactions with the characters will be behind the bar, making drinks for them, which is the main gameplay element, since in the game, instead of choosing dialogue options, what drinks you get your clients can influence their mood, what they say in their next visit, and in some cases even the endings.
The bartending minigame isn't too complicated, and you don't need to remember how to make drinks, just what the person asked. From there, it's as easy as looking up the recipe in the in game computer and dragging the ingredients (or using qwerty) and hitting mix, or in some cases adding ice or aging the drink.
But that's not the most important part, where the game shines through is in the characters: The writer succedeed in making realistic (for a cyberpunk setting) characters, with real problems and personalities, who you are actually interested in, and made even more interesting by the volatile political climate the game is set in. Without giving spoilers, many things will happen in the background that you don't take part in, but definitely affect you, your clients and the whole city
I wholeheartedly recommend valhalla. If you're a weeb this game is for you, but even if you're not there's much more to the game than waifus, if you just ignore the anime artstyle
