This game is suppose to be a soul successor of the famous title Socom Us Navy Seals, but falls short with many many fundamental problems.
I wouldnt recommend you to pick up this game till maybe about 3-4 months down the road, where I can see the Devs picking up their act and implementing a competitive side to the game.
Details:
Character/movement - The Characters you control are very robotic, very little sway or any fluid movement, when controlling the gun you dont see or feel like your receiving any kick back from the gun. its like the gun was mounted on a rock that can have the ability to move around. Jumping around feels like your on the moon, being able to shoot as if you were standing still or your running through the air. lots of things that your character will get stuck on, like pivots in the ground, rubble that should be easily cleared, or inclined terrain that anyone can walk up on. Your Character doesnt seem to have any inertia, or body weight when moving around and can change direction(strafe or back pedal) on a drop of a dime with no transfer of weight being displayed. your back pedal is the same speed as if you run forward. you cant dive properly and with many bugs with Dolphin Pop Up Animation exploits(sliding off the ground being able to shoot accurately and still be mobile).
Characters dont feel like they receive damage from anything. Bullets, Pellets, Grenades, or Fall Damage. Character does not slow down when receiving damage untill dead.
Movement Speed is way too fast and arcady to believe you are playing a human character with combat gear and weapons.
There is no Sprint button, You either Press a button to walk, or you move around at a run/jog speed in all directions. No Ability to put your gun down to sacrifice for top flight speed.
Gunplay - The Aiming system is One Dimensional which is point and shoot, There is no general aim or focused aim. There are scopes for the Snipers, but if you have to make a long range shot with a AR or SMG, you will have to scope in with your binocular zoom out and shoot in the regular point and click Classic View). There is no depth in the shooting mechanics, you are set in a battle stance that you are shooting as if you are looking down the sights of the gun all the time(and still are able to move around at jog-running speed in all directions)
- Stances play no role in how you control your gun. Same bullet pattern, same spread.
-All guns pretty much do the same damage, have the same kind of bullet spray, and dont have any feel.
- Fire Rates and How many bullets the gun has really makes the difference in the game.
-Holding down the trigger will only kick your spray pattern so much till it stops at the top of the cross-hair circle. And it will automaticly return to the original point where you started shooting.
Sub Machine Guns can out snipe any gun class. If you want a challenge use the Assault Rifles or Sniper and feel the struggle.
Pistols suffer from bullet delay and do very little damage.(Desert Eagle is the pistol of choice because of its different damage)

Here is a cherry pie recipe that i love
4 cups fresh or frozen tart cherries
1 to 1 1/2 cups granulated sugar
4 tablespoons cornstarch
1/8 tablespoon almond extract (optional)
Your favorite pie crust or pie dough recipe for 2 crust pie
1 1/2 tablespoons butter, to dot
1 tablespoon granulated sugar, to sprinkle
Place cherries in medium saucepan and place over heat. Cover. After the cherries lose considerable juice, which may take a few minutes, remove from heat. In a small bowl, mix the sugar and cornstarch together. Pour this mixture into the hot cherries and mix well. Add the almond extract, if desired, and mix. Return the mixture to the stove and cook over low heat until thickened, stirring frequently. Remove from the heat and let cool. If the filling is too thick, add a little water, too thin, add a little more cornstarch.
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Use your favorite pie dough recipe. Prepare your crust. Divide in half. Roll out each piece large enough to fit into an 8 to 9-inch pan. Pour cooled cherry mixture into the crust. Dot with butter. Moisten edge of bottom crust. Place top crust on and flute the edge of the pie. Make a slit in the middle of the crust for steam to escape. Sprinkle with sugar.
Bake for about 50 minutes. Remove from the oven and place on a rack to cool.

Valve might not be able to count to 3, but they did something great when they made Portal. Sure, they did the same thing with Half-Life 2, but Portal is the big surprise. When most companies made a puzzle game, they give you puzzles to solve, and that's it. However, with Portal, you got a puzzle, some hilarious dialog from a murderous A.I., and when you solve the puzzles in the test chamber, you move ahead and get that reward of more funny dialog, and sometimes see something interesting such as signs of previous test subjects. This "reward" for completing puzzles, even if not a tangible in-game object, made Portal more fun for me.
Other companies have followed suit with this: The Turing Test has an A.I. that talks to you after each puzzle, Quantum Conundrum has John DeLancey (the actor who played Q in Star Trek) talking to you between puzzles, and even the Uncharted games, which do have shooting segments and such, have side characters like Sully to talk to you and say funny or interesting things between puzzles. "Just do puzzles" might suffice for some gamers, but Valve and other companies have lit beacon to show the way for making first person puzzle games now.
It costs a bit extra to add those bells and whistles of dialog between puzzles and interesting banter, etc., but it's worth it. The Ball couldn't keep me playing it long at all. Why do I want to finish? It's been long enough that I could play Portal, Portal 2, Quantum Conundrum, etc. and have forgotten many of the puzzle solutions, so I could just play one of those again and be more entertained thanks to the reward that isn't present in The Ball. Even with non-puzzle games such as first person shooters, unless the gameplay loop is a 9/10 or a 10/10 for me on its own, I'm probably going to stop playing after a little while, because story, interesting events, dialog, and characters are very important to me, and a game devoid of these things that hasn't completely ensnared me will have me walking away to a game I enjoy more.
TL;DR: In an era when puzzle games have already evolved to include rewards in the form of enjoyable dialog, The Ball ignores this evolution and sticks to its guns, for better or for worse. I felt it was worse for it. A companion either in person or over a radio, or an enemy in either of those positions, talking to you, would have easily had me sit to play through to completion.

As a fan of puzzle games, I find it hard to recommend The Witness.
The price point is very steep, the storyline is very barebones and pretentious, the (normal) ending is a royal kick in the balls, and the rules to new puzzles are often poorly represented. There are even some solutions that require you to take screenshots and solve them outside of the game. I'm not sure about everyone, but I prefer to have all the tools to solve a game within the game itself. I'm not a fan of solutions that break immersion.
It's a shame because I would consider myself a fan of Jonathan Blow. Even with the game's faults, the environment is gorgeous with thought provoking set peices. Despite everything feeling 'dead' and 'sterile', there is a persistent sense of mystery that makes you want to explore all that the world has to offer. Every zone has a theme, every theme has a new rule, and every new rule causes you to think differently.
On paper, this sounds like a lot of fun, and I would be lying if I said I
have fun, but in practice this game is designed to be solved very slowly with every zone containing several mental road blocks. While I'm all for challenge in video games, it should not come at the cost of proper pacing. There are quite a few puzzles to solve and though some are genuinely clever, most involve contorting the camera to the 'exact' angle required to complete a path, look at the environment a certain way, see through a specific window, look at just the right reflection, and so on. It gets to be more awkward than enjoyable.
If you're a fan of puzzle/artsy games, I would pick this up for a 1/4 of its current price. Everyone else: Avoid.

This is not a bad thing because it meant that satisfying, rollling progress was made steadily, and you would be hard pressed to find a puzzle that you couldn't find a solution for after a few tries.
A HUGE plus for this game was the respawning. All to often in games, the respawn puts you way back -looking at you Styx- but the respawn and autosaves meant that even if you died, your progress on an area was almost exactly where you were when you died; Made it a lot less frustrating.
I wouldnt say the game had much of a story, more a pamphlet of explaining why this crazy crap was underground, but it was very satisfyingly brought full circle-pun intended-.
All in all, if you like puzzle games, with a bit of action/extremely mild horror elements, this game is worth about 10 hours to do puzzles and survival levels.

The Ball is a rather poor first person puzzle game with some tacked on combat. You play as an archeologist who falls down a hole in Mexico and finds a strange device that can be used to manipulate a mysterious ball. The ball is your main tool for solving puzzles and defeating enemies in the game.
The Ball was one of the early Unreal Engine 3 games and the visuals were probably pretty impressive once. These days the textures look low res and the models are blocky, but overall the graphics still hold up reasonably well. Unfortunately the game suffers from uninspired art design and you spend way too much time in caves and corridors that are visually quite boring.
The audio in the Ball is rather weak. Voice acting is pretty bad and the sound effects are not very good either. The sound for dragging the ball in particular is quite annoying and you'll be hearing it a lot during the game. The soundtrack is nothing special either.
The way you manipulate the ball is reminiscent of poor man's gravity gun. You can either pull the ball towards you (from any distance) or push it away (if it's next to you). Otherwise your ability to manipulate the environment is extremely limited.
Most puzzles involve the ball in one way or another. There are some clever touches like being able to spread oil with the ball and then setting it on fire. Unfortunately most of the puzzles are not particularly interesting and pretty much all of them have very obvious solutions.
The levels themselves are fairly linear although on a number of occasions you can complete a set of puzzles in any order you want. The game also uses a lot of invisible walls to make sure you don't take any shortcuts or come up with creative solutions to the puzzles.
In addition to the puzzles there's also a fair bit of combat. Unfortunately the combat isn't much fun either and the enemies tend to be rather boring. Most of the time you just use the ball to crush your enemies.
The story mode is rather easy. None of the puzzles are particularly difficult and the combat encounters are pretty easy too. And any time you die, you just spawn at the previous checkpoint with full health and no progress lost.
The controls with mouse+keyboard are pretty decent once you disable the horrible mouse smoothing that is enabled by default.
The story is not particularly engaging and the quality of the writing is quite poor.
Overall the game is reasonably polished. The game did crash a couple of times, however, and in one section the ground was completely invisible.
I didn't find the Ball particularly enjoyable and I wouldn't recommend it unless you are a huge fan of first person puzzle games.

It's taken me a while to get to The Ball.  There are a few reasons for this, but it's mainly because my DVD code never worked properly, so I waited for it to be out on Steam...
The Ball is an interesting game... It takes a mechanic from other games (i.e. some world object you need to manipulate to solve a puzzle / defeat a boss), and turns it into a fully-fledged game, complete with Inca mythos...  You are an archaeologist, who'se fallen into a mayan / inca temple, and with no other way out decide to procede further into the mountain..There unfolds an interesting story (so long as you find the secrets), of The Ball.  If you don't find the secrets, you get the same story, but omitting a few of the interesting personal viewpoints of the people who wrote the stone tablets...
You proceed through amazingly well preserved temples, structures, factories, and underground obstacle courses which play out like giant MouseTrap(tm), with your trusty companion, a gigantic glowing steel and copper sphere.  Your only interface with this sphere is a weird pneumatic skull gun which can either lure the ball closer, or smack it away from you.  To begin with, you feel like it's a dead weight.. it doesn't do much, except slow you down... Later, however, the ball gets certain 'powers', and the levels are set up so that you and the ball have to be in certain places to open passages, or trigger events...
The ball is huge... in-game it must be about 5' high, and made of what sounds like solid iron... When it impacts anything living (or undead), it squishes them to frags... When it collides with you, it just stops dead...  No squishing for you.   Also, you're protected from falling great heights, or having the ball fall from a great height onto you.. so the game becomes a giant game of crazy golf, with you as the putter.
The story is interesting, and slowly reveals the history of The Ball, and how it came to be in your possession. It also explains why it seems to be pivotal in the underground cities and villages you make your way through.  By the time you reach the end, the reason for the ball becomes very clear, and the ending leaves you with some mixed feelings... The same as when you flush The Weighted Companion Cube into the incinerator in Portal 2...
The levels are lush, and cavernously huge.   Caves disappear into the gloom high above you, and massive halls stretch away into the darkness ahead of you.  Laval bubbles and hisses around molten rocks, and in the deeper levels, bricks are superheated, revealing glowing mortar behind them.
The music is lovely and ambient, largely leaving you to ponder and the wondrous scale of the levels, and evoking the unusual aspects of the game.  Sounds are limited, but great in surround-sound.  The rumble of the ball as is revolves around you is great, and in a battle you can really use the slingshot to great effect if you know where it is.
Since it's based on the Unreal engine, the game is supersmooth, even at high resolutions.  The levels are mostly quite low-poly, with angular arches and flat floors.  It relies on interesting textures to evoke actual texture.  There aren't even bump maps, I don't think, so any graphics card post 2012 should be able to run it at full res without breaking a sweat.
The controls are extremely easy, and once you get the hang of the pushing and pulling, the ball becomes just as much an extension of you as the chains in God of War.. You use it to much the same effect.   By the end of the third or fourth level, you're smacking the ball into clouds of enemies with worrying precision.
Each level has a different 'feel', and it's split into two sections.  There's even a driving section, although I feel that the vehicle isn't really utilised to its fullest.
The game has a few survival modes, which I've tried, but are just darned hard for me.. I get to level 7 or 8 and can't dispatch the enemies fast enough.. I'll try a bit more after this to get those last few achievements which can only be got by tackling the survival maps.   The game has a handy in-menu achievement tally, so you don't have to alt-tab or shift-tab to get them.
All in all, I was very happy with the Ball.  Yes, the level design is old skool, and the gameplay is VERY early 2000's, with some shonky monster AI.  But it tells a great story, through some lush levels, with good music, voice acting, and a simple, but effective mechanic.    I really enjoyed playing it, and will play some more when I have more time.

This is a bad♥♥♥♥♥game. It is a no–holds–barred action slasher bullet hell boss battle gallery of a game. This video just list my quick thought on FURI and what I think of it.

The aesthetic is interesting, and the concept is good. Overall, I like this game, but there are some problems with it that I hope get adjusted.
This game seems like it's aiming to be the kind of challenge that you should expect to have to trial-and-error to overcome. Often there's no visual indicator (at least none that's obvious to me) of whether attacking at a given moment will result in success, or being blocked, or the enemy flying into a frenzy, or an unavoidable parry. The moments when you can successfully attack are different for each pattern, and it seems like the only way to figure it out is to try it. When you finally master one pattern and make it to the next phase, everything the previous phase just taught you about when you should attack could be wrong, so expect to start failing again.
There are similar problems trying to parry, or even to figure out what attacks you can feasibly parry.
So, given that Furi is aiming to be that kind of challenge, you can expect to come up against a boss that you'll have a lot of trouble with, and have to retry many times. This is where the game shows its biggest problem. No matter how completely you master early phases of a boss fight, and no matter how easy they become for you, they will always be TIME-CONSUMING. If you're struggling with the last phase of a 6-phase boss, you'll spend a lot of time completely bored as you work your way through the early phases again and again. It really ruins the pacing of what's supposed to be a fast-paced combat game where you're constantly encountering new things.
On the topic of pacing, the cutscenes are sort of a pain as well. THey came up with an interesting system to make them semi-interactive. You are in control of your character during the cutscene (able to walk around), but you can enable a sort of auto-pilot, and just let the scene play out. The problem with the cutscenes is the sloooooow lumbering walking pace of your character. Is there a run button I haven't found? I don't think so.
I believe the intent was to give time for the atmosphere to establish itself, for tension to build, for you to admire the ambiance, and for the narrator/companion to speak. But the pace is at such an extreme of slowness that it's absurd. Surely the character can walk just a SMIDGE faster without ruining the atmosphere.
Haven't finished the game yet. I'm alternately enjoying it, and hating it. That's in the nature of difficult games, but I wish it wasn't exacerbated by the other stuff.

To the developers:
Such a great "couch" co-op game. Just recently tried this game with my Nintendo Switch Joy Cons with my mom and boy do they feel just right for this game. Switch version through Nindies when? I'd gladly buy this game a second time. Not even kidding. The sooner this gets there the more sales it'll get before the other indies overflood the eShop, trust me.
To everyone else looking to buy this game:
Highly recommended, if you're looking for a Halloween game that isn't all spooks and jumpscares but laughs and frustration (the good, entertaining kind) with a friend or family member, then this game is totally for you.
Death Road to Canada is a rougelike game, meaning it's maps and encounters are all randomized and when you die, you die for good and have to start over. But you unlock things the more you play, so dying isn't bad... Unless you die right away if you have terrible luck.
You can make your own characters and let them "inhabit" the world of Death Road to Canada and have a chance of meeting or even recruiting them as you play the game or choose a mode where you only meet the rare characters; each being super risky but super fun to have in a run.
The game has a ton of references to other games, lots of jokes and is overall hard not to enjoy or crack a smile at while playing it. It gets even better if you play it with a friend or family member. Some might not enjoy its humor, but I certainly do!
The music is also pretty good and I really dig its pixel art style.
One thing I have to mention, though, is that this game is probably not made for super long sessions solo. I think 30 minutes/until you die per day is more than enough, because otherwise you might get tired of this game fast. Personally I only play it when I can convince my 63 y/o mom to play it with me (I'm a 24 y/o loser with no friends and social anxiety, don't judge me too hard) and I get bored of it on my own after 30 minutes.
This game is entertaining solo, too, but not as much as when you play co-op, in my opinion. If you expect a similar experience like Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon, then I'll have to disappoint you.
All in all, though, I'd say this game is great if you need a co-op game for Halloween that's fun. I don't think online co-op is a thing yet, but I hope it will be.

Who wouldn't want to go to Canada to escape the zombie-ocalypse?!
Death Road to Canada is a rogue like beat-um up with a fairly healthy dose of Oregon Trail like survival elements.
Although you do have a great deal of control in the game, between what locations you scavenge, what choices you make (like whether to say give up supplies or ram a barricade set up by bandits), whether to sleep and rest or push on through....
The outcome will usually leave you guessing, or well... suffering. Even when you think you are making the best deicion, just like life, things don't always go the way you would hope. Your friend may stab you in the back and your forced to leave him behind cause morale is low. Or you may struggle through a horde due to injuries from a previous encounter.
Every time you play it will feel like a whole new narrative is unfolding. There's even a surprising degree of customization too. You could choose a randomly generated character... or create your own set of familiar faces to use in the game. Give them personalities, and perk traits and see how far you can get with them.
There's a lot to love with the games charming and odd humor, it's appealing pixelated visual style, and it's all over the place music (well that one is both love and hate.... sometimes the music doesn't really fit the mood, but you take the bad with the good).
In the end it's a game worth picking up, and sure to give a solid amount of replay value to retro game loving zombie fanatics. Or anyone who just like to laugh their♥♥♥♥♥off at how it all plays out.

Look, if I really try to talk about this game, we'll be here all day. What all of the above boils down to, is that this is a fantastic game. If you're unsure about buying it, just buy it.

VA-11 HALL-A is what you get when 2 venezuelan weebs get together and put their love of cyberpunk, anime, and cute girls into one package and sell it for 14.99. Valhalla is a good game. Or is it? Can it really be considered a game? Are VNs games? All valid questions, questions that don't have a single answer:
Valhalla does have a lot of reading, and there's no voice acting, so reading is the only way to play the game, but it's not like a traditional VN where you read a bunch of stuff, make some choices, choose a girl you want to ♥♥♥♥ and go into her route, Valhalla is a cyberpunk bartending simulator, and most of your interactions with the characters will be behind the bar, making drinks for them, which is the main gameplay element, since in the game, instead of choosing dialogue options, what drinks you get your clients can influence their mood, what they say in their next visit, and in some cases even the endings.
The bartending minigame isn't too complicated, and you don't need to remember how to make drinks, just what the person asked. From there, it's as easy as looking up the recipe in the in game computer and dragging the ingredients (or using qwerty) and hitting mix, or in some cases adding ice or aging the drink.
But that's not the most important part, where the game shines through is in the characters: The writer succedeed in making realistic (for a cyberpunk setting) characters, with real problems and personalities, who you are actually interested in, and made even more interesting by the volatile political climate the game is set in. Without giving spoilers, many things will happen in the background that you don't take part in, but definitely affect you, your clients and the whole city
I wholeheartedly recommend valhalla. If you're a weeb this game is for you, but even if you're not there's much more to the game than waifus, if you just ignore the anime artstyle

SOCOM 1 in September 2002 was my first experience into online gaming as a college freshman.    Thirteen years later, I am still playing with people I met during my first year playing SOCOM (If my wife gives me trouble, I joke and tell her I met these friends before I met you :)  SOCOM will always have a special place in my heart.
With the failure of recent SOCOM games and my utter dislike for most "popular" FPS out there, I have been casually playing games mostly for the social aspect with the friends I made along the way.   Until I started playing HHOUR...
For the first time in a very long time, I got what we like to call the shakes or heart pounding or heart flutters or that frog in your chest.  If you played S1 or S2, you know what I am talking about: your the last guy alive, you already killed one enemy and four more are now on the way to plant the bomb in your base.  You get a little anxiety building. You surprise one and now there's three left.  You double back and check your flank, there he is, got em.  Two left.  You Double back again and check the door in time to see one guy go inside and the other is close behind, you pop out and take him down.  One Left.  You work your way to the side of the door and peak in, looks empty, enemy must be behind something.  You risk it feeling cocky and as your heart is about to explode, you just need the round to end.  You enter, enemy pops out, gun fight ensure and you somehow are still standing while you watch your enemy fall.
What I just described happened to me not in a SOCOM game but last Friday while Playing H-Hour: World's Elite.  (If Domtron1 saves his broadcasts on twitch or youtube, you can go check out what I just described, May 15th I believe was when it happened).
Thank you SOF Studios for reminding me why I fell in love with with online gaming in the first place and for demonstrating that sometimes, companies do listen to their fans.
I highly recommend anyone and everyone to try this game, just know that it is still early in the development process and is not a fully polished game.

Alicia Quartermain is a balanced, fast-paced, and fun time management game, but one that falls in the easy category even for a casual genre.
Alicia Quartermain: Secrets of the Lost will surely feel familiar for many, since it not only uses the standard time management game mechanics of ordering around some workers to gather resources for glorified road works or building construction, but it is also largely reminiscent of the
.
One of the core aspects of this game is its fast pace: the stages are small and crowded, so it is easy to clear them out, even with our 2-3 workers, with next to no downtime. Additionally, stockpile is very limited and production buildings are either automatic or replenish in seconds, so the game emphasises constant action instead of strategic resource management. Since this means we never really run out of anything, there are no parts on any stage we cannot solve by simply waiting a few seconds.
Despite this speed, the game is still easy on any difficulty. There are plenty of levels (50+5) to entertain us for a good while, but do not expect to spend more than a few hours getting the perfect 3-star score on each.
It's a short but fun game. I like it, but do try to get it while it's discounted, replayability is a bit low, imho.

Not unplayable, but if you're used to Jet Dogs other offerings, you'll be disappointed. Hopefully Whalebox's next offerings will be more polished.

Alicia Quatermain: Secrets of the Lost Treasures is basically 12 Labours of Hercules dressed up in different clothing, and I'm completely fine with that.  JetDogs has the time management formula down to perfection, and as long as the tuning remains tight yet forgiving while allowing for flexible strategies and featuring top notch presentation, I will always gobble these games up as fast as they can make them.
Once again, you're tasked with completing a set of goals in order to proceed to the next level. While the goals vary, the general concept is the same; collect resources and perform specific tasks before the timer expires. Efficiently managing your workers is at the heart of the gameplay, although it's by no means necessary if you want to play more casually (and there are 3 different difficulty modes to fit a variety of players' tastes), but doing so adds strategic depth to what is in essence a very simple game. The more effort you put into challenging yourself, the more reward you'll get for it.
There are a couple mechanics that are unique to this series.  Bandits will leave timed bombs on paths which need to be defused before they blow leaving a gaping hole in their wake which takes quite a bit of resources to repair.  Not being prepared for these can mean the difference between snagging 2 and 3 stars.  You can also repair and upgrade buildings that give a steady income of resources without the need to gather.  Juggling these buildings with how quickly you can gather your own resources from replenishable nodes adds flexibility to the gameplay, and I'm always for more strategic options in these games.
The presentation is great with simple yet pleasing cartoon graphics, quality acting by Alica's VA, and another great soundtrack.  There are also story snippets in the beginning of each level which give a short description of what's going on.  Sometimes a bit of dialogue is exchanged between Alicia and her workers or the enemies too, which makes the characters feel a bit more dynamic. The only complaint I have is a few typos here and there, and a handful of story snippets that don't completely fit into the description window and cut off part of the last sentence.  I didn't find this to be a deal breaker as the gameplay more than makes up for it, but others may be more annoyed by it than myself.
If you're a fan of time/resource management games, there's no reason not to buy this game.  The value for your money is phenomenal, even at full price.  I certainly hope further entries in Alicia Quatermain's series makes it over to Steam.  These titles would make excellent additions to my time management game library.

I haven't quite finished everything, but I have completed a very significant portion of the game without any guides. Not only does this succeed in being the most consistently mind-blowing game, I've ever played, it's also unique from any puzzle I have ever seen because it requires both inductive and deductive logic. All puzzle games, whether it's sudoku or portal, give you the rules up front and then just rely on you to make deductive steps to reach the solution. In The Witness, the rules of the puzzle are never given to you. It is up to you to inductively guess what the rules could be, abductively test your supposed rules, and then deductively solve the puzzle based on the info that you yourself have been able to gather. Because of this, I would not hesitate to say it is the most challenging puzzle game I have ever played. This in turn creates the largest temptation to use a guide or look for hints because we naturally associate "more challenging" with "less doable". This is, however; not the case. The game is just as doable as any puzzle game, and it facilitates the learning of all of the rules naturally. If you go for this game, do not bang your head against the same puzzle for more than a few minutes. The world is open, when you get stuck, explore. The answers are never all in the same place.
The creator very cleverly draws parallels between the relationship of the player and the game world to the relationship between the scientist and his testable environment. Jonathan Blow's philosophy of what we need to know, what we can know, and what is useful to know is very profoundly expressed through the game, although I can't say I totally agree with his rather cynical philosophical outlook. Very enjoyable, one of a kind experience. If you are willing to allow yourself to legitimately struggle with the unknown, you will get so much out of this game.

You must ask yourself if this game is for you. It's not for everyone. There's no action, items, or enemies. The game is ponderous, challenging, and vague. Not everyone wants to spend over 25 hours solving puzzles, and thats ok. But if puzzle games are interesting to you, The Witness is certainly one of the best. To like this game, you must enjoy and be satisfied with learning new concepts and experiencing breakthrough moments in your understanding. If this sounds good, just buy the game, its fantastic. If its not enough, maybe skip it (or challenge yourself).
This game is about puzzles, but it is also about learning, discovery and epistemology. In the end, it is about teaching you to solve its mazes while organically guiding you to moments of epiphany. While the game certainly takes itself seriously, I think that it deserves the attitude for how well it accomplishes its design goals. This game sticks to its morals and realizes them fully. The result is something beautifully unique that doesn't compromise if doing so would undermine its goals.
It surprised me how versatile the maze puzzles are. The simple concept of drawing a line through a grid from the start to the finish is complicated by gaps in the grid and symbols whose meaning you must learn through sets of puzzles designed for that purpose. Eventually you are solving problems with multiple sets of symbols that must be satisfied simultaneously, speaking a new sort of visual language.
Oh, and the visual are effing superb! Really, this game deserves to be played slowly, stop and look at all the pretty things (it may even be usefull...)

The Witness is different. Extremely different. The closest thing to it is probably The Talos Principle, or in a small sense Antichamber, but that's a stretch. The only reason I bring this up is because those are the only two other games I've bothered to review, because I've loved them so much. And same goes for the Witness.
First, as every other review tells you, its a puzzle game with a philosophical flair. However, a significant portion of the challenges is just figuring out what the puzzles are themselves. I could go into depth as to how it does things differently, but I feel many of the other reviews have covered that. Instead, I want to focus on some of my key experiences playing the game, which hopefully will give everyone a fuller understanding as to the experience that is the Witness.
Throughout the whole game, I could not stop feeling a sense of wonder. The artstyle, the lay of the land, everything was designed so you had to just stop and look around going "whoa." What's better is that there are so many little details that you don't notice on the first pass. Sometimes the second or third. But once you really start developing an understanding for the world, you start paying more and more attention. And when you do finally notice that little detail, you realize why you missed it the first time. Originally you didn't know what to expect, what mattered and what didn't, and what details even existed. This is what allows the game to have such depth; it's amazing world and level design.
There were puzzles I didn't even realize were puzzles! This sounds annoying and frustrating, but it is actually wonderful design. It forces you to explore, to discover other types of puzzles in other areas, and building an understanding for the problems presented to you. Then, as you explore, you start thinking "maybe I can apply this new technique to that puzzle I skipped way back when?" BAM. Epiphany. Best feeling in the whole damn world.
Building off of this, the exploration of the game is nonlinear. You do not have to work through areas in a predetermined order. It gives you total freedom. So I recommend not getting too stuck on areas, and instead just continue exploring and learning. Eventually you will have the knowledge to attack that one puzzle.
This game is not easy. Even when you fully understand the puzzles presented to you, the challenge doesn't end there. It pushes you to actually use this new understanding in more and more complicated ways. Patience is truly a virtue in this game, but trust me, the rewards are worth it. In fact, I started writing some of the more difficult puzzles down to try and use logic to solve it. However, like all formal logic, you need some assumptions. Many times I made faulty assumptions. Eventually I'd realize it couldn't be solved, and I'd learn which assumption was false, and overall I'd learn more about the system. It's an amazing feeling.
However, I think the best experience in the game for me is when I had "beaten" it. Instead of finishing the game, I chose not to. I thought about all the stuff I might have missed, or didn't fully understand. The actual process of exploration, discovery, and problem solving is just that rewarding.
So, do I recommend this game? HELL YES. Do I think it's for everyone? HELL NO. Again, it's probably most similar to The Talos Principle or possibly Myst (never played it :( ). Hopefully this convinced someone on buying this game; if you have the patience, it is an experience you will never forget.
Tips if you actually get the game:
- Take a screenshot of the map as soon as you find it. It's helpful
- Do not be afraid to scour the same places you were before and have "completed"
- As I said before, do not get bogged down by puzzles for too long, especially ones that you do not understand conceptually. Explore. You will most likely find something in your travels that will help you understand it.
- Take screenshots of puzzles or solutions if you feel it may be helpful later
- Do not be afraid to write things down. Not at all necessary, but you might find it helpful as I did.
- Open your mind. The overall experience is wonderful, but it easy to be bogged down by skepticism and impatience. Please, it is so much more enjoyable if you force yourself to be accepting and patient.

The Witness is an Incredible game for those wanting a challenging, intelligent puzzle game. The game leaves you alone to discover and explore the mysterious world at your own pace. It's like the Dark Souls of puzzle games.

That said, navigating the world can be a bit grating, but when all you want to do is explore the magical world, yet the limitations placed on the player character's movement can be frustrating.
Once you accept those limitations, this game opens up and is full of the wonders of discovery that games in the 80s (and early 90s) had, before handholding became a trade practice. The Witness treats you like an adult and let's you learn things on your own, let's you fail, let's you choose where to go next.
I love this game. Well done, Jon Blow and team.

Interesting little game..
Mixes elements of bullet hell games and classic hack and slash combat...
Also neat because the game is just one string of boss fights, you literally fight nothing but bosses with the exception of one that has some adds you have to deal with...
Basically it goes bullet hell phase--->hack and slash/reaction speed--->bullet hell ... rinse repeat until you expend the bosses lives... if you get downed during a phase boss regains its health for that phase and you try it again until you expend all your lives at which point you restart the fight..
Its a pretty decent challenge,.. beat it on normal difficulty but I can see where replay  value is here..
is it worth the current asking price? Im not really sure, its quite the little visual novel and the story is kinda interesting.. its never really directly apparent if you're the bad guy or not until the end and a choice is to be made...
The graphics are very well done and pretty artistic, its very apparent that the designers wanted you to experience their version of this little world and show it off every chance they can between the boss fights.
Also the ability to just press a button and have the character autowalk in the correct direction during the crazy camera angles was much appreciated.
Its a solid little experience if your looking for a good distraction that you can play  through multiple times and get some enjoyment out of it... maybe wait for it to be on a 50% sale or something if your tepid about it. Otherwise I enjoyed it start to finish and I intend on trying to clear it on the higher difficulties and attempt to get S ranks on the bosses.

This game deserves more attention than it has gotten. The flight system is a modified version of the one used in War Thunder and expirienced players will have no trouble. It can take a few minutes to get used to flying with no down or up (because in space down is where ever the floor is and up is where ever your head is pointing, not because this is one of those crappy 2d space games), but it can by fun to disorient players by coming at them along an odd attack angle. The game forces players to think in 3d, going under and over to flank instead of around. The crafting system works well and forces you to carefuly consider your play style. Best of all the dreaded "Pay to Win" system is mor limited than most. Synergy (exp) transpher, DLC, and Premium ships are the only noticable advantages. Premium ships are usually much weaker than their Synergy (XP) required counterparts and are so over priced only the desprat and the rich bother to get them outside of a very generous sale every year or so.
Over all the game is well ballanced (except for the occasional max level russian), and easy to play. There is controler support and Occulus use is avalable. The graphics are exelent if you can run at max level, and are better than many paid games of similar age.
The only real drawbacks are the dwindling player base because the developers put all of the advertising budget into their flagship game Warthunder and allowd Star Conflict to fade into relative obscurity. It has a server infrastructure to match and it is not uncommon for the NA players to end up in Russian, Europian, and even South Asian servers with clear favoratim for Russian players as they are the majority of the population.
If youre a fan of arcade space flight and combat sims, this game is for you.
*EDIT* The pay to enjoy scum system has infested this game. Events giving out exclusive ships require you to have no life away from the game, OR spend $20-$50 on a slot machiene style pack that only costs $1-$3 each but only have a 5%-10% chance of dropping what you actually want.

On me: Over 2000 hours in game, 4500 matches, all ships played and maxed, build a corp from scratch to 150 members and top-10 PvP leaderboards, organized and played dreadnought matches. Considering myself a casual player - can take on almost anyone on a good day, or die like a newb on a bad one.
On the Game: Great, addictive game. Maybe the best space combat game currently on the market. Spaceships, fights, PvE & PvP, open space, pirates, aliens, missions, ship customization, great graphics, low requirements, linux & mac support - everything you want from a space combat game and much more. Also much more mature than most other space combat offerings on Steam, and far more dynamic and  interesting than e.g. Elite:Dangerous. Basically it's War Thunder in Space.
Try it, it's free, and up to the mid-tiers the grind is moderate (and mid-tiers are much more fun than high-tiers anyway). If you have the time and patience to improve your gameplay to competitive levels, this may be a game worthy of long-term engagement.
As reference: without investing any real cash, it will take you about 100-150 matches to maximize all Tier-1 ships. With licence etc. it will take 3000 to 5000 matches to maximize all ships in the game, if that is your goal.
However, you need the frustration tolerance of a tibetan monk after Tier-1:
- Matchmaking is super-broken and will put new players with 100 matches against unbeatable veterans with 10'000. Often. And in every Tier (except 1). Only thing worse than "normal" matchmaking is squad matchmaking - the only balancing there is the amount of players in squads to be near-equal. The game doesn't even try to match based on skill or experience - I've seen squads with 300 matches total placed against squads with 30'000 matches total. Matchmaking generally feels worse than random - it seems the goal is to frustrate players on purpose, to get them to buy "better" stuff and spend more money on the game. Newer players complaining about the frustrating game experience are told to simply "gid gud", as if every casual player had the intention to spend 2 years of his life in the game.
- Tiers are supposed to be skill-related, but that is not the case. There are just as many new players in T5 as there are experienced veterans. Lower Tiers (T2/3) are chock-full of uber-leet veteran players and  - even worse - elite kill squads "seal-clubbing" / "farming" newer players for easy wins which yield stats and Iridium for the corp.
- A lot of the vet no-lifers are extremely abrasive, insulting other players at every opportunity. The vets basically "own" the game (or at least act as if they did), and vet squads and corps dominate the whole gaming experience. Newer players (anyone with less than maybe 3'000 matches) are treated as cannon fodder. This, together with the disgusting matchmaking, greatly contributes to extremely high player fluctuation in the mid-tiers and an environment very unfriendly towards casual players. Woe upon the newer player daring to use the same OP builds and tactics as the veterans. For example, it's OK if you're getting killed by OP vet drone pooping tacklers 20 times in a row, but if you so much as dare using a drone in your interceptor, be prepared for a veritable ♥♥♥♥♥torm.
- The whole "Dreadnought" match experience is a huge hassle and pretty repetitive. Timeslots are limited, setup horribly complicated, and strategic sector gains are basically reserved for the vet corps due to the inherent  mechanics.
- Testing of changes is reserved to/done by some of the vet players, which in turn leads to  major and minor changes which generally favour the veteran player community.
- Veteran players incessantly ask for more advertising to get more players (more lambs for the slaughter), not realizig that this game's primary issue is not gaining new players, but to retain those who give the game a try. I have led a major corp for some time, and the speed in which the game is bleeding players due to frustration is absurd (about 2% each day).
Over 1.2 million players have tried this game. Only about 2k play it concurrently, maybe around 7k  over the course of a week. Less than 100 vets "own" the game. Are you the one out of 10'000 that can stand the frustration and has the skill and time to make it into their ranks?
If not, give this a spin for a great casual game experience - until it's your time to rage-quit.

Ever since I started playing Spore back in 2009, I have always had fun bringing life to my imagination and sharing it with other people, and the community was amazing - Parkaboy, flamestar, and Pat(There were numbers after but I never learned them all) to name a few. Imagine my glee when I found out Spore can be bought on Steam when my computer broke down and was replaced. And since I can play GA without the disc, since the discs I have are for some reason not working (Likely age, this game is somewhat old afterall), Steam was a lifesaver for Spore.
First off, it's great Steam has Spore, I can download it and play it without any of the discs (For GA anyway) on any desktop or laptop if I felt like it. The vanilla game of Spore off Steam is great, the CnC pack is good to add to your collection but is never really needed to complete the game, GA however is fun as you get to play adventures made by Maxis and other players and the ability to make your own. Unfortunately GA, unlike the vanilla game, has (ATM) two small problems but problems nonetheless.
1. Everytime I make an adventure or captain and share it, it never shows up in the Sporepedia - both in the game itself and the website, I have checked. I never had this issue when I used the discs 5 or so years ago, every creation created with the GA expansion shared normally on both Sporepedias, so this has to be an issue on Steam's part.
2. A more recent problem; the buttons on the button of the screen (Edit, Share, Delete, etc) no longer seem to work for some reason. Everytime I bring my cursor to it the button is highlighted briefly then becomes uninteractable. And this is also a problem in the Adventure Creator/Editor: when ever I'm editing or creating an adventure, the Save, Cancel (Rex X), and "Finalize"(Green check) no longer work as well. And it's not exclusive to those buttons, the menu (Spore emblem button), Sporepedia (Squares button by menu button), and even to add text in the adventure's description box AND intro, objective, and victory/failure buttons no longer work at all either. I can't even add a goal to the adventure since all the buttons on the lower part of the screen is no longer interactive it seems. Whether it's a problem from the Steam version of the game or on EA's part is unknown to me, but I would like you two to talk this out and come up with a solution. Because of this problem I really saw no reason to continue playing if it persists until it gets resolved (If it ever will).
So to those thinking of playing this game for the first time, it's up to you. Bringing your ideas to life is fun but the small problems can be small thorns in your side, irritating you at every chance they get. But if you truly wish to try it out, don't let me stop you, I just want to let you know of two problems I have run into.

It's almost been a year since I've purchased Death Road to Canada, and I must say that even after all this time the game still holds up as incredible. The sheer concept of the game is brilliant, and the built in upgrade system for better future runs as well as laugh-out-loud dialog makes this game a must buy. It's so easy to start up and then pick up the game whenever, as the saving system allows you to complete one event at a time if need be, or complete an entire fun yet challenging run to Canada in one sitting. The game isn't easy, but that's where the bulk of the fun is with the game. Trying to figure out what character combinations go well together to ensure a good run is crucial, but if you want even more of a challenge you can attempt the Death Road solo, or better yet a BERSERK! solo run, which I plan on attempting in the future. Speaking of characters, the built in custom character creator is an outstanding feature of the game. Make your family, friends, favorite YouTubers, or even celebrities, give them their own perks and traits, and then upgrade them through Zombo Town. It makes the game feel especially satisfying when you and your brother make it to Canada, and when your custom character dies to a zombie it makes it even more heart-wrenching. Overall, I can't help but recommend Death Road to Canada for anyone who's considering purchasing the game. It has a ton of replayability, and is really cool to think a four person team made such an incredible title. Can't wait to buy it again once the Android verison releases the 26th! 10/10

Far Cry 4 is an overall well put together action adventure game driven by a slightly underwhelming story. This is unfortunately topped off with characters you never truly fall in love with.
Dislaimer: This review will contain very minor spoilers.
The Good:
The amount of weapons and ways to accomplish missions is something that has been carried over and added upon from the thrid installment. Graphics have seen a massive improvement and optimization is good as well. Lots of little random wtf moments that are fun for the first playthrough.
This game was purchased for $20 during the winter Steam sale. I am currently 40% complete with 30.2 hours on record so it checks off my personal value for money quota (1$/hour).
Voice acting for side characters is very well done: Longingus, Sabal, Amita, and the radio host have all done an excellent job at adding emotion into the game where it is otherwise lacking.
The bad:
I initially bought this game due to my infatuation with Far Cry 3's story. Throughout that game you are made to really appreciate the subtleties of characterization not only among the protaganist but also the side characters. That is what was primarily missing from this game. Sabal and Amita, the two you interact the most with through your playthrough offer relatively black and white solutions to a Civil war. There's no real middle ground.
Pagan Min had another excellent voice actor but wasn't in the game often enough for you to really get to know the character other than he was supposed to be a benevolent dictator. This was the most dissapointing aspect of the game for me, especially after playing Far Cry 3 which had one of the best villians in all of video game history with Vaas. Pagan was never able to terrify or shock the player as much as Vaas was, and for this I resent him.
Conclusion:
While the villian and story may have been lackluster compared to the third they were in no means bad. When you combine this with stellar graphics, fun gunplay, and an immense world you get an overall solid but slightly stale fourth installment of the Far Cry series. As long as you set your expectations appropriately I would say purchase. I would not recommend buying this game at full price, wait for a sale like I did and you will be much more satisfied with your playthrough.
Overall: 7.5/10 (Wait for sale)

The witness is a puzzle game, with mild elements of exploration. Having come into this game expecting akin to Braid I was sorely disappointed. I am dissapointed, not because this game doesn't have puzzles or atmosphere, but because its a very isolating game. While figuring out the puzzles there is no background music, no overarching narrative - just the complusion to better your puzzle solving skills.
Don't get me wrong, the puzzles in this game are great. The build up of the puzzle design is great. The art design is great - but it feels hollow overall. I guess I could liken this game to someone making a rubiks cube simulator with hundreds of different rubiks cubes. Is there hours of game play here - yeah - is it misleading in its purpose - no. Would I play it for hours on end - no.
In regards to the puzzles specifically, as mentioned previously I feel like they are well done, but at the same time some of them start to feel gimmicky. I can't think of a good example of this, but I feel like puzzles should be self-contained, and should not require the environment outside of the puzzle to solve.
Is the witness a good puzzle game? Yes
Is the witness a game that I would recommend? No

There is absolutely no ambient music. Only the noises of the enviorment you're in. And I have to say that the developers did an excellent job at making sounds effects, every step sounded like what I was stepping on/in. If I was walking on concrete, it sounded like I was stepping on concrete. And the same for all of the other materials in the game. It was really well made as far as little details go.
As for gameplay I would have to give The Wittness a 8/10. The game is a puzzle game that is open world and relies on you exploring the beautiful landscapes to find out where to go. Now, that being said there are several areas you should go to before others otherwise a lot of the puzzles the game puts you through won't make sense at first. I had this issue multiple times and I had no clue where or what I was supossed to be doing. This was frustrating at best as I had to go look up what I was supossed to do for a specific puzzle because I didn't know what the hell I was supossed to do. But I like that about this game. There is absolutely no tutorial and the game does not hold your hand at all. It is extremely challenging and forces the player to think about the puzzle they are trying to complete. There were clues hidden throughout the enviornment which made me look about to try and find something to try and help me complete the puzzle. It is a very clever idea and the concepts for a lot of these puzzles are some that I have never seen in a game before. The "you have to look for clues" aspect of the game also led to several different secrets in the game which IMO is really cool.
All that being said this game isn't easy at all. The game starts out relatively easy, however that's about it as far as easy goes. The game is extremely difficult and challenging. I wasn't able to play the game for more than about an hour per session because my brain would melt and be in a puddle on the floor. But when I was in a good mood and ready for a challenge the enviornments were very relaxing, and being that the only sounds in the game are the ones you and your surroundings make just exemplified that even more.
I would definitely recommend this game to those who are ready for a challenge and don't want their hand to be held or be stuck in a super linear puzzle solving experience. Excellent work.

Making things worse - I followed its development for years and was a Jonathan Blow fan after Braid, but at this point I feel duped out of $40. I feel certain I'll never again feel compelled to play this game. This is my first refund request on Steam after many years, and I'm embarrassed for having bought it. Lesson learned.

In one sentence this game is too good to be free.
First of all, the graphics. The game runs very well, even on my low end computer (about $250 US). The game is crisp, bright, and has tons of particles, but runs over 30 fps on the default settings, so it isn't very demanding.
The gameplay is very different then most others. It feels basically like War Thunder and Star Wars had a kid. The game has very similar controls and styles to War Thunder, but the fact that you are in space makes the oreintation during combat very difficult at first. Star Conflict is very fast paced, so if your reflexes aren't the best then this game isn't for you.
The learning curve isn't that harsh, but I would recommend trying War Thunder first because it is a tamer version of Star Conflict. You are quickly thrown into two tutorials that spell out what you need to do and how to do it.
The connection times aren't great, you may wait three minutes to get into a ten minute game, but you are with players of a similar level. I don't have to worry about my ping even though my internet is crappy.
All in all I give Star Conflict a 9/10 because you don't need Alienware to run it at all, the graphics are great, and the game is fast paced, but it takes a while to join a match. (I have a short attention span)

VA-11 Hall-A, Valhalla, is a relaxing jaunt through a cyberpunk dystopian setting. That's right, I just used cyberpunk, dystopian, and relaxing in the same sentence and I'm not even being sarcastic. This is the type of game that you sit down to play while snacking on delicious treats, drinking a nice warm up of tea (or whatever you fancy), and just enjoying the slice-of-life visual novel about a bartender, Jill, working in a soon-to-close bar in a city rife with troubles happening in the background. This is a game where you play as the character that would normally be the NPC in most other games serving drinks to a cast of interesting people, many of whom could probably be the protagonists of their own games.
The gameplay is simple and easy to learn, all you do is mix drinks and change lives. Customers order drinks, you mix together all the necessary ingredients, and listen to them talk. Each character has their own preference of drinks, you the astute player is able to pick up on and learn, which helps when a customer asks for a drink using a vague description that you have to figure out yourself rather than just telling you what they want. The conversations the characters talk about are diverse, interesting, and humorous, with conversations ranging from social commentary, philosophy, crime, technology, politics, science, the sex industry, and more. I found myself deep in thought concerning some of the heavy concepts the game so casually comments on, making it a rather intellectually engaging game. The characters are all interesting and fleshed out, each with their own views and ways of speaking. It's subtle, but you can influence the dialogue through the drinks that you give the customers.
Aside from the bartending gameplay, there is also a collecting aspect to the game. You can buy items for your apartment everyday before going to work, spending money you earn from bartending. Occassionally, JIll will want to buy certain items, which influence how focused she is during work.
The game has a terrific soundtrack reminiscent of synthwave and other retro electronic genres of music. The music adds to the relaxing atmopshere of the game, and you get to select which tracks play throughout Jill's workday, allowing you to get familiar with the soundtrack.
VA-11 Hall-A  does, however, draw much inspiration from other visual novels and anime, so those wary of such media may not have the best experience with this game. Character archetypes commonly found in anime can be found here; however, the silverlining to this is that, more often than not, I feel like the usage of these anime / visual novel stereotypes are commentary in and of themselves.
Overall, I highly recommend playing this game--it's a nice game to unwind and relax to after a long day of work or school. I look forward to whatever game Sukeban Games makes next.

H-Hour Early Access review:
Prepare for the long awaited return of a gaming legacy.  Today’s First Person Shooters (FPS) games have catered to the individual.  Where teamwork is unnecessary and experience points has been allowed to set the tone of the game objective.
H-Hour brings something not necessarily new, but fresh to the gaming scene.  SOF Studios revives the Sony Socom legacy from the ashes with this “no respawn” tactical shooter.  This game is not for the casual “Lone Wolf” gamer, but the experienced mature gamer.  You will find no respawn, a minimap showing only teammates, no kill cam; and all by design and demand from those who are hungry for the next challenge in their evolving game play.
H-Hour World’s Elite takes your experience to a whole new level where the actions made by you or a team-member can quickly become the deciding factor of win or lose.  This game will train you through trial by fire to learn how to move more tactically, coordinate with team members to pull off objective goals and bring you a clutching experience that will have you almost as excited spectating your teammates as when your boots are on the ground.
Fight alongside up to 7 additional team mates across intimate maps that provide a “tactical” environment.  Play in one of two game modes (more to come) to accomplish your objective of eliminating the opposing radical force by any means necessary.  With only one life to live each round, you’ll be forced to abandon your solo “run and gun” ways. After playing the game and completing the campaign as well as a good load of side missions, the game feels way to repetitive. Kill Baddies > Sell Loot > Buy Weapons > Kill Animals > Craft Items > Kill Badies > Repeat.
The game has very little replay value and the characters are very, very hard to form a bond with. Sure, the story uncovers a-lot about our protagonist, yet it does it in a way that makes it near impossible to really FEEL like you are in his shoes and that you know him on a personal level.
There is much this game could have improved on and there are parts this game has done very well. It did a great job creating a new unique environment that still feels familiar to FC3. It adds in new modes of transportation and new forms of combat. However the game could have used a decent chunk of features. For example, closing off half the map until you progress further in the story? No. That is bad. Close off the main compound sure. But half the map? The idea of open world is for you to be able to explore the OPEN WORLD. There are players out there who right off that bat, want to see the world and unlock the towers so we can get that gun we want. Yet we have to make it through half the game to get to that point.
The grind is there, as in any crafting game. This game has an issue of making that grind a little too much. Let's take for example, the Rhinos. From personal experience I can tell you it doesn't take 30 bullets to put down a cougar. It doesn't take 5 arrows. It takes 1 bullet or 1 arrow. Keep it cool. Nerf the animals. Focus on making the game more unique and focus on character bonds.
I rate this game 5/10 and with that do not recommend it. I have hopes that the next Far Cry will be better.

The Witness for me has been a presentation in opposites - beautiful and ugly, graceful and clumsy, plain-spoken and pompous. I wish I could give this game a rating between thumbs-up and thumbs-down, but since that's not possible, I'm going to have to choose not to recommend this game, despite the fact that there are many things about it I really like.
The game places you on an island, and the way to move forward is to solve various puzzles throughout the island, which all have different rules and different levels of difficulty. Most of these puzzles take place on flat-panel screens, and involve using a cursor to draw on the panels and solve the puzzles by obeying the varous rules, like keeping blocks of a certain color together or blocking out specific tetris-like shapes.
+Island is beautiful, at least in terms of color palette and geometry.
+Seems to run fairly well.
+Puzzle rules are very clever, and you will feel smart when you figure out the hard ones.
+Teaches you the rules organically, you learn the rules naturally most of the time.
-Island is pretty, but there isn't much to actually
on it, other than interact with panel puzzles. Invisible walls are everywhere and it ends up feeling like a pretty-looking, but ultimately shallow façade.
-Puzzle difficulty ramps up quickly, a bit too quickly sometimes. Prepare to be frustrated.
-Story is so threadbare it might as well not exist. Bits and pieces are around, but nothing is ever explained, which along with the non-interactive island makes the setting feel even more pointless.
-no musical score.
-Some puzzles feel downright cheap. I'm not sure how people with vision/hearing problems will even complete this game.
-Puzzles are presented in the most repetitious, boring way possible.
At first glance, The Witness appears to have a lot of things going for it, but when you spend some time with it you find out that all it really has to fall back on are the puzzles themselves. The problem with this is that the puzzles are presented to you in such a monotonous fashion that by the endgame I was getting pretty bored. Combine this with the non-existent story and un-interactive setting, and this feels like a "game" I could play on a piece of paper.
Jon Blow wants to make games for smart people and I get that, but there is a difference between not suffering fools and spitting on them. It's been a while since I've played a game that felt so hostile to the player. Some of the stuff the game pulls near the end feels less like an intellectual challenge and more like a big middle finger.
If you are a puzzle junkie AND you are good at them, you will probably enjoy this game. If not, look elsewhere.

I have video review of the game available Here.
For those of you not interested in watching the video, here's the basic rundown of my thoughts on The Witness.
In short, The Witness is the most engaging and addicting puzzle game I have ever played. I've never seen a game more completely built around the experience of puzzle solving than this. And I do mean the whole experience: learning the rules, the sudden flashes of understanding, the satisfaction of solving a difficult problem and, eventually, the way the puzzles begin to rewire your brain.
The Witness marks the first time I have experienced full-blown Tetris syndrome since...well...Tetris. Even when I wasn't playing the game, I'd start to see grids and lines all over in the world around me, and my brain would constantly be imagining and solving puzzles in the background. This one time (and I absolutely swear this is true) the solution to a particular puzzle I was stuck on came to me in a dream. It was such a strange but amazing feeling. I thought that sort of thing only happened in movies, but The Witness made it happen.
It's really unfortunate that the game is so strongly centered around letting the player figure things out for themselves, which means that even the slightest details about the way puzzles work and the way the puzzles interact with the environment (and they do interact with the environment quite a lot. This game isn't just logic puzzles with a nice backdrop) can ruin the experience for someone. So buying into The Witness takes a bit of a leap of faith, since it really is better the less you know about it. I made the leap and couldn't be happier. So I strongly recommend that if you have even a passing interest in puzzles, that you make the leap as well.

This game took me about 19 hours to beat (without consulting a guide). Overall, I'd say if you like puzzle games you'll probably really like this. If you don't like puzzle games, avoid.
Pros:
+Pretty. Visually interesting without being distracting. One of the few games I found myself actually just walking around looking at the sights. There's something really nice about the low-poly models, saturated, colorful textures, and ambient sounds.
+Puzzle games that kind of put you in the position of a scientist and rewards skill at figuring out how things work (as well as actually solving the puzzles themselves). It's a sense of discovery and experimentation and accomplishment you don't find in lots of other games. Most puzzle games explain their mechanics up front and the core gameplay involves working with those mechanics, but this game makes figuring out the mechanics part of the experience. It reminds me of the enjoyment I derive from trying to solve mystery novels while reading them.
+Plenty long enough. Even after you get an ending there's still more you can do.
+There's more to it than just solving line puzzles by themselves in isolation. Many of the puzzles heavily involve interactions with their surrounding environment. There's also stuff to do that doesn't involve line puzzle boards at all.
+All sorts of stuff to discover (in addition to just figuring out the puzzle mechanics).
+They preserve the mood throughout the game, all the way to the end. Some games with a peaceful mood suddenly end with a credit scroll accompanied by obnoxious and over-energetic or overwrought "deep" music. This game doesn't have any music at all. I didn't find anything that really "took me out of the experience" through the course of the game.
+It's first person but didn't cause motion sickness (at least for me). Some puzzle games that have a lot of turning and wandering around can make me feel really nauseous. I feel like certain design decisions in this game contribute to lowering the chance of getting motion sickness (like turn rate and FOV).
Cons:
-Some tediuous and annoying puzzles whose main challenge is obstructing your ability to get a sense of their state (by being distorted and skewed or far away or other annoying gimmicks) or who force you to re-do earlier puzzles or walk back and forth a bunch. Some of them even made me feel a little nauseous. There aren't many of these - I get the sense they just wanted to play around with the existing puzzle mechanics in certain ways to change things up, but I kinda just wished they wouldn't or that they would just do away with those puzzles entirely. I usually get really frustrated and end up quitting games when stuff like this happens, but for some reason I found it pretty tolerable in this game.
-The final section drags on a bit too long for my tastes.
-A few puzzles will be impossible if you have colorblindness, but they are optional.
-Not a whole lot of story to figure out. Coming into this, I thought it was going to eventually answer all sorts of questions I had about the island and that that was kind of the point of continuing to play. It really isn't. In retrospect, I think this doesn't really hurt my enjoyment of the game much. And you actually can figure out the story, it's just not going to be something as elaborate as games like Myst or Riven. Despite the ending not being a big reveal or tell all, I actually really liked it (it's quite understated and not flashy, which would've killed the mood had it been).

I first found out about Death Road to Canada when I watched a friend stream it. I had a great time watching and decided to get it myself. 57+ hours of gameplay later, I know that it was definitely well worth the purchase.
The best part of Death Road to me is that each run is a new adventure. Events and choices are randomly given for you to make, many of which throw in some great humor. In one run, you could end up having to fight your way to a UFO that you can somehow drive, and in another, you might have to use your trusty shotgun or chainsaw to reach the end of a sewer. There's many different things and places to discover and enjoy.
Death Road also strongly delivers in its gameplay. It might look easy enough in the trailers to fight through zombies, but when you play the game, it's engaging and offers a unique challenge. You have to manage your resources wisely from the beginning of the run to (hopefully) the end, and you've gotta use your best skills wisely, like your shooting and strength. It might seem like a lot at first, but once you get the basics down, it's really entertaining.
Piece of advice: Don't expect yourself to win the first time you play. In order to have a winning run, you've gotta practice your techniques and how to manage your resources. However, with each run being unique and the gameplay being as engaging as it is, getting better and better is nowhere near boring. Each run builds confidence, and you find yourself strongly looking forward to the day you finally cross that border. Once you win the first time, more modes are unlocked, each of which provides a new challenge for you to face.
One last thing that I want to briefly mention is the ending to a successful run. I won't spoil what it is, but I'll just say that it's greatly rewarding after all the hours that you put into the game. When I won for the first time, the ending made it greatly satisfying, especially since I never used a wiki along the way.
This is a remarkable game, and I definitely recommend getting it. It's often on sale for 10 dollars, but if you're impatient like me and pay the full 15, you're still getting quite a bang for your buck.

I know what you might say: "They bought your vote!". But this is not true. Orlygift is a really awesome thing, because Commander Cool 2 easily could have been just another game in my ever growing Library, but since I had 1 week to write a review, I had a motive to play this game, and I'm glad I did.
Commander Cool 2 is a max 4 player platform game. According to its story, a grumpy janitor steals a time machine, so the company calls YOU to use a time machine prototype, travel back in time and recover the original. The levels take place in pre-historic times, where your enemies are cavemen and slightly more evolved people. On each level you have 4 tasks to do for 100% completion, collect all coins, complete the level in time, don't take any damage and collect the hidden crystal. Of course, you don't have to complete all on one run, so a maximum of 4 playthrough each level should be enough for maximum completion. Most of the time you just have to get from A to B, where B is your time machine, but every fifth level features a boss battle.
Graphics are okay. Nothing extra, but they aren't ugly either. Same for the sounds. Generic, but okay. And since this is a co-op game (too) you expect me to say something about the multiplayer too, right? Well I can't say much, since the game only has local co-op yet. This may or may not change, since it's Early Access.
VERDICT
A nice little platform game, which is perfect for older machines too. If you love platformers, go for it.
