At the time of writing this review, I've made it through the first three jailers of the game, and I can already say with conviction that this game was worth the purchase, especially if you're a fan of challenging games. It's also worth noting that I've been playing with a controller, and my guess is that playing with a keyboard is a much different experience.
The gameplay can be difficult, yes, but not to the point of feeling unfair in any way; the more you play, the more you learn how to spot 'tells' in the middle of the fight and react to them. The combat feels incredibly smooth, and you'll get a feel for the rhythm of things -- so to speak -- fairly quickly. Even though you have a limited set of moves, I can't say that I've found the combat repetitive, likely due to the pace of the fights and the phase system that is implemented. The art style is amazing, and the soundtrack is incredible, and both lend themselves heavily to the overall atmosphere of the game. I will admit, however, that the segments between the fights are a bit slow and awkawrd to maneuver, though they are heavy on exposition; but there is the option of just hitting A/X (depending on what controller you use) to have the game take over your movement controls until you reach the next boss.
All in all, a challening, fast-paced game with a great soundtrack and fluid controls. Would recommend.

This game came out of nowhere and I'm glad I checked it out. Fast, frenetic, fun. This is the best old school-style arena shooter to come out in a really long time. DOOM wishes that it had this game's multiplayer. The graphics are gorgeous, sound design is good, the maps are varied and well designed (for the most part), and all your favorite arena FPS modes are in there. It's simple, has a small but varied selection of weapons, and does just about everything right. This game does not seek to reinvent the wheel, and that's what makes it so good. For all fans of the old school Quake-style multiplayer FPS, this is the game for you.
EDIT: I'm still enjoying this game quite a bit so I thought I'd respond to some of the criticism I see in negative reviews.
"There's nobody playing" - These were all during early access. The game has a consistent player population at least right now, shortly after release.
"You can't play with friends/It's hard to get into a game." - Pay the cheap price for the full version to gain access to the server browser, solving both of these problems.
"If you want to play Unreal Tournament, just get Unreal Tournament. It's free!" - Yes, and it's also currently in a highly incomplete state whereas Toxikk is a complete experience. In addition, Toxikk handles differently with different weapons and movement mechanics. There's room for two good Unreal Engine arena shooters in the world.

Commander Cool 2 is a fairly generic platformer. It's definitely not an amazing game and there is no potential in the game to achieve that level after early access. It's just barely decent. There is however potential with some finetuning from the developer to make a decent game (from a 5.5/10 as it is now, to a 7.0/10).
My main motivation for this negative recommendation is due to the progression system. Every level you  can achieve three stars and one diamond. You get a star for collecting all coins in a level, finishing the level within a time limit and not getting hurt in a level. The diamond you just have to find. The problem with collecting stars is the fact that it's mandatory. Progress is blocked when you haven't achieved enough stars to progress. The fix is very easy: make it optional. For me it killed the flow of the game and my enjoyment of it.
It seems impossible to finish a level within the time limit. Because I cannot achieve this star in any level, I'm stuck at level 9 (of 33) and cannot progress any further. The main reason why I cannot complete this star is because of a second problem with the game: the controls are way off and not responsive at all. This needs to get fixed before the release. If you fail it should be because you made a mistake, but not because the controls let you down.
Also the graphics has two main problems. The animation really, really sucks. It's very noticable that they have used Spriter in the most basic way possible. It can be a lot better. The second part is the rock textures. They are ugly and detract from the overall visual quality. The rest is decent enough, but the rock textures are plain bad. Because they have a very strong presence, it negatively affects the perception of the game.
The price is pretty high for a generic platformer that's very light on content. Even with extra planned content, it's impossible to think €7,99 is a good price. I would urge the developers to not raise the price, but instead lower it to at least € 4,99. The game isn't good enough and never will be to warrant that price.
If the issues I have mentioned are fixed on release and if I didn't already had the game, I would have considered to buy the game in a sale (€2,49 - €2,99). Using the steam review system you can only choose recommended or not recommended. If there was a third option called maybe, I would have chosen that instead. But in it's current state I cannot recommend this game.
FULL DISCLOSURE: I have recieved this game for free from the developer.

It's an entertaining platform game where your goal is to hop into the time machine at the end of each level and defeat the ultimate boss. Although it's pretty traditional platformer genre, its colorful and comic design has been a spotlight. As the game progresses, you will be able to unlock all kinds of skins. You, riding a dinosaur, equipped with rockets, is getting chased by a giant dinosaur.
As of the gameplay, it now consists of 33 levels as of Early Access 1201. Each level has similar missions--beat the level within a certain time (vary between different levels), collect all coins, and take no damage. While passing the level may not be difficult, it definitely takes some practice to achieve all the goals. Actually some levels, especially later on, can get really challenging depending on how the traps and obstacles are laid out. With enemies throwing stones and spears, the level becomes harder to achieve the no-damage mission. For speedrun, you may allow yourself to take some damage and overlook some enemies, as all you do is catch up time. Fortunately you can achieve all the goals in different playthroughs, so you don't have to worry about killing all enemies and collecting all coins while trying to be fast without getting hurt. In later levels teleporters will become critical to pass the level, those portals may transport you to some surprising locations, though--you may find yourself in the middle of enemies or spike thingy, or empty space that makes you fall to death. The final level majorly consists of the giant dinosaur whom you must beat with rockets. Keep in mind the rocket is only effective when hit on the dinosaur’s back, so take full advantage of the wall since you are able to jump higher through walls, land on the temporary platform, and get yourself some time for the dinosaur to move away.
Meanwhile, I have noticed some minor downsides in the game. The program does occasionally crash for some reason I haven't figured out. There is no option to sprint, so player might feel a bit uncomfortable. Even though the game is in story mode, there is actually only a beginning cutscene, but as you go through the levels you will not see anymore, even after beating the final boss. When getting back to the main world and choosing levels you might find hopping through every level a hassle since all the 33 levels are connected by a winding route and cannot be chosen with a faster way. Nevertheless, as early access stage the entertainment is very satisfactory and performance issue is nearly imperceptible other than the occasional crash. As the development goes on I believe that bugs will be fixed and more content will be added.
In general, this is a game worth playing, it's quite entertaining because of the challenges as well as the graphics. The game is not perfect, but I can see the hard work behind the developers and would play more if new maps and more playing modes are added.

Love the art style, beautiful well animated and well drawn out.
Characters:
Well fleshed out characters, that cater to different tastes. A dangerous yet polite hitman, a childish and playful robot, a cat girl(?), Daily Bugle's Jonah Jameson replica?
All lovable and relatable.
Story/Writing/Lore:
The world of VA-11 HALL-A is dystopian(very tamed), cyberpunk future. And it doesn't go the "anything I write must make sense to reader since it's in the fiction category" direction. It tries and succeeds to make sense and to explain certain futuristic elements in the game. And balance it out pretty well. My favourite example is that, even with all the advanced technology that even allows you to replace your body parts, it comes with a price of the probability of getting a "nanomachine rejection syndrome". (play the game to find out more)
The writing and the pace that it delivers is just right for me.
Jokes are well placed, and well thought out.
Really subtle build ups that you wouldn't pay much attention to it, but once the joke is delivered, it will leave you smiling or laughing.
Gameplay:
It's a visual novel with afew gameplay elements:
-like mixing the correct proportions of ingredients to get the correct drink
-guessing a regular's favourite.
-getting an appropriate welcome drink for someone new to bar or alcohol.
-guessing an appropriate drink for a customer's mood.
-create an abomination for that streamer girl.
But do not underestimate them. I find myself subconsciously trying to get flawless perfomance everytime.
Soundtrack/OST:
Feels like an action movie, but appropriate since the world of VA-11 HALL-A, is a cyberpunk, tamed dystopian future?
Funky, Jazzy, Glitchy, Electronic-ish... I can't list them all, it's really diverse.
Personal favourites:
I love the sounds in the menu screen after the music finishes. Lets you have a better idea of how the world of VA-11 HALL-A looks like. With all that beeping and foreign sounds that you just can't identify.
Anna, because coming up theories for her during your own time or before going to bed is a good way to kill time or fall asleep. seriously.
I love how even though the game's lore setup just screams the potential of being an action rpg game. It decides to go with a really cozy visual novel, that still uses the game's lore elements keeps you really curious. Nothing really major happens to your character, but you still feel impacted by these little small things.
Overall: I'd recommend anyone looking for a relaxing game but as equally impactful as undertale. This is a very forgiving and entertaining visual novel, for anyone who wants to start exploring the genre. Instead of cheesy generic romance characters, you get to be a cool bartender.
Personal(unprofessional) thoughts:
The game has alot more potential. The world of VA-11 HALL-A is just dripping with potential. So much left unexplained. So much left unexplored. It feels wasted.
I'm also not a big fan of "thats the beauty of it, leave it to the audience to decide/guess" stories. Where things are left unexplained. It's unsatisfying, and I personally feel disrespected. Dragging it before explaining it all is fine, but dragging it only to explain nothing just really feels terrible, and I hope VA-11 HALL-A doesn't do that.

When I saw that "The Solus Project" was the spritual successor of this game, I had to buy both. I thought to myself, how bad could "The Ball" be?
I was pleasently surprised to find that it was not bad at all. It's by no means perfect, and similarities to Portal are obvious, down to the gun that doesn't fire bullets of any kind. That said however, if you enjoyed Portal and Portal 2 as much as I did, you'll likely enjoy "The Ball." A FPS puzzle game that makes you think and encourages you to explore to try to find secrets. The physics are perhaps the only part of the game I had issues with, and that was pretty rarely to. The music is lovely, the enviroments are beautiful, the controls are easy to understand and the game does an excellent job of letting you know what's expected of you most of the time without holding your hand the whole way.
All in all I'd give "The Ball" a solid three and a half out of five stars and would very much recommend it. Especially if you enjoyed Portal.

The Ball is a very simpler puzzle game that I feel accomplishes what it set out to be. That being a physics based puzzle game with a weak and mysterious story that binds it all together and gives it purpose. If you are looking for a game that makes you think for a cheap price of 10 dollars, then look no further than The Ball. The puzzles are well-designed and the developers managed not to get repetitive even with the extremely simple controls. However, it is important to note that the combat is extremely bland and the graphics are very lackluster, but that being said, the graphics do not take away from the raw gameplay experience. Overall, I recommend this game because it is a decently challenging puzzler that keeps you wanting to delve deeper into the ancient underground civilization and find out what the conclusion to the enigmatic story could be, and though it has minor flaws, for 10 dollars it is definitely worth picking up for the puzzle enthusiast.

This game seems fun at first, but it's filled with extremely frustrating RNG mechanics. You can literally have everything great, going your way and then with the turn of the next RNG event you're now doing horribly. Most fun games with these mechanics make it hard to get what you need, but if you get what's required you're usually ok unless you take dumb risks. Even playing it safe, you will get screwed by this game.
I've done at least a dozen plus runs now, gotten to the last day and had multiple rare characters in my party with good loadouts and supplies, but even with a four man party it's not fun and was not possible to win. I'm sure if you waste enough hours playing the game you'll get the lucky specific combo needed to win, but it rapidly becomes unfun. I am a huge SOCOM fan and have eagerly been following this project way before it ever reached kickstarter. H-Hour was promised to be a game that revived the third person tactical shooter formula that I loved and at the start it was on course to do just that. Unfortunately it has been a downward spiral of lies and deception that leaves me today feeling betrayed, untrusting and scammed by SOF Studios. This is a company that censors its community on the most extreme levels, doesn't hesitate to hide key information from its customers and sadly that's not even scratching the surface. Overall SOFs is the most unprofessional game studio I have ever witnessed. It is no wonder why funding was never secured from any investors in two years and we are left with the empty shell you see today.
Gameplay is extremely barebones and lacks heavily in features. Do not expect anything more than a third person perspective that allows you to run, crouch, jump and fire your weapon in the games two maps (yes two), one of which is a poorly designed open linear level. While advertising itself as a tactical shooter the game plays nothing like the series it is trying to imitate. Gun mechanics are horrible and teamwork is impossible due to the game not including voice chat among other basic and simple features. Overall this is as basic as a shooter gets and gives you no reason to play again after your first game is completed. While the one life round based structure is there, each round turns into a boring and bland team deathmatch. Technically the game offers horrible animations, awful sound quality, muddy visuals, numerous bugs and lacks heavily in content. Call it early access but I have been a day one public alpha tester and the progress made has been abysmal.
I do not trust SOFs to ever improve upon the game that is for sale today. Avoid a purchase at all costs until the developer proves they have the intentions and capabilities of delivering the product that was originally promised and begins to treat its paying customers like a professional studio would. As of today there is hardly any game here and what it does is beyond unimpressive. This has been such a massive letdown as a SOCOM fan to write this review. I am also disappointed there are delusional members of the community who are shilling themselves falsely hyping this up just in hopes of the project being saved by mass sales. As a steam user I am disgusted that another game and studio in such poor condition was let into the "early access" program. How a two map multiplayer only shooter with zero features was approved is beyond me.

I feel as if I've played this game enough to finally write a review. I downloaded this game back in it's beta, and I was really impressed by it. Not only was the game fun, but the aspects of the game as a whole were a new thing entirely. This was the first game in which I've experience true 3-D. What I mean by this is that there is no up and down on the map. Sure you may start faceing a certain way, but unlike games such as Battlefront 2 (first space battle game that I thought of), you can face your ship any which way. The controls are easy to use and understand. The maps big, detailed, and contain various interesting environments. Their a plenty of ships to chose from from three different factions. Different classes of ships have different special abilities. And you can customize your ship's loadout, getting more options as the game progresses. A couple of negatives to the game follow:
In the free roam aspect, the goals and objectives are sometimes unclear as to where to go and the map is very big and easy to get lost in.
The customization of your ship is limited to it's modules and weapons, with the option to use "standards" for paint schemes and emblems.
It seems to me that despite your amount of kills, deaths, captures, whatever, the game will give you more xp if you are on the winning team.
Sometimes the matchmaking will put you into games in which the other team has  better ships by a few ranks, this is because the tiers for matchmaking contain multiple levels of ships. For instance, tier two contains ranks 4-9.
Despite all of this, the game is very fun and addicting. At one point I had stopped playing back in the beta, but I got back into it due to the enjoyment of grinding even if only for that one double xp game per day. This game has a similar appeal as War Thunder which is made by the same company who made this game. The game is overall very fun and has the grind appeal as well as the enjoyment I find in every game, even if we lose. I definately recommend this game. I can't wait to see what more will be added. Oh, and did I mention it's free to play! Don't worry, paying doesn't seem to help players too much, except for the increased xp gain.

TL;DR at the bottom
Looks more fancy than the last time, the shiptree and missions pages especially. The new ships - the Destroyers - look very good (much like the rest of the ships) but are, like everything else in this game, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly expensive. PvE is still godawefully boring but at least I managed to destroy that alien commander now which I failed miserably at the last time. Guess they nerfed them.
Update 01.10.2015:
Played it for about a week again to give it a fair chance at not being bad - I really like space games - but alas to no avail. Let's see
- Matchmaking is a lot quicker now than it was before but no more balanced which means it can be attributed mainly to rising player numbers
- PvP balancing... yeah no don't get me started on that
- PvE balan... PvE is godawefully boring - admittedly that's the general problem of PvE everywhere in every game but this here takes it a step further
- Ships are still the way they are after the evil wizard (see below) but somehow they managed to make it half decent with the weapon locks to classes and so on. Still bad though as you have to grind redundant ships to get the ones you really want - e.g. Jericho Guard-Frigattes are jsut way more sensible than Federation as former have way more base shielding to use their special with. Oh yeah and they are still absurdly expensive.
Once upon a time -
this was a fun game where you could do space dogfighting as though there was air. The factions were pretty starkly contrasted in their attributes and special abilities on ships making for some interessting choices. It had an OK progression for a FTP game - the premium content was actually more powerful than what could be gained from grinding but it wasn't gamebreaking.
Then came the evil wiz-----a patch.
Aaaand suddenly it doesn't suffice to grind enough "standing" - now you have to grind synergy to unlock new ships that might or might not have a similar ability to the one you currently grind. Abilities got spread around more and some ships received things that are completely pointless on that hull and should've stayed where they once were. Then they switched around the weaponsystems, removing the cool ones and limiting the selection for ships even more than it was before (where at least you could find cool weaponsystems for all classes of hulls). Once you actually grinded enough synergy you hopefully have an astronomic amount of currency to actually buy that new ship as well. Did I mention volunteer secondary missions that lock the ships you select for them out for up to AN ENTIRE WEEK? Yeah - very fun gameplay element that. The premium content is basically mandatory if you ever want to get anywhere.
Now it's a shipwreck (literally) of what it could've been, heck of what it WAS.

The first thing that came to my mind after playing Commander Cool 2 for a while was: Damn, this is exactly like Mechanic Escape! In fact, there are a lot of similarities. Most of the mechanics are the same, for example, such as double jump, wall grind or even unlockable skins for your character after a bunch of rounds done. Some silly achievements are also similar, like die x times, then die xx times, kill x enemies, collect x coins.
Now, does this make CC2 a bad game? No, not at all. Even if they did got inspiration from Mechanic Escape, they did created a new valid game, fun to play, and with a complete different "face". The pre-historic theme is well developed, appart historic fails, but overhall they did a good job on putting it all together in a fun to play fashion. Most of the achievements are pretty easy to obtain, too, so if you are a achievement-dude, it is well worth spending some time in here.
Some levels are very easy - others not so much. But by playing on you will get to understand all the game mechanics, which will help you understanding what or how you have to do.
The terrain graphics flicker a lot, not as much as to the point of hurting your eyes, but when you notice it it's a bit irritating. I also noticed some "bad" finishing at the pink-dinossaurs that you use to jump (the begging of their tales seem very very irregular).
Includes trading cards, which is always nice. I have no opinion on the versus mode as I haven't found anyone to play with so far.
Overhall, yes, I do recomend this game, and since it is in early access I am hoping the devs do work out the little things on the game.

First of all, it must be said that this game is more visual novel than bartending simulator - you only serve drinks during lulls in conversation, and most of the game takes place through dialogue between the MC and characters that come to the bar.
That being said...
This game is awesome. The characters are far from generic; they aren't cookie cutter stereotypes you typically see in other visual novels. They seem to be people unto themselves, and that makes your interactions with them all the more interesting.
The stories that are told vary from being hilarious to being heartbreakingly sad. Combined with the fact that these are personal stories, not tall tales about toppling regimes or killing evil lords, makes this even better. These characters are down to earth, and their stories are all relatable (to a certain extent).
If you enjoy visual novels (or if you enjoy reading in general), buy this game; it won't disappoint.

This is the best puzzle game I've played since Portal.  For me, it's better than Portal was.
I don't want to spoil anything about the Witness, because the true enjoyment comes from discovering the essence of the game as you go.  So I'll speak in terms of Portal.  This game is tremendously longer (it took me ~40 hours to complete both achievements), and in my opinion is incredibly harder.  There are some puzzles I spent way too long on, and others where I literally laughed with excitement when I finally figured them out.  Whereas Portal had fantastic narration and at least some story-centricity, the Witness relies on mystery, discovery, and exploration to capture players.  The Witness is non-linear and each player's experience and discovery of the game is assuredly different.  I was able to solve enough puzzles to complete both achievements without any external assistance, although I know there are more facets of the game I haven't fully explored yet or just can't figure out.  This game does a good job with that adventure game trope: you discover interesting features in the world, which very likely have some function, but you just don't know how to interact with them yet.  I have a piece of paper here on my desk with reminders of such mysteries, as well as a bunch of puzzles I drew out to help me solve them.
Worth knowing, I fit squarely into this game's target demographic.  It will likely appeal to players who are stubborn, inquisitive, and have taken at least one philosophy class in their life.  I refuse to look up any how-to guides or walkthroughs for games, knowing that the enjoyment comes from frustration followed by the joy of discovery.
One critique of the game is that the puzzles themselves can be a bit repetitive.  By that I mean, they overall follow the exact same format the entire game, although with myriad variations on that core theme.  I do believe this was a conscious design choice for the sake of unity, however, I posit that the game would not have suffered, and perhaps would have felt more constantly fresh, if there were other types of puzzles.
Braid was great, Portal was amazing, and this game is a step yet above.

This is a zombie survival road trip simulator full of dad jokes.
In Death Road To Canada, your goal is to survive a trip from Florida to Canada, acquiring cars, looting ruins, and running from a truly monstrous amount of zombies.  Up to four people can fit in the cars you find - and a bevy of strange special encounters make each run unique.
The humor is the weirdest and best part of the game.  Each game has a bit of a "you had to be there" element to it which makes it hard to explain (I just survived an encounter by having a circus clown sign up for a pose-off with bandits), but since each game has so many weird traits, learning these encounters and mastering the weirdness for yourself is a huge part of the fun.
There are some qualms - the controls occasionally stick, and the language isn't quite well translated - but if you want an over-the-top serial-encounter game to scratch the itch that Super Amazing Wagon Adventure left, this is one road trip you'll want to take.

Review from a previous Dev Tester of the game:

The cheating/hacking/exploiting has overtaken the game as of Sept. 2015. With a dev on their team openly admitting to the public that this isn't a primary concern of the game, I have lost all interest.
With the game only able to maintain 16 players at peak playing times on a Friday/Saturday night, the players have become stale and over abusive. Speculation has occured that anyone who dislikes the game and makes negative conditation towards it will recieve harsh punishment from the creators by going to lengths to tarnish your reputation. If you are a streamer, there is little to no support as well when running into issues. If you are streaming this game you will run into countless issues and problems that seem so easy to be fixed on the dev's side. If you are brave enough and consistent enough, you might bear thru the growing pains to show this game to your viewers.
Overall this game went from full potential, to waste of time and energy. The way the company and development team handles the community and general public is disgusting to say the least.

H-Hour World's Elite: By design, this game is the spiritual successor to the original Socoms (1&2). A tactical shooter that relies on teamwork and communication. This game has come a long way and SOF studios is committed to making the best game possible. I have seen that in the process that they have put in place. I can vouch for that this game has recreated that  Socom feeling on more than one occasion. 3 guys left, they have the bomb and it's up to me to stop them. I took out the first two and threw a nade through a window taking out the last one hiding upstairs in the bomb plant site. That was a rush, with palms sweaty and a great sigh of relief when I got the job done.
That Socom feeling isn't something you will get every round for there are so many variables. It's like a big game of chess. Where do I spawn start? What Loadout? Do I rush and possibly give my life to stop their rush tossing grenades? Or do I take a slower approach and try to pick off the enemy and then try to get around them somehow? This game has all of that.. even in it's early state.
If you are a fan of the old games and you want this game to succeed, be a part of the Early Access and make H-Hour, a game that isn't like every other shooter out there.

If you loved the SOCOM series back in the day, then this is the game for you. They're trying to reproduce the same feeling as SOCOM but not copy it exactly.
It's a third person shooter with medium-small sized maps with demolition (like CS:GO), one life per round, and will eventually have ranks, clan battles, more game modes and features of course, and SOF Studios actually read their forum and implement changes that the community asks for. You know how an entire community can get angry and rise up in the forums because something in the game is terrible or stupid? They read that, and generally they adjust it to what we want. That is, MOSTLY. Some subjects, like bullet velocity, remain untouched and are out of whack, yet the company won't address it.
Remember that this game is not COD and it's not Battlefield, and if you come on to the forums wanting changes that resemble those games, you're going to get shut down. Only buy this game with intent on helping it get to full release. Do not make a review and thumbs down the game because you think it's bad because it only has 2 maps and 2 game modes. They'll be adding weapons, game modes, animations, tactical equipment, maps, etc as they grow with your help. Review the game based upon core mechanics and gameplay, not upon the lack of features currently.

Go, liberate that outpost -you can do it stealth or frontal attack-, unlock that gun or that other by completing transports, bomb defusals, hunting missions over and over. Liberate fortresses and go on with the story until it ends.
Let's be honest, these games are repetitive. They aren't bad but the things you do are the same, and FC4 to me lacks that Vaas madness element of the 3, so the story was somewhat more interesting than this one.
All in all if you are more into "open space FPSs" sort of thing, you aren't going wrong with this one. Even if you beat the game you can reset the outposts so they get populated again by enemies and you can go on killing or showing your stealthy prowess but that's it.
Positive? Yes. Negative? Hell, Ubisoft try to do something new other than sequels and sequels over sequels on games that have the same structure over and over again.

WELCOME TO A MOBA THAT ACTUALLY DESPISES LOW MOBILITY AND GOING THROUGH 30 MINUTES OF FARMING.
Good points:
* No towers, no farming, you level up in teamfights, killing.
* Even when there are no towers, each team can build defenses for their respective sides in
the form of mistic animals or plants (They provide bonuses or utility, but with enough skill you
can actually pass them and keep fighting).
* Incredibly well designed characters. You know about Garen from League, or Juggernaut from Dota, the
spinning to wining guys; well, here you have Tyto the Swift, wich is a persian assassin of crazy mobility
that can actually keep striking between dashes and after dashes. Every character combines abilities
that you already know, but gives them new pasive efects that help to keep the game fresh.
* FAST matches (My longest match was of 7 minutes) in very small maps, believe me, there will be
ALWAYS a teamfight for you to join. How little can the maps be? If you want a reference
think about Zanzibar of Halo 2 but with all the excitement of the abilities that a MOBA game can provide.
* Beautiful graphics. Please, read again, beautiful, not realistic. Each monster, map and character has incredible
aesthetic visuals and you can understand their theme in one look.
* Mobility. Every dam character has a dash, a running, jumping, flying or blinking ability, and you can perform
different kind of atacks depending of your current position on the ground (If you jump, or fall from a high place
you can land using a falling atack, and ETC, THIS can be done with practically all the characters).
BAD POINTS:
* Buy a controller. PLEASE, buy a controller. It is obviously from the first time you try to use an skillshot
that it was designed to be casted with a control and not keyboard/mouse. (You can learn how to
properly use skillshots with lot of practice, if you feel confident enough this will not stop you).
* Ridiculous amounts of RAM requirement. I can perfectly play any other MOBA with better graphics such
as Dota 2 without mayor lag, i can even play Dark Souls smoothly, but this game, with its cartoonish
graphics, is almost half of the time running slowly because of it. I need to literally close every other single
thing im doing to let the PC put all that RAM into the game even when i set it to the lowest quality.
* FREEMIUM. Yes, everything is free, but you will unlock the heroes and custom items very, very, VERY
slowly. The game is almost desperate for your money. Yes i know this is a problem shared with League
of Legends, but this has something to do with the next problem:
* Few players. I had to wait 4 minutes after finding my first match. This can variate from 2 minutes to 6 minutes of waiting while the system tried to match me with a team, and sometimes the system is actually unable to find a propper match, and fills the thing with BOTS for both sides. If you are suffering from a lack of players WHY DO YOU INSIST IN MAKE ME PAY TO HAVE ALL THE OTHER CHARACTERS? This makes every match to feel limited, because, if someone else picks first the character i wanted then im screwd, for i have to choose other of the remaining 7 weekly characerts, and sometimes the other players have the same issue, making you limited to 3 or 4 different characters per week.
Im beggin you, Gigantic. You have AMAZING gameplay and AMAZING characters, but if you keep being so close minded even in this desperate times, no one will come to play.
Do i recommend this game? HELL YES. Even with its defects you can still have a great time, even when playing against bots, its really dynamic and innovative.
Cool tip: Take 3 hours hours of your time to proof every character on the practice tool map untile you find the one that makes you feel the more confident in gameplay level, believe me, you will not regret this.

What if I told you that you play as a man in a shark suit, defeating cavemen with a severed unicorn head that shoots rainbows? If that doesn't get your attention, you can also wear Half-Life's armor while carrying a gatling gun and running from a tyrannosaurus rex! Oh if that's not enough for you, you'll also fight a dinosaur with a rocket launcher while dressed as Futurama's Bender, Sailor Moon or anything else you want. There's even four player local coop and death match versus.
Commander Cool 2 is a platforming shooter that has you fighting your way through the stone age in all sorts of unlockable costumes with a variety of weapons. On paper, the game sounds like a blast and for the most part it is. There are just a few things holding it back like jumping issues, game length and how easy it is. Since this is an Early Access game, the short length is forgivable. There's hopefully more to come and the thirty levels show enough promise and let you get a real feel for the game and what its capable of.
The easy difficulty makes it the perfect game for kids. The first twenty levels are easy, but the final ten do get challenging. In a way that's quality game design, but in another there are so many hardcore platformers out there that forget that even easy games can be fun.
On the surface, there's not much going on here, just a simple shooter, but then there are boulders to roll and hop on for extra height. Hop on a sleeping dinosaur's back as a springboard. Keys to unlock switches that control moving platforms. At some point there are teleporters. With all  these goodies, I don't feel like the game used them enough, but that could be because the game is so short. Like all platformers, you'll find plenty of spikes that will instantly kill you.
Commander Cool 2 is a forgiving game. You can take three hits of damage before you're dead. You have infinite lives, so death means you respawn at the beginning of the level. Defeated enemies are still gone, coins are still collected. Later levels even have checkpoint flags due to trickier jumps. Nothing too difficult though.
You'll find plenty of guns from crates. Commander Cool starts with a boulder gun that has a short range projectile that drops to the ground. The arc is rarely put to good use. Other than that, you've got short range shotguns, long range crossbows, even if cavemen never had them, a chicken that fires long range eggs, a gatling gun that sprays at a quick pace. The other weapons seem to have a slow deliberate pace that forces you to aim or it'll be another second before you can fire again.
These cavemen foes are no pushovers, they can take a lot of damage, and shooting one means they'll charge at you. Most people would run away from a slick dude wearing shades shooting at them, but these foes charge! You'll find giant Venus fly traps, cave men that throw rocks, others that throw flaming spears and all sorts of hazards. Smashing rocks, flying spiked boulders that get dropped out of no where. It makes for some good timing sections, but its never too difficult.
The game is setup like a mobile game, you've got ten levels in each section of the campaign. You select a level and unlock them by completing one. At the end, you hop in your time machine and receive stars for three things: getting to the exit in under par time, never dying and collecting all of the coins. These are just meaningless goals for people that want achievements.
At every tenth level is a dinosaur chase that really helps break up the pace of the game. You'll fly on pterodactyls, get chased by a dinosaur and even fight one. There's no going back here, so you'll need to quickly collect the coins or if you're like me, you'll miss them all and just exit the level.
Each level has a crystal to collect in order to purchase  the costumes. These costumes are just personal preference and don't do anything different. In four player cooperative, its a good way to tell yourself apart from everyone else. You're bound to find something you want, even if they don't have a license to use them and might get forced to be patched out.
There' 360 controller support, but you're still forced to use a mouse for the menu. Other than that there's keyboard support. The controls are simple they could have been played on a NES controller. You have  left and right to move, one button to shoot your gun left or right, a jump and mid air double jump. Commander Cool can also wall jump, but it feels a little stiff compared to other games. You'll need to push into the wall and jump then pull away from the wall to get distance. There's also a button to change your costume and an action button for pulling levers. Pushing down does nothing, unless you're on a floating platform, then you'll automatically fall through it when other games require you to push down and jump to fall through.
With that said, the jump feels floaty, almost to gravity defying. That's just how it is, but the major sticking point I have with the double jump is the lack of control. If you jump out once, you can't jump back for your second jump, instead you'll need to go out further or else you'll drop like a stone. You're stuck unable to move from this drop. There are vertical levels that I've fallen a few screens before I had control to move left or right again.
One of the only consistently difficult parts of the game are hanging rock platforms. You need to land on them precisely or you'll be wobbling all over the place. If you fall off or hit the rocks too hard they'll begin to swing and once they're swinging, they'll never stop. It just makes a tough moment far more difficult. Of course restarting the level is a good option. None of the levels are too long, most are under two minutes. There's a good bit of exploration for the coins, but nothing that will ever take you away from the map. Every level is contained in one map.
In terms of frills, there's a versus mode for local death matches. There are even custom maps, but no map editor in game. This can extend the game's life, but only if the fans take to it. The developer has included a few map scraps so that you can use a third party editor to make something. These maps only have a beginning and an end with nothing in between.
The story happens in a skipable intro. A downtrodden janitor hops in a television that's really a time machine. The corporate boss has just the man to call, Commander Cool of course who you'll see in shades on a beach surrounded by beautiful women. He pulls off his Oculus Rift to discover that it wasn't real. You'll then hop into a different rust bucket of a time machine and the animated introduction ends. Normally I don't discuss intros or stories, but this was entertaining and I missed it completely by jumping straight to the menu.
As for the animation arms swing with no elbow movement. Maybe that's just the cavemen. As for the music, its nothing memorable or detrimental. It fits the vibe and the sound design is much better. Shotguns blasting, rockets exploding and happy joyful chimes at the end of each level.
One of the pet peeves I have is when you start the game and go to select one of the three campaigns to play, you'll discover that the game only has one campaign. The other two are future DLC. While I have no problem with DLC or playing for an extra campaign, the last thing I want to see after I've bought a game is being lead to believe that I only bought one third of the game. I remember back in the days of Shareware when you got the first campaign free, but teased with everything the full game has to offer.
In the end, Commander Cool 2 isn't a game for everyone. Its easy, imperfect and short. Its still a fun game that leaves me wanting more. I'd like to thank Christian for giving me a copy of the game. If the game didn't have its charm and silliness I'd say avoid it. There's just something fun about the costumes, predicaments and weapons that overcomes any jump issues.

My review for this game as it stands is tentatively positive.
Commander Cool is a retro style platformer with colorful modern sprite graphics and a comedic look, where you play Duke Nuken lookalike hunting a time machine stealing janitor through history (although only the prehistoric era is available now).
The platforming elements are really solid, including some of the physics elements like the swinging stones and rolling bolders, although I'd still say the weapons/enemy gameplay needs a lot of work. Some weapons, like the default rock launcher are awful and require too many shots to kill anything, slowing things down, while others one shot enemies with ease. And there's no logic or effort to getting the upgrades, the maps just toss them in your path (or don't).
The game has three challenges and a hidden item per level, which are all pretty short. Only the time trial mode tends to be challenging, but its usually very hard, which does provide something nice for platformer enthuiasts to shoot for, even comparing their scores on each level.
Ultimately, this is an OK game right now, but with the level editor and promise of online (instead of local) multiplayer it should have some room to grow in the future.

Th Witness is a difficult game to talk about, but I am comfortable saying that it has been my favorite game this year and quite possibly my favorite game of all time (certainly in my top ten).
Aside from "I hate puzzle games" and "There is no plot", most players who down vote this game do so because they lack whatever quality it is that would give them the big "ah-ha" moment. The Witness is just that: one big ah-ha moment. If something doesn't click for you and/or you get frustrated easily, The Witness may not be for you.
For me, The Witness never went beyond your typical "difficult". It started easy, got harder, and challenged me to think outside of the box, but I never had to stop. I never really left an area stumped to return to it later. The ah-ha moment typically came between 10-15 minutes each time I was stuck. This created a VERY positive feedback loop for me as a player.
But anyway, here are some recommendations if you want to give The Witness a chance:
1) Play with a friend. I played with a fellow developer. Perhaps the fact that we are game designers helped, but if one of us got lost, the other person usually caught the solution right away. It was very seldom that we were both confused.
2) Accept that not every area is required in order to complete the game. I have a very busy schedule and have yet to 100% the game. Only seven of eleven main areas are required (any seven) to view the game's ending. Many have complained that Blow did not work to accommodate the visually or hearing impaired. Puzzles like this are NOT required and he claims to have even worked hard to try to include a puzzle that was only accessible to the color-blind (sadly it didn't make the cut due to the large gamma differences across displays).
3) Sleep on it. The ah-ha moment is what you're after. The puzzles are almost never any more difficult than the previous puzzles (to an extent). A fresh mind and a change of perspective can help.
4) If all else fails, take it to paper. A lot of friends made paper models to work out some of the more difficult puzzles. I believe that my friend and I only had a sheet or two of paper notes, but I am assuming that we weren't the norm.
Aside from all of that, the game is beautifully designed. Many, many memorable moments and puzzles. Great visual and audio design for a game that can seem so constrained by the overall plot/setting. A remarkable experience, in my opinion.

The witness is a divisive game to say the least. The people who like it, really like it. But those who go in expecting something this game is not, are almost certain to walk away disappointed. The following are just some general things about the game. I dare not call them "facts" since some things are still subjective, but I try.
Whether you will like the Witness or nor depends largely on whether you consider any of the following to be pros or cons.
1. A number of puzzles rely on color and sound, more so than you might be used to in other games. Colorblind or tone deaf players be warned.
2. Similarly, there are a handful of puzzles with brightly flashing colors which may cause discomfort.
3. The Witness is a puzzle game, far more than it is a puzzle-adventure game. It's not Myst. Solving puzzles doesn't give you a new piece of the story. It gives you more puzzles. Story is an afterthought at best.
4. The witness has decent atmospheric sound design, but is devoid of almost any background music.
5. Some sections you may do 10 or 20 puzzles in a row that are similar except for increasing complexity.
6. This game has no tutorials, no hints. Everything is determined by the scientific method. You have to experiment with puzzles to understand how they work.
7. When you solve a puzzle in the Witness, there is no fanfare, no sparkles, no gold star rating. For the most part, the only reward is unlocking the next puzzle.
8. The Witness is open-world. You can very early in the game go nearly everywhere in the island. It is also likely to throw puzzles at you in the early game that you will need to step away from and come back to much later.
9. You will always be drawing lines in this game. There are many different mechanics at work, which make for many unique puzzles, but the method of imputing the solution is always the same. Even switches and levers are line puzzles.
10. This game can be really hard, obtuse, and often frustratingly mind-bending. Sometimes, very rarely, it might also be just a little cheap.
- The bonus totally not objective section
Unpopular opinion inbound, but I think I liked this more than The Talos Principle, to which it is compared quite a lot. I like the mental process of solving puzzles, but not really the act of having to show my work, which in Talos Principle might mean 5 to 10 minutes of carrying around boxes through force fields and trying to get a laser angle just right. I already know the answer. I don't want to have to do all the grunt work as well. I want to do a new puzzle.
This game allowed me to do just that. Once a puzzle clicked, it took just a few seconds to draw it out, and move on to the next challenge. This wasn't always true. At times the pace set by the puzzles is broken by the languid pace of the world around you, which I suppose is fine, if you are taking the game at a slow pace. Near the end of the game, getting around the island between the few puzzles you might have remaining was also not that much fun anymore, and one or two puzzles were maybe just a bit too obnoxious in the way it regarded my time.
Despite this, for the most part, I loved it. It this was one of the most inventive, original and gorgeous puzzle games I had played in a long time.

Excellent concept, bland execution.  The core concept is there, but nothing ever builds on the original push/pull ball mechanic. This game could have been a pretty awesome coop puzzle game, but it is single player only.
PROS:
-Nice idea
-Ball moves around easily and without headache (this COULD have been a major frustration point, but is executed almost perfectly).
-Voice acting is ok (for what very tiny bit there is).
NEUTRALS:
-Graphics are just barely acceptable (quality/resolutions)
CONS:
-Walking/swimming/railcar simulator. MASSIVE amount of just walking around for no reason. Areas are large and excessive for no real purpose, especially since there is very little to explore (a few secrets but thats it). No other drops, items, collectibles, etc.
-NO SPRINT/RUN.  For a game with massive amounts of walking, why can't we run!?
-Barely two game mechanics (push/pull ball and magnets in the levels that do the same). No additional mechanics are introduced over the first 3 levels (8 levels total so little less than half the game). No other items, gear, or abilities. The core concept is good, but nothing ever builds on it.
-Environments are very bland with the exact same textures over and over.
-Puzzles are very straightforward; barely require thought. Almost every "puzzle" is just push these switches in linear order.
-"Survival" mode (and all combat in the game) is extremely boring and repetitive. Just  hold the ball and swing side to side. Although a number of cool traps exist, using them is usually to your detriment as it is more effective to just swing the ball.
-No plot/narrative. Every now and then there is a tiny bit with a voiceover, but as a whole characters just show up and virtually nothing is explained. Given how expansive the environments are, you would think they could use this space to tell a story....but no, it just adds to your playtime by making you walk longer between areas.

The Ball with some pretty big flaws.
First, I'll start with the good: The environment design. The vast caves and ancient mayan/aztec/central american cities are very captivating to look at and explore. There are some great vistas in the game. Similarly, the design of the enemies is pretty good. Also, the ball puzzles are, for the most part, fun, if quite easy to solve.
However, there are a lot of problems. The first thing that hits you is the wya the game is renderd. It has a sort of "cell-shaded-but-not-really" feel to it, and it looks as if someone was toying with the saturation filter a little too much at times. But this isn't anything major, and is probably more a matter of personal taste.
One of the biggest gripes I have with this game is the level design. Yes, I just praised the environments, you would think the level design was good too, no? Unfortunately, this game suffers very badly from "invisible wall syndrome". Rather than design the areas you can walk around to not have areas you can cheat your way around, the devs simply slapped an invisible wall wherever you're not supposed to go. This is really jarring and annoying when I encounter it in a game, especially one that involves having to more around an object like the ball. It ggets so bad that at one point, thanks to a physics glitch, I had trapped myself floating in mid air, standing on top of an invisible wall, and was unable to get back into the level because it was there.
Also, on the subject on exploring the nvironment. There comes times when you try to explore the area to find more "secrets", but find yourself being forced onto the next area because you solved a puzzle or boss fight too quickly, which prevents you from finding the secrets. This is very annoying.
There are also some "boss" fights which range from incredibly easy to beat to downright impossible without dying many times first. You shouldn't have to rely on the game saving your progress on dying to get past bosses.
I would also like to touch on the story. It starts with you trapped down a hole. Fair enough, an archaeologist is bound to have that happen to them once or twice. But then it appears they have no rope to send down the hole. And apparently they need a crane to lift you out. None of this makes sense, the hole isn't really that deep, and pretty early on in the game, the player mysteriously produces some rope with which to tie the ball to things.
So in short, The Ball is a fairly mediocre puzzle game, which if you're just a new and casual player, you may enjoy, but if you've played games for a while, you will very easily spot the flaws in it.

Those are the first words you hear in
, a character-action game where you perform one-on-one battles against similar-sized bosses, using your limited repertoire to slash and shoot through an atmospheric world. But does it live up to it’s idea of a game featuring a gauntlet of bosses? Or did it need something more?
To start, I initially was afraid that
’s moveset would be incredibly limited. And it is. You don’t exactly have a lot of tricks or really any “combos” in your moveset, but what you do have are a simple set of mechanics and systems that drive the player to instantly master what they’ve been given. And as a result,
’s fights become a tense, fast-paced gauntlet that taxes reflexes just as much as adaptation against strategies and a full understanding of your combat moves.
The fights are incredibly well-designed, with the enemies all having just enough variety to constantly change up your tactics and shake up the otherwise simplistic routine of “See Warning - React - Punish”. While it can lead to the game looking repetitive at times, it certainly doesn’t feel that way, due to each fight having multiple phases that shake up strategies and throw all sorts of wildcards at you. The final phase in most fights often combines most of the attacks and spray patterns you’ve dodged against and throws them all at once, making for a satisfying if incredibly challenging end to a fight.

Initially, I was incredibly frustrated by the game. I found myself wasting hours on a single boss fight and I honestly felt that some of the attacks were cheap. However, it further hammers in the point that
is something you have to absolutely master as soon as possible to progress. You can’t blindly mash the Attack Button or just wait for the enemy to continuously let you parry, you have to really understand what you can do to quickly and efficiently defeat the Guardians. As an example, there’s a move (Mentioned in the “How to Play” section of the game but never mentioned at all otherwise) that allows you to charge up your sword while in the 1v1 blade mode, which leaves you vulnerable for a short while but makes your next hit super powerful. Combine it with a charged Strike, you can efficiently do an enormous amount of damage to enemies, and it’s mastering tricks like these that really elevate the skill cap for this game. The end result of this is a combat system that’s gratifying, elegant, and has enough substance behind it’s flash.

What I feel like is the biggest downer are the sequences in between the fights, in which you just walk a long path down to the next area. While the set-pieces in these sections are visually pleasing, nothing visually or truly engaging happens in these sections (Other than your fellow rabbit-hat companion talking to you about your next opponent). These sections are both uninteresting and perhaps worse, not a good breather for the fights. This is mainly because these sections sometimes last way too long for it to really be a good breather or good break from the fights. As a result,
’s pacing is way too off and doesn’t strike a good balance between gameplay and waiting before the next fight.

Where
steps up in its gameplay, it also steps up in both its presentation and story. The game’s visuals and character design (which was done by Takashi Okazaki, known for the Afro Samurai Manga) oozes in style, with a distinct set of colors and setpieces that give
its own identity. And this identity is further discovered in the stellar techno soundtrack, which really makes the battles feel alive.
While I won’t be spoiling what the story really is about, the one thing that made it an overall interesting and intriguing plot was how vague the game was about who the characters were or the world. It makes it clear at times that the characters clearly know what’s going on, but the player doesn’t know any of it, meaning figuring it out through self-discovery becomes a satisfying and huge part of the game.

Unfortunately, none of the characters felt interesting or had any real character beyond their movesets. This is made worse by the voice acting, which appears to be incredibly inconsistent in quality and tone. In the English Voiceover, some of the characters would often say something in a harsh tone, only to instantly make an awkward voice delivery in a more monotone voice. It’s here where I see the polish in the game somewhat drop a bit, as characters constantly repeat the same voice lines.

So ultimately, the game comes down to replay value to really entice you in.
is being priced at $25 (launch), and it may be a bit worrying for some. For me, it clocked to around a 4-6 hour playthrough (This can vary depending on how long it takes for you to overcome a certain boss). Fortunately, the game offers a wealth of additional modes (Including a Furier Mode that ups the difficulty and a Speedrun Mode) to play following your first playthrough, but it may still not be enough. Ultimately, whatever or not you think the price point is worth it is up to whatever or not you think the game’s concept or gameplay will keep you coming back hours after the credits roll. $25 is quite the steep price which what can be an experience that might be difficult to pick back up if you found yourself really annoyed by its pacing.

In conclusion,
is something I would highly recommend. But it may be off-putting to some who want an experience that can last them just a bit longer. Or a game that flows naturally through its levels.

Remember that kickass fight at the end of Kill Bill Volume 1? Yeah, Furi reminds me of a series of fights based on that encounter. With the game focusing on nothing but bosses, it doesn't over complicate things with lots of different mechanics and moves. What it does is focus on the little things in battle: blocking, positioning, and pattern recognition. Bosses change up their styles reasonably between the different waves of their fights, and it's up to you to quickly figure out how to take them down, and what skills in your arsenal will counter each of their attacks. It's simple but effective, and the bosses bring a strong variety on how you go about defeating them. With that said, you will see hiccups from time to time, as some of the games rules get changed on the fly, and the game doesn't do a great job of indicating that the rules have changed. And certain moments will take you right out of the immersion, as clipping/graphical issues can make things a bit hard to overlook. In the end, you're here for the technical combat, and it works due to the KISS principle (keep it simple stupid). Just don't expect Bayonetta or Devil May Cry mechanics, because it's not that.

Furi is a game about you, a hero, who was a kept as a prisoner, but now you're out of your jail, and your goal is to regain your freedom. While you attempt just that, you piece together the story and ask yourself whether or not what you are doing is the right thing.
You'll be fighting various bosses, all unique in their moves and fighting-style
While the controls are very simple - Shooting, slashing, parrying and dodging - and some of those charged up - Furi doesn't force the player to learn Combos or do Button Mashing, but rather how to outwit your enemy and fight them with what you have. Your timing, reflexes and execution will be deciding if you can emerge as the stronger fighter. Learn how your adversaries fight, parry, dodge and punish their mistakes!
Furi has two standard difficulties, and upon completing the game on Furi (Standard), you'll unlock the more difficult Furier difficulty.
You also may compete in Leaderboards and Rankings or in the Speedrun mode that is unlocked upon finishing the Story.
From the games atmosphere and soundtrack, all I can say is that it is gorgeous. If I wouldn't have to dodge hundreds of projectiles, I'd listen to this music all day long.

The bosses all vary, one boss you maybe need to fight close up a lot, the other one keeps distance and avoids close up fights - There is just ONE thing all bosses have in common, and that is the challenge they offer.
Furi is the best Bullet-Hell I ever played, and a unique Gem, that shows how a game looks when in every aspect the game developers know what they do.

-No minimap

-Extremely poor interaction between forum moderating team / end users.
-Extreme censorship of feedback.

I'd heard great things about The Longest Journey, so I got it on sale and decided to settle in and get ready for what I expected to ben an incredible story and challenging point-and-click adventure.  I want to state that I am an avid and proud classic gamer.  I have an embarassing amount of classic gaming gear in my closet of shame, and I fully appreciate classic games of all genres.  I've played many classic point and click games, and I'm aware of how the genre has evolved over time.  That is why I was surprised at how disappointed I was with playing The Longest Journey for the first time in 2017.
The game's dialog seemed forced - as in they literally force you to sit through all branches of the conversation tree (with ALL NPCs), and you better do it or you'll miss out on some info that lets you continue the adventure.  Seriously, there is so much exposition in this game, you'd think it was an exhibit at the 1999 World's Fair (if there was one).
The puzzles were either too easy or completely ridiculous.  You'll see other reviewers complain about the "Rubber Ducky" puzzle, and they should.  It was a masterpiece of communicating to me that this game hates me.
The voice acting might have been good for 1999, but now it is only passable on average and unbearable at times.  The guy who did the Slingblade impersonation made me think about switching to subtitles only!
I didn't connect with April (the main character).  There was something about the character that just seemed too young and inexperienced to be relateable.  Then I found this wonderful review which helped me identify what my problem was:

In case you don't want to read that article, the basic idea is that games have gotten really good at being serious.  Mass Effect, Bioshock, Batman, Skyrim, The Witcher and a ton of Indy titles have accepted the challenge to deliver a compelling and inspirational story, but in 1999 that wasn't the case.  As a result, the almost self-mocking tone that TLJ takes comes off as overly apologetic and holds the player back from truly identifying with the characters.
Finally, I literally fell asleep during every extended playing session with this game.  That is probably mostly my fault, but I just couldn't take it anymore and had to quit.  If the game still came on CDs, I think I would have made it to somewhere in disk 2, but that was enough for me.  I cannot recommend The Longest Journey to my friends or anyone unless maybe it is the first story driven adventure game you'll ever play.

Recently I decided to see if I could try the trilogy out, just to see if it was even possible for me, this was a total pure clean slate run with no history with the series, no lore known, no story known, no secrets, only that I know vaguely of April and of Zoe and that Chapters took a long time to make in order to finish the series in some meaningful way.
Anyway I fire up the game, and quit-out 10 mins later in utter frustration at what can only be described as the worst point and click adventure game I have ever encountered in my gaming history. No hints, tips, help, guides or advice of ANY kind can be found in the game, you are literally stuck trying to figure out the first of presumeably many puzzles in this so-called award-winning, critically acclaimed game...which it's not...in any way/shape/form and those defending this game are outright liars for not seeing it's flaws and mistakes.
Now the music is good, the voiceover work is fantastic given back around 1999/2000 VO work was extremely rare in video games and almost never done, however the storyline/plot will leave you confused as hell and even on that 1st screen I have no idea what's going on. You have to redirect some waterfall to help a tree that in turn will save an egg for some giant phoenix type bird and I can only assume you get to move on from this, but my brain was hurting just trying to figure out how you re-direct the water with the stick you found. Cue the rage quit.
Now you can argue this is only the start and yes that's true, however I watched some YT videos /wo spoilers and they do state the game has several puzzles that require logical thinking to solve, which is fine...IF the game had proven more helpful, but you get nothing, and bare in mind yes nowadays you can find the answers online, however:
1. If this had been 1999/2000 early internet would NOT have given answers so you lot would have been just as stuck if your a veteran of this series so you should understand my anger
2. I had ZERO interest in cheating my way through this game with help guides, I was expecting it to be enter game, play through story, work my way through the trilogy, it's all done, game was flawless, no issues, but this is not the case
A good game will ease you in, help you settle into the game and progress through it, TLJ does not accomodate for this and your first few mins with a game really factors into whether you will like/enjoy that game or not and games that don't help you out when they should (especially in RPG types) really let themselves down in that regard.
I cannot recommend TLJ to either new or old players, the repeating VO text from clicking and zero help on any of the puzzles is too mentally detrimental for the game to win you over and succeed in immersing you into it's world.

My husband and I recently got addicted to VR and have been fairly desperate for a brand new computer with all the bells and whistles.  That said, my decision to pursue a graduate education has left us penniless for the time being.  One night, the gaming bug bit me particularly hard after seeing some of the puzzle/adventure PSVR releases that have just come out, and I rather desolately fired up the 7 year old laptop that occupies space under my bed, hoping to find something on steam that it could run (generally hit or miss, with more miss than hit) and could also be entertaining enough to occupy my time.  I knew that with the graphics being as bad as they were, something point-and-click would probably be the best.
I found this game on a list called 100 best point and click adventure games or something like that.  It was $10, so if it only brought me a few hours of middling entertainment, it was probably a decent value.
Wow.  It's now two days later.  I have done nothing in my free time except play this game, despite the fact that I am in my last week of grad school and I literally have the final exams that will make or break my graduation in two days.  I can't help it--it's really well done, with very tricky puzzles (I am a dedicated puzzle gamer, artifex mundi, myst, name it) that really had you trying just about everything, tons of lore from a bunch of different races, and cutscenes that while old, are really impressive and almost emotional in how cool some of the effects are.  I have no idea how many hours it took me to finish this game, but it is the kind of game that you really shouldn't start unless you have a few days free, because you probably won't be doing anything else for a while.

To be honest, I have to open with this:
I have never experienced the bugs people complain about in this game.
My computer is higher-end, so the 6 GB RAM requirement does not affect me.
Having said that, boy do I love this game. I'd probably have more hours and more time played in the past couple weeks if League of Legend's ranked season wasn't ending soon, but I really want people to know this is a fun game. I don't write reviews often, so I'm really sorry if I don't have much of a format. The game is in a rough spot right now, so I wanted to throw this out there and see if maybe I can reel in some players.
People liked to talk about how Overwatch was if Team Fortress 2 and League of Legends had a baby, but this game is if League of Legends and Overwatch had a baby. Two teams of five, picking from a (decently sized, for its age) roster of "heroes" (like Overwatch, not all heroes are on the "good" side, morally), fight to destroy each other's nexus... Except it's not a nexus, it's a GIGANTIC (ahyuck), invulnerable monster called a "guardian" (either a griffin or a naga. depending on the team). Teams summon creatures (cyclops to build walls, plant-bois called bloomers for healing, cerberus for vision, and a few others) and fight each other to gather power for their guardian, and once their guardian has enough power, it flies across the map and attacks the enemy guardian, making it vulnerable to attack. The guardian has three health bars, and depleting one "wounds" it. First team to wound the enemy guardian three times wins.
That's just the premise. The mechanics are greeeaaat :D
It's like League in that you have a set of abilities that you can level up, unique to each character, and you can't switch once you've picked for the match; while it's like Overwatch in that it's third person, you don't have to unlock your skills, and there's all sorts of fun things you could do that nobody would expect since you can jump around and platform in the map (ex. as a marksman hero, you can get up on a perch and snipe people, but as an assassin or fighter, you can totally run around the marksman's blindspots, up the map, and just pop out behind them to fight the hell out of them). There's four maps right now, which each have very different layouts, so matches are very different from map to map, and of course there's the added variety of having this or that hero in the game, changing what you have to deal with/look out for.
It's not like either in that the skills you level don't get stronger, per se; they give you more abilities to go along with that skill. For example, the hero Tripp (my favorite, though people who play currently might judge me for that) can level her skill "Electric Slide" (ahyuck) to give her 100% crit chance if she lands it, and the hero Beckett can level her basic attack (dual-wielded pistols) to have more ammo in a clip. Depending on how you level your abilities, you can end up with a pretty different style of play than someone who would build differently. You can experiment with each hero and see what suits you best :D
I have to give the current downsides, too, otherwise this wouldn't be honest. Like I said at the beginning, the game has a 6 GB ram minimum, and I don't have to worry about that cuz my computer's higher-end. My friend plays with me sometimes, and her computer isn't the best by any stretch of the word, so I don't really know about that.
Apparently it can be buggy? I've never run into a bug... at least not a game-breaking one. The only one I've seen was if you jump on a certain platform on a certain map, the hero Ramsay T-poses til he hits the ground, but that was just funny.
The one thing I have dealt with is the small player base. Like many good but underrated games, the player base for this game is on the smaller side, so queue times can be long... but only recently have my queue times reached eight or nine minutes.
The issue is that the developers of the game, Motigo, have been for the most part laid off by the people who picked them up, Perfect World. The game wasn't making enough money, it would seem. Part of the team has been kept around to maintain and update the game, or so we've been told/hope. The reality is that if the game doesn't start picking up soon... it'll die. The people who have been posting since its launch on the discussions and in the reviews that this is a "dead game" definitely haven't helped at all... bunch of... rude people. It's a fun game, and more people should give it a chance.
This is running long, so I'll cut it off here. I'll probably continue this in the Discussions section, so if you wanna hear more from me go there. But for people who made it this far and don't really wanna continue, thanks for reading this! I hope you give this game a shot, it sure does deserve it!

Play it for the puzzles, not the 'story'.
I found the puzzles in this game to be excellent and intriguing. The solutions aren't arbitrary or ambiguous like the puzzles in Myst or Riven, and the rules are introduced gradually and organically as you explore the island. The difficulty scales satisfyingly, and I found them challenging but enjoyable throughout. If you enjoy sudoku or crosswords, you'll probably like the puzzles in this game.
The 'story' however... well, it's basically not worth a damn. It's literary nonsense that pursues pointless ambiguity, sacrificing meaning on the altar of 'complexity for it's own sake'. Good stories are ambiguous because they address complex issues, not the other way around. This story doesn't adress much of anything - even if you drill down far enough to grasp what's really going on, with the second ending and hidden audiologs. There's just nothing of weight to it, and it's wrapped up in so many layers of secrecy that even if you do manage to wade through the pseudo-intellectual ♥♥♥♥♥♥y, the dissapointment at the end is doubly disgusting.
Blow's made a wonderful game here.

Th Witness is a difficult game to talk about, but I am comfortable saying that it has been my favorite game this year and quite possibly my favorite game of all time (certainly in my top ten).
Aside from "I hate puzzle games" and "There is no plot", most players who down vote this game do so because they lack whatever quality it is that would give them the big "ah-ha" moment. The Witness is just that: one big ah-ha moment. If something doesn't click for you and/or you get frustrated easily, The Witness may not be for you.
For me, The Witness never went beyond your typical "difficult". It started easy, got harder, and challenged me to think outside of the box, but I never had to stop. I never really left an area stumped to return to it later. The ah-ha moment typically came between 10-15 minutes each time I was stuck. This created a VERY positive feedback loop for me as a player.
But anyway, here are some recommendations if you want to give The Witness a chance:
1) Play with a friend. I played with a fellow developer. Perhaps the fact that we are game designers helped, but if one of us got lost, the other person usually caught the solution right away. It was very seldom that we were both confused.
2) Accept that not every area is required in order to complete the game. I have a very busy schedule and have yet to 100% the game. Only seven of eleven main areas are required (any seven) to view the game's ending. Many have complained that Blow did not work to accommodate the visually or hearing impaired. Puzzles like this are NOT required and he claims to have even worked hard to try to include a puzzle that was only accessible to the color-blind (sadly it didn't make the cut due to the large gamma differences across displays).
3) Sleep on it. The ah-ha moment is what you're after. The puzzles are almost never any more difficult than the previous puzzles (to an extent). A fresh mind and a change of perspective can help.
4) If all else fails, take it to paper. A lot of friends made paper models to work out some of the more difficult puzzles. I believe that my friend and I only had a sheet or two of paper notes, but I am assuming that we weren't the norm.
Aside from all of that, the game is beautifully designed. Many, many memorable moments and puzzles. Great visual and audio design for a game that can seem so constrained by the overall plot/setting. A remarkable experience, in my opinion.
