Angeldust is... OK.
Although you could call it Walking Simulator or THE NEVER ENDING JOURNEY...
When you start the game, you choose 1 of 4 classes, each class has several unique abilities only available to them.
I personally chose the Builder; so I had a Turret I could Spam, a Dispenser that gives me Infinite Health Recharge, a Springing Board that I can use to Troll Players, and a Bomb/Detonator so I can cause Massive Destruction to both the Terrain and Monsters.
So after choosing your class... you spawn on your PLOT of land that only you can use/edit and you can then place blocks to build a home, a garden, a d1ck - whatever suits your fancy.
And thats really and sadly about the only purpose the home serves is that its just merely decoration.
You can "Play the Game" without even touching your plot of land.
If you go NORTH or SOUTH you will find yourself on a NEVER ENDING JOURNEY where you will see other players "works of art" as you walk very slowly for hours.. only to find a few handful of players who are most likely either AFK or pre-occupied with decorating.
If you go WEST or EAST outside of the Village - you will find yourself all alone, as you venture on yet another NEVER ENDING JOURNEY through different types of terrains such as a forest, a desert, a jungle, yada yada yada.
Sadly, the odds of you meeting another player the further you venture become more and more.. and MORE less likely but you may have some sort of social interaction at Level 1 by a 0.01% chance or less.
After Reaching Level 2 of the Wilderness outside of Town your odds of social interaction are about 0.0000000000000001% or less.
And by Adventuring out into the Wild, you will make  "Discoveries" as a new player (such as: finding a new type of terrain, killing a new type of monster for the first time, or digging up a new type of block) and that nets you a sum of gold that you can use to change the color of your characters clothes on there website, unlock your unique abilities or purchase different textured blocks for decorating your plot of land.
So.. after a few entertaining hours at most... you will find yourself inevitably... BORED out of your MIND!
And that about sums up the game.
Now with that said... here are several things that could actually make this game way better imo:
+ Social Interaction - Add more ways where we can actually MEET Players easier
+ Mounts - Good god do I feel like a human snail at times.. give us a Horse to ride or something...
+ Give Homes a Purpose - Take Minecraft for Example; you build a home not only for decorative purposes but for Protection, to Store your Items and so your Friends can build with you, etc.
+ Give Homes Interactable Objects - Like a Bed, A TV you can Turn on/off, a Music Box that players can only hear while inside the house, a teleporation machine maybe for tele to friends homes, a kitchen where you can cook.. I could on and on...
+ Items you can pick up - Would be neat to actually find 1 time use items that I can pick up and store in a treasure chest at my home like say a piece of meat from a slain monster that regens my health, etc.
+ Crafting System with Collectable Items - I was disappointed at the lack of a crafting system (i.e. when I cut a tree down it just disappears instead of collecting sticks that I can use to maybe craft wooden armor, a fence, a crown made of sticks or whatever)
+ Give Friends The Ability To Edit Your Home - It'd be fun to log on and see what new stuff my friend did to my house or even still be able to build a home on my plot of land with another player who I've given permission to do.
+ Add a Menu IN-GAME that allows Players to add Friends - There should be a place in-game where I can type a users name and then maybe warp to his house or location!
+ Add Group PvE Dungeons - So instead of wondering through the wilderness alone and bored; maybe at home you can interact with some sort of object that adds you to a wait list and then send you to complete a dungeon/boss fight with other players
+ Add PvP Games - You could add anything from DUELS, to Group Battles with 10+ Players vs 10+ Players on a random generated small battleground where players can interact with the terrain during the match (For Example Red Team Builds a Castle but Blue Team Manages To Tunnel Under it and Steal a Flag say for a Capture The Flag type of game) OR you could even add a PvP Challenge Game where instead of players killing each other... they simply kill monsters and see who can get the most kills by the end of the round.
+ Fishing - Pretty easy to implement and would add a nice little social feature for the game.
+ At the very least if these ideas are too hard to develop... you could add a (X,Y) Point that all Players have available on there warp devices so everyone can warp there and be able to Team Up to go off into the Wilderness.
That way Players don't have to walk the NEVER ENDING ROAD that goes North and South for Hours and Hours in order to find a single soul to interact with...

I didnt play The Longest Journey when it came out, so it is new to me.  Im about halfway through and I can honestly say I like it.  However, I do not love it.  I know some rank TLJ as one of the best adventure games ever...Personally, I would not.  Its a solid "good," not "great."
It has decent voice acting, which is present throughout the entire game (thus far).  Some of the speech goes on for a long time and I found it myself reading the text and skipping through the speech to move things along.   Some of the voice acting  is a little cheesey, but for the most part, it is solid.  The story is derivative and brings nothing new or exciting.  However, even though it is unoriginal, it is presented well.  There isnt much in the way of music or sound effects that stand out, which is both a positive and a negative.  Graphically, the game is playable on a modern high resolution monitor.  It doesnt look great, but it is definitely passable.  The graphical models low polygon count definitely show the games age.  And the backgrounds seem to get washed out from being stretched to higher resolutions.  The interface is simple and easy to use.  Everything accessable from the mouse, which is nice.  There is no need to use a keyboard, unless you want to skip through the lengthy spoken dialog.  As I said before, its faster to read the subtitles.  Some of the animations while interacting with objects, especially people, are annoyingly long and unskippable.  This is especially annoying when you are trying to do something repeatedly.  Some of the puzzles are really simple and require no thought.  While some are a little more complex.  There is one puzzle in the game that is so ridiculously difficult that it is considered one of the hardest puzzles in adventure games.  This game definitely falls into the category of clicking inventory items and just seeing if they interact with what you are doing.  This game defintely has the failing of many adventure games, in that the solution is something you wouldnt think of.  You simply solved it by clicking inventory and interacting with the environment.
Again, this game is good, but nowhere near the likes of other adventure games.  Still, for the cheap price, it is worth it if you like the genre.

Really strong and fun early access tower defense game.
* Has good progression of different types of enemies with different abilities (fast, armored, flying, burrowing, building jumping, etc)
* Interesting mechanic where the bugs get to the cake and then go back along a ground path (which would only be different if they are flying/jumping.)
* Fun different building types that balance different tradition TD buildings with some fun modifications (fast, slow, aoe, high damage single target).
* Interesting boss enemies with different mechanics.
* Pretty easy to complete a level, but has a nice visual representation of if you were able to protect the cake without any insects touching it, which I have yet to fully complete.
If you like a Tower Defense then is a fun replayable and cheap game, my only wish is that it was 3 times the price with three times the content as 18 levels left me wanting to play a lot more.

My favorite aspect is the unique mechanic of limited actions. In between rounds, you only have four (later six) eggbirds to build, upgrade, or gain extra resources. While you can undo immediate actions, you cannot sell or move towers later.
During a round, your only action is to temporarily power up towers, then wait a few seconds for the recharge. This might sound limited, but especially in later levels, it keeps you busy with quickly deciding when and on which tower to use your power best.
The maps are very open, giving you many different options to figure out the best set up by replaying a level.
The art style is not for me, personally, but also doesn't turn me off.
Overall, the game is all about strategy and planning ahead, which can make it frustrating at first, but more enjoyable on replays. As a fan of strategy and tower defense games, I love it.

I just finished my first playthrough of Defend the Cake's 18 levels, and I am very excited to go back and play through all the levels again.

Defend the Cake is relatively easy to beat if you don't care if some of your cake is taken by ants or rocket powered snails, but difficult if you're trying to get a perfect score.
The aspect of Defend the Cake that distinguishes it from other tower defense games is that all 6 towers have their own purpose and no single tower feels overpowered.
I highly recommend purchasing this game if your're a fan of strategy tower defense games.

TOXIKK joins in on the trending resurgence of niche gaming that was once popular near the turn of the century. More importantly, it is equipped to quench the thirst of many arena/twitch shooter fans that have been left wanting more after playing DOOM's new multiplayer. The fans I'm referring to, by the way, are other Millenials that have been dying to play a new Unreal Tournament clone. Now I'm not saying that TOXIKK is without fault, or that it is capable of bearing the title of UT's illegitimate successor (excluding UT4), but TOXIKK presents an admirable effort and foray into a genre that was once forgotten by many. It deserves a chance to prove its worth to the arena veterans, and newcomers alike, waiting for UT4 to finish development – which is currently in pre-alpha.
The developers have provided a free version of TOXIKK for anyone to enjoy, for as long as they like. Their reasoning behind this, and differences between the full version can be seen
. Bottom line, TOXIKK is
F2P, and the free version will only have access to the
experience. As an Early Access supporter (full version owner), I am perfectly satisfied with their decision to release a free version in order to help bolster the online community, spread awareness of the game, and ensure longevity of community support. If this fact isn’t enough to sway you into at least trying out the game, or if you are on the fence about purchasing the full version, feel free to read the rest of this review.
Online multiplayer is, of course, supported offering classic deathmatch, team deathmatch, capture the cell, and area domination modes. A server browser helps you navigate custom, private, and public matches alongside a quick join feature. Game customization options include: mutators (Instagib!), # of combatants, score, time, etc. A single-player mode is also available for play, tasking you to complete contracts to advance your career.
There are no classes, loadouts, weapon carry limits, or health regeneration as seen in many modern FPSs. Going back to the good ol' days, every weapon or item must be picked up after the game starts (excluding a common starter pistol). As expected of an arena shooter, some of the types of weapons you will see include: automatic assault/sniper rifles, rocket launchers, plasma blasters/shooters, flamethrowers, and a razor blade thingy. Also, every weapon has a primary and secondary fire mode, effectively doubling the variance of gunplay.
Some maps offer the ability to operate futuristic vehicles, such as: an assault bomber, battle mech, 4x4 SUV, hoverbike, and hover jet. These vehicles are extremely satisfying to use, yet do not cause any major balance issues gameplay-wise. And don't be alarmed, it isn't that difficult to take down a vehicle, especially if multiple allies are helping.
12 available maps, a few taking heavy inspiration from classic Doom and UT arenas, provide varied battlegrounds for you to wreak havoc. They each have so much style and themed scenery, ranging from: jungles, ancient Italian strongholds, Canadian Rocky Mountains, Cambodian temples, Bolivian Andes, sci-fi Chicago, Hong Kong slum districts, to a secret research facility in Moscow. In the same vein as the classic arena shooters, the map design tends to incorporate 3 levels (upper floors, ground, underground), multiple staging areas for hostile engagement, and various hidden/side-paths for flanking. Also, a native level editor is provided for use, and synchronization with Steam Workshop allows for the creation and sharing of amazing maps!
Standard arena shooting controls are utilized; however, advanced movement controls derived (with changes) from UT2K4's system are also implemented, including: WASD movement, jump/double jump, 4-directional dodging, crouch (avoid falling off edges), high elevator jumps, wall-dodges, slope jumps, and so much more depending on how well you can utilize the combinations of moves. I have seen some straight up high-tier Lucio movement going on, making me think that I was in the wrong game for a moment. These fluid combos are made possible by retaining velocity after jumps (unlike in UT2K4). If you seem to be lost in the wealth of information, or scared that everyone will be Spiderman'ing around you, worry not. There is a competent movement tutorial and everything will become second nature after a while.
Going back to my previous statement that TOXIKK is without fault, I would definitely love to see a better UI. It is very minimalistic as is, and detracts from the futuristic sci-fi immersion that everything else manages to put forth. I also need to see bunny hopping servers (obstacle courses) to be able to finally replace UT as my go to arena shooter. But other than minor personal preferences, TOXIKK seems to be one of the best arena/twitch shooting experiences (multiplayer) that is currently released, especially on Steam. Until UT4 is released, which may be a very, very, long time, I can easily recommend fans of the classic shooter genre to tryout TOXIKK, at least the free version, and support the full version.

Gigantic equates to the casual gamer's hero-based MOBA, but it has a lot to offer for competitive players as well.
Choose between a weekly rotation of five heroes ranging from assassin to tank and every hybrid class in between. Matches consist of summoning creatures that gain power toward attacking the enemy Guardian. Level up your hero and gain power by upgrading summons, racking up kills and destroying the enemy's creatures. It's as straightforward as that, and perhaps what makes the game oversimplistic.
However, there is some strategy involved in this casual F2P title: having no medic on your team means spawning a healer as your summons, as opposed to cutting off lanes with the Cyclops' walls or visualizing enemy map positions with Cerberus. Also, players who've farmed enough in-game currency to purchase the two accessory summons (the fiery artillery Drake and the paperweight Obelisk) add a layer of tactical considerations for their enemies. While there is variety in which you level-up your hero, there's almost always a surefire build that dominates the playfield for each character. Thankfully, Motiga have recognized certain imbalances and attempts to mix up the meta periodically.
Overall, I like to imagine Gigantic as the casual gamer's over-the-shoulder MOBA; the community is tight and friendly, and toxicity is yet to be found as I've played. Match waiting times can be a hassle, considering the size of the game's current audience; but it's worth a shot if you've been windowshopping for a MOBA and haven't really been convinced to buy one.

After about an hour or so and having completed the first two levels I am not sure if I will go back to this game. I realize that I still have roughly 5 to 7 hours of gameplay left, but I think after the first level something more significant should have occured.
The game just feels like going through motions. Hit switch, move ball, hit switch, go through door, hit switch, move ball, watch out a bad guy, hit switch, go through door, etc.
The game looks fantastic, even after all these years, it plays well, controls well, and mechanically it does what it sets out to do, but there is just no real reason to keep going.
And while I hate to compare this to Portal, the game does showcase how you can have simplistic mechanics but keep the player engaged and entertained at the same time. With every succeeding level Portal lays out a narrative through audio and visual cues, one that makes you want to engage with the game and see and hear what comes next. But with The Ball, you get none of that engagement. A few story elements thrown around in what seems like an afterthought, and some one off expositives via secrets.
The worst thing I can say about this game is that it is disappointingly boring. It's not bland, it's not ugly and it certainly isn't a waste of time, it's just ... there.
It's no Portal, but it's kind of like Portal. Fun, interesting mechanics, and beautiful scenery. Well worth it.

I love this game, I haven't played it a lot, even less on PC, but it's a great game that I can't wait to play right now. However, I stumbled onto a little problem I thought I ought to share. IF YOU ARE PLAYING WITH MINIMUM REQUIREMENTS OR SLIGHTLY BETTER, after all the cut scenes, the screen just goes black the first time. This is because Ubisoft locks all their games at 60fps and the default graphic settings are high. Just go to the main menu, settings, video, and lower the graphics quality. You can also lower the locked framerate to 40. This and a few other adjustments (optional) fixes the problem and you can go about your killing. Now keep in mind, I have a 6GB 2.5GHz Intel core i5 laptop, and this fixed the problem, I'm not sure if it will change it for you, but anyone without a super beefy desktop should do this, just for the wellfare of you computer if not for anything else. You can go higher than these settings on my PC, but I did this to start and it worked.

Co-op is different though compared to FC3, because the co-op is just playing the story with a friend as Hurk from FC3, and isn't really the 4-player shoot everything, which I kinda liked in my opinion, I wish they could've had both in the game. For the multiplayer I didn't really get to play it because it was dead, which is kinda sad, because I think it would've been pretty fun, but I can't really guess what it would've been like. Stick to the story. The graphics compared to FC3 are WAY better in my opinion. I thought they were the same until I loaded up FC3 and saw how terrible they were compared to FC4. The weapons have amazing sounds now as well compared to FC3. There were a couple new weapons, and there are signature weapons, which introduce special weapons for a high price, which have different attachments you couldn't put on before, and so on. The crafting system is also the same, where you kill animals to get the upgrades, and then find special animals to get the very last upgrade and so on. There might've been new syringes, like the hunting syringe, which allows you to see everything through walls and so on for a certain distance. I could be wrong. The animals were much more detailed, and much more aggressive than in FC3, but they weren't as distracting.
The vehicles are the same too, but there's a buzzer, which is a helicopter you can fly around and even shoot down at the enemies with your secondary weapon. It's pretty fun to ride in, and the majority of the game, I flew around to get to places much easier.
I loved the Characters in the game because they were given so much personality and detail that it was really hard to make the choices I had to make. Personally Pagan Min is one of my favorite
of the franchise. He's a pretty cool guy but I don't want to explain why otherwise it could ruin the story. Ajay Ghale (protagonist) felt like another Jason Brody, except Ajay fit more to his killer instincts. I felt as though he just did what he was told all the time, but he got to make choices. Jason Brody just killed everyone, regardless of him claiming he couldn't kill a person. Ajay had more personality and involvement in the story, rather than just a story reader like Jason. Amita and Sabal gave off weird vibes throughout the story. They tend to argue alot and brings out the choices that the player can make, and can affect how the story is told. Both of their storylines lead to different consequences, and  both are quite baffling to say the least. They had just as much involvement as Ajay and Pagan. Characters that didn't really have an impact on the story was Noore, Paul De Pleur, and Yuma. I never really understood why they were there in terms of playing the game. You only see them for a couple minutes, compared to Sabal, Amita, and Pagan. They seem to have been just put in there the last second, because you really never hear from them at all.
I loved the soundtrack in the game, but I personally loved FC3's soundtrack ALOT more because it fit the intense gameplay much better. There were certain times where it did get intense, like when you had to get the thangkas for your parents' house, which played a mini-story to follow.
When it comes down to it, Far Cry 4 has to be one of the best of it's entire franchise, and it's really fun to even explore the beautiful environment given to you. It has given me a story that I wish I could see a second part of and makes me want to play it back again someday.

The Good
- Graphics are beautiful
- Weapon variety (once you get any money) is decent
- The voice acting seemed fine.
- If there were any bugs they were relatively minor (like enemies getting oddly placed in the air) or I just didn't notice them. The game never crashed on me, I never experienced any slowdowns, and generally it ran smoothly.
- Flying around in a buzzer and blowing stuff up with the grenade launcher is fun for the first 10 minutes
The Bad
- I spent the majority of time in this game actually being bored, hoping that the plot would make up for the repetitive nature of the gameplay. It doesn't.
- It seemed way too familiar to Far Cry 3. I mean I got this game on a discount, so the price wasn't bad for me, but I can't defend Ubisoft for trying to sell this initially as like a $50 game. There was a 4 year time frame between Far Cry 2 and Far Cry 3 and I think it showed in terms of the change in quality between the games (not just graphical quality but also gameplay improvements). Far Cry 4 on the otherhand had only two years after Far Cry 3 was released. It seems like it could have used more development time to make it more distinctive from its predecessor.
- The map colouring for mission icons is terrible. Normally I wouldn't even think to mention something this minor in a review but it honestly was bad enough to warrant it. It was actually hard to find main quest missions at times on the map because of how close
- The game needs more proper side missions (and not just random side missions where you kill X lieutenant) and fleshed out secondary characters. Make me actually feel like I'm in a civil war and make me relate to the people in it. Just having generic NPC's that I get quests from doesn't do this.
- The writing seemed pretty weak (especially my characters motivation for fighting through a civil war). If it were me I would have just dumped the ashes in a pretty lake in Kyrat and called it a day. No need to get my head blown off for my mom's sake (and yes, I know about the secret ending).
In short: There isn't anything about this game that I felt was unique enough to warrant recommending someone try it.

The Witness is wonderful, meaning full of wonder, and awesome, meaning it elicits awe.
I think this game could inspire a love for learning in a child.
I'm only probably a tenth or so in to the game, but I've already gotten my money's worth. The island is opening up in layers of meaning, layers of understanding. The whole island is a series of allegories layered atop one another and beckoning the curious explorer.
Blow's design objective -- to model epiphany -- requires inductive reasoning of the player. This game is entirely inductive reasoning. It's the most dense use of this rare mechanic that I've ever seen presented in a game.
I heartily recommend this game as an excellent use of your time.

First and foremost: This is a puzzle game.
I don't mean that in the obvious sense. I mean in the sense where it is the closest game possible (besides possibly the brilliant but flawed game "Pandora's Box" made by Microsoft) to a jigsaw puzzle. As such, each fragment of the game you complete - each panel, which you can see in the trailer - is meant to take a small portion of your time to complete, and be challenging in and of itself. If you know the solution, you can solve it within a couple seconds maximum and then immediately start on the next "piece." If you cannot solve it, place it down and pick up another. I see a lot of people complaining about lack of reward for completing each panel; your reward is the information you've gained mentally and your greater grasp as to how the puzzles work. If you do not get a sense of euphoria from understanding puzzles and completing them (or if you are failing to gain understanding of the puzzles as you play), this is not your game to begin with.
This game also heavily rewards observant people. There is a particular puzzle in the game that I solved within minutes, because I quickly realized more information was needed, and sought out such information, finding it almost instantly. I watched someone else who took hours on the puzzle because they failed to recognize where they were missing information. No puzzle in the game has a solution that is obtuse or arbitrary; all the information you need to solve every puzzle in the game is given to you in creative ways; you just need to recognize it. 98% of the time, it is immediately around you, staring you point-blank in the face.
Comparisons are hard to draw. I see plenty of reviewers likening this game to Myst or The Talos Principle. Neither of these are good comparisons at all. Myst had obtuse puzzles that were not explained fully with little depth. In The Witness, each puzzle is obvious and doesn't require vague clues from elsewhere. You are required, however, to fully understand the puzzle itself. Knowing how to solve it is not enough; there are many puzzles within the game with several possible solutions, and you are required to figure out them all. As such, each puzzle has incredible depth and complexity, which cannot be said of adventure games like Myst.
Each puzzle also does more than form a small part of a whole; you are required to understand and learn what works within the puzzles and what doesn't. Once you understand the puzzle itself (which in my case, sometimes required graph paper, Legos, or both), solving it was trivial and took seconds. The same cannot be said of The Talos Principle, where each puzzle had a few variables which, with trial and error, could be used to create a solution, and even with the solution in mind could take several minutes.
The Witness is not a game for everyone, and both positive and negative reviewers need to understand this (In fact, a negative reviewer explained in such depth what he disliked about the game that I realized this was 100% my kind of game and bought it immediately). If you are a curious player who pays attention to detail in every game you play, and who enjoys brilliantly-crafted mental challenges just for the sake of the challenge, this may well be the puzzle game you've been waiting for. If you suffer from impatience while attempting jigsaw puzzles, or often charge through games without peeking around every nook and cranny first, watch someone else play the first few minutes of The Witness to get a better feel. This may just not be for you.

Firstly I'm not saying it's bad because it's hard. Whn I first got this game I really enjoyed the game wounding what secrets I would learn but after a few hours I noticed what the reward is MORE LINE PUZZLES it just not rewarding to play alone maybe with friends.

I didn't absolutely hate the game, but as I got further and further in it, I started not caring whether I solved the next puzzle or not. Sometimes I would discover a door and I would care until I opened the door the puzzle was blocking.  For the most part, I learned that most of the doors just led to shortcuts through the world and really didn't reveal anything. Sometimes the doors
, but those weren't very rewarding as they didn't really give you insight or reveal what you were doing on the island.
Many times I'd be presented a puzzle where I knew I could solve if I pulled out yet another sheet of graph paper and worked it out, but simply didn't feel like it. So I ended up quitting, playing something else and coming back the next day until the same thing happened. It turns out that is exactly how I approach sudoku or maze puzzle games on my smart phone. Binging on those is exactly what playing The Witness started feeling like. So I got through to the "easy" ending in small doses. Fortunately with everyone complaining about how bad the easy ending was, I was already prepared to be let down. So it wasn't shocking.
The puzzles in the mountain almost made me stop completely. The only way Jonathan Blow could make the puzzles any harder were to
. That's when I felt he stepped over a line from intellectual challenge to using cheap tricks to make them harder. It's one thing to present a gauntlet that makes you think outside the box with all you've learned, it's another to have someone jump in front of you waving their arms while you're trying to solve a puzzle. Having to look at those puzzles was unpleasant. Giving your players headaches and motion sickness is not good puzzle design.
Interestingly enough, it wasn't until AFTER the mountain when you
did the game become fun again. I'm currently going through those puzzles, but I'm yet again, approaching it as I would the sudoku and maze puzzles (Flow Free) on my cell phone. A couple of puzzles at a time and then moving on to my other games. I'm using the same method to find all the environmental puzzles too. I'm simply in no rush to see the other endings.
The only reason it's worth $40 to me is I enjoyed exploring the Island and the game has lasted a long time. It was a "pleasant" way to pass the time, but the game itself didn't knock my socks off.  Talos Principle still remains as my all-time favorite puzzle game.

That being said, so far, this game has been very fun.  From the perspective of a new player, the game plays well and rewards teamwork and skill as much as good equipment and passive buffs.  Using different ships with different strategies and weapons allows for a multitude of approaches right from the get go.
Three interesting game modes make this game quite fun and promise more fun in the future:  Skirmish, Attacked sectors, and a conquest mode.
Skirmish:
People are matched together by their ships and rank to fight in 3 demisional battlefields in a variety of game modes (I've only played in the two basic modes allowed for early beginners).  Bots fill in the blanks and if you're just looking for a casual bit of fun, these early teir 1 fights are entertaining and relatively easy to do well in.  As you upgrade to better ships (mostly just stat increased versions of the pervious ships with maybe some different modules and a new paint job as far as I can tell), more game types and maps become available.
Attacked Sectors (free roam):
A sort of open world type of game play that allows you to use jump gates to explore.  While the servers are occasionally laggy or glitchy causing players to get stuck in certian zones, it's certianly an interesting and fun place with missions and such to do as you go on.  Also, note that as your progress and unlock better stated ships, (pretty easy in the lower teirs) you will also unlock new zones to explore and new missions.
Mechant ships will fly though the sectors at regular intervals with their escorts, often getting harrassed by cartel ships, biomorphs, and aliens wheneven they're around.  It can be good money for a new player to hide behind the escorts and help out from a safe distance until you feel confident enough to fight them off yourself.  Be warned,  if you die with things in your cargo hold (often either valuable scrap, or usful crafting materials for fancy weapons and ammo), you will loose them.  Also not sure you get to keep the raw credits you find either but I could be wrong there.  When in doubt, hide behind something else and use missles to express your disapproval of them chipping away at your armor.
Conquest:
Requires a corperation to play.  I'm in a corp now, but I've yet to actually try it out!  From what I can tell, basically players fight over each chunk of map in the name of their faction and corp.  Winning enough or maybe capturing enough within the zone for a certain amount of time claims it for your side and also marks it as owned by your corperation.  Once again, will get back to you guys once I've actually tried it.
Ship Ranking system:
Each ship has a rank (1-16) and their teir is determined by their rank (1-4 is teir 1, 5-8 *I think* is teir 2, ect, ect. going up to rank 16 (teir 5) and a "secret project" ship or two which is a step above and I've no idea what they do other than probably kick a lot of♥♥♥♥♥
Personal experiance with the ships:
Ships are split into tiers and from there into ranks.  There are 5 tiers and 16 ranks that I saw.  Each faction has it's own ships with their own styles but you can buy and train into any ship class of any faction while contracted to any other faction so don't fret too much.  You can also sign up to aid one of the other factions at any time though I'm not sure you can be in a corp of one faction while contracted to an opposing faction.
Also, while this seems to be more of a mission type thing, factions obviously tend to favor you using their ship types.  (one of the missions I got required me to use a faction's ship to get three kills though it was not effected by me switching to another ship I had from an opposing faction.  Should be noted this was a skirmish match.)
The federation Lynx excels in ambushing and flanking enemies using it's cloak and debuffs to make targets weak and slow while the federation Raptor is a quite tanky support frigate that can move around the edge of the battle spamming shield regen and repair or using it's drones to engage any enemies that come close.  it's accurate lasers and cruise missles (or additional combat drones if you decide to manufacture them) make it and excellent general support ship with a fair bit of tankiness.
I've also tried a ship who's name I forget which is quite akin to basically a big sniper ship with devastating damage.  I've not played around with it much and it is highly specialized to dealing damage so using it for other roles tends to not go too well but for someone who needs to crack the shell of some of the larger, tougher ships out there, it's a good choice.
The Ghost is also a fairly decent fighter, you get it by playing War Thunder.  (not sure on the specifics)  It's basically a full attack ship that specializes in killing things as quickly as possible.  It's got flares for countering missles, and some modules that mostly just increase attacking power.  Be aware that a drawn out fight will put you at a disadvantage as it's not quite the fastest or the toughest.  It's strengths are in the massive amount of damage it can lay down in a very short amount of time, and does it ever.
I should also mention that in skimish missions, you can switch ships between respawns meaning that ships that might be a bit too specialized can simply be kept in reserve for when you need them.

I had seen this game on the steam front page on and off for quite a while and decided that since none of my other games were scratching my gaming itch, I'd try this out. Previous reviews of this game being of poor quality are somewhat outdated. Apparently this game has received a major overhaul in the past several months and is now much more fun than it used to be.  Despite being a bit of a pay to win game, skill and good reaction times will ultimately determine who wins a fight. Microtransactions are clearly visable, however I don't think they entirely ruin the experience. At it's core, Star Conflict is an entertaining 3rd person space fighter game, with some MMO elements. (To actually call it an MMO at this point would be a bit of a stretch to me)
Pros -
Easy game to get into with straightforward controls.
Mechanics allow for player skill to trump pay to win blingy ships
Several different game modes to suit most everyone's fancy (Large PVP, Small "arena" style pvp with small objectives, and PVE)
Cons -
Pay to win style game - Set up is extremely similar to World of Tanks in several different respects. WoT players will find a similar feel. (Note again that how the game seems to work, P2W doesn't guarantee you a win every time, or even a noteworthy advantage if you don't know how to use the ships you're flying.)
Confusing UI - I got a bit of sensory overload from my first 20 minutes of gameplay trying to figure out exactly how to upgrade my ship and make money. While the UI is nowhere near as daunting as EVE's, it still had me referring to google occaisionally to find an answer that should be readily apparent.
"Open World" - Before I begin, note that this Con comes with a rather large caveat that, at time of writing I have only put a dozen or so hours into the game. However, from what I have seen there is very little to do in this open world. Further, what little there is to do (collecting loot and manufacturing parts) is made arduous by AI opponents that are extremely difficult for a new(er) player to kill. This combined with very little player activity outside PVE and arena style PVP leads me to wonder what the point of it all is, at this stage of the game's development.
Final Thoughts - I would recommend this game to you if you're looking for something to divert yourself for a while and just want to watch things blow up. I have recommended it to my gaming community so that we have other games to play besides EVE and Wargame. Will this be a game that the average gamer sinks hundreds of hours into? Probably not, but I still feel that this is a good game to play when you're just wanting to unwind after a long day.

A classic point & click adventure game, first released in 1999.  The story concerns a young woman named April Ryan who discovers that she's instrumental in preventing a catastrophe that threatens the Balance between two worlds; Stark and Arcadia.
The story.  I wouldn't necessarily call it "original" these days, but it's thoughtful, moving and VERY well told.  It challenges some common tropes of the genre without denying their necessity.  The characters are also well-rounded.  April Ryan is the perfect example of what a female protagonist
in my opinion.  She's not a damsel in distress, but neither is she an♥♥♥♥♥♥kicking, hyper-sexualized, I-am-woman-hear-me-roar style character, the likes of which Hollywood (and many other video games) love to put forward under the label "strong female lead."  April has strengths and weaknesses, hopes and fears.  She has a realistic body type and she dresses in reasonable outfits.  She feels like a real person, which only makes you as a player identify that much more with her plight.
The graphics were considered pretty good when the game first came out, but they have NOT aged well.  The game is still perfectly playable, but it shows its age.  Likewise, the voices.  Some of the voice actors really go all out, others not so much.  (Thankfully April herself is in the former category, since you'll be listening to her more than anyone else.)  In 1999, when the concept of having voices
was still a novelty, this could be overlooked.  Today, it takes its toll.
Also, with the Steam version, there's one significant bug: confirmation dialogs for
or
, etc do not display properly (at least on Windows)!  Press "Y" for "Yes" or "N" for "No" to get past these mysterious empty white boxes when they pop up.
The Longest Journey is probably my favourite P&C adventure game of all time.  The story is the purpose for a game like this, and this story is worth experiencing, even if the audio/visuals are showing their age.  It's also the first installment in a trilogy which does not disappoint as it unfolds in full.
There is strong language in this game (multiple F-bombs) which you might not expect, given the presentation.  I don't personally find this offensive, but others might.
If you've read the review this far and are still considering it, buy this game!  You won't be disappointed.

IMPORTANT: This game had trouble starting on my Windows 7 (64-bit) PC. If I started my PC and tried to start the game, it would never start the first time, giving me a DirectDraw error, which also made my mouse cursor only work on half of my desktop, so I would have to ctrl-alt-del and log out from windows. BUT, when I would log back in to Windows and start the game again, it would work perfectly, every time. So, if you have the same problem, just start the game the first time when you don't have any other important applications running, hit ctrl-alt-del when you get the error, log out, log in and start it again. For whatever reason, that works. I don't know why.

Being a fan of point and click adventures, there was little doubt I'd like the game. However the game differs quite a bit from your traditional adventure of the era. For once, Puzzles are a little bit rarer and more confined to certain areas of the game, making them more accessible. Also the game is skewed towards telling its story, so there is a bunch of lengthy conversations happening instead of puzzles all the time. Knowing this era only from puzzle-heavy titles like Monkey Island or Sam&Max, I really enjoyed this shift. Overall the gameplay feels quite slow, with a lot of running and listening involved.
Now as all point and click adventures, this game also suffers from the gamplay problem of being stuck. Sometimes you are bound to miss things or interpret situations differently from what the developers intended. Given the more straightforward and limited nature of the puzzles in this game, I found myself being significantly less stuck and able to keep a good pace through the game.
The story was really engaging for me. A nice mix of science fiction and classic fairy-tale fantasy made for some funny and likeable moments. Now the story isn't really anything out of the ordinary nowadays, but the way it is being told and the characters used made for a nice unique experience in my view, with a certain sidekick stealing the show. There is also a nice portion of geek culture references, so if you belong to the target audience, you get some more laughs out of it.
There's no way aroung it, the game looks old, having your standard run-of-the-mill prerendered Backgrounds with some live rendered foreground, as was common for the time. I didn't think any of the voice acting was particularly bad, but some of the voices really stood out from the crowd.
I can wholeheartedly recommend the game to fans of point and click adventures. Others might be put of by the slow gameplay or the dated tech. If you can look past such things, the game has an engaging bundle of science fiction and fantasy for you in store with a healthy chunk of humor.

This is a really frustrating game because the concept is brilliant for a puzzle game (you have a giant ball and a tool for moving the ball, solve puzzles) but then they felt the need to implement combat. Combat has absolutely no place in this game - the mechanism for killing the standard enemies is just "run them over with the ball" and for the miniboss creatures who show up at the end just in time to stop the momentum dead in its tracks every one boils down to "place ball here, lure miniboss into damaging effect". If you're lucky that just involves hitting them with the ball, if you're not it involves luring them near electricity or landmines or oil trails or some other damn thing.
And don't even get me started on the recurring worm miniboss which spoils perhaps the best chapter of the entire game, which is just a rehash of the tentacle alien from the original Half-Life, only instead of distracting it with grenades you wait for it to go into an idle animation and then dash from place to place.
Honestly if they released some special no-combat-we-swear version of this then I'd have next to no problems with this (although there are always nitpicks, like how the game throws down checkpoints regularly but only saves after like a third of them) but as it is the game feels like it's stretched way too thin and it means that even the interesting ideas such as the anti-gravity field are woefully underutilized and undeveloped. Can't honestly recommend it in this state.

Being a fan of point and click adventures, there was little doubt I'd like the game. However the game differs quite a bit from your traditional adventure of the era. For once, Puzzles are a little bit rarer and more confined to certain areas of the game, making them more accessible. Also the game is skewed towards telling its story, so there is a bunch of lengthy conversations happening instead of puzzles all the time. Knowing this era only from puzzle-heavy titles like Monkey Island or Sam&Max, I really enjoyed this shift. Overall the gameplay feels quite slow, with a lot of running and listening involved.
Now as all point and click adventures, this game also suffers from the gamplay problem of being stuck. Sometimes you are bound to miss things or interpret situations differently from what the developers intended. Given the more straightforward and limited nature of the puzzles in this game, I found myself being significantly less stuck and able to keep a good pace through the game.
The story was really engaging for me. A nice mix of science fiction and classic fairy-tale fantasy made for some funny and likeable moments. Now the story isn't really anything out of the ordinary nowadays, but the way it is being told and the characters used made for a nice unique experience in my view, with a certain sidekick stealing the show. There is also a nice portion of geek culture references, so if you belong to the target audience, you get some more laughs out of it.
There's no way aroung it, the game looks old, having your standard run-of-the-mill prerendered Backgrounds with some live rendered foreground, as was common for the time. I didn't think any of the voice acting was particularly bad, but some of the voices really stood out from the crowd.
I can wholeheartedly recommend the game to fans of point and click adventures. Others might be put of by the slow gameplay or the dated tech. If you can look past such things, the game has an engaging bundle of science fiction and fantasy for you in store with a healthy chunk of humor.

Un juego que posee sencillez estética, pero a nivel jugable se puede volver una locura de disparos y golpes llenos de acción,  que cuando se disfruta con amigos puede ser sumamente divertido, pues ofrece  distintos modos de juego, así como muchas armas y hasta un editor de niveles en el cual podremos hacer de las nuestras a la hora crear escenarios divertidos y en los cuales sea difícil maniobrar para conseguir eliminar a nuestros adversarios.
Para algunos puede ser confuso entrar por primera vez al juego pues la interfaz es confusa con respecto a las características que escogeremos para la partida, pero nada que un poco de tiempo  dentro del juego remedien para irse acostumbrando.
La interfaz es simple y da poca información
Pero esto no es tan malo, pues si vemos el juego como un título de acción retro, Square Brawl hace bien su trabajo, pues muchos de los juegos de antaño no tenían un tutorial ni podíamos tener una visualización del mapa en el que lucharíamos y cosas por el estilo.
Nuestro objetivo será destruir a los demás contrincantes, podremos escoger partidas locales ( no hay multijugador en línea) de 1 vs 1 y hasta 4 vs 4, en equipos o todos contra todos, siendo la ultima la más divertida de todas, y sumando la posibilidad de utilizar más de 10 armas o ataques distintos, con  4 modos de juego entre los cuales destacan “partida a muerte por equipos”  y “free for all” (todos contra todos), donde nos toca darle muerte a nuestros contrarios en niveles donde podremos  hacer plataformeo y brincar de un lado al otro haciendo una suerte de parkour muy divertido, y es que el juego también tiene un arte simple con uno que otro destello en las sombras que le hacen ver bonito y más vivo.
El empleo de partículas da un toque mas bonito al juego
En lo que respecta a las batallas en sí, el juego no tiene barras de vitalidad, en su lugar nuestro personaje ( nuestro cubo ja ja ) ira disminuyendo su color y entre más pierda su color original estaremos más cerca de morir, las armas tienen rebote así que le añade rasgos divertidos a tomar en cuenta, no podemos hacer ráfagas de disparos, pues habrá que esperar unos pocos segundos para volver a disparar, lo que le hace más desafiante pues si fallas tu disparo deberás ponerte a cubierto para no acabar hecho trizas, la música podría ser más variada,  pero no es algo a lo que le prestas real atención cuando estas riendo con tus amigos por la manera en que te deshiciste de ellos o ellos de ti.
Corre súper a los 60fps, podemos incluso acelerar la velocidad del juego para hacerlo aún más frenético, y el único punto realmente que hace de este juego talvez no tan apetecible para muchos es la falta de multijugador online, que estamos seguros podría ser un plus tremendo para el juego ya que eso algunos jugadores lo ven hasta necesario hoy en día para un título de esta naturaleza, pero que aunque esté ausente no deja de ser un buen juego, que a $5 está muy bien.
el editor nos permitirá dejar volar la imaginación
En resumen,  Square Brawl  viene siendo algo parecido a Super Smash Bros, en lo jugable y en lo artístico  tiene su toque personal que lo hace adorable y te puede sacar una que otra carcajada.

This is good 4 player fun.
Square Brawl is a sweet local co-op brawler with a simple art style. The idea of the game is to get points by killing your opponents. This is done through a number of cool weapons and the occasional enviornmental hazard.
Underneath it's simple exterior lies a pretty intuitive movement system that manages to put itself ahead of the pack due to the way that jumping and climbing "hang". Rather than just falling your cube glides along through the air.
There are many different maps and the game includes a map editor. It's pretty simple to use and adds a good of additional content to the game.
Right now there are twelve availble weapons. Prior to starting a match players choose any two that they want. Each weapon is unique and creats a large variety in play style. My current favorite is the dash weapon; it allows you to slam into opponents to damage them.
The game has four different game modes: Free for all, Team Deathmatch, Head hunter and a team variant. On top of the four game modes there are a number of modifiers that can be activated (i.e health regen, one life, etc). This adds yet more depth to a pretty simple game.
The game is local co-op only but has a pretty good bot system in place in case you still wanted to play. The bots have a good range of difficulty settings and the game is definitely still fun with only bots.
The downsides for me lie in the cube aesthetic and rather repetitive synth music. If it had online multiplayer it would probably be a pretty solid hit. With all that said the game is only five dollars and at that price is a good deal
Cheers,

The Witness is a puzzle game with a minimal amount of story but an absolutely beautiful world to explore, with an excellent merging of the puzzles you solve and the environment you're in.
It is unabashedly a puzzle game, and it has extremely well-crafted and insanely difficult puzzles, while still providing a natural learning progression without hand-holding and annoying tutorials. You start by solving easy puzzles, then harder, then harder still. The reward for solving puzzles is most often more puzzles, like the games Hexcells, Hook, or Snakebird. Occasionally you find audio logs that give philosophical perspective from famous thinkers like Einstein, Nicholas of Cusa or Heisenberg.
But make no mistake about it - this is a
, and like the other games I listed, the reward for tackling a grueling puzzle is
. Some people will not like the lack of RPG Puzzle Experience Points™ or new and exciting guns with which to take down tougher puzzles, but it's not that kind of game.  The game is about taking in the surrounding and using it to solve puzzles.
The puzzles themselves are brilliant. Even though they all take the same general form (You need to find a path through a maze) there is an ENORMOUS amount of variety. Furthermore they are brilliantly paced and the game does an excellent job of teaching you the rules non-verbally. You'll come up across two or three puzzles with a new symbol, think you understand it, but then the game will force you to deal with a puzzle that makes you tweak the way you thought it worked.  Regardless of what some detractors say, there is not a single puzzle in the game that 'breaks the rules'. It is perfectly consistent.
Some real criticisms: The trailer promises a story about regaining your memory, but that is absolutely 100% not in the game. Some of the areas are incredibly unfriendly to people with disabilities like color-blindness or deafness. Some of the quick but tough puzzles turn off on wrong guesses (to stop people from bruteforcing them) and you need to resolve the previous puzzle (the solution remains on the panel, so it's not difficult) so that can be annoying.
However these flaws are minor compared to the excellent puzzle crafting, the beauty of the island, and the mind-opening fusion of the two. This game is heartily recommended to people who like puzzle games.
Small spoiler for people who "don't get it": If all you've done is walk from puzzle to puzzle, making guesses until you move on, and then finish the game without looking around, you're going to have a bad time. The environment
. Go to the mountain. Take a look down at the river. Open your eyes.

The Ball centeres around a large sphere that you can manipulate with a gravity gun like device. Needless to say it's a ton of fun. Most of the game is driven by solving puzzels with zombie fights inbetween. You have no weapons other than the ball, so this can make things tricky in a good way. There is also lore to be found that reveals secrets about The Ball and what happened to the ancient civilization that left the ruins the game takes place in.

Buy? Likely.
The Ball is a first person puzzler from the same developers of Killing Floor that draws similarities to Portal and Q.U.B.E, set in a ancient South American cave and ruins network from a civilization that centered around The Ball. This ball can be "kicked" and "attracted to you" with an acient tool called The Hammer to activate switches and transmit effects like spikes, fire, electricity and mines, which are either used to solve puzzles or occasionally deal with hostiles. The majority of the puzzles are pretty easy to figure out, even if you are not into puzzle games, save for a couple moments that may require you to "think from another angle". Combat sometimes feels inconsequential, but gets more interesting when there are tons of enemies or you have to deal with foes that can be killed directly by the rolling of The Ball. The game is at its best near the end game, though, some situations like an oil and fire  combat part and the last puzzle were annoying.
Take my timeplayed and subtract about 7 hours to get a more accurate play time. The game also includes extra missions including a Portal 2 like test chamber series. Owning the game entitles you to a skin of the main character in Killing Floor, though it is odd that you never see the guy until you play KF. Has X-Input support. 1920x1080 is the highest resolution. I can recommend this to any puzzle gamer and those who don't want a hard puzzle game.

In this review, I am going to compare Square Brawl to Nidhogg. If you dont know what Nidhogg is, then look it up.
First off, like Nidhogg, Square Brawl (SB) has graphics that are very... square. Unlike Nidhogg, however, SB takes advantage of its art style, and somehow makes it look beautiful. That, combined with the screen shaking and other interesting effects, make the game very pleasing to the eye.
Also like Nidhogg, SB is an indie game. That means that only a few people are working on it, and it has a very limited budget. However, unlike Nidhogg, SB actually has a decent amount of content. In fact, it has way more content on release day than Nidhogg has now, almost 2 years after it was released.
So, all things considered, SB should cost at least 2-3x the amount of Nidhogg, right? Wrong. SB costs 1/3 of Nidhogg's price, and in my opinion, is way more enjoyable. If I had one gripe with this game, it would be that there needs to be more variation in weapons. I think that the best way to solve this issue would be to create more weapons, and keeping the current ones as well. I think perks would be intersting too.
Overall, I rate this game an 8.5/10

The Longest Journey is the reason I got into video games as a child. I connected easily with April Ryan (the protagonist), and the disbelief she initially expresses at her fantastical predicament injected an element of realism that even my younger self appreciated. Anybody in the real world, having found themselves transported to a fantasy realm, would react with skepticism much like April's.
The story itself is not tremendously original, but it is well-told, in a unique (and beautiful in its own way) setting, with characters that I found, and continue to find, memorable and endearing.
I loved this game as a child, and I love it more as an adult --- although there are parts that I still needed to consult a walkthrough to get past ;)

After having this gem gathering dust in my library for quite a few months I finally managed to fully play it through. And when I say 'gem' I really mean it.
I originally bought it simply because I wanted to play the two first games before getting to the actual Dreamfall Chapters. Now I'm actually really glad I made that decision.
Of course this game is seventeen years old by now, which means the graphics might not be suited for everyone's eyes, but I don't think that should be seen as a negative factor. The story, however, if not the longest (depending on whether or not you're quick with point-and-click adventures) did impress me. For such an underrated and not well-known game it has one of the best fantasy-plots and worlds I've come across so far. And even if there isn't that much to be seen of some of the characters I did come to like them quite a lot.
For some of the bugs others have mentioned I can't say anything, since I haven't come across any (the text was screwed up on time, but reloading a previous save fixed it and it hasn't appeared again).
If there's a game that deserves a (graphical) remake it's definitely The Longest Journey and I am happy to say that I'm very excited for the other two games.
Can't wait to see what they'll introduce in the future!

I'm never quite sure what to make of fighting games. I really enjoy them, especially in local multiplayer, but don't quite have the passion to develop a half-decent win record in online play. In a lot of games, this can be pretty limiting even if I really enjoy the mechanics. Injustice 2, however, has a rather enjoyable campaign mode and a relatively robust system of singleplayer questing through The Multiverse. Problem solved right?
Well ... a lot of those Multiverse battles are obnoxious. Too many of the modifiers are just random bursts of damage that can't really be played around in an enjoyable way rather than things that change the landscape of the fight. AI difficulty fluctuates a fair bit over the course of a single multiverse event and the way events chain together to provide player rewards are often exceptionally frustrating--requiring certain characters at certain levels and whatnot.
Between these minor frustrations with Multiverse pacing, the tedium of working with the item inventory, the five different currencies, the level-up mechanics and the loot-box system, despite providing more robust single player content than any other fighting game I've played, it can often feel like a bunch of chores the game is forcing on me.
All this leaves me in a somewhat weird position. I love the game's core mechanics and the multiplayer (without the silly item stats, at least) is breezy and accessible and fascinating offering all of the depth and strategy I like about fighting games with less of the analog stick acrobatics many combo and special systems in other games demand (outside of the inevitable high demand in terms of raw reaction time). But I spend most of my time with it in singleplayer modes in between local multiplayer sessions with minimal ability or experience with online multiplayer--and I have mixed feelings about all of the singleplayer content outside the rather excellent campaign.
A few other caveats: the publisher seems determined to make the currency and DLC system as obnoxious as possible without getting too deep into the waters of gambling on loot boxes. While not worse than the comics, and better in a few cases, a lot of the costumes for women in the cast are kinda weird and it's disappointing that the whole alternate universe conceit didn't create space for much more imagination and a little more balance in costume designs across the cast.
All in all, I think I recommend it more than not.

The Ball is a first-person puzzle game where you can control a single giant item - the Ball - via attraction and repulsion. Using these abilities, you then use the ball to solve a variety of chambers, working your way through the game to its finish. Additionally, the Ball can be used as a weapon to take down enemies that attack you, leading to a bit of first-person crowd handling while you maneuver them into a position where you can mow them down.
In addition to the core story, there are a couple other modes, such as survival mode where you seek to survive successive waves of enemies.
The core gameplay itself is quite solid, and the puzzles are fun, if a tad too long - much of the scenery is repetative, so it feels padded and artificially stretched out. Additionally, while I found survival mode to be quite fun, the combat which is put into the main storyline feels a little out of place.
Ultimately, if you enjoyed other first person puzzle games such as Portal, you'll probably find something to like in this game. While it's not quite up to that series' quality, there's a good bit of fun to be had.

I usually don't write revies unless I'm very passionate about a game -- so thats a start!
This War Of Mine is seriously a unique experience, and the game is brutally emotional. The game is bapstism by fire, and the controls are extremely simple which is a plus.
Logic is a key role in this game, and it was implemented beautifully. After the first in game few days, you'll have the basics down very quickly (about 15-30 minutes roughly.) You start out as 3 survivors, and I promise you will probably utterly fail at least once. Failure IS NOT and option later on, as this will be your downfall.
The game is so emotionally griping, making you contemplate your past decisions endlessly, especially as this affects your characters will to live aswell. (Suicide is a possibility...)
The combat is very simple yet slightly cinematic and very cool. The Stealth in the game is almost flawless, and very well done. There are many ways to stealth, sticking to shadows, walking slowly, climbing, hiding, lock picking, sawing through grates to open up passags etc.
Another amazing feature is the non-linear play style. The concept is very similar all around, which is survive, (although, all character personalities and back stories are different, so this can alter the play-style too), but every play through is different, with random appearances and events, which all tie very well into one another. Such as weather, fighting, sickness, famine, economic changes, etc.
Equally great is the fact that possible enemy (soldier/looter/survivor) presence and behavior will change throughout time, and this will also affect your night time scavenging. An area can also be repeatedly scavenged, and enemies do not respawn -- enemies have a very adamint search mode I might add.
Real time updates -- if you have crafted a radio, then you can listen to it daily, with its 5 stations. 1 weather, 1 classical, 1 punk-metal, 1 Local news, and 1 Political news. The weather, and news stations will change according to the situation, as the music stations stay fairly similar. Any updates are also posted in a time logged journal for your convienence. :)
Overall, the graphics are beautiful, and orchestrate the game in a way that makes it seem like a story, more than a video game. With much emphasis on a "sketch-like" artstyle. The colors are dark and depressing, which pars great with the art styles. The audio is great, and the soundtrack is very subtle and fitting. It can be peaceful, and in too much downtime will get you thinking about your actions, alot. \
All in all, this game is a must play for any survival/military-dystopian/slavic style/stealth/murderous gamers with a knack for decision making.
- "Do unto others, as you would have them do unto you..."

You can tell your mice where to go, and THAT actually goes way farther then you might at first thing. This means you can control where the weight goes before hand; unlike in world of Goo where the goo simply goes to the closest point to the end goal.

This is a very good, if old, adventure game. Certain things about just didn't age very well - such as the 3d character models, fonts, and fmv sequences. However, the rest, the core or the game, from the voices to the story to the puzzles and gameplay held up very well.
The voice acting is very good, and when paired up with the dialogue it is really good at telling the story. It can be funny when it needs to be, or sombre when the occasion calls for it. The story itself also flows very well, with good pacing from when April is just going about her daily life and how it slowly builds into this long journey.
As far as the gameplay goes, the puzzles are pretty good. With plenty of characters to talk to, and the very useful diary mechanic to keep track of everything, although you can get stumped at times theres almost always a way to puzzle out the answer.
As far as the art in this game goes, it can be alright. In-game some of the models used in characters look extremely low resolution, but it's not too off-putting. The fmv sequences are just ugly to look at. But all of the static backgrounds in this are great, from the downtown of venice to the seaside cliffs in arcadia. They just look fantastic, even at such a low resolution.
Technically, the game runs okay-ish. But you need to remember to quit the game properly, else it messes with the Windows Font settings. Also, you may wish to create a "power plan" to use, as by default these old games tend to use 100% of your cpu resources, which can be undesirable.
If you can look past some of the quirks of the technology it was built with, its worth playing for fans of this genre.
There were a few parts I had to look things up online, because I got completely stuck.  Other than that, I love the game.  Cool storyline and fun to play.

The Longest Journey is a 1999 point-and-click adventure game set in two parallel worlds, the cyberpunk-based Stark and fantasy-inspired Arcadia.
The game features some of the best lore of any game I've played, spectacular voice acting, and amazing writing.
Despite the dated graphics, the game has still held up extremely well, and is in my opinion one of the greaest adventure games ever made. The graphics are worth looking past in order to enjoy the great story hidden underneath.
I highly recommend playing this game before any of the newer entries in the series, because it really is a spectacular story and provides a lot of important background and characterization for many of the characters in the universe.
Great immersive story! This classic defines what point-n-click puzzle games should be! The graphic may be out-dated but the story will live on forever!

When this game was released (late 1999, early 2000) it was several months on no#0 (they had this 0-9 top10 thing) spot in the best TV show (in my country) about latest video games. The kid I was back then wasn't very much into adventure games but have remembered that fact as probably no other game spent so many time on that spot. El Duderino that I'm now is still not a huge adventure games fan but likes to try something from that genre now and then (Dracula and Sam&Max series being the favorites). The reputation this game has as one of the best in the branch is well desereved. Those funny Norwegians have done a great job!
Playing this was just like the title says...it was like taking a very long journey. A thoroughly enjoyable one.
Some would say that the graphics are awful but in all honesty if that is true it didn't bother me at all (played on 1080p monitor and the picture wasn't stretched or anything). The moment I dived into such an interesting story with completely believable characters I was just there. It felt like I could actually touch the person I talk to or stand on a cliff and look into the depth of a beautiful landscape while the breeze on my face. The mixture between magic and logic, fairy tale and (futuristic) reality is done great and you never get tired of either. I slightly liked more the magical part. The struggle within the main character is also properly served before the player and progresses in adequate tempo as the game rolls out. Voice acting is spot on as well as the music. I'm not going into any details on purpose, you gotta inhale them on your own.
I would suggest playing in little doses (those 25 hours you see happened over last 4 months but no need to have such a slow tempo xD), couple hours per day tops. That way you won't be annoyed by long walks/runs across new or known screens which this game (unfortunatelly but not tragically) delivers. Don't worry about forgetting parts of the story if you stay away for some time, it won't happen I asure you (but if it does there is an automatic in-game Diary that will help out in a jiffy). ;)
If you have technical issues with menues or something there is a very quick solution for that (Google is your friend).
The puzzles are perfectly balanced, not naive but not "head-breaking" either. About 90% I figured on my own and for the rest I used
which I find to be a wonderful solution when you're stucked because that little wink pointing you in the right direction always feels better than watching/reading a blunt walkthrough.
Summa summarum...an absolute must-play for any gamer that likes games with a soul.
And if this will one day be taught in art history schools or something similar it won't be so by accident as this really is art.

I came to this with no prior knowledge or nostalgia. Initially the awkward, low poly character models were quite jarring in comparison other things I've been playing recently. However the pre-rendered background locations were awesome. As the game progressed I got more and more drawn into the story and the world that I started to forget I was playing this on a tiny window in the corner of my screen. That is the defining characteristic of this game, the brilliant story. Despite how much I much I enjoyed this game, I know it is not for everyone. This game is mostly dialogue and whilst the voice acting is excellent and engaging some people are going to just get bored. Similarly the game has various grand locations which give an excellent sense of the world, it does mean lots of protracted running back and forth. And of course it has its fair share of baffling point and click logic but I didn't need a walkthrough any more than any other game.

Only for big point-and-click fans.
I played as someone who has only played a few point-and-clicks and graphic adventures, being a fan of Broken Sword, Snatcher and Policenauts. Point-and-click fans will no doubt love this; it's relatively well made. But for those who don't list it as their favourite genre, this will be more of a miss.
My major problem was how long everything took - there's a lot of walking/running to and from locations, and even just running across screens can take too long. The amount of needless, unskippable walking (and other movement), not just by you but by other characters in a little cutscene or to begin conversation, is obscene. Imagine a 20-hour movie where 10 hours of it is walking. This might be an underestimation. (Note that there is an option to skip the animations, however the game tells you not to as this skips any major plot points that happen during the animation - these are mini cutscenes after all - and is only meant for those who are doing another playthrough.)
This combined with the hefty amount of talking, but a script and voice acting that didn't keep me glued (all but one character had me just reading the subtitles fast and skipping through), I tapped out after a few chapters. To continue would've been a slog of watching pointless walking and little arm gestures that take 10 seconds a time.

What a beautiful game! Certainly one of the best point and click adventure game, if not the best ever. It didn't age well (had to play in 640x480 windowed mode on a 24" monitor) but the story makes that up. Which is really good. Actually I was thinking about the golden age Final Fantasy games while playing this. Because it's really similar to some of them (like 7-8-9). Ofc it's not an RPG but an adventure game... but the story, the settings, the music etc. a lot of things reminded me to the Final Fantasy series.
Really hard to talk without spoilers but if you don't mind the graphics then you will definitely enjoy the game. Starts a bit slow and sometimes a bit tedious (mostly the puzzles) yet I never felt that I play it just to finish as quickly as possible.
The character development is interesting but at one part the game just stops caring about it which is kind of a let down. There are a lot of undiscovered areas in the game (more background story of the world, the characters etc.)
I'd love to see a proper HD remake!

Another match 3 or more game but this one has 6 kinds of play.
The 6 boards have no levels so you play until you lose though they will get harder the longer you play.
Power-ups will show up in most of the play modes but most just give extra points but there is 1 that will remove gems from play.
Snazzy swap
This is just like any other match 3 game.
Swap 2 gems placements to match 3 or more of a like color to remove them only to be replaced by more gems until there are no more matches left.
When you make matches a bar will counts down that gives extra points if you can make another match before the bar runs out.
Clearing clusters
This starts like the match 3 one but in here new blocks will not fall and you need to clear all the blocks to move on.
if you do clear the board the next one will add 1 more kind of color gem.
As matches are made gems will gravitate down and to the middle of the board.
Falling star
Gems will fall down a few at a time (they come down faster as time goes on) and you can swap any 2 gems to match 3 or more like colors.
Gems will not swap back if they do not match like in snazzy swap.
Moving 4-ward
On the left you will see gems in a pattern and you can make this on the board or match 4 like color gems in a square.
Any connected gem of the same color connected to the 4 square will also be removed.
Gems will keep falling every sec as you play.
Pathfinder
Here you need to put like color gems in strait rows of 4 (4 squares will not work but they can be diagonal) to be removed.
Every time you move a gem and do not make a set more gems will fall on the board.
These gems are shown on the left as well as the gems for the next 2 turns.
Gravity Switch
This is like clearing clusters but in here the gems will only fall strait down, up, left, or right.
You control what direction they will fall and can change it to any of the others at any time.
As with clearing clusters if you clear the board the next one will have 1 more kind of gem.
