I usually don't write revies unless I'm very passionate about a game -- so thats a start!
This War Of Mine is seriously a unique experience, and the game is brutally emotional. The game is bapstism by fire, and the controls are extremely simple which is a plus.
Logic is a key role in this game, and it was implemented beautifully. After the first in game few days, you'll have the basics down very quickly (about 15-30 minutes roughly.) You start out as 3 survivors, and I promise you will probably utterly fail at least once. Failure IS NOT and option later on, as this will be your downfall.
The game is so emotionally griping, making you contemplate your past decisions endlessly, especially as this affects your characters will to live aswell. (Suicide is a possibility...)
The combat is very simple yet slightly cinematic and very cool. The Stealth in the game is almost flawless, and very well done. There are many ways to stealth, sticking to shadows, walking slowly, climbing, hiding, lock picking, sawing through grates to open up passags etc.
Another amazing feature is the non-linear play style. The concept is very similar all around, which is survive, (although, all character personalities and back stories are different, so this can alter the play-style too), but every play through is different, with random appearances and events, which all tie very well into one another. Such as weather, fighting, sickness, famine, economic changes, etc.
Equally great is the fact that possible enemy (soldier/looter/survivor) presence and behavior will change throughout time, and this will also affect your night time scavenging. An area can also be repeatedly scavenged, and enemies do not respawn -- enemies have a very adamint search mode I might add.
Real time updates -- if you have crafted a radio, then you can listen to it daily, with its 5 stations. 1 weather, 1 classical, 1 punk-metal, 1 Local news, and 1 Political news. The weather, and news stations will change according to the situation, as the music stations stay fairly similar. Any updates are also posted in a time logged journal for your convienence. :)
Overall, the graphics are beautiful, and orchestrate the game in a way that makes it seem like a story, more than a video game. With much emphasis on a "sketch-like" artstyle. The colors are dark and depressing, which pars great with the art styles. The audio is great, and the soundtrack is very subtle and fitting. It can be peaceful, and in too much downtime will get you thinking about your actions, alot. \
All in all, this game is a must play for any survival/military-dystopian/slavic style/stealth/murderous gamers with a knack for decision making.

If you've ever played a turn based game in your life and even somewhat enjoyed it, you really need to play DOFUS.
I've been playing on and off for 10 years. Occasionally I'll take a break because of life/boredom and I'll go try out another game. Yet DOFUS always pulls me back in due to how frequently its updated and how unique it really is. How many mmorpgs do you know that offer an enriching turnbased combat? I have yet to encounter a single one outside DOFUS/WAKFU. Not only that but the class system is great. 17 soon to be 18 classes that are both distinct from each other and so unique from many mmorpgs. How many games do you know where there exists a class solely devoted to getting drunk and throwing people across the map? I acknowledge that without subbing you can only get up to levels 40-60 or so without really pulling your teeth out, but the subscription cost is very cheap as far as sub-based games go and definitely worth it.
Final comment on the matter is the pvp system. 1v1 pvp is very enjoyable but the rewards are mostly cosmetics. However the 3v3 pvp system that unlocks when you hit level 50 is amazing. I'm someone that usually avoids pvp, but turnbased pvp with friends (or even randoms) in a small team like that just somehow works so well. Not to mention you get tons of money and various rewards for winning.
I don't have much else to say besides please give this great game a try. If you ever need help starting out just message me and I'd be glad to show you around and get you started.

Tiny Bridge: Ratventure
is a physics based puzzle game developed by Estelion, and released in 2015. I feel like this is a tablet game that got lost and found it's way on steam.
You are the bridge builder helping two Rats get cheeze. It's probably the story of the century, lets be honest here. World of Goo didn't have much of a story either, but they had some existential thing going on in the background at least. I could weave a crazy story about how Top-Hat-Mouse is an entrepreneur that is venturing with his friend stocking-hat-mouse to invest in the cheese market.
...But that would just be cheesy.
The gameplay is straightforward, but agonizingly difficult at the same time. You put down points to create a bridge for your mice to run across to get cheese. At that description alone someone could easily say "okay, why don't I just play world of Goo instead? What does this game do differently?
You can tell your mice where to go, and THAT actually goes way farther then you might at first thing. This means you can control where the weight goes before hand; unlike in world of Goo where the goo simply goes to the closest point to the end goal.
I would describe this as an "Encore" to World of Goo, but not quite as charming, it was clearly inspired by world of good, and mechanically speaking it's pretty solid. There was just something about this game that didn't quite connect with me. But that's not enough of a reason to give it a negative review, it does what it promises it goes on sale often.
If you wanna play a game similar to world of Goo, and have a little money to through at it, it might be worth a pick up.
I wish I could be more helpful, but I don't really recomend, or discourage trying this game out. This one's on you. But, as always thanks for reading my review.

The Witness provides the joy of discovery, exploration, and solving puzzles in a way that abstains from the trends of modern game design. It is less like a filed-down meticulously crafted experience and more like a beautiful expanse in which many truly beautiful experiences are possible, and in that way it is less like a "game" and more like a world. It conveys very profound messages, never explicitly, but it leads you to moments of introspection and thought, extremely open to interpretation and personalization, and yields many individual variations of self discovery, just as experiences in real life would. It toys with many strong concepts, and often the messages are typically supplied internally as a reaction to those concepts (the most effective way of truly resonating and teaching). I think this game will most appeal to those who find themselves living their lives in the pursuit of truth of any kind. If you want a familiar comparison, it is like Myst, but done properly, and a million times more captivating and powerful.
The main rewards in the Witness are knowledge and understanding. In the tradition of Jonathon Blow's games, you have the ability to choose which puzzles you want to solve first, and you may often find yourself leaving a string of puzzles to try a new set, and finding that new set providing you with a key understanding that will help you complete the old set. Sometimes you will turn to life and introspection to solve these puzzles, and draw on your own talents and personal backgrounds, many times I found myself taking pictures of the puzzles and scrawling out symbols in my sketchbook, as if I was some kind of archaeologist. A lot of the puzzles are as ruthless and uncatering as a real life puzzle or problem would be, which makes them incredibly more satisfying when they are solved, because there was no assurance that you would complete them. This helped to make the game feel like a grand mystery, or an ancient artifact that I was dusting away and piecing together. This strongpoint would not have worked if it were not for the non-linear, open, choice-driven atmosphere that is presented, as many of the puzzles, will no doubt, drive you mad. But I sincerely discourage anyone from looking up the solutions or seeking help, even if you feel they seem impossible, there isn't nearly a speck as much joy of reaping the rewards of the puzzle, than discovering within yourself the ability to solve them. In fact, until completion, I refrained from looking up anything about the game until I completed it, because I didn't even want to know that anyone else had solved the puzzles before me.
The only major complaint was the weak ending, as all the mystery the game built up, led me to so many imaginative ideas of what it was all leading up to, what was possible, and what grand truth could be revealed, and unfortunately, the game didn't live up to what those mysteries led my imagination to produce. Nevertheless the experience was unforgettable, and this was a true work of art, visually as well.

TL;DR: In short, the game does not have many puzzles that require much thought. In most cases instead the game just makes the actual act of solving the puzzle difficult.
If you're looking for a puzzle game that requires actual thought, get this instead:
Here's the point where i personally gave up:
Ran into the sound puzzles. Puzzles where one has to draw lines at heights indicated by bird song. Doable. Then the game overlays cellphones, wood instruments and more birds. These were entirely impossible for me. Game provides no way to make them easier whatsoever, and has no compassion for people who aren't great of hearing.
---
Some more rambly details:
The game is basically a very beautiful, mostly static 3d landscape you walk around in. It might actually be kind of relaxing if that was the point, but the point of the game is puzzles.
The game's puzzles are largely not "solved". There are a few exceptions, but for most puzzles you don't look at and think about them much. In fact, for many of them the solution is just to look around and trace the line as indicated  by shadows, reflections, bird chirps or similar. (If you're colorblind an entire section of puzzles will be impossible, as the game lies even to non-colorblind people.)
That is, for many puzzles the "puzzle" part is in finding where in the surroundings the solution is hidden so you can enter it. Usually they're either not hidden at all, or hidden such that you need to work out how the reflections ingame work (i.e. not at all like in the real world).
Then there is a number of *actual* puzzle that require pausing and thinking. Those are actually more annoying than the previous ones, because the *actual* puzzle in them is figuring out what the rules of the puzzle are. You're literally just reverse-engineering a black box. This would be fine if there were a lot of different things to try, maybe have the ability to rearrange the pieces on the board and see how that changes the solution. Instead however you have a fixed set of inputs to which you can add your solution and get a yes or no for whether it is right. Sadly often the inputs don't explain all the details of the rules however, so when the complexity steps up, you're just left guessing and hoping and eventually brute-forcing it.
Some rule-based puzzles i still don't know what the rules are, even after having looked up the solutions, and i'm a programmer by trade.

1. warning!
this is not a usual puzzle game. this game is about finding out how the puzzles work. figuring out the mechanics is the meat of the game, so don't spoil it by looking it up. if you don't understand a puzzle, go somewhere else. every puzzle type has a tutorial area, where the rules are explained. also don't rush those tutorials. some of them can be beaten by a little bit of luck or perseverance, however, you probably don't want to leave without a firm understanding of that particular game-mechanic. go back to each piece of the tutorial puzzles, and see if your understanding of the rule does indeed apply. btw googling it might not even help, there is a lot of misinformation out there, especially about the star or sun icons. figure it out yourself.
2. pros
the core gameplay. although based around the same apparent structure, the puzzles are actually highly varied. the interaction between the world and the puzzles are two-way and smart. amazing how much juice you can squeeze out of one puzzle type.
the world. is lush, beautiful and interesting to explore. explore just for the sake of it. to watch from every angle, visit every last bit of it.
3. cons
the software itself aka production value. considering the thousands of hours went into designing the world and the puzzles, the main puzzle is why the developers could not allocate a few dozen more into making a proper UI, rebindable keys, comfortable movement, somewhat less painful mouse control in puzzles, some music or at least interesting ambient sounds, a little less broken sound for the recordings and movie clips, and such basic qualities. the programming is borderline incompetent.
ending. or the lack thereof. it is OK though, we don't really need one. but we need to admit that the ending is laaazy.

The steep price point is more than justified, The Witness is without overstatement the single most well designed game I've seen. Everything is connected to everything else on The Island. The simplistic, yet complex line puzzles might look similar, but are in fact extremely varied: there's always a new twist to them that gets introduced.
The game is however undeniably not for everyone. The puzzles will get hard, and you do need a certain type of logical thinking to get through them.
Unfortunately it is near impossible to truly show or explain what The Witness really is. It is a gaming experience that has never been seen before. If you like puzzle games and would like a challenge, buy it right now. (But whatever you do, do NOT ruin it by looking at gameplay beforehand!)
The Witness is a divisive game. Personally I enjoyed my time with the game very very much and recommend the game even at full price to anyone who enjoys puzzle games.

+ The game is stunningly beautiful
+ The small yet dense world is fun to explore
+ Puzzles are mostly skillfully crafted and fair
- Some puzzles are challenging only because they cause nausea or are physically hard to see
- Some puzzles are not colourblind friendly
- Puzzles are devoid of reason and lack any meaningful context
- The game description promises a narrative that is nonexisting
- The open-world nature clashes with the puzzles occasionally, as in you may stumble upon puzzles that include mechanics that have yet to be thought in the game
+/- Some well read monologues/quotes that seem meaningful but ultimately amounts to nothing
Overall a strong intro that transitions into frustration as it goes along until the ultimate "slap in the face", the ending.

I know this is supposed to be one of the best adventure games of all time, and I really wanted to like it, but it just kept dropping me right when I thought it was getting good.
The character development at the start of this game looks detailed and promising, but it doesn't follow through with a complete theme. It starts with one theme, then abruptly picks up another, starting with a unique character and ending with a stereotype.
The puzzles are difficult, and there are a lot of them, but they aren't very intuitive. They're good for a brain exercise, but I didn't find them fun. I ran to the walkthrough a lot (and I hate walkthroughs) because the game design didn't get me to care about the puzzles. This could very well be personal preference, though.
You can sprint or walk, but even while sprinting....You. Run. So. Slowly. Over. Vast. Distances.
The game world tried very, very hard to be immersive and one-of-a-kind. It offered a lot in the way of lore and history to the world, locations, etc. But I found it all to be ultimately lacking. It felt like somebody who loved fantasy and sci-fi writing one of their first stories. Not bad at all; I can tell they loved their creation, and I appreciate their efforts. But it's not something I would want to PAY for, if you know what I mean.
It's not a bad game. Don't get me wrong. I did enjoy parts of it. But, for the most part, I found myself continuing just for the sake of finishing, and in the hope it would get better along the way. I did buy the sequel, so, again, it's not a bad game. But it's not a great one, either. Just average.

You have reached the peak of gem shuffling. You guide the cursor with finely tuned skill; your soul has fused with these ancient space stones. So finally after it's release on consoles, we're honored with Injustice 2 on PC, but is it worth the hype? Well the game won the game awards 2017 for the best fighting game, so what does it have that makes it stand out to its prequel or even other fighting games?
Graphics: They look outstanding for a fighting game.
The level design is unique and you can transition from one part of the level to another through special moves like in Tekken 7.
My concernes before release was that quality of the PS4 port, especially because Warner Bros has a history as a publisher in rushing out buggy and badly ported games (ex: Batman Arkham Knight, Mortal Kombat X), but it turned out to be a great port with just a few moments when things are framelocked to 30 fps that happen during the cutscenes and during the super moves.
Sound: DC universe iconic voices, immersive music and great sound effects.
Gameplay: Combat style is similar to Mortal Kombat X and there are an insane amount of combos you can perform. Luckily this game can be played perfectly with a keyboard so no controller or fightpad is needed. You'll have a blast exploring every characher's combos.
Story: The story continues from where Injustice 1 left of and also reflects upon the Batman vs Superman movie conflicts within the game. Story was easy to follow and captivating. It tries to create the illusion that your choices matter, but the truth is the only choice that matters is the last one.
So the good news is, compared to Street Fighter V, it actually has a single player campaign that actually has an interesting plot. The bad news is this game has fallen predator to the lootbox tumor that's been spreading too much in 2017. Are they pay to win? Yes and no. They contain gear that increases your character stats so depending on how you see things it might be what makes you buy the game or not.
To separate the pay to win players from the regular ones, they have divided the queues for that, so there is one queue where gear is used by both players and there is a queue where it is not.
It sounds good on paper, but the problems start with the way the matchmaker works. There is no matchmaker! Literally you will be matched against the same oponent 10 times in a row even if you research for a new oponent after cancelling. The game does not even care about your own experience in Injustice so it just finds completely random people for you to fight. There are not enough people playing that non-gear mode to actually have fun in a fair way, whereas the gear mode queue has enough players for you to either stomp or be stomped due to gear stats.
The multiverse is an alternative to fighting players as you can train and get some flashy lootboxes while at it, yay!
Conclusion: From my point of view it's worth buying it for the single player part of the game, but for the multiplayer, despite having a great netcode, I would strongly discourage you in not buying it if you intend to focus your time on that.
TL:DR
Pros:
-Mostly good PC port
-Amazing graphics
-Immersive music
-A large cast of heroes to choose from
-Great single player campaign
-Multiverse is an awesome way to spend your time training
-Flawless netcode
Cons:
-Lootboxes hitting a game like this
-Game longevity questionable due to its small playerbase and lack of a matchmaker
-Gear is affecting online games and lootboxes guarantee that you'll never get the gear you want
-Despite gear being optional, both players have to agree not to use gear
-Overpriced dlc

Hello, Unreal Tournament veteran here. I'm not necessarily recommending the game, I wish I could give it a neutral rating, but I definitively don't want to give it a bad review.
Me and a couple guys from the UT forums jumped in and gave the Free Edition a try, see what it's like on high-level plays. This is one of the only afps games that imitates Unreal Tournament (more specifically UT2004) rather than Quake/CPMA.
The UT community has always been very fragmented, because each UT game is very different. If you liked UT2004, you will probably like this game, as it has dodge-jump in it - a feature that half the UT community likes, the other one doesn't. I happen to be the latter, but I won't go into detail why,
. Just like in UT2004, the problems with dodge-jump start showing here as well, once you start entering high-level play, and can handle Godlike bots. Admittedly, this game noticeably tries to do something to mitigate those problems, but it does come at the cost of weapon balance - the rocket launmcher in particular is outlandishly powerful and so are most of the hitscan weapons.
But that's not really the problem with weapons. I'm sure balance will change over time. The bigger problem is the lack of imagination. UT has flak cannon, which is many people's favorite waepon. This game has a regular double barreled shotgun, which is hitscan. UT has a minigun. This game has a regular assault rifle (which is quite OP). Of course there's at least one shining examples of fun weapons like the Stingray - a combination of plasma and shock rifle, but without the shock combo (what a shame). Then there's the outright weird one, which is the flamethrower - I really don't know how the mechanics behind its primary fire work. None of the weapons have a particularly interesting effect or mechanic behind them. Not even knockback/pull or any sort of combos, or movement lockdown, blocking... nothing.
Another thing to note is the vehicles seem very week. A little bit of spam from the stingray kills even the big mech. The vehicles seem to be loaded with firepower, but could really use a little bit more tankyness,
EDIT: apparently your #1 melee weapons alt-fire can repair vehicles and it costs suit energy.
I do like the invisibility ability! Such a wonderful revamp of the stupid Adrenaline system from UT2004. Your suit energy recharges slowly and you get to use that for a very limited invisibility, which does create some interesting comebacks! I love it.
I also like how in DM and TDM the enemies drop health packs on death! What a wonderful solution to the problem of always being low on health after every fight and all the nearby health pickups being on cooldown. It might not be a good idea for CTF, Domination and Duel, but it's sure as hell a welcome addition to DM/TDM.
I must also compliment the devs for their work on some of the maps. The mayan ruin/jungle themed maps are very good and visual clarity is very good on them. Lots of verticality and places to use wall-dodging :)
I am wishing the devs all the best and hopefully there will be some small ctf or duel tournaments in the near future. That would really help this game's reputation.

A puzzle-adventure game with action segments
Rating 6/10
The Ball feels like an extended UE3 tech demo that's been fleshed out into a full game. This means there is a lack of real plot, narrative and character. Each new area feels like an excuse to show off puzzles or the environment rather than the story dictating locations and pacing.
Puzzles and combat are at the heart of the game and they both work together nicely with neither one taking precedence over the other. The game starts by dropping you into an undiscovered and mysterious ancient civilization buried deep beneath the earth. Of course like most ruined and ancient civilizations it comes beset with dangers; luckily you also find the ball of the title as well as a hand held artefact that controls its movement. The ball is a large and powerful weapon but also unwieldy, you can either magnetically draw the ball towards you or punch it away using a piston of varying power. Control of the ball is key as it'll be both your protector from arrow traps and monsters as well as solving numerous puzzles littered around the ruins.
Combat is bowling on a grand scale as you launch the ball towards the enemy watching as they topple like skittles; it's a great effect and really feels like it has an impact when it strikes down a horde of mummies. And they do come at you in hordes with combat often a quick affair as you fire the ball around trying to knock down as many of them in one go as possible. Firing the ball with too much power will strike down more enemies but also leave you vulnerable as you slowly draw the ball back, it's a fine balance and knowing when to fire the ball as well as when to bring it back is key to survival. Thankfully the combat never overstays it welcome and after clearing a room of enemies you'll end up with a new puzzle to solve.
These puzzles are probably the highlight of the Ball, it will obviously be compared to Portal and whilst not quite as ingenious the puzzles are still well thought out, neither being too complicated nor too easy. The majority of the puzzles require you to guide the ball over various obstacles to reach buttons that allow you to progress. The element of solving puzzles and exploring new areas as you descend further into the ruins is what makes the game.
Once you've completed the main storyline there are a number of survival arenas which are hectic battle against the clock as waves of monsters stream into small arenas as you fire the ball around and set off traps in a desperate attempt to survive the round before it starts again. They are a nice time diversion after completing the game but no more than that.

This is a puzzle/brain teaser game. For me, I was a part of the Unreal community for a while and had the opportunity to play this game in beta mode. Really fun trying to figure out what needed to be done to advance on to the next area. Game play, of course, is limited to exploration.....but not too mundane to a point of disinterest. Overall the game can give you immersion, but only if you use your imagination as you go along through the caves and whatnot.
You will need a decent pc with a decent graphics card as there are areas that can tax your screen fps.
I enjoy puzzle games so this one kept me entertained. I recommend this game for you puzzle players out there.

I'd like to start this review by saying, the Ball wasn't a bad game, I just found myself bored a bit to often to confidently recommend.
The game itself functions well enough. I never encountered any game breaking glitches, never sank through the floor,  lost the ball, or had a button simply not work. It plays just fine in that regard. The ball control is a bit wobbly in terms of getting it to shoot precisely, but it's very slight, and most of the puzzles allow for that little bit of wiggle room.
The puzzles are pretty easy, and never really force you to do any huge mental gymnastics. The hardest part of the game are the survival levels and those just involve surviving waves of enemies. The enemies are easy enough to kill (rolling the ball over them) but they're a non-threat for the the campaign and appear so sparingly in the campaign they almost feel a little out of place. They aren't there as a puzzle impediment like the turrets in portal, most times (a few exceptions), they're mostly just thrown at you to be a momentary antagonist.
The story is interesting. However you only get it through finding secrets and once you've clicked out of the text screen there's no way to recall that text without playing through the level and finding the secret again, so if you miss one that's unfortunate. The secrets themselves are easy enough to find, you just have to be patient and willing to hunt around for hidden alcoves and the like. They do however have a stage selector so if you really want to play a level over it's easy to do.
The game looks nice enough. The graphics are consistent, and I never saw any graphical glitches, but the ball itself is a bit annoying. Even transparent it's very noticeable and still impedes vision to a degree. The problem there lies in the design of the ball. The ball is made up of two parts. A round solid peice, and a complex framework. Everything fades out except for the framework, which there is a lot of, causing a sort of cage like effect on your vision.
Overall the game was alright. I don't regret buying it, or playing it. If you're looking for a game similar to portal, while this is in the same vein (logic puzzler), it isn't in the same league. If you want to have some fun walking through mildly Aztecian ruins, smashing some zombies, and solving some puzzles give it a shot.

Although it says I currently only have ~4 hours of in-game time for Star Conflict, I've actually played for 22.5 days (540 hours) as of the time of this review, and just reinstalled it using the Steam client. Star Conflict is an arcade-style MMO space shooter game, offering PvP (team deathmatches, capture the beacon, etc.) and PvE (set missions, instanced "open space") game modes.
Overall, I have enjoyed it and would recommend as a fun game, primarily for its PvP modes, but with caveats. This game is for people who like flying around in pew pew space fighter ships; it is NOT a macro/econ type game (e.g. EVE) on a vast scale. Playable maps are bound (but rather beautiful to play in IMO), and "open space" feels obviously instanced, i.e. it isn't truly "open space."
PROS:
- Fun arcade-style space shooter game (primarily PvP--again, IMO)
- Multiple ship classes to choose from, build customization
- Pew pew lasers, missiles
- PvP modes are fast-paced
- Free to play (F2P), with purchasable extras (game is not Pay to Win (P2W), IMO)
CONS:
- Small game population (queue times, matchmaker can be annoying)
- Grind becomes rather evident
- Underdeveloped econ system; no player trading
In conclusion, it's a free game, and can potentially be a lot of fun. It does take a bit of time investment, but for someone who's looking for a space fighter game, this might be a good one to take a look at. GL HF!

Hello, and welcome to Dofus!
Dofus is a turn based strategy MMORPG. It started out with 12 classes (hence the name "World of Twelve"), but in the past couple of years they've added more and more classes which have spiced up the game a lot! This is one of the best games I've ever played, and I'm not just saying that. I've been playing this game for over a decade and I've loved every minute of it.
This game will challenge you in almost every way a game can. There are 17 classes (with hints of an 18th), and each class has 22 spells that are unique to that class. There are even more spells that all classes can have, but you must overcome different challenges to obtain them.
Dofus takes a little getting used to when you first start playing, but as soon as you start getting on a roll the fun is endless! There are over 16,000 achievements that you can unlock ranging from extremely easy to damn near impossible! Unlocking an achievement will give you a certain amount of gold and experience depending on how difficult it was to unlock it.
This is a game for both the hardcore gamers and the casual gamers! It just depends on your playstyle.
There is an awesome system for Guilds, and Alliances in place that allows the players to control the map. If your Alliance is in control of the area you get a boost in EXP and drops! Other Alliances can attack areas they don't own to try take them over and you have to defend in a timed King Of The Hill that can result in a warzone of PvP fights!
The players own the economy, so depending on which server you play on, the item that you want to buy may or may not be in the market. Unless you want to make the item yourself you can level up to 18 different professions by creating items using all the materials in their respected recipes (harder to make items give you more EXP, but require more mats).
There is an enormous variety of monsters of different skill levels that each drop their own unique materials that you can sell, use, or make into certain items!
You won't find yourself sitting around looking for things to do!
There's so much more, but I would be typing for days, and even I don't know everything about the game!
USEFULL EXTERNAL SITES:
Use this site to find certain item combinations that will make your character even stronger!
This is the Dofus Wiki page; it will help you a lot with your journey if you ever get stuck, or want to know what a certain monster does, and how to beat it. Keep in mind though that it is player made, and so it might not have everything about the game in it.
I HIGHLY recommend you play this game, I know you won't regret it!

I waited for this port for so long, but it was worth the wait!
1. The Combat is much better over all than Injustice: Gods Amoung Us's. The movement is much faster, and so are the fights. Although, the supermoves, cutscenes, and intros are stuck at 30fps, the combat is a solid 60fps. A small price to pay for this great game!
2. The story kicks off right where we left off in the first and even though it didn't have the 2 worlds colliding concept going on, it turned out better than I could of hoped.
(I'll try to make it sound good without spoiling anything major that we didnt know from the trailers)
Superman is locked up, and Batman/Bruce is trying to rebuild what was destroyed in the first game, but the major threat of the new cabal of villians brought together by Grodd forces him to call on allies, like the Green Arrow from the Universe that collided with this one, along with Black Canary. Also Harley Quinn is an ally like in the first, along with the newbies Firestorm(my personal main in the game) and Bluebeetle. But, we all know Braniac is the real threat. Batman confronts Superman about him, and Superman excailms he needs him to beat Braniac. Now whether or not that is true, you will have to play to see how the story pans out for yourselves.
3. The Graphics are just gorgous. I personally have a Gtx 1050ti OC with an i5-6400k, and I can run a mix of medium and high settings at 1080p60fps. But really any grahphical setting, and this game still looks good, definetly an improvement over the first.
4.The Gearboxes are there but Injustice 2 handles it way better than EA has been handling them lately. Yes, they do give you more stats, but in ranked multiplayer, it is made so that everyone is at an even advantage, in both strength and framerate. They can be quite easy to obtain as well, especially thanks to the Multiverses which is my next point.
5.The Multiverses make the singleplayer experience extremely supieror compared to the first. These allow for a constant flow of new singleplayer content, with challenge and great rewards. Plus new multiverses appear every day for hours upon hours of playtime. I personally spend most of my time playing with them more than I do in multiplayer.
6.Last but not least, the roster of heroes and villians is huge, with 36 to pick from and with Enchantress and the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles coming out in early 2018. So the Season Pass is worth it for a huge varaity of playable characters to choose from. Also, like the first game, there are premire skins that let you turn 9 of the heroes into diffrent characters like The Flash to Reverse Flash or Jay Garick, or Supergirl to Powergirl. So if you count them, along with the heroes still to come, thats a grand total of 50(if all 4 Ninja Turtles will be playable) heroes and villans, almost doubling the roster of the first game.
Overall, I have to say Injustice 2 is a worthy if not superior sucssesor to the first game. It looks amazing, combat is more smooth, the story is more intense, the multiverses makes there always something to do, the roster is huge, the multiplayer is fair, the gearboxs arent a pain, it is a much better port than NetherRealm's MKX, and although the 30fps cutscences would be better in 60fps, the good definitely out ways the bad.

It's not a bad game but I wouldn't reccomend it for two reasons. I got motion sickness and it's a bit repetative.
By repetative I mean that even though the puzzles themselves are varying difficulty they are very similar in design and very 2d. Feels like just walking in a 3d world to get to and start a new 2d puzzle.
I expected a bit more after all the positive reviews and I thought it reminded me of "The Talos Principle", but this game feels a bit simplistic in design (the puzzles are varying difficulty though, and absolutely a challange).

Very beautiful graphics and soothing sound, excellent atmosphere and feeling.
The difficulty of puzzles is next to impossible to evaluate because many are easy, some medium and few are hard. Some are even impossible or require unbelievable will to solve -- but for every person it is different. There may be a kind of probability but I was stuck on an extremely simple puzzle for a long time and then swept through many following puzzles without a hitch, and it was not a matter of comprehension. It is just a bit of luck on how you look at it and not necessarily a matter of comprehension, intelligence or other personal traits.
You'll have to live with those "dumb feeling" moments if you want to enjoy the game.
My advise is to play as far as you feel comfortable without spoilers but if you feel like you need it, don't think it is wrong to cheat and look solutions up on the 'net. Afterwards you'll feel guilty and like you've ruined the fun, so do this with caution. But sometimes I can tell you some very hard puzzles I was HAPPY to have them looked up, because I knew I could never do those. For example the ones where you have to pay attention to "something" (I don't want to spoil here) and then "translate" that "something" into the solution. Well, it happens that I simply can't perceive that "something" even if I know what it is, I have the solution and try hard. I simply don't "perceive" it that way so I'd never come up with that solution.
Other times I solved puzzles without having a clue how, even hourse later and all, I still don't know how I did some. Maybe just luck?
Then there are the citations from literature. They are interesting but they feel more like overshooting or wannabe genius. No denying that "The Witness" is a masterpiece that will be remembered for a very very long time. I value it a lot, it's one of the best games I've played in the last years. But, come on. Einstein and philosophers? It certainly is meant as a tribute to those luminaries, but this is still a game and a COMMERCIAL PRODUCT, not a piece of art.
To be true art it must be something to put into a museum, teach in school or to release into the public domain for all humanity to enjoy for free. And neither of these is the case. This is still a commercial game, and as such the altruistic citations don't sound sincere enough to me.
You want the real deal? Stop playing computer games and read an academic text about any topic (philosophy, art, social sciences or whatever) that you can download for free from any university. You'll get pretty soon the difference between this "intellectual posing" and the real thing.
That said, I still recommend it over and over again. If you like puzzles, Myst or exploration games on solitary islands.. then this is the best you can get.
Also, take some screenshots of beautiful sights and use them as desktop wallpapers! You'll be surprised how beautiful this game really looks.

The Witness is a first person exploration puzzle game that is highly remarkable for a variety of reasons, some of which sadly can't be discussed easily (or at all) without risking spoilers.
For those of you considering the game, please take this to heart and limit or (preferably) just abstain from looking up more info about the game. Many reviews contain spoilers at some level (including the top reviews)! The forums and community hub also do (even though there is a Spoiler subforum, there are still spoilers in the other sub-forums). I will try to keep this review as spoiler free as practical.
, The Witness manages to evoke even in a seasoned gamer like me, the sense of wonder I felt when playing games like Myst for the first time.
That is, among other reasons, because the game is a gorgeous piece of virtual art. Most of us are no longer easily impressed by pretty, expensive, mass produced graphics. This is more than that.
While indeed technically excellent, the world (well, island) of The Witness is crafted in a way that feels something like walking around in a masterpiece painting (or series of paintings, as there is considerable environmental variety). Aside from the overall beauty, there are so very many wonderful details to admire. I don't think I have played any other first person 3D game that approaches this level of artistry.
, which consists primarily of exploration, puzzle solving, and a sort of scavenger hunting is surprisingly enjoyable.
The classic CD-ROM game Myst is perhaps the closest comparison and the biggest inspiration for this game, but The Witness is much more accessible, less frustrating, more beautiful, and, I think, more rewarding an experience.
It is a game of epiphanies, repeatedly producing quite nice feelings of accomplishment in ways that not many games do, even most puzzle games.
This is largely because the puzzle solving mechanics are never directly explained to you, but the world presents you with ample visual and symbolic clues to make your own inferences. This is the core design principle, and, to me, indeed a key selling point.
Based on preview videos I saw initially, I had significant reservations about the seemingly simplistic puzzle mechanic. Simple it is indeed, but it is presented in such clever, varied, often challenging ways that it never really felt tedious or overly repetitive to me (although, I am quite good at puzzles). And, yes, there is somewhat more to this than solving 2D puzzles on flat panels.
Going into more details about the mechanics would spoil the sense of discovery that is the highlight of the game, so I will not, but I will say that this game will exercise your mind in a wide variety of wonderful ways.
It's not an easy game. While getting to the "easy" ending can be done without much effort, the game holds substantial challenges for those that wish to take them on.
During my playthrough, I ended up using three sheets of graph paper and taking numerous private screenshots for future reference. It's
type of game - the type of game (almost) nobody has dared to make in decades.
It takes maybe a 10-20 hours to reach the easy ending, and another 10-20 to reach complete the second achievement. However, there is quite a bit more to do, and doing all of it, even with a guide, would take quite a lot longer.
So, to those of you wondering about the $40 price point, the game has
to offer to justify it.

This game is a masterpiece and my personal game of the year for 2016.
If you don't like puzzles, you shouldn't even bother with this game.
If you love puzzles (or even simply like them), I highly recommend it.
Puzzles are a somewhat unique category of game. Most of the magic happens in the player's mind and doesn't translate well to a non-participating observer. Because they typically have logical solutions, puzzles have practically zero replay value. So even ignoring the fact that portions of this game are "spoilable", know that watching a gameplay video or using  walkthrough defeats the purpose of playing it at all.
Puzzles are the meat of this game. Some people see footage of the first-person exploration and mentally categorize this as a first-person exploration game where puzzles must be solved to allow you to progress. The truth of the matter is that the grid-based puzzles make up the vast majority of the game's content, and the first-person exploration is a means to allow the player to navigate between puzzles.
Puzzles with similar components are grouped together and placed within an environment that is visually distinct. Some puzzles have context clues placed within the environments. Some puzzles will affect your access to certain paths within the environments. Some puzzles are hidden and exploration is necessary to discover them.
Learning how to solve the puzzles is a puzzle in itself. There is no tutorial, except for a brief flash of the minimal controls. Any new group of puzzles presents you with numerous "easy" versions to solve before getting into the heavy stuff. Some players see this as a cheap attempt to inflate the total number of puzzles in the game, but even the easy puzzles are teaching you important lessons about what is or is not a valid solution. This becomes increasingly important as new types of puzzles offer more complex rules and start to combine components.
One of the great things about this game is that unspoiled players can, through observation, realize hidden significance in seemingly-unremarkable elements they encountered previously. The island houses a number of mundane (or even messy) environmental details that have a dramatic shift when viewed from a certain angle. Most of these details are visual flavor that would not be possible without the first-person exploration format. There are more layers to this game than many players realize, and there are whole chunks of game that many players will never see because they decided to speedrun or because they reached the basic ending and assumed there was nothing more.
If you explore beyond the puzzles, you may find references to philosophy (Eastern & Western). These are essentially easter eggs and will have no effect on gameplay, though they may provide some thematic context to players.
There is no background music. This was an intentional design choice made by the developer and apparently some people think it was some kind of oversight. Have you ever watched the comparisons of movie clips with/without music, or with different music backing the same clip? Music is commonly used to establish tone or to emotionally manipulate the audience. Lack of music is one way to avoid telling the player what to think or how to feel. There are still sound effects; it's not like the game is totally silent. I would even recommend headphones.
For the deaf or colorblind: there are a few puzzles that involve sound and some that involve color. They're not required in order to reach the ending, but they are required in order to reach a large chunk of optional late-game puzzles as well as one of the achievements.

This game let's you unravel it bit by bit, letting you feel challenged and intelligent without overwhelming you. And you do it at whatever pace you choose.

The Witness is one of the most divisive games you will ever encounter. To put it simply, to get satisfaction from the experience you need to be a hardcore puzzle fanatic. I don't mean puzzle fanatic in the traditional sense, either. The hundreds of puzzles scattered across The Witness' beautiful world are relatively one-dimensional. Instead of providing diversity through various methods, it uses only line puzzles. All variation is derived from the rules of these line puzzles, which are indicated by small icons.
In total, the game makes no effort to feel rewarding, or even substantiate its world. It's quiet, 100% puzzle focused, and can most be compared to a puzzle book you can find in a store. At $40, it's a risky proposition for the average consumer. In my case, it was a dissasisfactory experience despite the beautiful visuals and polished design.

A classic PC game that was pushing the medium almost 17 years ago. It's still beautiful, it's still emotional, funny and immersive.
It's a point-and-click adventure game unlike anything I've ever played. The game has a well-realized world that gives off a very European, 80s-90s sci-fi vibe. The amount of cinematic beauty such a low-budget game can come out with is impressive.
The story is very detailed and probably the most important aspect of the game, this isn't JUST a puzzle-solving point-and-click. I'd say it's a visual novel as well, with full voice-acting. Some NPCs can talk for up to twenty minutes about the well-realized lore created by the development team. It's got a snarky and relatable main character that keeps every moment interesting as she projects her personality onto any situation by using the "examine" feature.
My only gripes with this one is that the game drags on a little long near the middle, and a few of the puzzles are just ridiculous and you'll either have to get really creative with your problem-solving skills, or be following a guide.
Even if you're put off by puzzle-solving or point-and-clicks, I'd still say give this a chance if it goes on sale or you feel sponatenous. Its greatest strength is putting ADVENTURE in an Adventure game.
Buy it.

The Longest Journey is an amazing story adventure game and perfects the point & click genre. In terms of story, the game excels and the world is equally incredible as it incorporates both sci-fi & fantasy elements. The Longest Journey is imaginative in its way of creating a diverse and unique universe filled with lore and characters that remain memorable. April Ryan is fantastic as the game's leading protagonist. She is well written and stands out as a main character. The world is truly great from the moment the player enters the futuristic world of Earth, being set about 300 years into the future. Sci-fi alone is done so well in this game and so is the fantasy aspect inspired by classic medieval lore with a fantastical touch.
While filled with great lore and characters, the adventure filled game play can seem slow at times due to April's walk speed and this requires a bit of patience. This may be a problem as it can make the game experience seem a tedious one. Nonetheless, despite this The Longest Journey features amazing voice acting and dialogue coupled with a very well written script. This game is a true classic and really is one of the greatest adventure games ever made; nothing since has really compared to the degree of detail evident in the game's story structure and lore. Scale-wise, it is a series filled with imaginative lore containing creatures and characters from different worlds and backgrounds. This all combines to make an outstanding story adventure. The Longest Journey is the first of the Dreamfall series and anyone interested in fantasy, or sci-fi with an emphasis on narrative should definitely experience this game.

Far Cry 4 is straight up an absolutely amazing game. It improves on everything we thought made Far Cry 3 such a success. Its no revolution but the sheer amount of pure fun and enjoyability you gain from it is incredible and is an extremely solid entry in a franchise with high standards. The graphics here are definitely a step up from its predecessor. The heavily improved fur as well as the godrays make the game look as stunning as ever. The weapons remain solid as before but with more variety and realism added to them (most, anyway). A couple things that would make this the perfect Far Cry game would be a lot more customization options - not only for the weapons but also your attire. The land vehicles seem the same as before. They don't feel unique enough but the air vehicle (the Buzzer) makes what would have been long and boring journeys an exciting zip across the luscious landscape of Kyrat. The story was decent but what I thought was well done was the character development as well as the choices you are able to make between them. Overall, these features make Far Cry 4 a solid entry in the series and highly enjoyable. (The references to other games don't hurt) If you even remotely like Far Cry 3, this would be an obvious purchase

VA-11 Hall-A (Valhalla from now on) is a cyberpunk visual novel, and long story short, it's great.
Cyberpunk is usually associated with vast conspiracy theories, shady things corporations do, an increased role and influence of cyberspace/augmentations, and so on. Valhalla chose a different approach and instead decided to focus on everyday life of regular people, a hefty portion of which isn't exactly remarkable, at least not on the global scale. Jill, the game's protagonist, is a prime example of a person belonging to this group, and through her we'll get to know all the other characters and their stories. Given how strong Valhalla's character cast is, the process is incredibly enjoyable and fun.
In my opinion the best thing about Valhalla is its ability to neatly juggle comedy and light-hearted content with far more serious stuff. Sure, mixing genres, themes, and tones is hardly rare, but doing this seamlessly, without creating an obvious mismatch is definitely not an easy feat, and I feel that Valhalla managed to succeed.
Valhalla has some gameplay, namely a bartending minigame. Nothing fancy in this department, but it's perfectly fine. Visuals are fantastic, and so is music; the latter can be customized by fiddling with the in-game jukebox, which a very nice touch.
Overall, Valhalla quickly and easily exceeded my expectations. It was pretty much a day 1 purchase for me, and it didn't disappoint. Heartily recommended.

Dofus is not your typical MMO. It is designed, from the ground up, to be a fun, engaging, and visually stunning game... in 2D. Aesthetically, there are few games that can compare to the cohesive, stylistic beauty that marks Dofus, which transports us to a world where fantasy and magic feel real and new, much like my generation saw the bright, vast world of WoW at a young age and fell in love.
Dofus, however, is not a mass-appeal game. I can only compare its team to Eve Online in this respect: It knows its audience, and it does a damn good job of pumping out the kind of content that they love. There are many aspects of Dofus that are unorthodox in today's game market - Non-binding items, a robust economy where professions actually do matter (as they produce all the items in the game), and a class of professions where it is actually possible to change the stats of items and add stats that were not there previously.
It isn't all about professions, though. The turn based combat is carried by a gorgeous and well executed litany of spells, abilities, and animations that absoulutely showcase the dedication of the art team. This combat is made interesting not only by the mechanics, but your choice of character build. Character build in this game is, absolutely, your choice. Dofus features the old-style characteristics system where you allocate the points, rather then having them automatically assigned. There are still, of course, cookie cutter builds that some follow, but you do not have to be follow of them to excel: if anything, a person who learns the ins and outs of Dofus has innumerable opportunities to try out novel and interesting character designs that may surprise their fellow players.
On the topic of fellow players we reach one of the games many strengths. There are alliances that do nothing but PVE, if thats what you enjoy. There are alliances that do nothing but PVP as well, and of course a smattering that do all sorts of activities together. If alliances are too big a community for you (although alliances themselves vary greatly in size), you can choose  to be in an allianceless guild that is a bit more cozy. (Or you can play solo, talk to nobody, quit, and wonder why you can't enjoy MMOs.)
This game has been around for over ten years and I am still amazed by how many helpful, sociable veteran players there are. Although there are complaints about technicalities, as with all game communities, the Dofus community as a whole is passionate about the game they play, and more than willing to guide newcomers on their path to glory, loot, and lasting friendships.
I cannot recommend this game enough: Try it, and if you like it, welcome home.

Note: if you’re picking this up with friends, just make sure you’re put on the same server, so you can explore it together. When you first start, you’re going to be randomly sorted into one of the available INTernational servers by default. You can click the small “Manual server selection” to make sure you go on Rosal server together, for example.
Don’t be fooled by the cute artwork! Dofus is not a typical mmo, and has a lot of depth. The game was released more than a decade ago, and has kept evolving and growing since then. If you’re at all a fan or interested in tactical gameplay, you will like the combat. I’ve always compared it to FFTA (final fantasy tactics advance), but far more dynamic, and set in a large MMO world. It’s the many interesting classes and their mechanics that have kept me playing all this time.
This unique world has a wealth of stories, secrets, quests and achievements. You’ll also play the game through your friends, as this is an MMO after all, and play against them too: there are opportunities to fight against others not just nearby, but internationally and across all servers as well.
In the end, Dofus is a game set in a fantastic universe, that lets you choose what sort of experience you’d like, with no shortage of content. I’ve personally tried many other MMOs, and nothing (except for Wakfu somewhat, and it’s the same developer) compares
It’s free to download and try, and subscribing (not a recurring thing, you get 1 week/month/3months/6months/year at a time) allows you to interact with things outside of the first few areas. Believe me though, it’s definitely worth it. There’s also a system that will essentially allow you to play for free, and use the in-game currency to buy subscription time.

It really is a love hate game, when it works and you use all of your equipment and abilities to work around the challenges which are set, it's very rewarding. At the same time it's sluggish, sometimes you will be jumping around ledges (which is a major part of the game) and it will automatically open the wingsuit. When this happens you could just be jumping around onto some steps or something at ground level and half of your health will disappear. It's also a bit counter intuitive when you're sneaking up next to an outpost with stealth, and some eagle or even a leopard attacks you and the only silenced weapon you might have is a sniper rifle which is bolt action and useless for CQC. Some of the best weapons are unlocked far too late in the game to be of any use, such as the decent signature weapons like the heavy machine guns and the AMR sniper rifle which is just a one shot kill no matter what.
That said, I find myself coming back because of smart level designs, intelligent AI which makes stealth difficult, satisfying weapons and upgrades and a great world to explore. I only recently found that the only way for me to properly enjoy far cry games is to rule things out totally before moving on. Take all of the towers, then all of the outposts, then do the side missions and then the campaign, and I wish I had realised that about 200 hours ago! It makes the game feel less of a mess for me. I would also say once you have half decent equipment, don't be afraid of fortresses when the game says they're very hard early on because they're doable and are very rewarding when done early too, they just take a bit of strategy.

Death Road to Canada is a very good zombie survival game.
It truly feels like you are a survivor in a "real" zombie apocalypse
Your starting character(s) is a normal person and not a superhuman slaughter machine like in so many zombie games.
Your character gets tired after swinging his/her weapon at undeads for hours.
Killing zombies doesn't give you experience points, it will just keep you alive.
Running away is often the best thing to do.
You have to carefully manage your resources in order to reach the promised land of Canada.
On the death road you will find trader camps where you will be able to buy weapons and/or supplies, recruit characters and train your party.
On the flip side, you can meet and recruit rare characters such as : a pirate, a gnome, a ninja, a wizard ,a clown, a magical girl, a valkyrie, a goat and many others.
They are all very different gameplaywise and that makes every run feel fresh.
Death Road to Canada is filled to the brim with pop culture references.
This game has rogue like mechanics.
Upon surviving a siege you earn zombo points wich can later be used to unlock new traits and perks for your characters. Zombo points can also be used to upgrade perks.
Between missions you will experience random events that can save or destroy your run.
Some outcomes depend on your choices.
The duality between the "realistic" gameplay and the crazy situations is what makes this game great.
If you are searching for a solid zombie survival game that lets you experience whacky adventures, look no further.

“A nice change of pace from Bejeweled games.”
I learned how to switch with precision and speed while learning new phrases of positive reinforcement. I also learned how to plan ahead; foresight.
Casual to the very core, 3SwitcheD is a fun diversion that can easily make you sink in hours to get to that desired high score.
I find the voices that give you positive reinforcements very relaxing. The game praises you with almost every move you make and you even have the option to have it be male or female. It’s your standard mix of gem type games all in one, call it a clone or what have you, for me, what mattered was that they all worked well and that I had fun. One nitpick I have is that there is no feeling of progression other than getting high scores.
3SwitcheD doesn’t do anything new in the genre but it really doesn’t have to in order to shine. It’s a competent and fun game that made me feel like a winner in every step of the way, even whenever I do lose.
Although entertaining, I wouldn’t buy it for more than $3 US dollars.

This game requires a bit of compartmentalization. As a TL;DR for anyone reading, if you're into the kind of challenging logic puzzles the game offers, this game is well worth the money. But that's really the
reason to buy it.
Let's start with the good. The puzzles in this game are all based on an extremely simple idea: get a line from point A to point B. However, the game sprinkles in so many different rules and requirements the player has to meet along the way that some of the puzzles can be extremely difficult. It starts with simple maze puzzles, but expands with icons that reflect shapes that need to fit into sections the player makes, to color-coded icons that need to be grouped or divided in various ways, all the way to affecting the color of the icons using glass partitions and colored lighting. The number of iterations on the same concept is actually very impressive. I particularly like the puzzles that require the player to physically position themselves to gain the proper perspective on the board to see the solution.
The open-world nature of the island can lead to some frustration, though. The player can come across puzzles that require some fore-knowledge that they haven't gained yet. My advice to anyone looking to pick this up is to never be afraid of walking away from a puzzle you don't understand. Go exploring, and you'll eventually come across the tutorial panels for the information you're missing.
The puzzle portion of the game is the reason you should buy this game. Check out some youtube videos that show what the puzzles are, and if they interest you, the game is worth buying. If there's any problem with them, it's that there is an overwhelming number of them.
This game is gorgeous. There are likely some that aren't into the aesthetic of the game and want photorealistic graphics, but this game doesn't have that. If you're not that type of person, the extraordinarily colorful and varied landscape is actually very refreshing. I didn't run into any situations where the game ran slowly for me, but that no doubt depends on the machine you're on. Some of the environments also play into the puzzles, as mentioned above, and that's really the most creative part about the game. Going around exploring the island and discovering all that's hidden away is a nice way to give the player a chance to breathe in between puzzles.
If there's one complaint, it's that the environment suggests a bigger story with the island. The game has a Myst vibe to it that makes you feel like you're seeing a lot of real history and that people have been there before, but the game never really delivers on that. This actually makes the whole island feel much more artificial.
The Witness is pretentious. There's really no way to justify the "artistic" element in the game. On this strange island that has so much detail in it, the player starts to think there might be a greater message, a bigger story that happened in the past, and they're doing all the puzzles to figure that out. There seem to be experiments, archaeological digs, and statues of people that...might have been alive at some point? It seems like such a mystery, and it's fun to explore the environment and wonder what the answer could be.
Instead what the developers decided to do was record people reading famous quotes by famous people and scatter them as collectibles throughout the island. Yeah, the first one you find is kind of interesting, but after a couple more, you realize what the "artistic" message is supposed to be and that the developer couldn't convey that message themselves. They had to cobble together a selection of supposedly profound sayings from other people and create this Frankenstein's monster and call it "art". It doesn't take many of these tape recorders for the player to say, "Yes, science is the only true religion, I get it. Couldn't you have come up with an actually creative way of conveying this sentiment via gameplay or visual story telling?"
And around that time you'll likely find the theater room. This is a small area off the beaten path that includes a projector tied into a puzzle panel. The player can find secret codes behind locked doors to enter into this machine for secret surprises. These turn out to be complete videos of some of the people the tape recorders have been quoting saying more of the same stuff you've probably been listening to this entire game, along with some cinematic clips that seem profound. Look, that guy is carrying that candle, and it's all one continuous take, how artistic!
And this is a major problem with the game. I find it less enjoyable to solve difficult problems to unlock new areas if all I'm going to get is more puzzles and preachy quotes the developers substitute for artistic merit. I like the puzzles and the visuals, but this grates on my nerves.
And worse still, there is one thing that the game does that I would have loved to see developed more. While playing the game, you'll eventually see a puzzle in the environment. I first saw it as a reflection on the water, the distict circle with the line that has a beveled end. I thought it was weird, and was amazed when I found I could actually trace a line down it just like all the puzzles I'd been doing up to that point. I was even rewarded with a big booming noise when I completed it. Suddenly, I began to see those puzzles scattered all throughout the island, usually requiring I find the right perspective. Walking into a forest, I saw another puzzle start to form in the tree's canopy. I could even find some in the clouds when I was standing on the right hill-top.
This element of the game was facinating and clever, and I find this to be where the greatest potential for artistic merit in the game lies. The player spends so much time solving these puzzles that they start to see the patterns in the world at large. First on a building, then in the trees and the water and the sky. Isn't this a good way to make an artistic message about recognizing the same patterns from the smallest elements in reality to the great expanses of the universe and finding some form of spirituality in the surprising order of chaos? This isn't a new idea, but the way the game never forces you to spot these large environmental puzzles, yet almost guarantees the player finds at least one could have been such an interesting way to convey that message.
But these puzzles don't really do anything. To my knowledge, finding the dozens of them that exist maybe gives you an achievement. Unfortunately there are so many of them that hunting them all down is way more than I'm willing to do. Such a waste of a good idea.
So the game is fatally flawed, but if you approach it with the right expectations, you can still have a lot of fun with it. The puzzles are good and challenging, and the game does a decent job of giving you the tools you need to solve them, albeit in a way that sometimes requires you to walk away from puzzles until you get the information you need. This aspect of the game is the
, however. The game really wants to be artistic, but it's terribly misguided in its execution. Do not buy this game for a story, as you won't get any here.

The Witness is an open world puzzle game. Weird combination, huh?
That concept actually works rather well. You work on a puzzle for a while, can't figure it out, and instead just move on to another part of the island. This solves the everlasting puzzle game problem of not even wanting to start it up if you're stuck.
The (many!) puzzles are singular screens which have you drawing a line across a grid. A very basic concept. And with that very basic concept The Witness does absolutely everything it possibly could. It will introduce lots of new rules, need you to take the surroundings of the puzzle into account and even have you taking notes in real life.
"Then why are people complaining that the puzzles are too similar?" you ask. Well, that kind of line puzzle is all there is. The Witness really needs to be praised for how much it does with the limitations it set itself but it never answers the question why it limited itself so much in the first place.
The island is huge and even 5 or 6 hours into the game you will still find yourself running into new places you haven't seen before. And not because you just unlocked them, it just actually has that much content.
Content made out of puzzles that is, this game really is for the absolute puzzle game buff who wants nothing else out of it.
It also likes having some big fps drops and on some graphics cards it gets occasional random crashes but it's biggest downside remains its price! I don't feel like paying 37€ for a collection of puzzles and a pretty island (did i mention this is one of the prettiest games i've seen in a long time?) to walk around on is worth it.
I do however recommend buying it if you're really into puzzle games AND you can get it while it's on sale.

Dofus, Wakfu's older sibling. I would say Dofus is a lot like Wakfu, but unlike Wakfu, its older and has more content. I strongly recommend any Wakfu fan try out Dofus, or any MMO or RPG fan give Dofus a try one way or another.
Also be sure to check out Wakfu while you are at it.

DISCLAIMER: I've re-written this several times, unhappy with each. I have decided to stop doing that and just write how I feel instead of sounding professional.
As someone who found Dofus when it was first in beta, I feel almost ashamed to admit I've been playing this game as long as I have. In fact, It might be for the best that it's only now reaching steam, as I fear seeing the hours I've poured into this game might be traumatizing. Heck, the hours I might pour into this game AFTER this point intimidate me..... but alas, there's a reason I have stuck around as long as I have. THIS. GAME. IS. AMAZING. Why? because I said so! Okay, I'll be a bit more specific....
Appearance - I start here, because I frankly see little reason to go over it. You see the top of the page, you saw the trailer (granted it's a mishmash of the movie and the game, well done, nonetheless). And it's the thing that will catch people's attention. I, for one, LOVE the artstyle and direction Ankama has chosen to go, but something I should mention. It looks cartooney, and childish, don't let that throw you off, this game is VERY much aimed at young adults and adults. It might be a bit too complex for young children, and the dialogue and....ahem...references... assume a respectable level of maturity. That is to say, there is adult humor all over the place (think condom sword, and rabbits vandalizing fox(tanouki) statues by placing a giant wooden log between their legs...) so don't be afraid. Also note this game isn't just a ton of sex humor, Ankama is pretty classy, after all.
Gameplay - The main reason you'll get sucked in...or turned off. Dofus is a turn based strategy MMORPG, which I can understand some people not enjoying, I do. The game is very skill intensive, almost no reflexes needed. There are currently 17 classes to chose from, and I can tell you, don't bother asking what the "best" anything is. There is no "best" character, "best" build, "best" equipment or the likes. Ankama has done a marvelous job at keeping the classes ballanced. Speaking of the classes, the 17 classes all play VERY differently, leading many people to play multiple (oh yeah, multiclienting is a thing, and is supported in this game. That is both good and bad, depending who you ask). If you're just starting out, don't worry about playing multiple characters, it's not necessary to succeed, just keep in mind someone using 6 accounts will progress faster than someone using 1 or 2.
Uniqueness - The only thing even remotely comparable to Dofus is Wakfu, which is almost a sequel to Dofus, and is the same company. There's nothing even remotely comparable in the MMORPG market. If you've ever played Final Fantasy Tactics, or a similar game, you should catch on pretty quickly.
Accessability - The game is flash based, making it so it's not particularly taxing on even weak computers. After major updates, the game can be a little less comparable (such as the recent interface changes) but even with a mid-range laptop with integrated graphics, I had little issue playing several accounts at once. I also run on a poor net connection (I'm talking average ~200-250 ping, with spikes regularly) and it causes little trouble for me. There is a respectable free-to-play area that anyone can try out to find out if they like it before paying a penny. The game is also multi platform, working on mac and I believe still linux. The learning curve can be steep, and the initial game overwhelming, but that can't be helped with something as unique as this.
Management - Ankama as a company is one of the companies I respect the most. They have been phenominal at maintaining ballance between the classes, They are good at storytelling (granted they could use some work in the presentation in game...) and their use of the cash shop (Also known as the Ogrine Market, their cash currency) has been great. The items you can buy on the cash shop are almost entirely cosmetic, with a couple minor convienances. Also you can buy the currency with in-game money, as is the case with many games, and it's pretty reasonable to do so, and you can also use the method to subscribe characters. Customer support is famously aweful, by american standards, but when you look at it with the realization that the company is french, where customer support is a totally different perception, it's actually not bad. Izmar (the community manager) is also incredibly helpful and friendly, and very good at making sure things are running smoothly (she deserves a big raise!)
Longevity - I've been playing it for well over a decade..... I think that's enough said. I admit I am not a crazy hardcore player, but there's still plenty I haven't done and still want to do.
Customization - Character customization is a weak point here. Hats and cloaks are the only displayed equipment, you can chose colors of your character by picking 5 predetermined areas and coloring those to your liking, and you can chose between m/f and 8 different faces. Otherwise there's not a ton of options. The interface has recently gone through an overhaul and you are now able to move interfaces around to your liking, but even that could use a little more freedom.
Social - The guild system is O.K., the alliance system is interesting, and multiclienting people can play on their own no problem. With that said, You will meet some interesting people in this game, there are plenty of chat channels you can access, and the community is generally pretty friendly. In PvP obviously there is drama and hostility, but it's nothing comparable to what you'd find in arena games.
Bang for your buck - The game is relatively cheap for a subscription game, and the cash shop is nothing near necessary to keep up (in fact, you CANT realistically keep up with other people just by dumping cash into the game), and you can subscribe with in-game currency at a rate that is normally relatively decent. I would advise avoiding trying to use in-game currency for your first month or 3, but after that is when alot of people are able to transfer over, not that supporting ankama is bad by any stretch, and paying with real money makes the game less stressful, as you don't have to worry about upkeeping subscription.
Footnotes - Note that this game is oldschool. Level 200 (max) isn't when the game starts (or ends, for that matter), so you don't need to rush to high level. There is a huge amount of content. The official forums and subreddit are also great resources for newcomers, and those may help you avoid being overwhelmed. If you're into solo play, awesome, but keep in mind this game is designed for team content, and high level content will require you to team up at least some, or a ton if you find yourself questing.
