I begrudgingly choose not to recommend The Witness despite some excellent puzzle design because I feel that the majority of gamers (myself included) will not have the patience, stamina or desire to complete the grueling puzzles in this game with no reward other than a feeling of accomplishment for figuring out the solution. I completed the game only out of pride and curiosity to see if there was any kind of big reveal at the end. I was disappointed.
Ultimately, whether or not you will like this game depends on your philosophy about what a video game should be. If you haven't watched the Youtube video titled Jonathan Blow: How Mainstream Devs Are Getting It Wrong, I suggest you watch it before dropping $40 on this game. Blow is the lead developer for The Witness and Braid, and his philosophy about games is that they shouldn't be designed to be fun. Rather they should be designed to instill a particular emotion in the player. He also detests hand-holding by the developers, opting for an approach where the game lets players discover everything on their own. These principles are on full display in The Witness. Much of the game is not fun. It is often brainwracking and frustrating. The emotion he wants you to experience through this process is that "eureka!" moment from discovering everything all on your own. For some, that experience might justify the price.
However, I disagree with Blow. I understand his desire to use video games as an artistic form of expression, but ultimately when I play a game that has over 600 puzzles and easily over 20 hours of gameplay, I want it to be a fun experience. I contrast his philosophy on game design with Sid Meier's. Meier would take an interesting concept and attempt to develop it into a workable game. He would have testers play the game over and over, making changes each time, based on player feedback, until it was fun. If he could not make it fun for the majority of people, he would scrap the game. Jonathan Blow doesn't do this. Fun wasn't a design consideration in the Witness. Therefore, he decided not to incorporate anything into the game that might distract from his themes of exploration and discovery, despite the possibility of making the game more enjoyable for the majority of people. So what we have in the end is Blow's vision of what he wants the game to be, as uncontaminated by player opinions as possible.
It's too bad because if these well conceived puzzles and pretty open world were incorporated into a suspenseful plot where details were revealed after solving each area, I would have really liked this game. Sadly, there is no plot here, and for the majority of people the puzzles alone probably aren't rewarding enough to motivate you to slog through it without resorting to guides on the internet. Thus, I only recommend The Witness for those who just really enjoy puzzles or who are willing to play a game despite it not being an enjoyable experience much of the time.
If you do decide to get this game, take my advice: savor it slowly. The puzzles are much more enjoyable if you do them a few at a time, rather than binge-puzzling through entire areas. If you get stuck on a puzzle, minimize frustration by taking a break from the game or exploring somewhere else for a while. And the puzzles in the ending area are the worst in the game. They are all either extremely difficult puzzles, or they are easy but unoriginal, tedious, and annoying.
Pros: Experience of discovery and exploration, beautiful scenery, clever puzzle design.
Cons: Hours of frustration, no plot to discover, ending puzzles are terrible, and the ending itself isn't great either.
EDIT 3/10/2016: Many people didn't think I clearly stated my personal opinion, so "(myself included)" was added to the first paragraph to make it clear that my overall experience with the game was negative. I also clarified a bit in the paragraph which contrasts Sid Meier and Jonathan Blow's design process.

I bought this game because of Braid, and how beautiful it is in the trailer videos. Now that I've played it myself it totally exceeded my expectations, and now that I've beaten it, and with the rising amount of negative reviews on top about this game I feel like I have a responsibility to speak up positively.
First of all this is totally not a game for everyone, this is for those who loves to just chill and explore, this is for those who want a game that respects their intelligence. This game does a different take on many things. One of it is obviously not spoon-feeding the player about many things. I hate those games where they just bombard you with texts, or dialogues and all just to teach you every bits of what you can do in the game. Those kind of games are an example of bad game design. I mean looking way back we got Mario, did it teach you the mechanics through texts? No, instead it taught you by experience.
Moving on some other side, The Witness really focused on the gameplay side with a little glimpse to its narrative, that glimpse giving the player hints so it can interpret things on its own. Regarding the gameplay side it totally rocks! The puzzles are brilliant that you'll even think about how Jonathan Blow came up with it. I can't comment much on the narrative side because I was so into the world, and the puzzles instead. I'll probably focus on them on my next run.
Commenting on those people who did not recommend this game because "there are no rewards but puzzles", dude I just want to say that this is a "puzzle" game for a reason. The real reward behind this game are those "aha!" moments when you solve a puzzle that you've had a hard time with. There were also saying that the narrative is "un-insteresting", the game is dull. Yeah maybe it's "un-interesting" because the game doesn't present it to you by explosions, slow-mo epic moments and stuff, but it gets interesting when you dig deeper beyond the audio logs, the island, and what you do in it. Well at least for me it's interesting because it's a really clever ending.
Anyhow I just also want to point out the game content-wise. Is the $40 price tag worth it? YES! I've beat the game, I got 38.9 hrs as of the moment, and there are alot of areas that I haven't gone into yet! (I've solved around 450+ puzzles I think with around 30 secrets). For me I would even buy this game at $60. It's just that worth it for a puzzle maniac like me.
TL;DR version: The game is totally not for everyone, but if you're that kind of person who loves games that pushes their brain to its limits then this is totally for you. Content-wise, it has a lot in it. You just gotta dig deeper.

For a game that originally began as a mod for Unreal Tournament III, The Ball is a pleasant little distraction from the usual fare of first-person action titles.  I’m reticent to even call it a first-person shooter, even though it’s won awards as such, as it’s much more of a puzzle-solving game, and players receive exactly one weapon throughout the game.  This weapon, which looks and functions like an Aztec-skinned rip of Half Life 2’s gravity gun, provides players with a means of interacting with the eponymous Ball, which remains their primary tool throughout the game.  However, both Ball and control gun are disappointingly bereft of any ominous names.  For shame, Tripwire.
As a 1940’s paleontologist working a presumably remote dig site in the deserts of Mexico, The Ball quite literally drops players into a winding cave system lined with cryptic, ancient ruins. Quickly discovering The Ball and its control device, something draws the player ever deeper into a dangerous labyrinth of trap-laden, zombie-infested ruins.  Is it an insatiable curiosity, ancient mind control, or just a rail-roaded plot? I don’t know, it’s never really explained, but the puzzles players are led to are cleverly designed, visually appealing, and genuinely entertaining to solve, so a flimsy narrative is somewhat forgivable.
Hearkening to the addictive, puzzle-solving gameplay of Portal, The Ball was actually released just prior to Portal 2’s debut, and the influences are genuine and very much intended, even going so far as including a cross-over stage in The Ball’s challenge levels.  Trouble is, with just one means of solving The Ball’s puzzles, they do get a bit stale and predictable after a few levels.  Different environments allow The Ball to perform many more functions than simply rolling around like something out of Indiana Jones’ nightmares, but most of these functions are short-lived, and don’t feel like their true potential was fully explored, especially regarding the layering of multiple special functions at once.
Combat is another of the game’s shortcomings, as it largely consists of just  repeatedly blasting and retracting The Ball back and forth like some skull-embossed yo-yo from hell.  Boss battles and blinged-out Aztec zombie waves alike (Did I mention there are lots of zombies?) suffer from this repetitious bore, which is quite a shame, considering that one of those bosses happens to be a giant, zombified King Kong.  No, I am not kidding.
At the end of the day, The Ball is a fun little niche title, and to its credit, it never really feels like it’s trying to do more than it can.  What it sets out to do, it accomplishes, and does it well.  It may only last players a day or two, but for just ten bucks on Steam at the time of this writing, I’d say those are days well spent.

Similar to an actual zombie apocalypse, your plan should be to avoid the undead unless you absolutely HAVE to engage. You can throw a wide variety of furniture depending how swole your current character is, which makes you want to prioritize the big guy over the dork when it comes to the nitty gritty. You may ask yourself, "What do the Blazblue series even have?"
Well.. Buckle up cowboy 'cause it's about to get rowdy up in here.
Characters:
Want to be an edgelord? We got that.
Want to be a character that requires no absolute skill? We got that.
Want to control a machine who's actually your sister? We got that.
Want to be a cat? We got that.
How about a cat that fights with machines? We got that.
How about a cat with a sword? DLC.
Want to fight as your waifu? Wrong game but hey, whatever floats your boat.
How about a little magical girl who's actually two different humans in one body whose that body is actually occupied by a different women? I'm not even lying. We got that.
Music:
Ever heard a violin mixed with electric guitar?
No?
Trust me. It's good.
OST in Blazblue?
Stands for "Oh Sh*t, Time (to get hyped from the sick fire from this game)."
Gameplay:
You can learn to do combos from the move list which requires tons of practice.
But even Arc System Works knows that none of you are gonna spend more than 10 minutes playing one character which is why they have a Stylish option that plays the game for you! With a press of a button, with spamming that button after hitting, you can do these sick combos that do tons of damage.
Community:
They're really nice actually. You can meet people who use Stylish playstyle and have a battle on who makes the most mistakes. Or you could meet a Naoto main that completely bodies your face into the ground. But hey, practice makes perfect.
Story:
Hey, at least it's a better love story than Twilight. It's not the end of the series so don't be too down. Not gonna spoil anything except that Ragna's hair is white. It's straight to the point and honestly, I liked it way too much.
Modes:
You got your arcade mode where you will most likely put the game on Easy as you body through every single bot you meet. And sometimes you'll somehow get this scary jumpscare at the credits where you meet a CPU that will completely show you that you're sh*t at the game. But hey, 10/10.
You got this RPG thing that no one plays, but it's fun to check out.
Time attack = break keyboard/controller.
Extras:
Dude. This game has its own fan fiction and fan service. I don't think I need to say anything else about that.
Conclusion:
It's a really good game but the price is fairly high. I would recommend getting it whilst it is on sale. Sure you might find a flaw but finding a Naoto main that can 100% your main is completely normal.
10/10.

I normally write my reviews a bit differently and make them look more professional, however I'm not going to for this game as I couldn't really play it and here's why:
Why I can't play this and can't recommend it:
♦ No real graphics/resolution options (Launched the game and it didn't fit my screen, read you could change the resoltuin on the forums by opening a .cs file and editing it slightly. However, this meant that the map and menus were slightly off and made things look smaller)
♦ Alt+Tabbing after changing the resolution in the .cs caused them to be messed up (I say this as when you re-opened the game aft Alt+Tabbing, the game would be slightly off the screen and you'd have to close it and re-open it to get the game back on screen and be playable again)
♦ Can't change controls (This is annoying as pressing shift caused TNT to be thrown and since shift is how you open up the Steam Overlay... it gets annoying really fast)
♦ Levels seem to disappear and be replaced with new ones if you reload your save or die (This is one game related aspect I found weird in the time I did play. I find this annoying as I would have assumed you could finish the levels you already had, not get random new ones each time you loaded your save or died. Don't get me wrong, having unlimited levels seems good but planning the level order you want to do only to get new ones everytime you load is really annoying)
Overall, I know the game is made in 2009 and it seemed fun from what I played. It's a shame it's not optomised graphically to run at later resolutions and doesn't seem like it ever will be. However, if you can get around the graphical issues, I would recommend picking this up as it seems like a fun little top down shooter with some randomness to it as each level has something different about it.

I've played Warhammer themed games for years, more for the play style (as I love turn based tactical games) and never really got into the lore. When I first got Space Hulk: Ascension I was turned off by what I saw as overuse of narrow hallways and tiny rooms. I like to be able to move my units around more. Plus the campaign I was playing was very similar to the one from Space Hulk. So it sat unplayed for a long while.
Recently I've actually started learning more about the Warhammer 40k lore and revisiting some games in my library. This time trying Space Hulk: Ascension I'm able to get into it much more and have nearly completed the first campaign. And I'm amped to play the other campaigns and thinking about the DLCs too.
Pros:
It is a fun squad level turn based tactical game. The units seem limited and putzy at first, but once they start developing they do become the death machines you think they should be. Punching genestealers for melee sucks, but once you start getting claws and chainswords you really start mowing them down.
I love the graphics, especially the camera view in the upper right that shows a 1st person view from the selected unit's point of view. I loved that in Space Hulk too and was a selling point for me when I first bought SH:A. My only complaint with it is that it goes by so fast during the genestealer's turns that you miss all the action on that camera. Too bad mission video footage can't be recorded in game for later viewing.
I like the animations for the melee attacks. :)
Cons:
Well, lots of narrow hallways and small rooms instead of big battlefields, but that's the nature of a space hulk and just my own preference issue.
Other than that the only con I have with the game is that it doesn't have the multiplayer that Space Hulk had. Most of the hours I logged on Space Hulk were multiplayer rather than the campaign missions.

I've never played Space Hulk before, but I like the W40k universe. Unfortunately I can't say the same for this game. Now I'm not going to critique any gameplay since I don't know much of how Space Hulk is supposed to play, but I absolutely hate the UI. First, things are so dark and hard to see and I often have to strain my eyes just to see that I'm clicking on the right grid square. Second, I can't count how many times I've wasted AP and lost Terminators having them face in the wrong direction. Maybe make the direction arrow a bit bigger and more obvious? Because sometimes, I don't know if it's due to the intense lagginess I'm pretty sure I select one direction and a terminator will choose the adjacent one. It's so frustrating. I want to blame the sheer business of the interface and having incredibly tiny icons just below your selected unit.
I guess Space Hulk fans would put up with it, but approaching it as a first time player it's incredibly discouraging. Not the game's difficulty, but the eye straining UI and clumsy interface.

I don't recommend this title because of some design flaws;
It is based on the boardgame and should be better. The aesthetic is decent and the flavour, however you can't reverse movements if you make a mistake.
This is critical because the game often comes down to careful use of pre-existing action points to manage your squad. A mistake is insta-death a lot of the time once the Genestealers get up close.
Like a lot of conversions to computer games from board games, the random dice roll type element is enjoyable in a tabletop context but got tedious for me quickly, once my squad got wiped when I was 90% through a laborious mission.

I recommend the game mainly because I think that it delivers on what it is supposed to be.  It brings back memories of earlier strategy games and can be difficult.  Not be very familiar with the warhammer games, here is what I think could have been improved as a video game when compared to other stratey games.
1. Squad make up - you can't do much customization on the squad.  You get a sargent or templar, a heavy and 3 soldiers.  It would be nice to have a little more customization and flexibility.
2. Squad equipment - each squad member has set equipment.  Coupled with the fixed squad make up, it lacks the ability to allow you to customize the individuals in the group.  You get more options as you advance, but not enough to really differentiate the characters.
3. Maps - all of the maps take place on the space hulk ships.  So they are all cooridoors with small rooms.  It lacks a little variety.  It would be nice to have high / low areas, open areas, cover, etc.
4. Grid - the map is built as squares so there are only 4 directions.  This works because of the map layouts, but lack some of the flexibility that hex based map systems provide.

My only gripe is that no one seems to play online compared to other FPS games. I might recommend making this game free-to-play to bring in more players, but that could cheapen the quality of this game. I'm hoping with the recent release of DOOM that arena shooters such as TOXIKK get more popular.
Overall, this game is quite good for Early Access and I'm quite excited to see where the game goes from here.

This game provides a terrifying realisation that soldiers are not the only ones that experience the hells of war. You play as a small group of 3 survivors hiding in a bombed out house, and during the day you use these characters to rebuild the house (If you have the materials) or make food (Ifyou have food) or collect water (if you can) and do other important tasks. This is where the bulk of the actual story and what sold the game for me was. you see the horrors and brutality of war and what people will do to survive. and you find out a lot about yourself as a person as well. do I risk my life in ordder to defend a woman about to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by a drunk soldier? do i rob from the homeless encampment? do i help another group of survivors extract their friends from their bombed out shelter? Do i open the door of my shelter and take the chance of it being a raider or someone looking to trade?
so far i have made it almost 2 weeks in the game with all of my companions still alive. though there is no end in sight i am hopefull for the future... All-in-All this might be one of my most favorite games of all time, and i would highly recommend it to anybody, any gamer, and have them experience This War of Mine

The first thing I want to say about Gigantic is that it's visually spectacular. Character design, effects, and environments are a joy to behold. Character animations are slick and original, from the zippy attacks of Mozu to the visible heft in the lumbering Margrave. And I love the looks of the various creatures that players can summon.
Gameplay is quite smooth over all. Slight delays in some areas, but few games have such intuitive, satisfying and fluid movement abilities (e.g. Wu's leap, Tyto's dive, Tripp's slide). Unfortunately, character collision, especially with guardians, can be jarring.
Importantly, Motiga's take on the MOBA is a breath of fresh air - guardians, power, summoned creatures and rampaging are a creative blend of features that make Gigantic a stand-out title.
Adapting your hero with meaningful ability choices over the course of a match and feeling the benefits as you play is rewarding. Playing a different character feels almost like playing a different game - there's no shortage of meaningful mechanical differences between characters.
Sound is mostly good. The punchy sound effects and gripping orchestral soundtrack could scarcely be better. Voice-acting for guardians is terrific (approach the hostile Gren and hear his ~deeply arousing~ "I will destroy you"), but character voice performances are hit-and-miss.
There's one thing that, while not a major issue, got to me in particular.
The disparity in quality between the writing of some characters' voice lines and the character designs is puzzling. Motiga have done an excellent job of avoiding the tiresome pitfalls of visual character design present in so many MOBA titles - the typical 'brawny armoured sword guy' is absent, as is the exhausted trope of 'scantily-clad female assassin' - and have given us a line-up of visually unique, interesting and original-looking characters, but the voices fail to answer the questions that the intriguing designs raise (consider DotA2 - characters' personalities are present in nearly all of their lines).
Above all, though, Gigantic is a game that its development team clearly loves. They continued working even when the studio was temporarily broke, pre-release. Their passion really shines through in all the things that make Gigantic unique.

Spore. There are so many feelings related to this word. Galactic adventrures. These two words have been literally taking whole days of my life since I was only 10 y.o.
I remember how I was making huge Adventures, building insane empires and just taking all the Milky Way over. Spore is a kind of a game which you always find something new in. You never get tired of it, cause every day playing it you keep saying "Woow, how didn't I know that!?" over and over again. Also, because of Shooters and this stuff I have become very nervous through the time, but I have NEVER raged because of Spore. It's so magnificent that you just don't have time for butthurting! Highly recommended for relaxing.
About the game itself. Some people might find first stages uninteresting, for sure, "They are boring" - they say. But believe or not, every stage should be counted as a different game, and all 5 games are connected. Look: Cell stage - sth Agar.io(ish), Creature stage - Classic open-world RPG, Tribe and Civilization stages - Tactical Strategy, Space stage - doesn't even need to be said.
"Okey, this game looks like a mix of others, so what?". Noo, you are completely mistaken, Spore just contains everything, Maxis have put so so much stuff into a 5 GB  game, so anyone could find something interesting for them.
"Deym, what if I don't wanna make a ♥♥♥♥♥ in Creature stage like everybody does, what do I do then?". Here we meet the Redactor. Tons and tons of parts you can aquire, resize, move, replace, spin, color - do anything with anything! The only thing that may stop you is your own imagination. The farther you get - the more creativity you can show! Creatures, buildings, boats, cars, planes, even spaceships - create your own with these *pulls off a bag of parts*.
"Oh, I am gonna get tired of all this very soon, what will make me play this years and years?". The game is full of hidden(and not so) jokes. Spore makes fun out of every problem of nowadays. Religion, wars, racism, sexism(no women at all) etc. Spore touched each feeling and showed it without hurting. Ye, of course, it was made for 12+ kids but who ever gave it a spark? Kids play it because it's interesting to create stuff and explore the galaxy, teens play it because they are looking for their place in this world and Spore really helps with that, really. Adults, though, are the grown up kids, kek.
Galactic Adventures DLC(can I call it DLC?) is like another game in addition to what I've said upper but squared. Here you get even more space to make ANY-DAМN-THING! Just take planet(one of 52 different types), and change it the way you want, you can even decide, where each tree will be! Create seas, rivers, volcanos and stuff like that - all you need is there. On the other hand, you have all redactors in front of you - come and take! Created a new animal? Put some badаss devices on it - let it shoot rockets or summon bees. Got creatures that you needed? Now you can even adjust their character, moving, damage, health, even the phrases if necessary! Make your own planet with its own storyline, share it with friends, dude it's so undescribeable, that you just need to see it yourself.
In conclusion(I have only said about the most massive features, there are a lot more), if you want a game which you will wanna play more and more day after day, Spore is definitely one of them! You just have to have it in your library, I promise, you won't regret this. 11/12 just cuz the game is very old and if there was a rebirth of Spore, I personally would want kids from it :-)
Go ahead mate, buy it!

The Ball is a first person action-adventure game featuring a full single-player experience built on Epic’s Unreal™ Engine 3 technology. As a swashbuckling archaeologist working on the slopes of a dormant volcano somewhere in Mexico, you get stuck in a cavern. It doesn’t take long before you realize this is more than just a cave. You reveal ancient ruins that have been hidden from outsiders for centuries and discover a mysterious artifact, a gold and metal shelled Ball. As you progress towards solving the mystery of this amazing place you must unlock the secrets of the Ball and learn to control this ancient artifact. Venturing deeper into the volcano, you reveal some of mankind’s greatest secrets and you will start to encounter not just puzzles and traps, but also various strange creatures – the guardians of this mystery. These creatures have to be overcome, using only the Ball to defend you.

The Ball is a beautiful 3D environmental physics puzzler. That means: fiddle with stuff until you solve a puzzle. Then walk a ways, and get a new puzzle. Repeat. Think 'Portal', but without the sense of humor.
You've got a giant metal ball and a magnetic gun at your disposal, that only controls the ball. With this one mechanic, you face a series of increasingly-complicated obstacles. Also: undead zombies and mummies.
The Ball is creative and well-made, but I grew tired of the repetitive gameplay more quickly than I expected to.
However, if you see The Ball on sale, the fun of plowing over zombies with a giant metal ball is defintely worth the price of admission.  You throw the ball, kill a few, then kill a few more on the rebound. It's a unique form of combat, and always good for a laugh.

I'm a big fan of "twin stick" shooters, as I like the constant action and the need for good aiming and resource management. Larva Mortus, with its included mix of RPG and survival horror elements, is a decent addition to the genre but it does have its noticeable flaws, likely due to a low budget. So let's get the bad out of the way first.
The overhead graphics are passable, with some nice details on the walls like paintings and spider webs to add to the atmosphere of the creepy locales you'll be visiting. The particle effects of poison clouds and blood splatters look nice too. But the overall presentation here feels very flat. Enemies can hardly be discerned apart from each other, especially when they form close-proximity groups, due to the lack of visual variety among them. I'm not just talking palette swaps either, alot of the enemis tend to move the same, too. Add to this that the colors are dull and lack contrast and the whole thing just looks kinda "meh". I don't mind lesser budget graphics until they become an inconvenience, and Larva Mortus visuals tend to strain my eyes. Trying to pick apart foe from victim, when you're on rescue missions, for instance. Yeah, there's a glow around the survivors, but it is weak. There is too much going onscreen at once for such a flat look to inform you.
On the other hand, the story level, visual novel style cutscenes are rendered beautifully, and even slightly animated. I wish the rest of the game lookes as slick.
The game also suffers from level design due to waht seems to be randomization. Though there is a difficulty rank visible before choosing any mission, I've found they don't seem to really matter as levels just feel cobbled together from a random pool. You can die on easy levels too if you're in an unfortunate enough circumstance, such as enemies being RIGHT THERE when you come through a new door. If they swarm you fast enough and there are crates or coffins in your path of escape, good luck, my friend. It is really frustrating to have an otherwise good run through a level, only to reach one of the last rooms and have that happen. Because it feels cheap. This is of course especially bad if the randomizer throws a way-too-small of a room at you.
Finally, some aspects of the sound design really bother me. The shotgun sounds like a pea-shooter and the growls from the enemies grow really repetitive especially when they do so in unison. When items are picked up from the playfield, it cna be extremely hard to tell you did so, at least audibly. Some sounds are way too quiet, others way too loud. At least the music is nice enough.
Flaws aside, it can still be very rewarding to clear a room with death constnatly breathing down your neck (if you die, you just have to restart the level, although I believe you keep your experience and items from that round). And there's a solid arsenal at your disposal, from double pistols, to silver-tipped crossbows, each serving their respective purpose against the expansive bestiary.
As the player survives more and more rooms, he accrues eperience that he can spend at anytime on the skill menu. However, other than speed, it's difficult to feel much growth in the early going (read: slow progression). I would have liked to see more interesting bonuses and character specialization, but again, I understand there wasn't much of a budget here.
All in all, if you're a fan of the genre, then for the price, Larva Mortus should be a welcome addition. The action can be hectic and the pacing eggs you on just enough to say, "one more round". Just be wary that you are getting what you pay for.
FINAL VERDICT:
7/10

This was initially a negative review. In hindsight, I later changed it to positive.
The Witness is definitely a game that you'll either love or hate. For me, it was a love-hate-love-hate journey.
When it started, I was captured by the environment, the design, the colors. The puzzles looked smooth and fascinating. Everything was mysterious, and the promise of a hidden narrative pushed me onward. That was love.
After a while, I realized that the promised narrative (and I say promised because the Steam's misleading description clearly promises it, by stating "You don't remember who you are, [..] but there's one thing you can do: explore the island in hope of discovering clues, regaining your memory, and somehow finding your way home") is a failed promise. There is no narrative here, other than what you might imagine by yourself, as if looking at a stone cold sculpture. Solving puzzles has almost no consequence. Many little things I didn't care about before (like some puzzles requiring millimetrical positioning in the world, but the engine not supporting analog joystick movement) began to annoy me. That was hate.
I moved on. I decided to ignore the missing narrative, to try and just enjoy the puzzles, and the dedication with which the island was crafted. It worked. There is so much richness in The Witness' island, and so many relations between elements. Like that one statue which, if looked from the right perspective, wants to hold hands with a farther one. It's like a beautiful alien mechanism that pushes you to find its deeper connections (only later I realized those connections weren't really meaningful and mostly random, which can still be a beautiful thing but, you know, it depends). That was love again.
Finally, I reached the last part of the game. And the puzzles (and the misleading narrative) decided to troll me more evidently. Instead of implementing new ideas, they used dirty tricks like flashing lights and colors and glitchy monitors. They were trying to hurt me, physically. To solve one batch I ended up nauseous. To solve another my vision became blurry for a while. And mind you, these puzzles are not skippable: you HAVE to hurt yourself to go on. Every game developer knows you don't do flashing lights and colors, because on a wide range of people they can have really bad effects, and the eyes are a delicate thing. That was hate, again.
Then there was the ending(s). I won't say anything about it to avoid spoilers, but let's just say that, when I connected the dots, I realized that The Witness is just a big FU to players, possibly to humanity. Its anti-philosophical philosophy sways from intellectual frigidity to adolescent depth, from incoherent nihilism to detached positivism, and is overall like a Möbius strip, rolling over itself without anywhere else to go. The Witness didn't have anything to say, other than that it hated me.
I never wrote a negative Steam review (other than for the horrible Godus), and I thought I'd write this while still recommending the game. Because, as I mentioned, the island is beautiful, and most puzzles really cool. But then I thought about it more. Yes, I did love part of this, but at this price (please note, I was initially a big supporter of its high price), I can't recommend a game that hates you, and cheats you into believing there's a narrative which is not there. So. My two cents.
It's been a few days now, and I decided to change my review to positive (while leaving my previous words untouched). When I initially finished The Witness, I was angry and very annoyed. In hindsight though, the game's merits feel bigger than its demerits. Sure, I still believe it's a carefully and beautifully crafted empty shell (I'm not really sure if it wanted to be more but couldn't, or if it decided to embrace/show its own limits with frustrated anger) with an overall FU message, but it has a lot of potential, and I hope it will pave the way for better games, both as a culture and as a media. Also, as I mentioned in the review, most puzzles, even if inconsequential, are really good. They have a great learning curve, are well connected to each other, and never feel frustrating (except the "I want to physically hurt you" ones towards the end).
So. The Witness is, in my humble opinion, a glorious puzzle game on possibly the most beautiful virtual island I ever saw. Other than that, even if it fails at being more, it still shows such potential that it's a game you should play, to see it for yourself.

I begrudgingly choose not to recommend The Witness despite some excellent puzzle design because I feel that the majority of gamers (myself included) will not have the patience, stamina or desire to complete the grueling puzzles in this game with no reward other than a feeling of accomplishment for figuring out the solution. I completed the game only out of pride and curiosity to see if there was any kind of big reveal at the end. I was disappointed.
Ultimately, whether or not you will like this game depends on your philosophy about what a video game should be. If you haven't watched the Youtube video titled Jonathan Blow: How Mainstream Devs Are Getting It Wrong, I suggest you watch it before dropping $40 on this game. Blow is the lead developer for The Witness and Braid, and his philosophy about games is that they shouldn't be designed to be fun. Rather they should be designed to instill a particular emotion in the player. He also detests hand-holding by the developers, opting for an approach where the game lets players discover everything on their own. These principles are on full display in The Witness. Much of the game is not fun. It is often brainwracking and frustrating. The emotion he wants you to experience through this process is that "eureka!" moment from discovering everything all on your own. For some, that experience might justify the price.
However, I disagree with Blow. I understand his desire to use video games as an artistic form of expression, but ultimately when I play a game that has over 600 puzzles and easily over 20 hours of gameplay, I want it to be a fun experience. I contrast his philosophy on game design with Sid Meier's. Meier would take an interesting concept and attempt to develop it into a workable game. He would have testers play the game over and over, making changes each time, based on player feedback, until it was fun. If he could not make it fun for the majority of people, he would scrap the game. Jonathan Blow doesn't do this. Fun wasn't a design consideration in the Witness. Therefore, he decided not to incorporate anything into the game that might distract from his themes of exploration and discovery, despite the possibility of making the game more enjoyable for the majority of people. So what we have in the end is Blow's vision of what he wants the game to be, as uncontaminated by player opinions as possible.
It's too bad because if these well conceived puzzles and pretty open world were incorporated into a suspenseful plot where details were revealed after solving each area, I would have really liked this game. Sadly, there is no plot here, and for the majority of people the puzzles alone probably aren't rewarding enough to motivate you to slog through it without resorting to guides on the internet. Thus, I only recommend The Witness for those who just really enjoy puzzles or who are willing to play a game despite it not being an enjoyable experience much of the time.
If you do decide to get this game, take my advice: savor it slowly. The puzzles are much more enjoyable if you do them a few at a time, rather than binge-puzzling through entire areas. If you get stuck on a puzzle, minimize frustration by taking a break from the game or exploring somewhere else for a while. And the puzzles in the ending area are the worst in the game. They are all either extremely difficult puzzles, or they are easy but unoriginal, tedious, and annoying.
Pros: Experience of discovery and exploration, beautiful scenery, clever puzzle design.
Cons: Hours of frustration, no plot to discover, ending puzzles are terrible, and the ending itself isn't great either.
EDIT 3/10/2016: Many people didn't think I clearly stated my personal opinion, so "(myself included)" was added to the first paragraph to make it clear that my overall experience with the game was negative. I also clarified a bit in the paragraph which contrasts Sid Meier and Jonathan Blow's design process.

I bought this game because of Braid, and how beautiful it is in the trailer videos. Now that I've played it myself it totally exceeded my expectations, and now that I've beaten it, and with the rising amount of negative reviews on top about this game I feel like I have a responsibility to speak up positively.
First of all this is totally not a game for everyone, this is for those who loves to just chill and explore, this is for those who want a game that respects their intelligence. This game does a different take on many things. One of it is obviously not spoon-feeding the player about many things. I hate those games where they just bombard you with texts, or dialogues and all just to teach you every bits of what you can do in the game. Those kind of games are an example of bad game design. I mean looking way back we got Mario, did it teach you the mechanics through texts? No, instead it taught you by experience.
Moving on some other side, The Witness really focused on the gameplay side with a little glimpse to its narrative, that glimpse giving the player hints so it can interpret things on its own. Regarding the gameplay side it totally rocks! The puzzles are brilliant that you'll even think about how Jonathan Blow came up with it. I can't comment much on the narrative side because I was so into the world, and the puzzles instead. I'll probably focus on them on my next run.
Commenting on those people who did not recommend this game because "there are no rewards but puzzles", dude I just want to say that this is a "puzzle" game for a reason. The real reward behind this game are those "aha!" moments when you solve a puzzle that you've had a hard time with. There were also saying that the narrative is "un-insteresting", the game is dull. Yeah maybe it's "un-interesting" because the game doesn't present it to you by explosions, slow-mo epic moments and stuff, but it gets interesting when you dig deeper beyond the audio logs, the island, and what you do in it. Well at least for me it's interesting because it's a really clever ending.
Anyhow I just also want to point out the game content-wise. Is the $40 price tag worth it? YES! I've beat the game, I got 38.9 hrs as of the moment, and there are alot of areas that I haven't gone into yet! (I've solved around 450+ puzzles I think with around 30 secrets). For me I would even buy this game at $60. It's just that worth it for a puzzle maniac like me.
TL;DR version: The game is totally not for everyone, but if you're that kind of person who loves games that pushes their brain to its limits then this is totally for you. Content-wise, it has a lot in it. You just gotta dig deeper.

Great fighting game.
Huge cast of characters with thirty six on the roster. They are very well designed and most play very different from one another.
There is a button called Drive for each character that is unique to that character making the game play different depending on who you pick. Some of these are simple things like a normal that life steals, and some or more complex like a move that charges or uses ammo or a normal that creates weak points making subsequent attacks stronger.
Also lots of universal mechanics like Barrier Block (Push Block), Counter Assault (Counter attack useable while blocking), Crush Trigger (Block breaking mechanic that stuns), air dashes, super jumps, and more! Check out
for info on the others.
If you're interested in it the story is also very good but requires either watching the previous games stories (it's a VN) or reading up on them. Blazblue Centralfiction is a very very unique fighting game. Going back to it's core gameplay BBCF has managed to make it's way back to EVO in the past year. Now I personally have been playing Blazblue since Calamity Trigger and I honestly have learned to play 2D fighters from Blazblue. This game has delivered some of the funnest gameplay I have ever experienced on a casual side and competitive side of gaming. However I can't recommend this game due to the looming net issues on the PC version.
Pros:
-Very wide veriaty characters. Each their own however small similarities allow you to try new characters without completely "starting over" with the fundamentals.
-Complex yet shallow. Complex enough that it is competitive however shallow enough that casual players can grasp all the mechanics and learn from them(even though many of them pick 1-2 things, usually DP and Exceed Accel, and utilize them). Each character has a level of depth that completely shys away from generic 2D fighters.
-Story mode does a fantastic job at finishing up the story and tying up holes(unlike some anime writers/game devs we all know). The action is fixed to the story so there is less actions however if you like visual novels the story fits in with abit of combat.
-Modes like Abyss mode are great for people who seek only a single player experience. There is even a section for pure information(sorry I forget what it's called v.v) incase you really want to dig into terms and story lore.
-Online Practice mode!
-Many balance improvements for CF that CP faultered over. Such as removal of Repeat Paration and stronger balance of damage.
Cons:
-Noticably horrid bad matchups and balance choice(yes I am refering to Bullet as bad balance as well as Bang).
-Netcoding related issues including: Region Locks(only can find rooms outside your region by being invited to them), finishing matches remove players from the room and put them back in resulting in a sprite position reset after every fight(sometimes resulting in players getting put in the main menuwithout any notification), HUGE and I mean HUGES hiccups and input delay as fights go on and my favorite, random infinite character select due to loss of connection to other player forcing 1 of the players to Alt+F4.
-When the game lags it stays at that input delay for the whole round. It can only get worse not better.
-Really high spec requirement compared to BBCP.
-Aggression of the game dropped greatly due to implimentation of more comeback mechanics. (Better OD punishment because damage nerfs hurt most characters non-OD damage alot, Exceed Accel is basically free 2k[4k if your have Active flow from blocking well, landing hits or doing mixup] and insane Overdrive refill rate from Active Flow letting players who turtle get a easier shot at the oppressor).
--Personal Con
-$8 DLC character is the long awaited Jubei. A character people have been asking for for 8-9years now. This is very expensive for just a character and in a game that is competitively played at EVO for money it's kind of a stab in the face to keep releasing extremely expensive characters. He's a great character and everyone should be able to play him. However ArkSYS will continue to hold out characters and sell them to players when Blazblue begins to die down.
---
Despite all the cons I would recommend it if it wasn't for the virtually unplayable netplay on PC. It used to be fine until BBCF2 update was released and now I can barely play any characters (my fault for maining Litchi and Subbing Haz though knowing they aren't lag friendly vs most characters). I will happily switch this to a recommended if they fix the netcode. The game is overall great. if you want a far more aggressive 2D fighter I would suggest Guilty Gear Xrd R2. It's made by the same company and if far more focused on reacting and aggression. However I don't have it on PC and can't tell you if that too has been poorly taken care of.

Just replayed this classic masterpiece some 15 years after my first run-through. And WOW does it hold up! A great old school adventure game of the point-and-click persuasion, with an amazing story, cool atmosphere and lengthy gameplay set in both a future bleak version of earth, as well as a magical fantasy alternative.
Unlike those extremely annoying old Sierra games where opening the wrong door, forgetting to pick up the red berry from the Evil Wizard's toilet 5 hours earlier, or just putting on the wrong pair of socks, will kill you instantly and set you back to your latest saved game where you'd still forgot to pick up the damned berry, TLJ encourages you to try everything. This game will never punish you for exploring, just like - for example - the original Monkey Island trilogy.
There were a couple of small but easily ignored graphical glitches on my Windows 8.1 rig, e.g. some characters walk around with slightly unmotivated see-through holes in their heads, but you don't play a game originally released in 1999 to dive into the realer-than-real pixelwork. This IS your parents' old adventure game. Also, if the Yes/No dialogue window turns out blank, kick it DOS style and just press 'y' for Yes. You'll be just fine.
Again: a classic adventure masterpiece. Highly recommended.

Far Cry 4 è un gioco che è come quello di Far Cry 3 in quanto offre molto da esplorare, ma al posto delle isole Rook in Far Cry 3, esplorerai una nazione vicino all'Himalaya conosciuta come Kyrat. Ha una forte somiglianza con la nazione vera e propria conosciuta come Nepal. Kyrat ha molte montagne ed è molto povero. Nonostante sia così povero diventa il tuo parco giochi perché c'è tanto da fare.
La narrazione inizia con Ajay Ghale, un Kyrati nato negli Stati Uniti. Tuttavia, il paese è governato da un dittatore denominato Pagan Min. Min ha una connessione con la famiglia Ghale e questo è reso noto nell'intro cutscene. Dopo che Min ti lascia da solo per un po ', sei libero di esplorare e cominciare a strappare le cose. C'è una guerra tra l'esercito reale di Min e i ribelli conosciuti come The Golden Path, che la madre di Ghale ha aiutato a trovare. Il sentiero d'oro è guidato da un uomo e una donna, ma ogni leader ha opinioni diverse su come abbattere il dittatore. La trama è spettacolare, mentre tu dimentichi che l'obiettivo di Ghale era quello di spargere le ceneri di sua madre. La stella più grande di questo gioco è Pagan Min, che suona vizioso e carismatico. Tuttavia, a volte sembra che la stella più grande del gioco sia Kyrat poiché incoraggia così tanto esplorazione e ha un sacco di casualità.
Mentre ci sono missioni di storia che esaltano la narrazione ci sono molte missioni laterali. Le missioni laterali familiari comprendono gli avamposti liberi in tutta la mappa, a partire da Kyrat meridionale. Il RPG come tigre e abilità di elefante. Le competenze della tigre sono aggressive e sono progettate per più potere e violenza. Queste abilità ti aiutano a togliere i nemici da dietro. Le abilità degli elefanti sono passivi e aiutarti a sopravvivere a diversi tipi di attacchi.
Le abilità che imparerai nel gioco saranno valide per tutto il tempo. Mentre cerchi di attivare una missione side-by-side, puoi essere attaccata dagli animali e dalle tue abilità. Kyrat è in agguato con la fauna selvatica come orsi, tigri, leopardi, elefanti, lupi tibetani, ecc. Alcuni animali sono predatori mentre altri non lo sono. Voi guardate 2 animali combattono alla morte, ma l'ultimo soggiorno cercherà di festeggiare su di te. Puoi anche lanciare strategicamente carne. Gli elefanti sono giganti pacifici, ma possono divertirsi una volta che si impara l'abilità necessaria per guidarli. È possibile utilizzare elefanti per rovesciare veicoli guidati dall'esercito reale. È possibile utilizzare un elefante per afferrare un soldato e lanciarlo nell'aria mentre urla.
La storia principale delle missioni e delle missioni laterali è non lineare, poiché ti consente di usare stealth o di utilizzare tutte le armi da fuoco. Puoi anche usare compagni per unirti alla tua avventura. La più grande aggiunta a questo gioco è il gancio di grappolo. Si può afferrare ganci sparsi in tutto il paese e anche oscillare da uno all'altro. L'aggiunta più grande del veicolo al gioco è il cicalino, noto anche come il girocattore. Il buzzer può portarsi da un punto A al punto B in modo rapido, ma ha un'altitudine limitata in modo da esplodere se si salta troppo in alto nell'aria. Mi sono trovato a dover affidarmi ai ganci afferrati per raggiungere l'altezza delle montagne, ma vale la pena esplorare ulteriormente per scoprire nuove posizioni, saccheggi e lettere nascoste.
La creazione è un'altra parte essenziale del gioco. L'uccisione degli animali è necessaria per farli scivolare in modo da poter portare più rupi o più munizioni di un certo tipo. Le rupie sono la valuta di Kyrat e saranno necessarie per l'acquisto di munizioni, nuove armi e siringhe. Ci sono molte erbe e fiori che puoi strappare con il tuo comodo coltello in modo da poter creare siringhe di guarigione e siringhe che possano fornire più protezione dagli attacchi.
L'arrampicata delle torri radio dovrebbe essere molto familiare per l'Assassin's Creed. La rimozione della nebbia consente di visualizzare meglio la mappa e di trovare ulteriori attività. Mentre si arrampica su una torre radio, è divertente e non è così. È una formula di Watch Cats e Assassin's Creed.
Oltre agli eventi collaterali, la serie Far Cry, ci sono missioni in Shangri-La che si sentono come un sogno. Si muove con un arco e una freccia con la tua tigre bianca e come sui demoni. Shangri-La offre una partenza dal mondo a Kyrat. Altre missioni laterali simili agli altri giochi Ubisoft includono la strappo di manifesti di propaganda da pareti sparse intorno a Kyrat.
La storia principale può essere turbata se muori. C'è solo uno slot di salvataggio per tutto il gioco. Credo che sarebbero state le slot migliori, ma è solo una minima perdita da me. Il gamepla FPS

Injustice 2 is an EXCELLENT fighting game. The mechanics are quite similar to Injustice: Gods Among Us but definetly have been improved. I like to think of Injustice 2 as an alternative updated version of Mortal Kombat X just with new additions. Speaking of that Injustice 2 does offer some new things such as, the gear system, a loot box system, (which is actually done really damn well) multiverses, and having the AI to play battles for you.
Starting off with the gear system. Throughout your time of playing Injustice 2, from your battles you will receive pieces of gear for each part of your character. Head, Torso, Arms, Legs, and the characters accessory or weapon. The gear is classified in rarity as well, common, rare, epic and legendary. The gear gives you extra stats to your character, and if you have specific sets of gear pieces you can even get unique augments. For example I have two pieces of epic gear for my Batman that are from a set. If I equip the two pieces of gear 2/2 then I receive a special augment, +200 Strength to my stats. If I get equip the full set 4/4 then I get a buff to my character power. Augments tell you how much pieces of gear of the set you need to get a specific buff. What's really cool about the gear in Injustice 2 is that they are constantly bringing out new gear pieces for you to farm.
Another way of receiving gear is from loot boxes. The loot boxes are also classified in rarity, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Diamond. Loot boxes have chances of giving you gear from all rarities AND character abilities. Character ablities either give new special moves or replace a special move with an alternative move. Of course, the chances of loot boxes giving you epic gear and character ablities depends on the rarity of the boxes however Platinum and Diamond will ALWAYS give you guaranteed, an epic gear piece. I'm saying this now, the rates are really damn good. I've pulled multiple pieces of epic gear from even bronze and silver motherboxes. The most trouble I had with this loot box system was when I wanted SPECIFIC gear pieces, or I wanted gear for a specific character. Have no fear however there is a way to get gear for a specific character.
Moving onto the multiverses. Boy oh boy, the amount of HOURS you can put into these multiverses is crazy. Multiverses essentially are missions you do under certain conditions and you get rewards for doing them. Whether it be pieces of gear, abilities, or loot boxes. Multiverses are constantly changing, so it's good to keep an eye out most of the time to see if you are hunting down any missions to do. Multiverses offer a way to get pieces of gear for a specific character. There's usually 2 multiverses for each character and they last for about 4 days.  Doing each of the missions will reward you with a full set of epic gear for that characters multiverse. There is an alternative to this but it's not guaranteed to give you a full set. There is a 3rd multiverse that is similar to character specific multiverses however it lasts for about 5 hours and change. It give you epic pieces of gear but it's not guaranteed to give you a full set. The thing with these are that if you do the missions, along with getting a character specific epic gear piece, you get a random epic gear piece for a random character.
Now this all sounds too grindy? have to fear, your AI is here. Injustice 2 gives you the option to make the AI play missions and battles for you. You build how you want the AI to function and depending on your build you will win battles or lose battles. Usually you would want to go online and check out the best builds for a characters AI. For example I have my Batman on 30 counter and 30 rushdown, so he'll focus on countering the enemy AI and doing combos on them. You will find yourself using the AI quite a bit of times. Want to farm some gear pieces but too tired or lazy? AI. Getting your♥♥♥♥♥kicked by the extremly annoying Multiverse bosses? AI. Want to level up your character but can't play atm or lazy? AI. Your AI is your best friend in Injustice 2.
In terms of the PC port, It's not terrible or bad, it's just dissapointing... I've heard people are experiencing random crashing in which, the crashing I have experienced myself. The crashing RARELY happens for me, from the time I have had Injustice 2 it only crashed on me twice. Regarding the online play, I find myself getting into matches multiple times. It isn't really dead. The netcode is amazing, I remember they released the beta to have people test out the netcode, it's exactly the same here no problems whatsoever.
I say that Injustice 2 is worth picking up.. but not exactly at the current price. It offers new additions to make you spend hours into a fighting game. For a fighting game it offers so much single player content that I just can't keep my hands of this game. What sets it back is the PC port.

Pro's:

- 10/10 soundtrack

- Attention to small details
- Humor and memes
- Waifus
- Gotta pay bills while buying random crap to keep yourself from getting distracted
Con's:
There aren't any glaring flaw; however, I do find have some petty complaints.
So this game tries to make the experience as immersive and realistic as possible, making it so that you actually feel like a bartender who is currently working. Due to this, it compromises on some conveniences. For example, you can only save your progress during your breaks or at the end of your shift.
The game employs this jukebox which allows you to choose the songs which get played during your shift. I was suggested this game by a friend over on discord, watched them play for maybe 20 minutes, and knew almost immediately that I wanted it. This is zombie apocalypse survival meets Oregon Trail in a nutshell, but with so much more to offer than the current videos display. The devs want to pack this game with as much content as possible while avoiding too much micromanagement, and they do this very well. You have a team of four people, randomized, picked up off the side of the road, or customized, and the objective is to make it to Canada. There are many different game modes, which change the kind of events and encounters that occur, and give much replayability. Frequent stops at camps, bunkers, stores, and other locations offer chances at great loot or terrible misfortune. In between stops there's always amusing dialogue and short events that can make or break your journey's success. The music wonderful and creates the perfect atmosphere in every scenario, and as this game still gets very frequent updates, they're always adding more. There's also just the right amount of pop culture references without including so much as to take away from the originality of the game. This means you might run across a character from another game, some anime fans eager to protect m'lady, feral dogs who will join you if you manage to turn them to your side, or the occasional bandit that joins you just to run off with half your stuff when their morale plummets too far. You can assemble a team purely of your own design if you find that you're better at shooting than melee, or want to schmooze your way out of things, or be one step ahead of everybody - there are traits and specialties, more unlockable over time, that allows you to play the game how you want and have an advantage in differenct scenarios. If you're looking for something a little bit RPG, a little bit hack & slash, and a little bit strategy, without the over the top and often frustrating loot systems of other games, this is perfect.

I strongly recommend this *if* you love puzzles and exploration.
I was on the fence at first. I love puzzle games but everything I had seen suggested this was just a bunch of panel puzzles which could have been a phone game, with the island being just a five-million-dollar 3D menu system which took seven years to make and made the game cost £30 at launch. I was going to wait until it was on sale, but I kept hearing there was more (but never specifics) and a friend said it was good so I took a gamble and I treated myself. I'm really glad I did. I got my money's worth, as you can see from the playtime, and did & found almost everything myself, which was very rewarding.
The island is not just a menu system. It is part of the game. It is part of the puzzles. It is needed to solve the puzzle panels. It *is* the puzzles in some cases, and I am not just talking about large walk-on puzzle panels (although those do exist as well). I personally love exploring large 3D environments, and it is full of incredible detail, which makes everything feel real. It is not just the amount of polygons on screen but the way everything feels made out of solid stuff. Scaffolding and supports are in the places they would be in a real decaying building that needed them, and things like that. Things like the shoreline of a beach are really well observed, with so many tiny details. And every detail may matter, because it may be part of a puzzle or a clue, so you have a reason to look at them, too.
The island feels large and varied, but it usually only takes a short time to get from one place to another when you need to, so it is never a trek. It would be more accurate to call it dense than large, but the density makes it feel large. You'll often run the same route several times and discover something new on the way in a place  you thought had nothing left to give.
The puzzle panels are everywhere, but they are not the only things you can interact with, and the panels themselves are actually a UI for doing varied things, with a consistent theme and visual language. Some of them act like switches. Some are just puzzles. Some are both. The puzzles themselves are varied, and not just simple mazes (although there are a few), nor just logic mazes (although there are many). Nobody minded that Doom 3 had lots of interactive computer terminals which looked and worked in a consistent way, and the panels in The Witness are not entirely dissimilar, but obviously also more the focus of the game than in Doom 3 (and you won't be shooting any demons from hell).
The puzzles themselves are very, very well designed. Puzzle design is hard to do in games, getting the training, progression and learning curve right without it feeling too hard, too easy, or too repetitive. The game nails this overall, although there was one type of puzzle some people may find a little hard (but you can always use a walkthrough for that one type if it comes to it, and my advice is to repeat the patterns yourself as that seemed to help me visualise them). A sign of a good puzzle game is that, once you've learned the basics, you'll face puzzles where you try the obvious solution but find the designer has thought of that and added a complication to make you have to think laterally to solve it. This game is full of things like that.
The engine ran very well on my PC staying at a solid 60 FPS at 1080p on my GTX 960. I could up the res to 4k and get about 45 FPS but 1080p + good antialiasing and 60 FPS felt better. My hardware isn't really up to 4k gaming, so the fact it could have done >30 FPS in this game at 4k is a positive. A week after launch the things it was missing like FOV sliders and joypad sensitivity were added (mouse sensitivity was already in the game, and I played using keyboard & mouse).
Any negatives? Well, the story is minimal, but that honestly didn't bother me. In fact, I'd have preferred if there was even less story as I felt the small attempts to give some background to the island in some of the more hidden audiologs did not really work. I disliked the audiologs in general, but they are more of a collectible and, I guess, an attempt to make the player think about philosophy and spirituality while playing the game. You can completely ignore them (whether you click on them or not) and it will make no difference to the rest of the game.
I found the (lack of) editing of the quotes and the voice actors' delivery made even the seriously profound quotations have me wishing they would just shut up and stop repeating the same idea again and again because I understood it the first time and I keep thinking the quote will end now but they keep adding more words to say the same thing I already understood, just like this sentence itself has become; it can get annoying, can't it, when someone won't just stop talking even though they have run out of ideas to say, however good the ideas were at the start? :)
I also felt that the game's audiologs & meta-story were pushing the concept of spirituality as a given, as how the world must be viewed to experience the wonder of life to its full, and then they literally complain that few prominent atheists/scientists provide answers to spiritual questions rather than criticisms of other answers. I can see how the conversation arose. The game aimed to present various philosophies' takes on the world, some of them conflicting, and without saying 'this is right, and that is wrong', and it achieved that in general, but ended up criticising atheism and only atheism. It's trendy to bash atheism lately, and some of that backlash *is* deserved, but the author-inserts' complaint in the game was that it doesn't fit the framing the game designers wanted, which is neither its duty nor its fault. It's like complaining that statistics won't tell you which lottery numbers will come up, when a clairvoyant will. It also occurred that the author-inserts making this complaint were guilty of the exact same thing themselves, but not self-aware enough to see it. None of this really affects the rest of the game, though. It's just audio you can ignore if you don't like it.
While I liked Braid a hell of a lot, I wasn't a particular fan of Blow personally. He has exceptional design & dev skills, but I disagree with a bunch of things he's said (although certainly not everything) and find his attempts at narrative a bit pretentious, to be blunt. But that does not matter. This isn't "Be Jonathan Blow's Friend: The Game" and restricting ourselves to art only made by people we'd be friends with would rob ourselves of many great experiences, including this. As with Braid, the game mechanics and designs speak for themselves.
Before the game came out, many assumed it would be like Myst, and then wrote they were disappointed it was not. Having played it, I don't understand this. It felt *a lot* like Myst to me, and that game is fresh in my mind from recently playing Myst, RealMyst and Riven for the first time. You have an island full of puzzles and zones, things you have to work out for yourself using observation, symbols, logic and experimentation, and things you learn in one area that were gating your progress in another (i.e. ability to solve puzzles & open new areas). You have the isolation and the beauty. The feeling that someone made this place, for some purpose, and that it is both real and surreal, and will probably never be completely understood, but definitely has some meaning. Some of the areas are direct homages to Myst, too (e.g. the treetops).
If you like solving puzzles, if you like exploring, and having your observation rewarded at almost every turn, if you want to be inside a dense puzzle-candy store, if you like getting lost in a beautiful island that is tightly packed with detail, with things to find and do at literally every turn, then you will love this game and get many hours out of it. It is worth every penny and, more importantly, worth your time.

The Witness is one of those games that’s hard to describe due to spoilers. In the most basic sense, it’s a puzzle game in which you interact with panels that are simple mazes, but really, the game gets so much more complex. Every area of the island in The Witness has a set of rules that govern the puzzles found there. You will learn what those rules are through what you could say are tutorial puzzles. Some later puzzles in areas will draw from the rules of other areas, so you start mixing two, three, four, etc… rule sets together and this results in some seriously complex puzzles.
Again, I cannot say too much as I don’t want to spoil anything, but many of these puzzles got so complex that I found myself grabbing a pen and some paper and actually writing notes and drawing diagrams. I took more notes while playing The Witness than I did while working on my Master’s degree. One puzzle, not due to the difficulty of it, but due to how it’s presented to the player, gave me a headache. This isn’t entirely bad and I can’t really explain why, again due to spoilers, but I just want to try and let you know as much as I can without spoiling, that the game does really spice things up and is far more than just solving some simple mazes.
I should also add that I played The Witness in a sort of co-op mode. I played it along with a buddy of mine and we went from puzzle to puzzle, area to area in our own respective game while we communicated via TeamSpeak. Where one of us struggled, the other helped. This made it so that we never had to resort to using any online walkthroughs. We never really lost that sense of accomplishment in solving the puzzles by having to cheat online.
The Witness is a game that will make you feel like a genius just as many times as it makes you feel like an idiot. It will haunt your dreams and warp your brain once you’ve finished it. You will start to see things in the real world and you will want to interact with them as you had in The Witness. The is most likely my favorite game of 2016, I’m sure it will have a place in my top 10 games of the last decade, and it is even in the running for one of my favorite gaming experiences of all time.

A good Space Hulk PC adaptation with some notable improvements over the prequel and its pretty basic rules based on a boardgame.
There are 3 Space Marine chapters for you to pick from (and 3 additional ones in DLC plus 4 more cosmetic successor chapters). Chapters differ in various ways (as per lore) and they all have campaigns designed for a specific chapter, however all campaigns are available to be completed by any chapter.
You upgrade your squads as they survive through missions with various skills, weapons and items with librarians now being fulltime party members, offering squads some psyker support. Dead marines can be replaced either with one of an equal level, to make the game a little bit easier, or complete a rookie - depending on a difficulty setting.
Combat itself was improved with several fire modes for ranged weapons, which themselves now have chance-to-hit mechanics instead of dice rolls. Overheating is gained by firing weapons and will require action points or time to cool down. In addition various obstacle and trap items are available that can hinder Genestealers and win some time.
Terminators are made more survivable in melee via upgrades and with the right ones it is possible to make a good close combat fighter (especially when it comes to Space Wolves), however avoiding getting close and personal with Genestealers is still a much less hazardous choice.
Genestealers themselves now have their own different classes to pose new challenges for the player.
In addition the game also features a "rogue mode" where your already premade (or randomly generated) squad can take part in a randomly generated campaign. Sadly your squad gains no XP for this, only points for high-score ladder.
Overall it's a pretty fine party dungeon-crawler in itself.

An OK mobile port with better options available on the PC.
Pros:
Tiny Bridge: Ratventure has some things going for it.  It has an attractive art style and a whimsical premise.  It is currently on sale and very cheap.
Cons:
Sadly, quite a few cons in this one.
- First, it is obviously a mobile port.  There doesn't seem to have been much done in this conversion, including a lack of resolution options.  Sound and music are only toggles.
- There is only one solution to three star a level, the solution that you can get by looking at the hints.  This takes away from any creativity that might have been part of the process.  Each level is simply a puzzle with one right solution.  That would be OK if not for....
- Sometimes there are bugs.  The thin mouse sometimes gets lost and does not move.  Also, for a physics based game the underlying physics engine does not seem up to the task at times.  Sometimes, despite standing on top of your goal (the cheese), your mice seem unintersted in picking it up.  Maybe because you didn't follow the hint button map exactly.
The presentation isn't bad, and if you don't mind a simple puzzle game timewaster with a single solution you can get hints for, this is the game for you.  If you are looking for the next World of Goo, look elsewhere.

"No classes", but there's factions
"No leveling", but there's ranks
"No loadouts", but there's deployable hover bikes
"No regenerating health", but there's regenerating invisibility
"No iron sight aiming", but there's secondary fire
The only thing good about this game is the graphics. For a game that's "taking the arena fps back to it's roots": the movement speed is as slow as Halo, there's vehicles (including a jet), there's a periodically spawning super weapon that can blow up half the map, the pickup items are virtually impossible to distinguish, there's dodge jumping and double jumping, you can turn invisible for 5 seconds with a 10 second recharge. Also most importantly: There are no players online, it's emptier than reflex.
EDIT: I recently started playing again. It's a step in the right direction to make a free version to get more players. But the ranking system prevents players of different skill/experience from playing with each other. For a game this new, the player population is too low for this restriction and Toxikk will continue to suffer of low player base. I criticize this game for having vehicles and what do the devs do? They invent a new vehicle, good job. Let me also emphasize the item respawn times are ludicrously long, 15 seconds for a weapon to spawn really? Also 1 minute for mega health and heavy armor?? We might as well not have items on the map, especially since shotgun ammo, sniper ammo, and 25 health look practically identical.
The ability to spawn hovor bikes is also another pointless additive just like the temporary stealth. Why does every FPS have to add these pointless additives for the sake of being unique or for the sake of adding "depth" and "strategy". If you're going to add these things, you might as well go all out and make it another class-based moba shooter, but please don't make an appeal to old-school shooters if you're going to add stealth, vehicles, and clumsy movement mechanics.
This game lacks strafe jumping, lacks rocket jumping, lacks 144 hz performance. The only thing good about the game is the graphics. But a real "frag like it's 1999" type of player does not care about graphics. This game's graphics serves more to hinder player skill by having too much glare, too much detail (even on the lowest graphics settings) and not enough distinction between the pickup items.

Great old-school arena shooter with weapons that all have their own strategies to be effective, twitch-timing and fast movement, lots of mutators, and a surprisingly lively playerbase--with one caveat.
You won't see other players until you spend a half hour or so in a server with a friend. Lobby-based games kinda killed server-lurking, and Toxikk requires some server-lurking to see it shine. Get a full 8v8 match with real people, and it turns into a freakin' gem.
It's still got some rough edges, and if you're expecting something with "modern weapon" values, you're best served to look elsewhere. Toxikk is tooled around spamming rockets, bullets, and not blinking for five minutes at a time. You'll probably see a lot of complaining about balance--but any player that remembers playing UT '99 when it was new will tell you that's a load. You'll see rockets, grenades, energy beams, shotgun blasts... and it's a riot. I nearly had an aneurism when I first read some of the threads cropping up about the rockets being OP--back in the day, you didn't get to tank three hits, you gibbed.
My only real complaint so far is limited to the Raven starting pistol. Don't bother with it--unlike the Enforcer of UT fame, the Raven is essentially there to keep heads from popping around a corner in time for you to snag a real weapon pickup; which is disappointing. Entire strategies existed for single and dual Enforcers, and I'd like to see the same come into this as well.
For an early access title, it's rather well assembled. The maps are pretty and hectic, with natural hotspots that gravitate players so you spend more time shooting and less time running, the weapons are cathartic and satisfying, and the play itself is quite satisfying when you rustle up three spare warm bodies.

This game is going to be huge. As is, it's more polished and playable than most AAA games on the market. The playerbase might be small but there are people playing, and it's worth the extra effort to link with the community. Might as well get a head start before 1.0, because there will be free weekends and sales. Tell your friends, this is the arena shooter you're looking for.

I'm not going to give this a negative review, but at the same time, it's a really difficult purchase to recommend. The free edition means it's definitely worth a look, though Reflex Arena offers a more straightforward arena experience with a larger playerbase.
The core of the game is fantastic and achieves what it sets out to do, though it more closely resembles Unreal Tournament 2004 than 1999 arena shooters. If you enjoy any of those games, you'll know what to expect.
Vehicle modes, which I found the most interesting aspect of the game and would actually set this apart from Reflex Arena, are downplayed in favour of routine run-and-gun arena shooting.
